chapters.title: Sundargiri
paragraphs: Sundargiri He who had set out to experience the world and search the divine was blessed. In the dark forest of night he had experienced the fear of death. His unconsciousness, akin to death, had made him deaf to the bloodcurdling roars of the wild beasts. The great black serpent had brought him face to face with death. But the band of ascetics had at last freed Sarasvatichandra from all fear and rescued him. Mohanpuri had carried him on his broad shoulders through the raging forest fire to safety. The ascetics lived in a monastery on Yadu Shrunga, the third highest peak of Sundargiri. The path to the peak was treacherous. The steep climb easily tired ordinary persons; after two hours of arduous journey they would reach the top, out of breath. But the ascetics climbed the peak effortlessly within an hour. Sarasvatichandra was passed on from shoulder to sturdy shoulder and carried up the mountain. The ascetics reached the monastery one hour after midnight. As they climbed, the air became cooler. Although it was the month of Chaitra in summer, Sarasvatichandra’s body felt the chill. The cool, clear mountain air revived his senses and infused him with new life. His weariness abated. He climbed down from the shoulders that carried him and looked around in astonishment, trying to grasp the meaning of this strange yet beautiful dream. Glad to see the youth revive, the sadhus at once surrounded Sarasvatichandra. Their Guru, Vishnudas, had already arrived at Yadu Shrunga. A lamp had been lit at the entrance of the monastery; Sarasvatichandra’s face was aglow in its soft light. Standing beside him,  Mohanpuri gently rubbed his back and anxiously asked him, ‘Bhai, are you now fully conscious? Does your body feel well?’ Sarasvatichandra, still uncertain if this was a dream or reality, asked him several questions in response, ‘Who are you? What place is this? How did I come to be here? Is this a dream, or am I awake?’ Mohanpuri replied, ‘Bhai, for your soul this is a dream, but for your illusory transient body this is wakefulness. You have neither gone anywhere, nor have you come. But it is we who carried your body here from the forest. In the kingdom of our Lord Krishna, all are equal. The land as far as human eyes can perceive is ruled by Maharaj Maniraj. You and we are one, not distinct, and all of us belong to the same kingdom. The land on which our feet rest is called Sundargiri. This is a monastery of Vishnudas and all of us are members of this monastery. But Bhai, do tell me, who are you?’ Mohanpuri spoke in this manner to find out if the future as foretold by their Guruji would indeed come true. The other ascetics also realised this and they eagerly awaited his response. As his senses revived, Sarasvatichandra, careworn as he was, felt extremely thirsty and hungry. The sadhu’s speech jolted him into full awareness of his present circumstances and of the group of sadhus surrounding him. He replied in a language appropriate to the context. ‘It is true—the darkness that surrounds us all has not yet been dispelled. You know who I am. Why then do you await my answer? To cut a long matter short, if you are an empowered member of this monastery, please give this famished body some sustenance and some place where it can rest, after which dream and wakefulness are but one.’ The ascetics were satisfied with this response. The truth of their Guruji’s words both surprised and pleased them. They called out, ‘Shri Krishna Paramatma ki Jai!’ ‘Shri Radhakrishna ki Jai!’ Their faith in their Guruji’s knowledge of the past, present and future was reaffirmed once more. They vied with each other to make their chosen guest comfortable. One of them brought food consecrated with basil leaf, another brought cool, pure water while the third made a bed for him on a raised platform under a neem tree. A light mattress was spread and covered by a clean, fresh sheet, free of creases. A fourth ascetic lit a small fire that dispelled the darkness and gave warmth. They wordlessly served food to their guest, and then retired to their respective places once he was asleep. Some smoked ganja, others chatted, some lay gazing at the clear night sky in silence while some others sang hymns. Finally they, too, fell asleep. Leaves rustled in the breeze. Stars twinkled in the sky. Nature was alive and awake while all else slumbered. Night reigned over all. The hours passed swiftly. It was almost four in the morning. The early risers awoke. The ascetics, like the tiger, had eyes that could see as clearly in the dark as in the light. They moved about doing their daily routine observances. Sarasvatichandra was awakened by their stealth-like movement. He remained in bed but allowed his ears to capture the soft sounds and muted voices floating around him. His ears focused on the conversation of two ascetics who slept just a few hand-spans away from him. ‘Bhaiya, who is this guest of ours? From where did you bring him? And why has Guruji taken such a liking to him?’ ‘He was lying unconscious in the forest, from where he has been brought here. Guruji, in his state of meditation, said that this man is destined to be a mahatma, a great soul, and that one day he will bring glory to this monastery. Did you hear his responses to Mohanpuri’s questions?’ Sarasvatichandra realised that it was he who was the subject of their conversation, and smiled when he heard the Guruji’s prediction. He thought: This appears to be a peculiar land where predictions are made and believed. There must be something here for me to see and experience. As his ears picked up the conversation once again, his train of thoughts was halted. ‘Yes, bhaiya, his intellect sparkles. What does Guruji intend for him?’ ‘That God alone knows. Guruji has commanded that the visitor be brought into his presence in the morning after he has completed his meditation. We have been instructed to look after the guest until then.’ ‘I feel that Guruji will ultimately reveal to him the mystic secret of our monastic order.’

‘That would depend upon his adhikar, his capabilities. It is not easy to be in touch with the divine.’ ‘But surely, he must have that in him; or else there would have been no prediction.’ ‘Radhedas, whatever is to be, will be. Let us proceed for our daily discourse. The sun will soon rise.’ ‘What shall we discuss today, Viharpuri?’ ‘Has there been something troubling you since yesterday?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘What is it?’ ‘Yesterday as we were returning in the evening, we halted under a banyan tree to take rest. I was at Guruji’s service. He recited a few verses. I sought explanation of their meaning. He said: “Child, not today. Meditate upon them and acquire the fitness to grasp their meaning. At present your capabilities extend only to hearing them. When you also acquire the fitness to receive their meaning, I shall discourse upon them.”’ ‘It is true—everything depends upon one’s awareness.’ ‘That is so. But their meaning may not be unknown to you, Viharpuri. Guruji will not bestow his gift on the undeserving; but you and I are fellow ascetics.’ ‘You spoke well. It is our duty to explain such things to each other. Tell me the verses.’ Radhedas thought for a while and then recited the first verse. Gokul ma gokul chare, Gopalak Gopal; Nandsadan Nandan thai, Madhuripu bhasat bāl. The cows graze in Gokul, their cowherd is Gopal; He took the form of Nand’s son to slay Madhu the demon. Viharpuri suddenly sat up and said, ‘Oh! I have been taught the meaning of this verse—it is mystical! Its secret is almost magical. You are indeed fortunate that Guruji deemed you fit to hear this verse from his own lips. He must have recited some other verses as well?’ ‘He gave me three other verses.’ ‘Which ones?’

Radhedas sat up and recited: Avani avani Madhupuri, Krishna Chandra avatār; Shesha bhār uteri ne karat dharti uddhhār. In Madhupuri on earth is manifest Shri Krishna incarnate; Relieving Shesha Nag of his burden, He saved the earth. Sarasvatichandra listened to them intently. Radhedas recited the remaining verses. Paras sparshthi loh no thai swaroop vināsh, Daitya hari amarata deija Sudarshan pāsh. Pamar ma pamar dishe Gopalak Gopal, Krishna bhakti vash bhasto bālak arthe bāl. Just as a touch of the philosopher’s stone can transform iron into gold, To be slain by Sudarshan is to destroy the demon within and attain immortality. In his devotion to Krishna, Gopal the cowherd appears gentle as a child. ‘Guruji did not teach me any further,’ said Viharpuri. ‘And that is correct. Guruji has decreed that all those who have received the verses from him are permitted to consult fellow ascetics to glean their meanings. I will share with you the meaning of these magical verses. But you must not share it with anyone whom you think is yet to acquire the fitness to receive them. The teachings of the Shastras are of two kinds: one, those which can be understood by all and the second, those which are understood only by those initiated in the mysteries of a sect. A sword can protect, but it can also kill when wielded by one who is undeserving. Therefore it has been decreed that such sacred mysteries should be revealed only to the deserving. The sword should always be sheathed around children. The apparent meaning is called semantic meaning and the intended meaning is called essential meaning. Hence, that our Lord Krishna was the cowherd of Gokul is the apparent semantic meaning.’ ‘Does this mean that the semantic meaning is false?’ Radhedas interjected. ‘No. It is neither true nor false.’

‘That is being non-committal.’ ‘No, it is not. Those who know the code can send a coded message through a messenger. The messenger cannot fathom the code but knows that his master has conveyed a secret message.’ ‘I see.’ ‘Now let us see, the term “go” has multiple meanings: in Sanskrit it means a cow; it also implies the senses, as well as the whole earth. Therefore, the apparent semantic meaning of Gokul ma gokul chare is: the cows graze in Gokul. But “Gokul” also means the entire human species that inhabits this earth. Thus, the essential hidden meaning of the stanza is that: sensory experiences abound on this earth.’ Radhedas was amazed. ‘What else?’ ‘A “gopalak” is a keeper of cows, a cowherd. But at a deeper level, Brahma created the sensory universe, and Gopal, that is Lord Shri Krishna, rules over this world of senses—that is the mystical or metaphysical meaning of Gopalak Gopal.’ ‘Brother, this is truly miraculous!’ Viharpuri continued, ‘Lord Krishna apparently manifested himself as a child in Nandji’s house and slayed the demon Madhu. Nandsadan Nandan thai suggests that he assumed the form of a child, but that he is not a child.’ ‘That means that even semantic meaning is complex and what seems is in fact not.’ ‘That is correct. The term “Nand” is associated with Paramanand, Satchidanand: one whose abode is the entire universe. When the slayer of demons manifests himself as a child and assumes human form, he seems to be ignorant, that is, to others he seems bereft of knowledge; while in fact Gopal is knowledge Himself. This is the mystical meaning. Radhedas, do you comprehend?’ ‘How wonderful, Viharpuri! What profound mystical meanings are contained in Guruji’s words! I will have to contemplate upon them seriously. Let us proceed.’ ‘Madhupuri, the abode of the demon Madhu, also refers to Mathura, or the earth. Shri Krishna was born in Mathura. Now let us consider the essential meaning. Burdened by evil, the earth is being crushed. It has become like Madhupuri, the abode of demons. Shri Krishna manifested Himself upon this earth in Mathura. What was his intention? The earth rests on the head of the great serpent Shesha. Can you decipher the meanings contained in the word “shesha”?’ Radhedas thought deeply for a few moments and replied, ‘No’. Viharpuri enthusiastically illuminated the mystery for him. ‘Pay attention. This body is formed of five elements. The soul is neither tangible nor made of gross elements; it is neither subtle, nor is it the cause of anything. In this way we negate everything; what remains is shesha—this remainder is the soul. Have you been taught this?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘Just as the Shesha Nag bears the burdens of the earth, the soul or atman is also burdened by this neti neti “not this, not that” of the anatman—all that which is not the soul, is mere appearance, illusion, disguise, phantom. The Vedantis argue that this burden must be forsaken. While we the Alakhvadis—those who believe that the Creator is without form, without qualities or attributes and that creation is uncharacterised—argue that this earth itself is mere appearance and maya. But, our Lord Shri Krishna bears the burden of this earth, and so we must do likewise. What right have we to despise or reject something that Shri Krishna Himself bears? If we humans, who are also mere appearance and illusion, abrogate such rights, the earth itself would be destroyed.’ ‘Then what must we do?’ ‘That is the mystery of the Alakhvad. Dust assumes a higher form and becomes food; food becomes prana, the vital breath of life, and similarly the earth that bears us all also rises in the care of Shri Krishna and attains a higher state. Evil burdens the earth and pulls it down, which adds to the weight on Shesha Nag. But if we take the earth higher by our good and pious deeds, the burden on Shesha is reduced.’ ‘What do you mean?’ ‘We began with the illustration of dust and food. Similarly, Shri Krishna saves three kinds of illusory body. That is, he saves the soul which is crushed under the burden of earthly cares.’

Radhedas covered his ears with his palms and said, ‘Bhai, this meaning is too difficult to grasp. At present, my shesha is crushed under the weight of its meaning.’ Viharpuri laughed and said, ‘Fear not, even that burden shall be lightened by the grace of our Guru!’ Then he solemnly added, ‘It is for this reason that one needs to acquire the fitness to be initiated in the mystical meanings. The meaning will become clearer as you understand the remaining verses.’ ‘No!’ said Radhedas, raising his hands in despair, ‘I do not want to acquire the ability to comprehend them all today itself! I will ask you again tomorrow. Let me ask you—do not offer to explain before that. Let me first digest what has been given to me, or else I will get constipated.’ ‘Very well. The day is upon us. We must rise now, clean our teeth and bathe.’ ‘Should we wake up our guest as well?’ ‘Of course.’ ‘Brother, it is morning. Arise.’ But Sarasvatichandra was sitting up before Radhedas could complete his sentence. It was not yet five in the morning. It was the month of Chaitra when the dawn breaks early. They were on top of a mountain and the rays of the morning sun had already spread all around. It looked as if the eastern sky was donning a skirt made of light even as the night sky, clad in a garment of stars, shed its dress. Stars, witness to the passions of night, hid themselves. Even the cool mountain air was changing as the curtain of dark night was pierced and all life concealed by it came to light. Sarasvatichandra had spent the previous day and night in the forest; but when dawn broke he had found himself on this mountain. As you may recall dear reader, it was just the day before yesterday that he had witnessed the pomp and glory of Rana Bhupsinh’s court in Suvarnapur. But the scenes now unfolding before his eager and astonished eyes were by far more dazzling, more glorious and even more baffling. He was surrounded by tall black mountains that stood like monstrous waves frozen in time. Even the boulders on the mountains seemed curious about this strange new visitor. Awed by the sight, Sarasvatichandra momentarily lost awareness of his immediate surroundings and of the tall, black-bodied sadhus of Sundargiri, who themselves resembled boulders. Just then, a song rose through the crisp dawn air. The monastery was some fifteen yards from where he stood. Viharpuri said to Radhedas, ‘Guruji has commenced his morning prayers. Do you hear him singing?’ All ears were focused intently on the song. Vishnudas was an accomplished singer; his voice was cultivated, his singing robust and unrestrained; he sang with a tanpura. There was an idol of Yadunandan in the monastery. His prayer urged the god to rise. I bow to Yadunandan I bow to Thee who frees one from the cycle of birth and death On this new dawn I bow to Yadunandan O’ Hari, it is morning Hari, a new dawn breaks His voice and his fingers on the strings of the tanpura moved as one as his song rose from the very depths of his being. It is dawn, O’ Yadunandan—rise What was concealed is now filled with light The night is gone, the day is upon us The day awaits You—O’ Lord, arise! The stars have set as the sun rises, Hari, the peaks of Sundargiri rise in devotion to the Manifest The sun pays obeisance to the sun of the Yadu family Will my heart, too, bloom with the blossoming lotus? This Vishnudas is powerless to comprehend O Hari, it is now morning Quite abruptly, Vishnudas stopped singing and his tanpura ceased to make music. Viharpuri kept his hand on Radhedas’ shoulder and said, ‘Guruji has entered a phase of intense meditation—he is now in samadhi.’ Radhedas exclaimed, ‘What splendid powers our Guruji possesses! His singing! His asceticism! His teachings! Intellect, music, discourse, devotion, yoga, samadhi are all combined in his being— such qualities are without precedence.’ ‘Well spoken, Radhedas! Yes, it is indeed our good fortune that by service to such a master we seek the divine,’ said Viharpuri. He turned towards Sarasvatichandra and said, ‘O fortunate youth, you are a guest of this monastic order of Vishnudas. You are a recipient of his special love. We are his disciples and it is our duty, as also our right, to look after you. Hence, have no anxieties. You are in a space that is pure and pious. You seem unhappy. But by the power of the divine, by the grace of Yadunandan and by the blessings of Vishnudas, all your sorrows shall vanish. Therefore, leave all your cares behind and receive our hospitality. We shall get to know each other at leisure.’ Radhedas brought some water in a clean utensil and a neem twig for brushing the teeth and kept them on a rock for Sarasvatichandra. From this vantage point, the valley on the west far below could be seen stretching all the way to the sea. The sight of the sea brought back memories of Bombay and his father, and tears flowed from his eyes. He splashed some water on his face and eyes, but the tears flowed unabated. Viharpuri, who noticed this, said, ‘Esteemed guest, leave behind your sorrows. By the grace of Shri Krishna, supreme bliss permeates Sundargiri. Your ordeal is also about to end,’ and he recited an ancient Sanskrit verse: The white rays of the moon spread around the world like the windblown barren stalks devoid of chaff. They are split into shreds by the gentle breeze arising from the Lord’s breath, which is the unfailing remedy for the three types of affliction.⟨fn:54⟩ Sarasvatichandra had many friends from southern India in Bombay who could recite verses in Sanskrit. It was for the first time after leaving Bombay that he had the opportunity to hear the recitation of this familiar verse once again. Many pleasant memories came flooding back and took him away from the melancholy thoughts about his father. Last night he had heard poetry in his own language, and this morning, in Sanskrit. It seemed that this place would provide him with the pleasures of both poetry and philosophical discourse, and this possibility made him happy. Sarasvatichandra was filled with affection for this tall, strong, scantily clad, black-bodied sadhu. He addressed Viharpuri affectionately, ‘Yogi Raj, that was a fine verse you recited. But I could not understand how the rays of the moon can travel during the day! The hospitality that your monastery has bestowed upon me has purged my mind of its sorrows. And your Guruji’s affection is certain to lift the burdens from my soul.’ ‘Well spoken, young man,’ said Viharpuri, as he and Radhedas exchanged meaningful glances. They were amazed—this stranger was already initiated in the secrets of their sect! And he knew that Guruji was partial towards him. Moreover, he understood Sanskrit and even knew the mystical meaning of the burden of the soul! All this seemed most magical to Viharpuri and Radhedas. Their faith in their Guruji’s prediction was reaffirmed. Viharpuri joyfully embraced Sarasvatichandra, and as he did, some of the sacred ash from his body got smeared on Sarasvatichandra. Viharpuri was delighted and laughing, said, ‘Young man before I respond, do tell us your name.’ ‘My name is Navinchandra.’ ‘Navinchandra! Wonderful! What a beautiful name! Navinchandraji, you are our new moon. Shri Vishnudasji, our moon, represents the divine bliss of Shri Krishna. Vishnudasji’s aura permeates everywhere. Those who come under its influence are healed and all their sorrows vanish. That supreme bliss will also alleviate your suffering, Navinchandraji. Do you comprehend?’ ‘Viharpuriji, your words are like nectar and they unburden my soul. Should it be any surprise then if the soft, soothing light of your Guruji gives my soul solace and peace?’ responded Sarasvatichandra. It was his duty to show his gratitude towards those who had given him a new life. Love needs to be answered with love. Viharpuri was ecstatic. He said to Radhedas, ‘With every passing moment, the true import of our Guruji’s prediction is revealed. I will report this conversation verbatim to Guruji. We shall always be prepared to provide all hospitality to such a wise guest. Guruji will take some more time to get ready. Meanwhile, you give our guest a bird’s eye view of all the sacred spots of Sundargiri. Also acquaint him with our monastery and the sublime power of our Guruji. Introduce him to all our fellow ascetics and do everything to please his mind. Until I return, this is your responsibility.’ And saying so, Viharpuri walked away taking long strides. Sarasvatichandra was left alone with Radhedas. The ascetic took him to different parts of the mountain and pointed out various sites in the magnificent scenery around them. The mountain range of Sundargiri comprised several hills. The monastery was situated on Yadu Shrunga. Right behind Yadu Shrunga was Tirtha Shrunga, which was the higher peak; some Jain caves and temples were located on it. Still higher was Matsyendra Shrunga, on which there were huts of Matsyendranath and Gorakhnath; only three or four yogis who practiced yoga shastra lived on this hill. In its thick forests there were monkeys, bears, snakes and tigers. The path to this hill was unpaved, steep, narrow and serpentine. One was required to negotiate sharp rocks at places and cut through tall prickly grass and thorny bushes. The winding path was flanked on one side by a deep gorge and by steep mountains on the other; one wrong step meant certain death. The chasms were so deep there was no chance of ever finding the body. It was said that many a traveller and pilgrim had lost their life on this path. Many would feel giddy and be compelled to turn back. But the faithful did persist on this treacherous path to pay their obeisance to the yogis and to seek their blessings. Radhedas pointed out these and several other peaks to Sarasvatichandra. On one of the peaks lived ascetic scholars of the Vedanta who had taken a vow of silence. On another, pilgrims had built a monastery and a few huts for the use of itinerant mendicants. One hill had four Shiva temples, two of which were looked after by a brahmin priest and the other two by ascetics. Further away was a temple to Goddess Chandika where the worship was conducted by brahmin priests. The pilgrims had to walk from one holy place to another. They also made offerings at every place but of course the largest share was always reserved for their family deity. Ascetics, yogis, brahmins and mendicants were all provided for. The ascetics who lived in the farthest and most remote spots under harsh conditions were regarded superior to others. Very few pilgrims managed to reach their abode, but those who did believed that they had earned higher merit. Followers of all sects came to Sundargiri. On concluding their pilgrimage, they inevitably praised their own sect and decried the others. They often got into arguments with the followers of other sects. Sometimes these arguments even resulted in fist fights but they rarely went beyond little skirmishes. The pilgrims preferred to spend their energies in debates and discussion. Having narrated several such stories to Sarasvatichandra, Radhedas finally said, ‘Navinchandraji, just like the sea, Sundargiri is also an abode of all kinds of living beings—but there is a difference. In the sea, animals prey upon each other; but on Sundargiri, Maharaj Maniraj’s authority reigns supreme. His forces are not required even to police the place—everyone fears the king’s authority. They feel that if any news of sectarian conflict were to reach Maniraj, the prestige of their sect would suffer and it would also pain the Maharaj. There has never been a duty-bound king like our Maharaj who gives equal respect to all religious. No one—neither a child nor an evil-minded person— wants to cause him any pain or trouble by their conduct. Maharaj is still young, but he is matchless in intellect, experience and statecraft.’ ‘Does the Maharaj ever visit Sundargiri?’ ‘Certainly. This place is so beautiful that every few years he visits us either in the month of Chaitra or Vaisakha. He is benevolent towards all sacred sites here. Our Guru, like the gurus of all other sects, pays him a visit every year. Every time our Guru Vishnudasji visits Ratnanagari, Maharaj Maniraj receives him personally and seeks new wisdom from him. Maharaj greatly values Guruji’s blessings and is partial to all those religions that teach peace and morality. Just as Shri Krishna rules the hearts of gopis, Maharaj Maniraj rules the hearts of all the gurus.’ ‘Is the Maharaj a follower of your sect?’ asked Sarasvatichandra. ‘Maharaj follows his ancestral belief. How can we fault him for it? The Gita says: “Better is death in the discharge of one’s duty; another’s duty is fraught with danger.” Each one must prefer his own duty above all else. One of the duties of the king is that he must protect and nurture every religion.’ Sarasvatichandra learnt much from this conversation with Radhedas. Statecraft has so many facets. One facet is the discharge of duties; another is splendour and glory. Action and the discharge of duties result in both affection and disaffection. A king must be loved by all his subjects. Hence, the king should act through his minister, the karbhari, and retain the ceremonial functions that accord splendour and glory to himself. The performance of kingly duties is far more difficult and dangerous as compared to the obligations of a minister. One who is responsible for the administration of the state must be prepared to face all types of criticism. Such a person is also in danger of losing his position and prestige. Therefore a trusted and devoted minister should shoulder the responsibility of administration while giving all credit, honour and glory to the king. Just as a warrior must be prepared to face death in battle, the minister must be prepared to face the consequences of his actions and decisions. The minister’s duty is to sacrifice himself to protect the glory of the king; he should administer ably and correctly and ensure that all praise for it is due to the king. The object is not that the king should be praised but that the subjects must develop a feeling of affection, trust and loyalty towards their king. For example, in everyday commercial transactions or management of the household, the master of the house should always appear generous, and the charge of parsimony should fall upon the servants. Similarly in statecraft, splendour, honour and glory are the preserve of the king. This does not imply that the minister should not seek honour and glory or that the king should not perform any action or take any decisions. Action is the soul of the king while glory is the body. It is the responsibility of the king to protect his minister from the infamy that is heaped upon the minister in the discharge of his duties. It is the king’s duty to be unselfish in this regard—only a king who fully understands and accepts this duty can separate statecraft from kingly glory. It is for such reasons that statecraft is divided between administrative functions and ceremonial pomp. But the division is only superficial; at the core both functions are united—this is the first and essential principal of statecraft. In absence of this strong foundation the edifice is certain to be weak, which is detrimental to both the king and his subjects. This was the principle on which Vidya Chatura’s statecraft was based; he had explained this to Sarasvatichandra in the course of a leisurely conversation one afternoon. Radhedas’ comment refreshed Sarasvatichandra’s memory. He also realised that these ideals were put in practice by Maniraj’s minister. He remembered the Sanskrit verse: Where king and friend in truth agree, Fortune’s favours love to dwell.⟨fn:55⟩ He recognised that this saying was not just clever wordplay, it also drew upon experience. He thought, Maharaj Maniraj, your authority extends even over these ascetics who reside in this remote wilderness. Their love for you is deep; their fear of your authority is grave and their desire not to hurt or offend you so strong that they have no use for your police. Vidya Chatura, you have achieved such high glory and splendour for Maniraj! What deep trust and affection you must share with your king! It is certain that you have obtained this art from Gunasundari! Gunasundari! Kumud Sundari! The sudden memory of Kumud hurt like a knife wound and a painful, sorrowful world came before his mind’s eye. But Radhedas took him away from this world of sorrows. He led Sarasvatichandra all the way to the top of the mountain through a narrow path strewn with stones, overgrown by weeds and shrubs. Once they reached the summit, they sat down on the smooth surface of a large rock to catch their breath. Sarasvatichandra stood up and looked all around. On the southern side was the teak forest; from the top of the mountain the tall teak trees looked small and shrub-like. Towards the east were Manoharpuri and the mango groves adjacent to it. The bright morning sun blinded him, forcing him to turn his gaze northwards. The various peaks of Sundargiri were awash with light. As he turned towards the south, he saw the distant sea and the river Subhadra flowing from the east to meet the sea. It was a grand panorama that lay before Sarasvatichandra’s eyes. Radhedas described the various points that made up the scene. ‘Navinchandra, do you see that cluster of temples? It is an amazing spectacle during the four months of monsoon. A cloud-laden sky, water flowing from the mountain top to the foothills, the distant sea, these white temples in between, and the Subhadra flowing full at both the banks. The falling raindrops weave their tapestry, white silken clouds brush past us, the rain casts its spell, and all that water comes falling down! It is said that Gangaji emerged from the nail of Lord Narayana. These waterfalls give an illusion that they are flowing from our nails. Sundargiri is at its most magnificent during those four months. You must stay at Sundargiri forever and enjoy its abundant natural beauty—it is otherworldly. Those who have not seen it have wasted their life.’ A weeping child is distracted by a new toy; adults, even in moments of grief, are stunned by the beauty of nature and the flow of tears is arrested; past sorrows are momentarily erased by present joys. Sarasvatichandra’s painful memories were erased by the scenic beauty of Sundargiri, by the vivid pictures painted by Radhedas, and the vision of the future he presented. ‘Wonderful, Radhedas! Sundargiri is indeed beautiful! Who worships in these temples? What are those villages in the foothills?’ Radhedas had a bird’s eye view of the temples. He said, ‘Navinchandraji, those black spots in the distance are the homes of Surgram; it is a small village but it is a sacred place. Originally Surgram was situated where the temples are. These temples have the idols of all deities. There are as many different sects as there are hills on this mountain. The temples belong to all these various sects.’ ‘Radhedas, you are a devotee of Vishnu; you must not have entered the sanctum sanctorum of other deities.’ Radhedas laughed in response and said, ‘It is an illusion that our God is separate from the gods of others. I think the fable of the blind men and the elephant is most appropriate for this world. You do understand, don’t you? We are Vaishnava. But the followers of Shiva sing in their prayers: Shiva and Vishnu are one Do not consider them distinct Do not take them to be different ‘We, too, accept this view. When the Formless One decides to manifest Himself in the world, each one imagines Him according to the illumination of their hearts. Shiva, Vishnu, other deities and even the gods of other races are all manifestations of that one Formless One. It is all a matter of perception. Vishnu is the deity of our hearts. We worship Vishnu’s incarnation as Krishna. But ultimately there is only the Formless One. The Vedantis describe him as Brahma.’ Radhedas seemed to hesitate here. Sarasvatichandra sensed it and asked, ‘Why did you hesitate? Were you about to say something more?’ ‘Should I say it? You are a householder and may find an illustration in the language of householders easier to grasp; but I am an ascetic, you see, and hence my hesitation.’ ‘Please do.’ ‘A beautiful woman: some are satisfied just by gazing at her face, some want her to sing and dance while others are not content until they have the pleasure of her touch. Some even desire playful sensuality, while someone may find in her a reflection of their own mother. Similarly, the formless and incorporeal, pure and unsullied one manifests in a myriad forms in the hearts of devotees.’ Radhedas’ philosophical aspect was a revelation for Sarasvatichandra. The man who had successfully cleared all examinations to qualify as a counsellor was delighted to learn that the Indic religions also produced able advocates of its beliefs, and Sarasvatichandra was filled with patriotic pride. But he was tempted to test the abilities of these ascetics further. He took the position that many English educated take and asked, ‘Radhedas, does idol worship also imply devotion to the unmanifest Formless One?’ For a moment, Radhedas was enraged by his question, but he remembered his Guruji’s prediction and controlled his anger. He gravely said, ‘Bhai, if you were to ask this question to anyone else in the monastery, they would take you for an atheist, and that would cause you pain. Please do not ask this question ever again. Our vision is bound by our faith in the Vedas and by our Guruji’s commands. A question or argument that seeks to transgress these limits is for us intolerable.’ Sarasvatichandra realised the difference between this place and the intellectual freedom of Bombay. He was confounded by this combination of advocacy and religious conservatism. He knew that even by norms of English custom it was uncivil to criticise someone else’s religion. He apologetically said, ‘Forgive me, Radhedas. I did not realise that my question insulted your sensibility. I asked only as a disciple seeking deeper meaning.’ ‘Bhai, but was that a question at all? What deeper meaning could it possibly reveal?’ ‘Your Guruji has said: “In his devotion to Krishna, Gopal the cowherd appears gentle as a child.” I feel that this must contain some mystical meaning about idol worship.’ Radhedas was taken aback. He has not only heard Guruji’s saying, but he also comprehends it! Most certainly he is more advanced than I am, Radhedas thought. He politely said, ‘Navinchandraji, forgive me. Only Viharpuriji or Guruji himself can satisfy your curiosity. My abilities are limited and much below yours. I cannot comprehend the deeper meaning of what you seek to know. You are indeed fortunate— it is certain that your heart is imbued with the presence of the Formless One.’ Wanting to change the topic, Sarasvatichandra made some queries about the natural beauty surrounding them. ‘Radhedas, what is the name of the river that meets the sea? Where does it originate?’ ‘That is the Subhadra; it branches out from river Bhadra. The Bhadra meets the sea near Suvarnapur while Subhadra meets the sea near Surgram.’ Sarasvatichandra climbed up to a higher spot and followed the Subhadra’s course from the east to the west. From that great distance and height, the river appeared like a meandering silver line, trees lining both its banks. He tried to locate the spot where he was robbed. He imagined Suvarnapur that was hidden from view. He imagined the teak forest infested with gangs of outlaws. Suddenly, in that broad light of day, he imagined a nightmarish scene—he vividly saw Kumud Sundari being captured by the outlaws at the very same spot where he had been robbed, and he was shaken. He saw a little white cloud floating by. He imagined Kumud’s angelic form floating with that cloud. The song that he had heard from the old woman travelling with him in the cart taking him away from Suvarnapur came back to him. He imagined Kumud draped in a sari woven with sunrays, looking radiant and singing a song in that bright blue sky. The melodious flute plays in Madhuvan But the beloved slips away the moment he is espied He teases mercilessly, setting hearts aflutter The dark one hides in shadowy teak groves The renunciate who once sought pleasure seeks it anew The hidden one reveals himself Sarasvatichandra rubbed his eyes and strained his ears. The little white cloud seemed ready to dive into the sea. He saw the cloud morph into Kumud. As Kumud dove to her death in the sea, she let out a soul-wrenching cry: ‘Sarasvatichandra, you left me and ran away from Bombay. You abandoned me in Suvarnapur and ran away once again. This sin of my death is upon you, Sarasvatichandra!’ And the apparition disappeared into the dark black waters. The dejection, the melancholy and utter desolation of the woman’s heart and her searing curse singed Sarasvatichandra’s being. He felt as if Kumud Sundari in her various forms was jumping to a fiery death in the funeral pyre that raged in his heart. Tears streamed down his eyes; even the bright sun could not dry them. In the distance, conch shells could be heard from the monastery. Radhedas broke Sarasvatichandra’s reverie. ‘Navinchandraji, let us go. It is time to meet Guruji.’ Radhedas had not seen his tears. As they began their descent from the summit, Radhedas observed Sarasvatichandra’s fair complexion, his noble bearing and thought to himself: He is the troubled son of a wealthy father. His bearing and complexion betray his upbringing. His wandering into this place and his lost, distracted air suggest an unhappy past. His suffering must be grave. Shri Vishnudas will be his saviour. Who but a godly person like him could save him? Radhedas sang aloud: Who but a man of religion can satiate the passions of the body? Drink deeply of the Lord’s cup, and you shall not suffer rebirth Sarasvatichandra’s eyes were still on that distant spot where Subhadra met the sea. He imagined Kumud in a ‘jolly-boat’, floating effortlessly down the Subhadra. He followed Radhedas’ song with one of his own. Subhadra, fair in name, be fair to me, too If my beloved comes to you, counsel the one with the withered body The cool breeze that blows over your banks also bears your fragrant dew My beloved’s heart is on fire: give her the peace and solace To douse the fire in her heart and share with you its story If she were to jump into your waters deep, Like the creatures who reside there, Hold her to your bosom Save her, give her life from the nectar that flows in your heart Kumud, the lotus, is born of water and shares its essence If Kumud seeks your bosom, Subhadra be her friend As he was composing this in his mind, Viharpuri, Mohanpuri and the other ascetics came up to meet Sarasvatichandra. He joined their group, firmly telling himself: I have gone mad. Kumud Sundari is happy in Suvarnapur. God’s grace is upon her. I must not desire her. Some are separated by death, others by life. What is the difference? How is one human being to care for another? God Almighty shelters all. He found himself surrounded by the ascetics, who were being introduced to him one by one and making his acquaintance. But all at once, they seemed to diminish and vanish before his eyes—what remained were the mountains, the black boulders, the blinding rays of the sun, the distant sea, and the sparkling, rushing waters of the Subhadra. Everything else disappeared from his sight. Can the world become invisible at certain moments? Who knows? But Sarasvatichandra could only see the Subhadra as he sang, She has become an apparition The air is redolent with her fragrance I shall be like the forest breeze, invisible but Carrying aloft the fragrance called Kumud He then saw myriad forms of Kumud floating around him in the sky—some danced, some sang songs that perhaps Vanleela would sing. Kumud seemed to be teasing him. The renunciate who once sought pleasure seeks it anew The aesthete who once sought knowledge seeks beauty anew Standing atop Sundargiri, he muses on the Sundari etched on his heart He hears her, he sees her, he pines for her anew “Why did we love at all, Sundari? Having loved, why did we forsake one another? Having forsaken one other, why did I seek you anew, Sundari? And having sought you again, why did I abandon you?” As the melodious flute plays in your heart Chandra and Kumud dance with abandon He heard Kumud singing in several voices. The flute plays, O’ renunciate, for you the flute plays: Come wait by the river bank Bathing in that roaring sea, I see you, O’ renunciate And there again you stand by the temple door Love may be blind, but it listens Love hears a distant whisper What is written in our fates cannot be undone Even householders renounce their homes You left the world behind, O’ jogi Dragging me along after you Now be my teacher, O’ jogi Keep this jogini by your side As you give learned discourses This jogini will come and listen The flute plays songs of love

Expressing what went unsaid Its music sings of Brahman—it sings of our union Contain the world in your flute, O’ renunciate And fill your song with bliss Standing on the shores of the river of time He plays his flute Kumud, lost in pain and sorrow, is Filled with the sounds of his flute
chapters.summary: After a perilous rescue, Sarasvatichandra awakens at a serene mountain monastery, where he ponders prophecies and grapples with vivid, haunting visions of Kumud.

chapters.title: Maniraj and Vidya Chatura's Family in Manoharpuri
paragraphs: Maniraj and Vidya Chatura’s

Family in Manoharpuri Soon after Manchatura left Manoharpuri in the company of soldiers to escort Kumud Sundari home safely, the rest of the family and Chandrakant lay down to rest; but sleep eluded them for long. Chandrakant finally fell asleep by three a.m., but he was haunted by dreams of Sarasvatichandra. Sundargauri cried herself to sleep. Gunasundari, troubled and anxious about her daughter, lay in bed staring vacantly at the walls. As the day broke, each of them got up and sought distraction in routine. Young Kusum Sundari, who was given the charge of looking after their guest, brought Chandrakant his morning tea and milk. She engaged him in conversation to keep him amused. As he sat brooding alone in the veranda, she approached him with a few books and said, ‘Chandrakantbhai, Gunial taught Kumud behn from these books, and she will be teaching them to me as well. Pitaji also likes them. Perhaps they might interest you, too.’ Chandrakant felt both happy and sad. This family’s abiding love for learning and fondness for books gave him joy; but the fact that his dearest friend had broken all ties with such a worthy family pained him. Kusum, alert to his disappointment, said, ‘Chandrakantbhai, I cannot blame Sarasvatichandra. I feel that perhaps he wanted to do something like Robinson Crusoe, and so he left home.’ Despite his gloomy mental state, Chandrakant was amused at this comment, and said, ‘Behn, how did you suddenly remember Robinson Crusoe?’

‘He left home to wander the world; Sarasvatichandra did likewise,’ came the prompt reply. ‘But was that wise?’ ‘I would also love to roam, to see the wide world. I tell Gunial every day—why should one be tied to the house? If you ask me, it was my idea to have this excursion to Bhadreshwar. I feel that Sarasvatichandra also wanted to see the world. The trouble in his family gave him the opportunity, and he left home to fulfill his desire.’ ‘But he could have done that even after marriage.’ ‘But that is like inviting trouble! Look at Kumud behn—all her problems are due to marriage, isn’t it? Do I have a care in the world? Those who marry are certain to fall.’ ‘But behn, you shouldn’t be saying this!’ Once I start talking, I have no control over my tongue, Kusum muttered coyly to herself. Then aloud, she said, ‘I spoke in jest, Chandrakantbhai. But I can find no fault with Sarasvatichandra. He is an intelligent man and his decision was well considered. What can the outlaws possibly rob him of? I feel that this, too, he wished to experience.’ ‘How can anyone desire such a thing?’ ‘When he visited us, he was reading Shakespeare and he narrated to me the plot of a play. A gentleman called Valentine of Verona joined a band of thieves and became its leader. Couldn’t Sarasvatichandra have also decided to do something similar? It would be such fun.’ ‘Do you think it is a good thing to join a band of thieves?’ ‘Are outlaws thieves?’ ‘Then what else?’ ‘No, they are relatives of the ruler. They become outlaws only when they are disaffected with the rulers. When kings kill in battle, it is not called murder, is it?’ This rather naïve and yet intelligent comment lessened Chandrakant’s gloom somewhat. But before he could respond any further, there was a great commotion outside. Kusum looked out. Mukhi, the head of the village, was galloping forth with glad tidings even as other men from the village followed in his wake, shouting with joy. In a short while they arrived; and Gunasundari, Chandrakant, Sundargauri and Kusum were given a detailed account of the encounter with the outlaws and the glorious victory over them. Gloom gave way to joy. Mukhi went back to join the soldiers. Now they all anxiously awaited the arrival of Manchatura and Kumud Sundari. Each moment seemed like a lifetime. Chandrakant went and stood on the veranda, staring at the horizon. The women waited inside the house. Gunasundari suggested, ‘Kusum, we are all by ourselves. Let’s sing the song of the wasp; it would help us pass the time.’ Sundargauri said, ‘Kusum should accompany you on the sarangi.’ Kusum promptly went to fetch the sarangi. As she strummed its strings and tuned the instrument, she told Gunasundari, ‘Gunial, I will sing the verses spoken by the lotus, and you take the part of the wasp.’ Chandrakant’s reverie was broken by the sweet and melodious sounds of the sarangi. The veranda where he stood and the room where the women sat were separated by a grilled window. Through it, he could clearly see the pleasing scenes within. Sundargauri sat on a bed. Gunial sat beside her, her hand on Sundargauri’s shoulder. Their glow merged into one another as if they were not two but one. Kusum stood facing them, resting one foot on a box. She looked as delicate as a tender plantain tree; the sarangi in her hands became the plantain leaf. Kusum’s sweet voice merged with the sarangi as she sang. Stay away, stay far away from me, wasp I am a delicate flower Your sting bites! Stay far away from me, wasp Lusting for nectar, You think only of yourself Stay away from me! Kusum repeated the last line again and again. Sundargauri also joined in the singing. The sarangi played unrestrained. Gunasundari joined in with her melodious voice. Even the servants stopped working to listen to her sing.

O’ delicate as lotus, you misunderstand me In your haughtiness, you err Night after night you imprison me In your diamantine petals Forsaking the forest of flowers For the love of your lotus I place your pollen on my head All the three voices merged in the last line. Kusum swayed to the rhythm of the song. Her dancing form reminded one of the divine dance of Parvati. Before her statuesque mother and aunt, Kusum gushed forth like a fountain. ‘Kusum, oh how well you dance! How wonderful! Let’s call Chandrakant, too; let him also see your theatrics,’ said Sundargauri. She got up and embraced Kusum and kissing her fondly on the head, asked, ‘Who taught you this? When did you learn to dance like this, tell me?’ Kusum blushed and hid her face in Sundargauri’s embrace. Still feeling shy, instead of responding, she went and sat next to Gunasundari. Her face had turned a warm red. Gunasundari caressed her affectionately and asked, ‘Kusum, do tell us—from where did you learn to dance?’ Kusum would not look up but she mustered courage and said, ‘Why? Is it such a lowly thing? Why do you ask?’ ‘No, no! It is high art!’ said Sundargauri in jest. ‘If it is such a lowly thing, then why did Malavika and Iravati learn how to dance? Ask Gunial about it!’ Kusum was thoughtful for a while, then she added, ‘And Samal Bhatt’s heroine Vidyavilasini also learnt how to dance.’ ‘All that is fine, Kusum, but where did you learn this?’ Gunasundari persisted. ‘When we had invited the Maharaj to our house, we had organised a dance. I watched it from behind the curtains. You seem to have no memory of it,’ Kusum replied, finally looking up.

‘Oh, my God! Kusum, you learnt all this just by watching one dance! Such things never touched my Kumud,’ said Sundargauri. Kusum’s face showed some irritation. Gunasundari winked at her sister-in-law and said to Kusum, ‘That depends on one’s abilities. But if you are fond of this art, I can ask your father and arrange for a teacher.’ At the mention of her father, Kusum hesitated. Gunasundari told her of the teacher that she had in mind for her. Kusum was taken aback. ‘Who, that rand! Who is she to teach me? Gunial, you are impossible!’ and she moved away from her mother to signal her displeasure. ‘All right. We will do whatever you want.’ ‘If I want to learn, I shall do it on my own. Did I need a teacher to learn this much? Why do we need to inform Pitaji?’ ‘If not him, then whom will you tell—your in-laws?’ ‘Why? Aren’t there things which neither parents nor in-laws know of?’ ‘Who else would know? Your husband!’ her aunt shot back. In response, Kusum brushed Sundargauri lightly on her shoulder and ran out of the room. Sundargauri said mockingly to the retreating Kusum, ‘Of course, some things you will only share with your husband. Now we know your answer!’ Gunasundari seemed concerned. ‘What are you worried about, Bhabhi?’ Sundargauri asked her. ‘Kusum is so quick to learn; she listens carefully and she remembers; she is given to speaking her mind and she is hard to pin down and argumentative. As long as she is in our house, she is all right. But who knows what kind of a husband she will get? These very qualities of hers might be taken to be her weakness at her in-laws’ house, and that would be a source of such misery for her. I wonder, how this delicate, doll-like daughter of mine will fare at her in-laws’?’ ‘Why worry about such things now, Bhabhi? Each one is bound to their own destiny.’ ‘Sundarbhabhi, are those days so far away in the distant future? How long can Kusum remain unmarried? Look at her—she grows with every passing day and night. She blossoms each day.’

Sundargauri saw Gunasundari’s reason and flowed with it. ‘That is true. She is younger than Kumud, yet she overshadows her.’ ‘And Kusum! She wants to be like Mirabai!’ ‘Yes, there is no match for your daughter.’ ‘She wants to be a Mira; she is unwilling to be homebound; she will even go to England if we let her. She learnt how to swim. And now she has taught herself to dance! To keep her safe and out of trouble is about as easy as carrying a bundle of snakes.’ ‘But, Bhabhi, she is still untouched by impure thoughts.’ ‘Yes, that is a relief. But she is not meek like Kumud. Kumud adjusts herself to the situation. Kusum is like a lioness; she needs a lion for a companion. Are they so easy to find?’ ‘That is true.’ ‘If we manage to trace Sarasvatichandra and could persuade him for this marriage ... But a man who gave up ten lakh rupees without a thought will not be easy to persuade.’ ‘Perhaps Chandrakant could do something.’ ‘Yes, and that is the reason I allow Kusum to mix freely with him.’ ‘You are doing the right thing.’ Chandrakant heaved a sigh. He could no longer bear to listen to this conversation. He got up and went to his room and lay down, despondent. In a short while Kusum rushed in, saying, ‘Chandrakantbhai! Chandrakantbhai, get up! Maharaj Maniraj is coming this way! We are going to put up a curtain here so that Gunial and all of us can see him. You sit on the other side and watch the procession.’ The servants put up a curtain. The women sat behind it, waiting for the royal procession. There was much excitement and bustle on the road. People waited impatiently. Then someone called out in the distance, ‘He has come! The Maharaj has arrived!’ Kusum hid behind the curtain. She raised it slightly and peered from underneath it, unseen by those on the other side. Sundargauri gave her an affectionate pat on the back. Kusum brushed aside her aunt’s hand and said, ‘Kaki, we should not be seen by them. But there is nothing that says that we should not look at them.’ Sundargauri whispered, ‘But why raise the curtain?’ ‘All right. But you talk as if I don’t know how to cheat a little. Tell me, what have I stolen from you? Have you any clue?’ ‘Little wretch, so you even know how to steal?’ said Sundargauri, and got up to search. ‘Now you can sit down. I only made you get up so I could have a little more space.’ ‘You could cheat even me! If Chandrakant were not around, I would have sat on your silly head!’ her aunt retorted playfully. ‘I take my chances. You can’t say a thing to me. If Chandrakant weren’t around, wouldn’t I have sat in your lap instead?’ ‘Do sit quietly now. You are so difficult!’ Kusum spread herself contentedly. They had spoken so softly that Chandrakant had not caught a word of what they had said. The royal procession was now right at their door. Maniraj, the ruler of Ratnanagari, was a young man of twenty or twenty-one. His father Mallaraj had died a few years ago. Vidya Chatura had become the prime minister during Mallaraj’s reign. Maniraj had acquired a taste for hunting at a young age which had only grown with time. The forests around Sundargiri and Manoharpuri were ideal hunting grounds; human habitation there was sparse and the dense forests, saturated with wildlife. Maniraj took personal care to protect these forests. No trees could be cut without royal sanction. Maniraj liked the modern argument that thick forests are a guarantee against famine. Of course, forests also made hunting possible. But in an age when the old was fast disappearing under the onslaught of the new, Maniraj found it particularly pleasing when the old could be preserved with a modern argument. This pure-blooded Rajput kshatriya was born with high aspirations, which were further cultivated by Vidya Chatura. Although a brahmin himself, Vidya Chatura believed that hunting was an appropriate means of inculcating the ‘martial spirit’ in these times. Following his counsel, Mallaraj had surrounded young prince Maniraj by the best and most valiant among the Rajputs. Under their watchful eye, he was imbued with the martial spirit. Vidya Chatura’s wise counsel had endeared him even more to Mallaraj. Vidya Chatura had fulfilled Mallaraj’s condition: ‘Do not turn my son into a brahmin or a bania.’ And yet, Vidya Chatura had never concealed his brahminhood. He ensured that Maniraj imbibed the qualities of Rajputs, but not their failings. Moreover, this arrangement also ensured that young Maniraj did not develop an attitude of ridicule towards Vidya Chatura’s brahminhood and that he did not mistrust his counsel. Vidya Chatura demonstrated that he recognised the value of Rajput valour—this confidence was the basis of the mutual trust and respect between the king and his minister. The Rajputs in the administration had no opportunity to complain; in fact they were grateful to him for the opportunities that he created for them to be around Maniraj. Vidya Chatura ensured that the young prince met him as soon as he returned from a hunt. Maniraj always shared without any hesitation all that had transpired during the hunt, including what he had learnt in the company of other Rajput boys. This gave Vidya Chatura an opportunity to weed out any undesirable traits in young Maniraj as well as his companions. He had become a favourite teacher of not only the prince but also of many other Rajput youth. The young boys would in turn share their learning with their parents. Vidya Chatura had thus earned the affection and respect of many Rajput clans. The divide between the brahmins and the kshatriyas was to this extent bridged. Vidya Chatura rid Maniraj of all the undesirable facets of hunting and fostered the advantageous aspects. It is the duty of the king to protect the innocent and the weak and to punish the evil; this is also a mark of his valour. Vidya Chatura argued that this sense of justice and fairness should be extended not only to human beings but also to animals. Maniraj was taught that it was beneath his dignity to hunt harmless animals like deer and rabbits. He was encouraged to go after ferocious predators like tigers and lions. Vidya Chatura ensured that during hunts, these principles were adhered to. This maintained a balance in the forest by protecting the herbivorous population of the animal kingdom.

Summer months were ideal for hunting. The previous evening at around five, Maniraj had set out on a hunt. He was delighted that he had succeeded in hunting a lion. Thereafter, he had been informed of the activities of Sursinh and his band of outlaws. Not negligent of his responsibilities towards his people, Maniraj had immediately set out for Manoharpuri. The people of Manoharpuri were eager to welcome their ruler. Gunasundari had sent out a soldier to bring back news of the king’s arrival. The soldier returned and reported deferentially to her, ‘The Maharaj and other Rajput royals are coming here directly from the hunt. The king and his attendants are in the front, followed by the riders.’ Gunasundari turned to Kusum and said, ‘He is probably aware that we have camped here.’ Kusum rushed inside the house swift as a foal. Gunasundari looked at Chandrakant. Satisfied that he was appropriately dressed to receive the king, she said, ‘Chandrakantbhai, if the Maharaj seeks your company, be gracious in your response.’ At this, Sundargauri looked questioningly at Gunasundari, who replied, ‘Maharaj, though tired from the hunt, will invariably look for intelligent company even in this village. Who in Manoharpuri but this learned guest of your brother-in-law could fulfill that desire? Do you really think the Maharaj is unaware that Chandrakantbhai is our guest?’ Meanwhile, Kusum came out all dressed in silken finery. She carried a large ornate tray made of gold and silver. On it she had kept flowers, incense, vermillion, an earthen lamp and various other things required to welcome the king. Her silk odhni with its border of red and green flowers was embroidered with gold and silver thread; it fluttered ever so lightly in the morning breeze. Her long flowing skirt with many gathers was the colour of embers and glowed like the soft rays of the morning sun. She looked delightful and fresh as a dewy flower. Her anklets tinkled softly, making musical announcement of her movements. She wore pure diamonds in her ears, on her neck and wrists, and a waistband made of pearls and precious stones which shone like the colours of a rainbow. She had read descriptions of adornments in Sanskrit texts and had persuaded her mother to get one made for her. Thus adorned, Kusum came and stood next to her mother. Just then the bustle outside grew louder and more urgent. Everyone stood up. Gunasundari addressed Chandrakant, ‘Chandrakantbhai, be prepared, Maharaj will be here any moment now. If you prefer, you could wait at the steps to receive him.’ Chandrakant followed this good advice. A large crowd had gathered outside Gunasundari’s veranda. People greeted the approaching king. ‘Welcome! Welcome, Maharaj! May you rule till eternity!’ Then suddenly, everyone became quiet and the crowd neatly parted into two and lined up on either side of the road—the royal procession now had a clear path. The Maharaj could now be seen approaching the house of his minister. Maniraj and his companions walked on foot. The riders had also dismounted. Two covered carts made up the rear end of the procession. The carts were protected by Bhil tribals who walked bare-chested, their bows and arrows in readiness. A soldier carrying Maniraj’s rifle preceded the royal procession. Maniraj was flanked by fully-armed Rajputs. They seemed relaxed and talked amongst themselves as they walked. All of them wore bright and colourful headgears, and tight pajamas which were clasped at the ankle with a button. Their upper garments were made of soft white mulmul suitable for the heat of Chaitra. They wore tight waistbands into which various weapons were tucked. Their bodies were sturdily built; some were dark-complexioned while others were fair. Their foreheads gave testimony to their courage. Their eyes were sharp as a tiger’s. Their aquiline noses reminded Chandrakant of Roman sculptures. Some had thick lower lips, which they chewed on, their muscular arms eager and ready for daring tasks. There is a belief that some Rajput clans were the result of a union between the Aryas and the Shakas who came from the areas between China and the Caspian Sea. Watching these sturdily-built men stride together, Chandrakant relived this historical fantasy. Today, we the natives are the defeated and the English, the victorious foreigners. Some centuries ago, the Muslims were the victorious foreigners. The Mughals came after that. Before the Muslims came the Greeks and the Shakas. They, too, were foreign invaders. In ancient times the Arya kings and sages crossed the Indus and defeated the native Dasa inhabitants. They, too, were fair-skinned foreigners. This play of black and white, native and foreigner, the vanquished and the victorious has been going on since ancient times. But the definitions keep changing and they keep moving from one square to another in this gigantic game of chess. The sages and kings, the Shakas and the Muslims, even the Parsis who were once considered foreigners in this land of ancient tribals, have all become natives. The English, the new foreigners, will also become natives in the future. Time blurs all differences between the foreigner and the native; and once they disappear, all are coloured by the same hues. Maharaj Maniraj’s procession was led by a Muslim; the Rajputs followed him and the tribals brought up the rear end. They were all different in some ways, but united by their devotion to the land and their ruler. Maniraj had his mother’s complexion and his father’s stout frame and strength. His skin was the colour of gold, made ruddy with the pure Rajput blood and valour that flowed fiercely through his veins. His features were handsome and delicate, the power of authority apparent on his regal visage. Even those who did not know of his kingly status felt awed in his presence. In many native states, the dissensions between father and son are perceptible. In some instances these differences are out in open, while in others they simmer just below the surface. But those elders who had seen Mallaraj in his youth said that Maniraj was a mirror image of his father. His leonine stride, his deep, grave voice, his temperament and character reminded all of the young Mallaraj. A yogi who lived in seclusion at Sundargiri was unaware of Mallaraj’s demise; when Maniraj went to Sundargiri to pay him his respects, the yogi addressed him as Mallaraj. The Raj Guru, Prassannath recited verses of Kalidas every morning. His majestic (or resplendent) form was the same, the valour the same, and the natural sublimity (or nobleness of nature) also the same; the new born prince did not differ from his generating cause (father) as [a] lamp lighted from another (does not differ from it).⟨fn:56⟩

Maniraj, like his father, was about six inches taller than men of average height. His build resembled that of some Russian men. Vidya Chatura used to say that heroes of ancient ages like Ram, Krishna and the Pandavas must have been as tall as Maniraj, if not taller. Usually men are taller than women, but some of our men are shamefully shorter than the English madams. It is not surprising that the English sahibs are taller, broader and stronger than our men. But even the Europeans had to respect Maniraj’s build. His imposing persona awed people the first time they saw him, and their respect for him would invariably grow on subsequent meetings. His people were proud of their ruler. As he walked towards Gunasundari’s house, the people of Manoharpuri felt renewed pride in their king. Four women belonging to the community of bards, tall, dark and not very beautiful, made their way through the crowd. They greeted Maniraj and welcomed him with a song filled with affection for their ruler. Welcome! We welcome you, Maharaj Maniraj! The moustache is yet to grow thick and long, but you are the son of a lion You hunt like the Lord of Death The earth quivers as you step on it And lions make way for you You uphold the throne of your father “Live long! Live long!” cry your people “Live long! Live long!” cries the wind They sang, they blessed him, and made way for Maniraj. Maniraj said, ‘Bhairvi, your blessings have reached me. Tell me, are your sons well?’ A group of boys came forward. Bhairvi’s son bent low to salute the king and said, ‘Maharaj, in a kingdom where even the deer and rabbits are happy, does one need to ask how Bhairvi’s sons are? These are my brothers.’ All of them bowed low to greet the king. Maniraj asked them, ‘How is your Talati?’ ‘Maharaj, you have so much concern for us, what more do we need? Please keep this Talati here forever.’

Bhairvi came forward and interjected, ‘Son, you have still to learn the proper manner of speech. You should say: Please appoint such a Talati in our village. It is praise for the Talati as also a recommendation that he be appointed to a higher position. The Talati is a good and clever man. If he spends his entire life here, how will he move up?’ Maniraj was amused by this intervention and he smiled. Bhairvi noticed and, hesitating, said, ‘Maharaj, have mercy. We villagers speak without really understanding the import of what we say. We have to be very careful while speaking in your presence. If we say anything unflattering about your officials, you will instantly have the matter investigated. And if you find a grain of truth in what we have said, you will punish even your favourite officials. Therefore, we have to weigh every word we speak, or else we might inadvertently commit a sin.’ Maniraj was amused. He asked, ‘Bhairvi, tell me what kind of an administration would you like?’ Bhairvi was annoyed with herself. ‘Maharaj, I have again made a mistake. Pray make no changes in your administration. If someone is punished because of something we have said, that person’s sorrow affects us, too. If we speak more than is necessary, you must fathom the truth.’ ‘Should you not be speaking truth to me?’ ‘No, Bapaji, that is not what I meant. We are like your children. Why should we speak anything but the truth? We should conceal nothing from you. But you must be compassionate towards your officials. Are they any less deserving of your pity than the animals you hunt?’ ‘Bhairvi, what is it that you are implying?’ ‘Bapaji, we know that you have tears in your eyes every time you hunt a lion, because you have taken its life. You must show the same compassion for your officials when you punish them,’ Bhairvi replied. Then she turned to her son and said, ‘Recite what you have composed on Maharaj.’ Bhairvi’s son came forward and recited: Sword at his waist, gun in his hand As the lord of this land takes aim

The lord of the forest wonders Who is this brave man in the forest? Who is this man? Why is he here? Even as the lion ponders this An unseen bullet pierces his head Not knowing if the beast lives yet The beaters quiver from afar Maniraj strides forward fearlessly And touches the lion’s head He who slayed the king of the forest Now stands weeping: “Vanraj is dead, the brave one is dead, And the forest is bereft.” Bhairvi came forward and said, ‘Maharaj, if we say anything more, we may say something inappropriate. Sukhashankar Maharaj will now speak about the shastras—pray listen to him.’ Sukhashankar came forward and said, ‘Maharaj, anyone found harassing the innocent in your rule meets the same fate as those who approach a lioness playing with her cubs. And this is as it should be. The king and his people must have such abiding affection for each other. But we all pity that former Talati.’ ‘Did the Talati approach you after he was transferred from here?’ asked Maniraj. ‘No, Maharaj. Is your administration such that these things can be kept a secret?’ ‘But this woman grieves over his fate.’ ‘Bhairvi, would you like us to be more compassionate towards the Talati?’ ‘Yes, my King,’ she replied gladly. ‘All right, it shall be done.’ Bhairvi touched Maniraj’s feet and moved away. He was about to move forward when he found his path blocked by an ascetic. The sadhu, clad only in a loin cloth, addressed the king in chaste Hindustani, ‘Maharaj, the shastras ordain that no one should approach the king without carrying a gift for him. But you have decreed that no one should present a gift to you. What is one to do? In one case we break the shastric regulations, and in the other, we break your royal decree. How is then one to approach you?’ Maniraj laughed and said, ‘Sadhudasji, it is I who should make you an offering. I accept only blessings from ascetics like yourself. I cannot rightfully accept anything else.’ ‘Your wish, Maharaj. But you must accept some sandalwood paste—it is sacred. It was offered to Shri Thakorji. I cannot come to you without a gift, hence I have composed a poem in Gujarati. Please receive it as my offering, Maharaj.’ ‘Sadhudasji, please recite.’ The sadhu’s tall, wiry frame was smeared with sandalwood paste. He raised a muscular arm and recited: Brave and compassionate art thou, O’ Maniraj Shelter of virtue, all evil trembles at your sight Beloved and feared art thou, O’ Maniraj Good to the righteous, all wrongs you smite You inspire hope in the good and true And from their hearts they bless you With this love and goodwill, O’ Maniraj May your glorious reign last for ever Steering you through every battlefield Is Chatura the wise, your charioteer In his Gujarati Ramayana, the poet Samal had made Angad recite a poem for Lord Ram; Sadhudas’ recitation was reminiscent of that scene. As he was about to complete his recitation, Sadhudas became aware of a presence behind him. The Maharaj’s gaze was on that person. The ascetic turned around and saw young Kusum standing with a tray, flanked by guards, waiting to welcome the king. Chandrakant was also with her. The ascetic realised that he had kept the minister’s daughter waiting. He moved aside and said, ‘Kusum behn, come forward and welcome the Maharaj with your flowers.’ Like the soft rays of the morning sun emerging from behind a mountain, Kusum stepped forward. And like water-laden clouds bend to touch a river with hands of rain, Maniraj bent forward and took the tray full of fragrant flowers from Kusum’s hands. Holding the tray in one hand, he picked up some flowers, gave a few to Chandrakant and to Kusum and kept some for himself. Then he handed the tray to a member of the royal procession and asking him to distribute the rest of the flowers to the others in his party and the villagers, Maniraj instantly struck up a conversation. ‘Chandrakant, so you are here! Forgive me, I did not see you; you were right at the back. Kusum behn, your mother must have by now received news of the outlaws’ defeat. Kumud behn will be with us soon.’ Kusum looked down bashfully and replied, ‘One is blessed by the darshan of great men; but in your case even before one meets you, one is blessed by good news. Maharaj, Gunial has sent a message for you: First appears the flower and then the fruit; first the rising up of clouds, afterwards, the shower of water; this is the order of cause and effect; but prosperity comes before your favour.⟨fn:57⟩ ‘Maharaj, I must say that Gunial is overcome with joy and gratitude for you.’ Both Maniraj and Chandrakant were moved by the message and unshed tears glistened in their eyes. Maniraj said, ‘Kusum behn, please tell Gunialba that this is all the result of her good deeds. God always puts the virtuous through a trial, but he is generous in granting rewards at the end. Chandrakant, a mother’s love is matchless. Gunialba must be delighted that the threat to Kumud behn has passed. She has loved me like a mother ever since I was a young boy. Kusum behn, please tell Gunialba that Pradhanji Vidya Chatura will be here shortly. But tell me, why did you wait right at the back?’ Kusum smiled and said, ‘Maharaj, Pitaji once told me that Bhishma’s advice to Yudhishthir, contained in the Shanti Parva of the Mahabharata, is very dear to you. He also said that one particular sentence is your favourite. As I saw you, I remembered that. I wanted to see for myself that advice being put into practice by you. But at the same time, I also know that to intervene while the king is performing his duties is to obstruct the kingly functions.’

‘Is that so? Tell me what that sentence is?’ Maniraj asked eagerly. Everyone present watched the enactment of this delightful drama, their unwavering gaze fixed on them. Gunasundari and Sundargauri looked on fondly from behind the curtain, their eyes on Kusum. Chandrakant was deeply vexed; in his mind he reprimanded his absent friend: Oh, Sarasvatichandra, you are ill-fated indeed! Who knows where your wandering has taken you? And here I am, following you without luck. Look at this precious jewel of a girl. You want to remain a brahmachari, and this one here wants to emulate Mirabai! How can that be? Because of the two of you, my legal practice has gone to seed! This conversation with the king made Kusum feel very shy. She turned red with embarrassment and her eyes refused to lift from the ground. Finally she looked up and her lips parted softly like a blossoming bud, and she recited the verse. That king is the best in whose realm the people live without fear, just as the sons live without any fear in the house of their father.⟨fn:58⟩ She continued, ‘Maharaj, the people approached you just as children approach their father. Why would I not want to witness a scene of such joy and beauty?’ Maniraj was delighted. Kusum withdrew, and Maniraj sought Chandrakant’s company. As they walked together, Maniraj spoke of his admiration for the Shanti Parva. ‘Chandrakant, in fact I am yet to read a counsel to a king that has such gravity. You must have read many books. So tell me, in your readings have you ever come across the essence of the duties of a king as relevant as that which is contained in these verses?’ Maniraj recited for Chandrakant. The king should always bear himself towards his subjects as a mother towards the child of her womb. Hear, O monarch, the reason why this becomes desirable. As the mother, disregarding those objects that are most cherished by her, seeks the good of her child alone, even so, without doubt, should kings conduct themselves (towards their subjects).⟨fn:59⟩ ‘I have placed these verses, etched in gold, in my bedroom as also in the hall of public audience.’ Maniraj and Chandrakant moved towards the royal tent that was pitched at the other end of the village. Others followed them. Kusum went inside the house and stood before her mother and aunt. Sundargauri was delighted with her beautifully adorned niece. Kusum’s conversation with Maniraj had been both appropriate and charming. Sundargauri gathered Kusum in her embrace and kissed her. Gunasundari looked on affectionately at this lovely scene, thinking to herself: Just a moment ago, we were drowned in sorrows, while at this moment only joy prevails. How joyful are these two! Mysterious are the ways of God! And truly, God’s ways are mysterious. Joy follows sorrow, and behind joy lurks grief. Kusum, the embodiment of joy, was kissed by her widowed aunt who embodied sorrow. The moment she kissed Kusum, the two soldiers who had rushed to bring news of Kumud’s drowning reached the house. They jumped down from their horses and, being granted entry into the house, breathlessly recounted the news of Kumud’s drowning in the Subhadra. Everyone was stunned. A profound sorrow enveloped the house like a shroud. Gunasundari sat stupefied, unable to move or say anything as tears streamed down her eyes like rain. Sundargauri sat lamenting, ‘Oh Kumud! What have you done? Oh my daughter, I raised you and loved you—you were the only one this poor wretch could call her own. How shall I bear this tragedy?’ Young Kusum, with all her ornaments and finery still on her, collapsed onto the ground. She clutched Gunasundari and wept, ‘Gunial, why are you so despondent? Why do you forget that we are under the protection of the Maharaj? At least have a message sent to him? Dadaji will not come back without Kumud behn. Pitaji will be here soon. Why have you have given up, Gunial?’ Everyone sobbed and spoke incoherently. Finally, Kusum got up and came out on the veranda. She saw a rider approaching in the distance, holding a bundle under one arm—you may remember dear reader, he was the messenger sent by Kumud’s coachman with her belongings. Kusum rushed inside the house and excitedly said, ‘Gunial, get up! There is a messenger on his way!’ All rushed out anxiously. Kusum ran towards the approaching rider and asked, ‘Has Kumud behn been rescued?’ The messenger replied, struggling to keep his voice even, ‘It is God’s will. The outlaws could not harm Kumud behn, but the river carried her away. These are all her belongings. Her coachman sent them with me. Vadil Manchatura and the other soldiers have gone in search of her. The coachman is waiting for them.’ Gunasundari’s tears were unstoppable. She held on to the bundle and asked the messenger, ‘Bhai, do you think she will be found? She had written to me yesterday. She wanted to talk to me about something; it has remained unsaid.’ The messenger tried to console her, ‘Gunasundariba, it is pointless to worry. The river cannot be controlled by anyone. But have faith that your good deeds will bear fruit. It was not easy to defeat the outlaws. Who can harm the one whom Ram Himself protects?
