He is all merciful, and you have always done good to others. Kumud behn was worshipped like Goddess Lakshmi by her in-laws. The children of righteous parents have virtue. God will not turn his back on two such families.’ The messenger, too, was weeping unabashedly by now. His words gave little comfort to Gunasundari. Kumud, her first child, the sweetest fruit of her youth—and yet so uncared for! Gunasundari, crushed by the burdens of the family and by custom, had no time to love her, to fuss over her and shower her with affection. As if Kumud were motherless, she was given away to Sundargauri to raise! Gunasundari had no time for Kumud. Kumud, gentle and meek Kumud! She had never said an inappropriate word to anyone. Kumud, abandoned by Sarasvatichandra, was flung towards Pramaddhan by fate and haste. The misfortune of such a virtuous daughter made Gunasundari inconsolable. Nothing in the world could have given her solace. It was futile to hope that she could be rescued. Gunasundari collapsed weeping at the doorstep and sat there, numb and dazed.

No one knew how to console her. Her grief poured itself out in these words: I could not love you enough, my daughter And hence you faced such despair I could not give you any joy, my daughter Ask, now ask anything of me O’ woe betide—my Kumud is lost! I rendered you motherless in infancy I had no pity for you—how cruel could I be? I placed heavy burdens on you, my daughter O’ woe is me—my Kumud has been crushed! Daughter mine, you were most wise You kept to yourself the burdens of your heart Not even to your mother did you confide your woes O’ woe upon us—my bud-like Kumud has withered! The river proved dearer to you than your mother O’ daughter mine, where have you gone? That you chose the river puts a dagger through my heart O’ where is my precious Kumud? Gunasundari hung her throbbing head in anguish. As she poured her heart out, she felt somewhat lighter and regained her fortitude. She wiped her tears and said, ‘Kusum, open the bundle.’ Kusum opened it. Vanleela’s letter was on top. In it, Vanleela had narrated the doings of Pramaddhan, Krishnakalika and their lowly designs. Gunasundari read the letter, and was shocked. She said, ‘Sundarbhabhi, if Kumud has indeed drowned in the river, consider that a cow has been rescued from an abattoir. Oh God! How could she have shared her pain with me?’ Vanleela had composed a poem. Gunasundari read it. My virtuous Kumud, do not be perturbed The Lord will look after you; we walk in His shadow The evil do not change their ways, as if blind to them May they lose their sight and turn lame. That black-hearted Kalika cast an evil eye Not knowing that she was watched by me I will not forgive her, for Kumud you are most dear to me I pray no harm befalls you; be patient,

I will shame her publicly. The minister will hear of this and Devi will know it all, That whore will weep long and copious tears; Alak will kick her out like she kicked Khalak And rid her naïve brother of this witch’s spell She will send for you to return home. Swear upon my head that you will fear nothing You are clever, wise and God-fearing Truth shall triumph, the untrue shall perish Remembering her dear Vanleela, Kumud must remain true to her word. Gunasundari said, ‘Sundarbhabhi, it is unimaginable—the cause of Kumud’s sorrow is similar to what Chandikabhabhi faced. Oh, my daughter delicate as a flower, how could you ever bear this? This agony is so intense that one wants to give up life. It is now certain that Kumud did not drown in the river accidentally—she jumped to her death to be free of this pain.’ ‘My dearest daughter, couldn’t you wait? Couldn’t you at least talk to us once?’ Sundargauri said as she wept. ‘But the capacity to bear pain comes to those like me who are born to pain. And you were delicate as a flower. How did you bear this vajra-like blow? Kumud, I never once saw you cry. What all did you not suffer.’ Kusum also wept, but her pain with tinged with rage towards her brother-in-law. Gunasundari read Vanleela’s letter again to understand it better. She was shocked that Pramaddhan had in fact made accusations about Kumud’s character. She read about Navinchandra. Her mind raised a few questions, but they did not persist long. She so longed to meet Kumud, to comfort her, to cradle in her arms and give her solace. Her mother’s heart was torn between this intense desire to comfort her daughter, and an overwhelming sense of despondency and failure. This was perhaps the most unbearable of pains. If Kumud’s death were to become a certainty, Gunasundari decided she would invite Vanleela to Ratnanagari and learn all the details. It would pierce her heart and increase her pain a hundred-fold; but that would be her way of repenting and doing penance for the sin of giving away her gentle and pure daughter to a family of butchers who slaughtered her, as a cow is slaughtered in an abattoir. But then Gunasundari realised that with the sole exception of Pramaddhan, all the others loved Kumud. She felt that she had been unfair in comparing them to a family of butchers. Saubhagya Devi, Alak Kishori and Buddhidhan were all good, pious individuals; the thought of them soothed her somewhat. And yet, Kumud’s unspoken, unshared agony hovered above her like immense black clouds—no amount of wisdom or reasoning could alleviate her anguish. Gunasundari longed for Vidya Chatura, her soul companion who shared her joy and pain, ruled over her mind and heart and guided her in all her actions. Her heart cried out for him. Just then a maid came in and whispered to her that Pradhanji was on his way. Everyone got up to go and meet him. At that moment, Gunasundari saw a sliver of moonlight amidst the dark clouds; she heard his voice, and her aggrieved heart felt soothed as if touched by ambrosia. “You should know that even someone who lives far away would not be late for this festival!” Addressed by her relatives in this way with honest words a woman found peace, as if drinking amrta, as if from out in the woods she had heard the voice of her beloved.⟨fn:60⟩
chapters.summary: Amidst family anxieties, young Kusum Sundari captivates Chandrakant with her spirited discussions and spontaneous dance, revealing a free spirit yearning for adventure.

chapters.title: News from Bombay: Dhurtalal's Machinations
paragraphs: News from Bombay:

Dhurtalal’s Machinations Dear reader, we must now turn our attention to Bombay to acquaint ourselves of the developments after Chandrakant’s departure in search of Sarasvatichandra. Old Sheth Laxminandan had realised that he was the cause of his son’s disappearance and he was the reason why Sarasvatichandra had left home. This hurt him. He now longed for his son to return. A man in his youth feels passionately for his wife and sons. A youthful mind also has greater flexibility and suppleness to deal with separation from wife or son. The wounds heal faster. But as old age approaches, the mind grows feeble and one can hear the approaching steps of the God of Death. The possibility of final separation becomes vivid in imagination. Old age looms large not just over the ageing man but also over his sons; they need the assurance of their joys and of support in their sorrows. Laxminandan pined for his learned and intelligent son Sarasvatichandra and withered with every passing day. He was prepared to spend his inexhaustible wealth to search him out. He spent money everywhere, among the Bombay police, among the officials and businessmen, and gave money to his servants to further their efforts. He left no stone unturned. He sought advice from all quarters. He handed over the reins of the business to his wife’s brother Dhurtalal and focused all his energies in looking for Sarasvatichandra. Food became tasteless, sleep deserted him. He would lie awake till the early hours of the morning preoccupied with only one thought—his lost son. Laxminandan became a wreck. He cried incessantly when he was alone. He even stopped bothering to wipe his tears. Sarasvatichandra’s visage was etched on his mind’s eye and Sarasvatichandra’s voice haunted his ears. He could think of nothing else, speak of nothing else. In a few months the Sheth had withered and aged greatly; his eyes had become lustreless and protruded from their sockets. Everyone said that he would either go mad or die. Almost everyone took pity on him. But his brother-in-law Dhurtalal was filled with a new zeal. He did not want Laxminandan to come out of his debilitating sorrow. Dhurtalal was quick to grasp that the Sheth had no affection left for his sister Guman; Laxminandan no longer had anything to do with her. Dhurtalal therefore no longer mentioned Guman to him. He tried to secure the Sheth’s confidence by making a display of excessive humility, impeccable honesty, and a big show of doing everything within his powers to find Sarasvatichandra. He gained the old man’s confidence and established control over all aspects of the business. The clerks working in Laxminandan’s office accepted Dhurtalal’s authority. He obtained the keys to the safe, the cash and all documents. He became the sole controller and master of the factory, and made sure that no complaint regarding his conduct ever reached Laxminandan. Mired in sorrow, old and feeble, Laxminandan was deceived. Dhurtalal’s treachery was played out behind the curtain of honesty. Dhurtalal accepted a nominal salary but he began to take a cut from every transaction. Apparently, there was no loss to Laxminandan as his arbitrage and commissions did not show any decline in revenue. But Dhurtalal took a part of these earnings for himself—he took a commission of two annas for every rupee of purchase made for the mill, the office and the household. The suppliers gave less and inferior quality of goods. Dhurtalal also took a commission on sales. He bribed Laxminandan’s clerks and made them part of his scheme. He even threatened those who hesitated to join his plans. But there were two individuals who did not join Dhurtalal. As long as Guman saw Sarasvatichandra as an adversary, she acted on her brother’s advice. But with his disappearance, Guman’s sole aim became to protect her son Dhananandan’s interests—she wanted all of Laxminandan’s wealth for her son. Dhurtalal, blinded by his own greed, had not anticipated this change. He assumed that his sister was still a partner in crime and he still shared with her his plans to strip Laxminandan of all his wealth. However, Guman had lately realised that her brother was in fact stealing money from her son. She had used him against Sarasvatichandra, true, but she now felt that Dhurtalal’s next victim could be her own son. Guman was well aware of Dhurtalal’s capacity for machination and guile. She grew to both fear and loath her brother. She now saw him as an adversary. Gradually, Guman put a distance between Dhurtalal and herself. Dhurtalal recognised this change. He began to threaten Guman of dire consequences on the one hand even as he gained the Sheth’s confidence on the other. In front of Laxminandan, Dhurtalal showed great contempt for his sister and concern for Sarasvatichandra. But this had an unintended effect—Guman saw that her brother had turned arrogant, and she decided to take him on. Once Dhurtalal was firmly cast in the role of an adversary, jealousy and animosity stoked her fire. Guman resolved to herself: Watch out brother—I am your sister after all. And so Guman kept herself out of her brother’s group and his machinations. The only other person who resisted Dhurtalal was a clerk named Haridas. An experienced and honest bania from a good family, Haridas was an old employee of Laxminandan’s firm; he was also quite attached to Sarasvatichandra. Haridas had a characteristic sense of self-preservation, cleverness, sweetness and patience. He did not challenge Dhurtalal openly; he remained close to Dhurtalal’s men without implicating himself in their activities. He unobtrusively observed their activities and hoped that one day he would be able to prove himself true to his salt. Dhurtalal’s ascent seemed unchallenged. But he had no doubts that his reign was temporary, and that with the waning moon, it too would wane. The day Sarasvatichandra returned, or Sheth Laxminandan’s interest in the business was reawakened, he was certain to lose his position. This fear stalked Dhurtalal day and night. He was determined to be wealthy before such a day came. He was also determined to extend his reign as long as possible. Propelled by this desire, he abandoned all considerations of good and bad, right and wrong and moved resolutely ahead to advance his goal, exploring every possible avenue to acquire ill-gotten wealth. He opened the flood gates. He stole not only from Laxminandan’s business, he also starting cheating other firms with which he had dealings. He opened a business in partnership with some of his friends. They traded with Laxminandan’s firm at arbitrary prices and borrowed money from the firm against promised delivery of goods. Once Dhurtalal’s own business was established, he began to entice Laxminandan’s clients. Many widows, religious institutions and other unsuspecting persons had deposited their savings with Laxminandan. Dhurtalal wanted to capture these deposits. Laxminandan had earned the reputation of a reliable ‘trustee’. Dhurtalal believed that a trustee must flourish at the expense of others. He used Laxminandan’s high reputation to acquire trusteeship. Like that cruel fisherman who wanted the entire season’s catch in one day, Dhurtalal cast his net far and wide. He had begun to swim in dangerous waters. Dhurtalal was not the kind whose greed was satisfied easily. His devilish mind plotted schemes to ensure that Sarasvatichandra was never traced and that Laxminandan’s abilities were paralysed forever. Under pretence of assisting Laxminandan in his search for Sarasvatichandra, he bribed those carrying out the search to ensure that Sarasvatichandra’s whereabouts were never traced—and that if he were ever traced, he should be killed immediately. Dhurtalal did not want to take any chances. He led Laxminandan towards a mirage, hoping that the old Sheth would get caught in the whirlpool of despair, hope, helplessness and confusion and lose his mental balance altogether. He kept Laxminandan’s fears and anxieties alive and would not let him forget about his son even for a moment. Ultimately, Dhurtalal decided to take things in hand rather than just wait for things to happen. One day, lonely and forlorn, Laxminandan visited Sarasvatichandra’s bungalow in Walkeshwar. The doorman opened the house for him. He went and stood before Kumud Sundari’s portrait. Haridas and Dhurtalal were with him. Laxminandan sat on a chair facing the portrait. Tears welled up in his eyes as he said, ‘Haridas, this was to be the bride of my son. He left the house, and she was married to someone else. I lost two precious jewels. If I had not been so foolish and blind, all the riches and glories of the world would have been mine. But fate turned against me.’ He put his head on Haridas’ shoulder and wept aloud. Haridas wiped his tears and said, ‘Shethji, you must not punish yourself like this. Can you fight fate? It is not for lack of your efforts that Bhai cannot be found. We can make the efforts, but it is for God to grant us the fruits.’ Dhurtalal also butted in, ‘Shethji, I am worried for you. You might lose your mental equilibrium. You have done all that one could for a son as deserving as yours. You are unable to pay any attention to the business. That may work against you in the future. I feel that you should plan for the future when you are in a position to do so.’ Laxminandan was startled. ‘Haridas, do you think I am losing my mind?’ Haridas had observed the changing facial expressions of Dhurtalal. He softly said, ‘Shethji, I believe that if you were to start taking interest in the business again, you shall never be in danger of losing your equilibrium. We should also know what plans Dhurtalal Sheth has for the future.’ Dhurtalal did not like this. He suspected Haridas and surmised that Haridas was either a fool or against him. He looked searchingly at the bania, and said, ‘Shethji, just as I am concerned about my nephew, I am also concerned about Sarasvatichandra Bhai. I do not think like a woman in this respect, and you know that well. You should make arrangements such that it would protect the interests of both your sons. If I do not tell you that you have lost some of your equanimity, it would please you, but it would also harm the interests of your family. I would not be true to my salt if I say things just to please you, disregarding the real good of your family. That I cannot do, Shethji. But I am convinced that right now you are not in a position to take business decisions— you are torn between love for your son, and the pressures of running a vast business. And I am pained by your condition.’

Haridas thought, what a crook! Sheth replied, ‘Dhurtalal, you have to show me the way. I am preoccupied with thoughts of Bhai. I am incapable of any other thought.’ Dhurtalal was not one to let go of an opportunity presented to him. He eagerly said, ‘That is what I am also saying, Shethji. I have already thought about it. You should make a document which gives the power of attorney to two persons—one who represents my nephew, and the other who could look after Sarasvatichandra Bhai’s interests until he returns. This you should execute at a time when your mental capacities are not in question. If you fail to do this, at some point the matter will reach the courts, and all your wealth shall be wasted.’ Haridas quietly asked, ‘Who could those two persons be?’ ‘If Shethji approves, I can represent my nephew Dhananandan and ...’ Dhurtalal hesitated, ‘Someone like Haridas could represent Sarasvatichandra Bhai.’ ‘No, I do not have such capabilities. Dhurtalal Sheth is capable of looking after the interests of both,’ said Haridas. Laxminandan thought for a moment and said, ‘We shall see,’ and he got up and went to look at other rooms in the house. Dhurtalal was left alone with Haridas. He felt that Haridas’ response had caused some uncertainty in Laxminandan. He decided to take Haridas into confidence. ‘Haridas, you do not understand.’ ‘No, Sheth. I am a poor, small-minded bania. I don’t have your intelligence.’ ‘Listen, if the Sheth follows my advice, both of us will be little princelings.’ ‘Both? Am I worthy of it, Sheth?’ ‘Do you think they were born wearing all their jewels and silks?’ ‘Bhai Sahib, I shall be guided by you.’ ‘Look here, in just two months I have filled my house with riches. Do you want that or not? How can anyone get rich on this measly salary!’ ‘That is true. But can anyone change his destiny?’

‘Why worry about destiny? One should seize the moment. Old Sheth has lost his mind, and if he hasn’t, we shall certify that he has— the day after he signs this document.’ ‘How?’ ‘There are many vaids and doctors available. A little money can make a slave of anyone.’ ‘But Sheth, I don’t even have the money to buy poison.’ ‘Why are you so black-hearted, Haridas? The money is someone else’s; the pen with which the doctor will certify him crazy will also be a borrowed one. We are only the beneficiaries. We shall use the Sheth’s money to rob him. How come you are so daft!’ Dhurtalal caught Haridas by the shoulders and shook him a little. ‘I see. Now I understand. But both of us have eaten Shethji’s salt.’ ‘Forget about being true to salt and all of that. Once the money starts pouring in, one can very well do without salt; we will have enough sweets to eat then.’ ‘But Sheth, I lack the courage to do this.’ ‘What a coward you are, Haridas! Come with me this evening, and I will provide you with the courage.’ ‘So what is to be done?’ ‘Once I leave, you must convince the Sheth of our plan. I will take you out in the evening. The Sheth has made out two-three promissory notes to me. I shall transfer them to you—that should give you the necessary courage.’ ‘Yes ...’ ‘Yes or no—don’t botch it up, Haridas. In time, you will also learn to have fun.’ Having said so, Dhurtalal proceeded towards his carriage, muttering to himself: I shall introduce the bania to some fun. I will take him to the prostitute Radhesani—Haridas will become my servant for life! The fool doesn’t know that Bhai will have to die. Once he is gone, his share will go to my nephew Dhananandan. And then naturally, I shall remove the nephew, too. I shall be the sole owner. This brainless bania I will push out in no time. I want a power of attorney that states that once Sarasvatichandra is no more, his executor—this bania—will also have no say. But this Guman has become quite a nuisance! Bloody woman, why can’t she be killed off as well? For a moment Dhurtalal was shocked that he actually wanted to kill his own sister, but it passed. He got into the carriage, thinking: Why should I care if she is my sister or my mother—all are secondary to my self-interest. How does it matter if it is ninety-nine or a hundred? I am going to kill so many mosquitoes, how will one more make any difference? The carriage moved on. He turned back and glanced at the bungalow. His conversation with himself continued: What if the Sheth refuses to sign the documents? But I will have my gang as the last resort, won’t I? If he does not sign willingly, he will do so under duress. Failing everything, Padamji Parsi can forge the Sheth’s signature even with his left hand. We will see what is to be done. The world can go to hell. Dhurtalal twirled his moustache, thrust out his chest and boxed the coachman, ‘Rascal, why can’t you move faster?’ The coachman looked back, lashed out at the horse, and the carriage galloped out of sight. Haridas, dejected and despondent saw the coach disappear. He sat on a chair, ruminating. Oh God! Oh Mother Earth! How can you bear such burdens? All this is beyond me. Once the brother-in-law takes control of this king’s court, the old Sheth’s business, Goddess Lakshmi is certain to vanish. Her place has been taken by strife and conflict. A precious jewel had to leave home because of the evil designs of this Dhurtalal. He turned Guman against the Sheth. He will now term the Sheth crazy. His evil ways have corrupted the old, trusted clerks. Now Sheth’s sanity and his wealth are both about to desert him. All because of this Dhurtalal. Times have turned against the Sheth. The Sheth has realised his follies. But it is already too late. He now weeps and wails and Guman is frightened at the sight of her brother. After all they are brahmins— they only have hindsight. And could even Brahma put some sense into women’s heads? If Sita had not compelled Laxman to follow Ram, she would not have been abducted. It is said that a woman’s brains are in her ankles; it is not without substance. But such is fate. But Haridas, you are neither a brahmin nor a woman. You are a bania. Can you put your brains to some use? The Sheth is not about to change, the Shethani will remain what she is, and that rogue will do his roguery.

They will be who they are. It is you who have to somehow rescue the situation. This body of mine has been nourished by food provided by the Sheth. Now it is my turn to rescue him from the high seas—yes, that should be my life’s purpose. Oh Haridas, God made you a bania. Now it is your turn to prove that you are in fact a bania. Haridas closed his eyes and sat in quiet contemplation. A few moments of silence revived his brain. He calculated something on his fingers. He was about to say something aloud, but checked himself. His train of thought continued: It is dangerous to open my mouth. One should only speak to oneself. It is not wise to converse with the Sheth. He is not in control of his emotions and he might even blurt out my name to that rogue. Guman Shethani is in complete control of her faculties, but after all she has the tongue of a woman. There is no one in the house or the firm who has remained unsullied. I will have to put my life at stake. I will have to work alone. And then there is God. God is first; Haridas is his servant. God will back me up. The rest can go to hell. Haridas, God is with you! He has renewed my hopes. He shows me the way. Chandrakant! Yes, very good. It’s a good omen. But he has gone in search of Sarasvatichandra. All right, I will write to him. But can I wait that long? I will get a note of introduction from him to Bulwer Sahib, who is a friend of Bhai. But what am I to do until then? I will rob even the rogue. He has promised to pay me a bribe. I shall be greedy and take all that he has to offer. I will use his own shoes to beat him with. I am poor and without resources. I will use his bribe to pay the police and the lawyers. But will the boat sail on the steam of a poor bania like me? It may not, but even the stones float when Ram’s name is invoked. So what if he is not with us, Sarasvatichandra Bhai’s name still holds sway in this city. Just as a pedigree horse feels proud when an expert rider rides it, Haridas felt proud and his faculties grew sharper at the possibility of doing a good, selfless deed in service of his master, and he was filled with new vigour and hope. He had promised to meet Dhurtalal that evening. Haridas went inside the bungalow to seek Sheth Laxminandan’s permission to leave. He found the Sheth standing near a window, gazing at the sea, his eyes searching for Sarasvatichandra. Laxminandan did not see or hear Haridas come in. ‘Shethji ...’ Haridas called softly to draw Sheth’s attention. Laxminandan was startled. He turned around and shot a question, ‘Haridas, where is Dhurtalal?’ ‘He has left.’ ‘Who else is in the bungalow?’ ‘Just the two of us.’ ‘Are you certain?’ ‘Absolutely.’ ‘Haridas?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘Haridas!’ the Sheth repeated, looking intently at Haridas. ‘Yes, Shethji.’ Haridas saw inflamed passions simmering in old Laxminandan’s eyes. ‘Whose servant are you?’ ‘Yours.’ ‘Say that again.’ ‘Yours, Shethji. As long as there is life in this body, I am your servant, have no fear. I will remain faithful to you even if there is no one else left.’ ‘Who will protect my Sarasvatichandra?’ ‘That you alone will have to do, Shethji.’ ‘Liar! Go away! I don’t need you.’ Haridas was shocked. He realised that the Sheth’s rambling had a deeper meaning and he grew alert at once. ‘Shethji, there was a time when you did not care for Sarasvatichandra Bhai. But now you do.’ ‘How long will this last, Haridas?’ ‘Shethji, as long as your heart remains in the right place.’ ‘If I accept Dhurtalal’s suggestion, would I be thinking right?’ ‘That is for you to decide. But is he not a well-wisher of Bhai as well?’ ‘A man may err once. A man who makes the same mistake twice is a beast.’ ‘That has merit.’

‘Either you consider me to be a beast, or you are a beast yourself.’ ‘I am a poor man, Shethji, more like a beast.’ ‘Stop it. Now listen to me. This is a pointless conversation. Dhurtalal has corrupted all my trusted men. If he has made even you his own, tell me so frankly right now and leave from my sight. He and you can both do whatever you like. But don’t forget, Laxminandan still has some brains left. These ruins you see speak of a glorious past.’ Haridas was stunned by these clear words. He saw the former Laxminandan re-emerge before his eyes, and realised that his task had just become so much easier. His eyes welled up with tears of joy and relief. Laxminandan was closely observing the fast-changing expressions on his face—his trust in Haridas was reaffirmed. ‘Haridas, you need not say anything more. You are the only one from my firm who has remained faithful to me. All the others are scoundrels. I know you. You cannot be made to turn against me. You are not one of them. But take a pledge, touch my feet and swear that you are still worthy of my trust.’ Before Laxminandan could even complete the sentence, Haridas was at his feet. He clasped them and wept, ‘Shri Vitthal is my witness, Shethji, if I ever turn against you, in thought or deed, I will incur the sin of killing a cow, a brahmin and a woman. Pray do reveal your mind to me.’ Laxminandan choked with emotion. He lifted Haridas up from the ground, gave him a seat adjacent and said, ‘Haridas, tell me, what is on your mind?’ ‘Shethji, I will tell you everything. But I fear that if you were to lose your equilibrium and blurt out my name, no one will be able to find even a trace of my bones. I would lose my life, and you would lose the one man who is still faithful to you. Therefore, do not force me to reveal my mind. Have faith in me, and tell me all that you want to. You can put me on trial whenever you want. Open your heart to me—share with me all the secret burdens that you bear. But allow my lips to remain sealed. I will bring you all that you need from my store room. But if I handover the key to the room to you, Shethji, all shall be stolen.’ Laxminandan looked grave. He thought deeply for a while, then said, ‘Haridas, you remain as truthful as ever. I am convinced that you have not crossed over to the other side. I trust you. Your advice is correct. I accept it just as a child obeys elders. You must give truthful replies to all that I ask.’ ‘I agree to that.’ ‘I was so perturbed by Bhai’s disappearance that I lost my equilibrium and I was even prepared to do that which would have robbed Bhai of all his inheritance. This I realised only today—and I do not like what I have done at all. Tell me, is my caution misplaced?’ ‘Excellent, Shethji. What could be more auspicious than the day of marriage?’ ‘Today I realised that my brother-in-law has been cheating me. In my madness and despair, I have paid no mind to what he has been doing, but I did notice some things. When I think back on it, I know I have allowed him a free hand. I realise now that my brother-in-law is a complete rogue and a scoundrel.’ ‘Yes.’ ‘Just “Yes” won’t do, Haridas. Tell me if I have thought it through or not?’ Haridas laughed. ‘Shethji, today you have changed your opinion of him. What guarantee do I have that you will not change your mind again? Tomorrow is another day. Hence, do not ask me what he did. You tell me what you have decided to do, and I will respond. You must follow the condition that we agreed upon.’ ‘All right. I am not going to sign the document that has been drawn up by that rogue. It is like cutting my own wrist and making a gift of it to him. Am I right? You must respond to this; you have no choice.’ ‘Absolutely right, Shethji, you could not have been more correct. I say this without hesitation.’ ‘Fine. Tomorrow, I will come to the office after lunch. My intention is clear. I will take control of the treasury, the cash, the account books and all other business-related papers. I will then throw out my brother- in-law and warn him that he should never again step inside my house or my office.’ ‘That I agree. But you should consider if all that should be done tomorrow itself.’ ‘You might have a point there, Haridas. We shall think about it. Now the next thing. I have written some names on this paper; they are clerks in the office and the mill. They will be dismissed from their job tomorrow. Take this and read the list.’ ‘I will read the list, but we don’t need to rush into it. They are lowly functionaries; they are moved by their hunger. If we provide them with enough to eat, they shall work with us.’ ‘All right. Once I drive this one out, you will have a major task to accomplish, Haridas.’ ‘What is that?’ ‘You must find Bhai. If it costs you a lakh of rupees, you must find him. If it costs you your life, you must find him. You must lead the search. But you must bring back Bhai—he must be brought back.’ Laxminandan appeared somewhat unhinged as he spoke the last sentence. Haridas became guarded. ‘Shethji, that I will do. Chandrakant is already on Bhai’s trail. Even Bulwer Sahib has some inkling of his whereabouts.’ ‘What? Is that so?’ ‘Yes. We should get a letter from Chandrakant in the next three to four days.’ ‘Haridas, this cunning rascal appropriated twenty-five thousand rupees of mine and made no effort to look for Bhai. And this Chandrakant took no money from me. You are right; Chandrakant genuinely feels for Bhai. But this rogue Dhurtalal was responsible for Bhai’s disappearance. He did not want Bhai to return—why would he look for him? But without thinking I gave him the responsibility.’ ‘Shethji, that was fate. Now tell me, what else do we need to do?’ ‘I am still not in full possession of my senses. I don’t know when I will lose it again. Therefore, we must have a trustee.’

‘But just now you said that you would not sign the documents!’ ‘Let me complete. I will not sign any document prepared by that rascal. I want to make a document that makes Bhai the sole trustee of all my wealth. He will be the sole trustee—not you, not me.’ ‘Wonderful, Shethji. But will Shethani agree to it?’ ‘If she does not agree, let her be. I do not trust anyone but Bhai. I will hand over all my wealth to him. I will make him a trustee of Dhananandan’s share as well. Bhai will be responsible for Dhan’s mother. He will be Dhan’s guardian. He will even be responsible for me.’ ‘But Shethji, Guman Shethani’s consent is necessary. Don’t be in such a mad hurry.’ Laxminandan got up and slapped Harilal. ‘Bastard! Traitor! You want her consent? You want to please her? Go away! I have no use for you.’ Haridas caressed his cheek and said, ‘Shethji, there was a time you wanted to please her to the point that you drove away Bhai. Am I so wrong in thinking about her pleasure in Bhai’s absence?’ Laxminandan mellowed. ‘You are right, Haridas. I won’t curse you. But you know what Shethani told me? She said that she did not know that her brother was such a rogue. She said Bhai is like a son to her, too, and that he would care for her. She said Bhai would not be able to sleep if she were hungry. Shethani told me that if she had known of her brother’s true character, she would never have allowed any of this to happen. Haridas, do you understand? Or is your brain slower than that of this woman?’ ‘Sheth, how can I, a poor clerk, aspire to the intelligence of a Shethani? But could she not have said this to test your intentions?’ ‘Stupid, you have still not understood. Dhurtalal gave some powder to his sister, which she was to administer to me. If she had done that, I would have either gone mad or died! Look, here it is.’ Laxminandan took out the packet that contained the powder and showed it to Haridas.

Haridas was shocked. ‘Dhurtalal! Oh, he is a demon in guise of a man. Sheth, now I understand things better. Did the Shethani give you this packet?’ ‘Who else? Do you think she fancies being a widow?’ ‘Oh God! Sheth, you are right.’ ‘Is there anything else?’ ‘No, but what shall we do till such time as Bhai returns?’ ‘I am around. I am still like a tiger. I shall have them for a meal.’ ‘That is true. But you are still not fully in control of yourself.’ ‘What if it persists? Do you think my abilities will be further eroded?’ ‘Shethji, who knows the will of God?’ ‘True, one cannot say what God wills. But if I were to lose my mental equilibrium, Chandrakant and Bulwer Sahib should take control of the business till such time that Bhai comes back.’ ‘Now everything is in place. I accept.’ ‘You can go now. Tomorrow at twelve noon I will be at the office. I will create a scene and drive out that rogue.’ Haridas realised that it was futile to restrain the Sheth any further. He decided to leave it in the hands of God. But he had to think about the next day’s plan. ‘All right, Shethji. I will see you tomorrow. Meanwhile, write me a note addressed to the Police Commissioner.’ ‘What for?’ ‘I want to ensure the presence of the police tomorrow at the office. That rogue will not give up so easily. He is certain to do some mischief.’ Laxminandan wrote a note to the police commissioner. He also wrote to Bulwer Sahib. He handed them both to Haridas and said, ‘This one is for the chief of police, and this one is for Bulwer Sahib. I have requested him to come home tomorrow morning. We will draft the document together. I have to act fast. He will also bring some news of Bhai.’ Haridas took the notes, kept them carefully in his pocket, and waited. Laxminandan said, ‘Now go. Go and bring back Bhai.’ Tears welled up in Haridas’ eyes; the Sheth was not in full possession of himself. He repeated, ‘Go, Haridas.’

‘Tomorrow morning, Dhurtalal will enquire about the document. He will also want to know about our conversation. What will you tell him, Shethji?’ Laxminandan looked at him meekly and said, ‘I will tell him whatever you want me to tell him.’ ‘Do not reveal your mind to him, Shethji. Just tell him that he should talk to me and that everything will be decided tomorrow afternoon.’ Laxminandan got up and hugged Haridas. ‘Wonderful! You have the brains of a bania, Haridas. How do you think so fast? It’s a perfect answer! I don’t need to think about it at all. I need to tell him nothing! Now go—we will meet tomorrow at noon. Go. Until tomorrow noon. Nothing else.’ Haridas was torn between conflicting emotions. He felt burdened, pained, and yet he was happy at what he had accomplished. He felt hope and enthusiasm, as also fear. He told the gardener to look after Laxminandan and pleaded with God to take care of his Sheth. It was almost dark by the time he stepped out of the bungalow into the garden and on to the road. He had to meet Bulwer Sahib, the police commissioner and Dhurtalal. He hired a Victoria carriage. The road was deserted. The fading light of evening and the peaceful road allowed him to calm his excited mind. He said aloud, ‘God, Your will is supreme. What a poor wretch like me could not have accomplished even with great effort will now be made possible because of a few words spoken by the Sheth, however unbalanced he might be—such is Your will. Morality and good shall emerge victorious and sin shall be vanquished.’ These words lingered in the air, swirled around and finally merged with the falling dusk. Everything looked in its place, undisturbed as before. Haridas went to the police commissioner’s house first. The commissioner was well-disposed towards both Laxminandan and Sarasvatichandra. Dhurtalal knew of this, and he had used it to cultivate his own nexus in the police department. At times he would use the commissioner’s name, at other times he used Laxminandan’s contacts, and when necessary, he would bribe his way to favour. Haridas was aware of Dhurtalal’s network among the subordinate policemen. He therefore thought it prudent to approach the commissioner directly. He gave Laxminandan’s note to the commissioner. Haridas gave a detailed account of all the issues and individuals involved, and requested for police presence around the office for the next day at noon. The commissioner agreed. Next, Haridas met Bulwer Sahib and gave him the letter. The Sahib was pleased to hear about Laxminandan’s decision, and he agreed to visit the Sheth’s house the following morning. Haridas went home, had his dinner, and without further delay hurried to Dhurtalal’s house. Dhurtalal was waiting for him as impatiently as a farmer waiting for rains. Haridas told him that the Sheth was not immediately agreeable to signing the document but had promised to consider the matter the next day at a time when he intended to visit the office. This irked Dhurtalal considerably. ‘Haridas, your help will be absolutely essential tomorrow. If the Sheth refuses to sign the document, we will have it forged, but we can’t afford to wait any longer. Tomorrow afternoon, we shall declare him mad and have him sent to the mental hospital at Colaba with the help of the police. I have already warned the doctor at Colaba, but I need to tell him the exact time. I will give you a note, which you shall carry to him tomorrow morning.’ Haridas was stunned by Dhurtalal’s brazen courage. He said, ‘Very good. It’s an unfailing remedy. Tomorrow afternoon we shall send the Sheth off to the mental hospital with his hands tied behind his back. What shall we do after that? How shall we get the police?’ ‘Take this note to Latif Khan Jamadar and Dhurkerao Havaldar. Tell them that the police must remain present at the appointed time.’ ‘All right. But who shall deliver that note?’ ‘You, who else? I am the end, and you are my means.’ ‘All right, Sheth; it will be done before twelve noon tomorrow.’ Haridas took three thousand rupees in cash from Dhurtalal to pay for all the arrangements. Dhurtalal took him to Radhesani’s establishment. Radhesani gave him a bidi and sang a thumri for him. Haridas pocketed the bidi. Dhurtalal spoke freely. Haridas learnt all his secrets. He pretended to be shy and did not respond to Radhesani’s advances. He left Dhurtalal in Radhesani’s company and went home. He kept Dhurtalal’s notes away safely. He went over the details of next day’s plan in his mind once again and went to sleep late. The next day, Haridas went to the office just before noon. Dhurtalal arrived soon after, followed by Laxminandan a few minutes later. Haridas spoke to neither of them. He opened his desk, took out a ledger book and pretended to write in it. Some policemen were patrolling the street outside. Laxminandan thought that they had come at his request, while Dhurtalal took them to be his. Both believed that Haridas was their confidant; both were certain of final triumph and their confidence was apparent. Laxminandan walked in, his chest thrust out, and accepted the salutations from his staff. Dhurtalal sat on his seat twirling his moustache. Apart from Haridas, there were three or four other clerks sitting at their desks. Surprised by the Sheth’s unexpected appearance after months, they made a great show of their diligence. The brothers-in-law said nothing to each other for a while. Finally, Dhurtalal broke the silence. ‘Wonderful, Sheth! Look how splendid the office looks just by your presence. Without you the office looks bald, like a head without a pagdi and an elephant without its palanquin.’ ‘But you have been present. Are we so different?’ Sheth replied, concealing his impatience. Dhurtalal leaned forward and asked, ‘Shethji, did you think about what we discussed yesterday?’ ‘Hasn’t Haridas told you already?’ ‘No, not everything.’ ‘It is just that I cannot make up my mind and until I am clear, I do not want to take any decision on it.’ ‘Sheth, you are mentally unstable. Therefore we should not postpone a good thing for another day.’ The Sheth sat down, put his feet up on his desk and said, ‘You are right, I am unhinged. Hence, I order you to leave my office right now. You are dismissed.’ Sheth turned towards the clerks and loudly said, ‘Clerks, do any of you need to ask Dhurtalal anything? I have dismissed him.’ The clerks were stunned. Dhurtalal turned red in anger, but his words were calm and measured. ‘Shethji, you are not completely stable. If you were in full possession of your mental faculties, you can dismiss me whenever you please—you are the master. But given your present condition, I have to act as a guardian to my sister and her son. I am also responsible for your wellbeing. I urge you to calm down.’ ‘Rogue! I dismiss you! I ask you to leave my premises this very moment. Come on, now get up and get lost!’ Dhurtalal got up and turned towards the clerks, ‘Brothers, Shethji has lost all sense. It is indeed very sad. If we don’t restrain him, he might harm himself.’ No one moved or spoke. Then Laxminandan walked up briskly to Dhurtalal and gave him a shove, shouting, ‘Clerks! Call my security guards or call the police. This rascal has no place in my office anymore!’ Laxminandan looked towards Haridas. Dhurtalal turned brazen. ‘Haridas, go call the police. The Sheth has gone mad. Clerks, restrain him! What are you staring at my face for?’ A clerk named Thakordas was the first to get up, and the others followed his lead. They tried to restrain the Sheth, but Laxminandan pushed them away, enraged. They tried to tie him up with a cloth rope. Dhurtalal and the clerks shouted, ‘The Sheth has gone mad! He is insane!’ Haridas quietly got up and signalled to the police to enter the office. Both Laxminandan and Dhurtalal were sure that the police was partisan. The police came in. They saw Dhurtalal and the clerks tie up Laxminandan. Dhurtalal told them, ‘Haridas, the Sheth has gone mad; therefore I have tied him up. Take him away to Colaba or wherever you need to take him.’ One of the policemen asked in Marathi, ‘You tied up the Sheth?’ Dhurtalal proudly replied, ‘Yes, it was I who tied him up.’ The policeman ordered, ‘Tukaji, first handcuff Dhurtalal, and then all these people. Untie the Sheth.’

Dhurtalal and the clerks were taken aback. In a moment the police had handcuffed Dhurtalal and his accomplices. The havaldar addressed his men, ‘Tukaji, we can testify that these people illegally restrained Shethji. You take them to the Commissioner Sahib. I will follow.’ The policemen dragged away Dhurtalal and his accomplices. Laxminandan, Haridas, the havaldar and a few policemen stayed back. The havaldar freed the Sheth and confiscated the cloth rope with which he was tied as evidence. The havaldar asked, ‘Shethji, what are your orders for me?’ Laxminandan replied, ‘Havaldar, I will follow you. I will meet the Sahib and file a complaint. You are free to go.’ The havaldar saluted Laxminandan and went away leaving him and Haridas alone. Haridas said, ‘Shethji, did you see the brazenness of the rascals?’ ‘Haridas, God was my saviour, and so were you. This rogue was determined to send me to the mental hospital.’ ‘Yes, I am aware of it. Here, read these notes.’ The news spread in the city. There was much excitement. As the Sheth read the notes written by Dhurtalal, Bulwer Sahib came to visit. Laxminandan got up, shook hands with him and offered him a chair to sit. The Sheth asked Haridas, ‘Haridas, shall I show these notes to Sahib?’ Bulwer Sahib took his seat. He had met Laxminandan in the morning and learnt about Dhurtalal’s treachery. They had decided to meet again in the afternoon. He read the two notes written by Dhurtalal; the plan to have the Sheth declared insane was apparent. Haridas produced the three thousand rupees that he had received from Dhurtalal the previous evening. Both gentlemen were pleased with the honest and dutiful employee. Bulwer Sahib was of the opinion that both the letters and money should be immediately deposited with the police commissioner and that the commissioner be made aware of all the details, but the plan of taking the case to its conclusion and eventual conviction should be left to the police. Bulwer Sahib approved the draft document prepared by Laxminandan, but they decided to seek the counsel of a senior barrister as they could not decide if the document should be signed immediately or if Laxminandan should wait until the criminal case against Dhurtalal was concluded. It was decided that Haridas should remain in Bombay until all these matters were resolved. Bulwer Sahib advised that Chandrakant should coordinate the efforts to find Sarasvatichandra and that the Sheth should give him all the financial assistance required. Laxminandan promptly sent three thousand rupees to Ratnanagari for Chandrakant. Bulwer Sahib returned to his house while Laxminandan and Haridas went to meet the police commissioner. The police commissioner was a courteous and noble officer. He promptly arranged to have Laxminandan’s formal complaint lodged. Haridas gave his testimony; so did the policemen who had witnessed the scene. He assigned the investigation to a trusted chief constable with an order that he should be immediately made aware of any development. Latif Khan and Dhurkerao met Dhurtalal in the prison with the letters he had written to them. They expressed their regret and said that they had received the letter somewhat late and had not understood its contents clearly. Dhurtalal explained to them his intent and read out the notes, thus admitting to his guilt. The serial numbers of the rupee notes that Dhurtalal had given to Haridas were registered in the account books of both Laxminandan and Dhurtalal, because the notes had been initially received by Laxminandan, who had passed them on to Dhurtalal. The police investigation thus moved at a brisk pace. All the news and rumours were reported in the newspapers. Dhurtalal and Laxminandan became the talk of the town. The newspapers also wrote movingly about Sarasvatichandra’s disappearance and Laxminandan’s state of mind. Bulwer Sahib was keen to publish such stories because he believed that no matter where Sarasvatichandra was, he would certainly be moved by his father’s plight and would put aside his hurt and reach out to his father. Bulwer Sahib printed short narratives and poems that described Sheth Laxminandan’s sorrow. The poems, printed both in Gujarati and in English, were certain to touch Sarasvatichandra’s heart, he believed. Laxminandan remembered a few lines of the poem that Sarasvatichandra had written to him when he left. A well-known poet, Tarang Shankar, used these lines to compose a poem, expressing Laxminandan’s anguish and published them in the Gurjar Vartik. What does your father care for your sorrows, you said He pines madly for you, of course He finds this earthly form burdensome The son may well have erred, the father took no offence; The father erred once, but the son’s pride couldn’t bear it. The world is home to many souls, but the father’s life is invested in his son’s He chants your name till his mouth runs dry He abuses Lakshmi: You robbed me of my son! He weeps so much he can barely see If the son is separated from his father, The father will surely die. Not content with the poem, Laxminandan decided to publish something under his own name. Bhai! Why are you so heartless? Have pity on my old age. I have no one else. Come back wherever you are. I can neither think nor breathe. For a month from today, I will wait for you. If you don’t come back, I shall give up my life like Dashrathji. Bhai, what has made you so heartless? If you are not with me, to whom shall I turn in my old age? The translation of this was read out to Bulwer Sahib by the editor of the newspaper where this was to be printed. Bulwer Sahib said, ‘Print it under the Sheth’s signature. If Sarasvatichandra reads it, he is sure to return. Just as the call of the hunter awakens a lion from its deep slumber, Sarasvatichandra’s unreasonable and stubborn silence will vanish the moment he reads his father’s heartfelt lament. Print it in bold type.’
chapters.summary: As Laxminandan pines for Sarasvatichandra, Dhurtalal cunningly seizes control of the family business, while secretly plotting to ensure Sarasvatichandra is never found.

chapters.title: News from Suvarnapur: The Guilty Son of the Karbhari
paragraphs: News from Suvarnapur:

The Guilty Son of the Karbhari Every good political institution must have a preventive operation as well as a remedial. It ought to have a natural tendency to exclude bad men from government, and not to trust for the safety of the state to subsequent punishment alone: punishment, which has ever been tardy and uncertain; and which, when power is suffered in bad hands, may chance to fall rather on the injured than the criminal.   —Edmund Burke The day that he had become the Karbhari of Suvarnapur, Buddhidhan had asked himself: what if people of his own faction and family were to turn tyrannical? Who would the people of Suvarnapur carry their woes to? Would they also face the predicament that had been his lot for so long? Who would be responsible for the sins of misrule? What if Pramaddhan or someone else in the intoxication of power were to begin oppressing the people? Would he, the Karbhari, be open to complaints against his own confidantes? These questions had troubled Buddhidhan the day he had assumed the powers of the Karbhari.⟨fn:61⟩ But at that time he had no inkling that soon this question would arise in his house, and that his own son would be the accused. And that let alone Krishna Kalika’s husband, even his dear Kumud Sundari would not be able to put a charge on his son but, in fact, would herself stand accused. Such events awaken the conscience of karbharis and other officials—if indeed they do have a conscience— who soar high with the support of son, brother, friend and other close relatives. Not just that, if a conscientious official who is aware of his responsibilities were to take pride in the belief that he has the capacity to punish an old friend or a close relative, such instances expose their weakness and belittle their pride. As he gathered more information regarding Pramaddhan’s doings, Buddhidhan was both shocked and greatly humbled. He could see shades of similarity between Shathrai who acted through his son Dushtarai, and himself who tolerated Pramaddhan’s activities. This comparison pained him. He looked for strength that would enable him to remove the cause of that pain. Within just few days after assuming the Karbhar, Buddhidhan was perturbed by questions like: Am I any different from Shathrai? Will I be instrumental in inflicting the same pain on others which it was once my lot to suffer? Events unfolded in quick succession which caused him immeasurable agony. Even before Navinchandra’s departure, Vanleela shared some stories about Pramaddhan’s doings with Saubhagya Devi and Alak Kishori, who in turn appraised Buddhidhan. We know that at the time of Navinchandra’s departure, Buddhidhan was perturbed. What followed was much more painful. On the day of Kumud Sundari’s departure, Vanleela spoke at length to Saubhagya Devi and Alak Kishori about Krishna Kalika and Pramaddhan. Mother and sister called Pramaddhan and without revealing their source or the details of his misdeeds, they reprimanded him for misdeeds which were certain to bring disrepute to his father. Pramaddhan’s guilty mind sprang to his defence and he employed the guile taught to him by Krishna Kalika. He took out from his pocket some burnt pieces of paper and in a great show rage, he accused his wife Kumud of infidelity. This confirmed for mother and sister the validity of Vanleela’s news. Saubhagya Devi’s eyes welled up with tears. ‘Alak, the sins of my past lives have come to haunt me. I gave birth to a demon! Shiv! Shiv! Shiv! My daughter-in-law meek as a cow has this suffering in her fate! I am going away. I don’t even want to look at the face of this son of mine! You deal with your brother. I, a daughter of poor parents, married your father who was destined for greatness. But does the fate of the wretched ever leave them? He got the Karbhar, and I lost my all.’ Unable to bear the agony, Saubhagya Devi went and lay down in the parsal, covered herself from head to toe and wept her heart out. Devi went away, but Alak Kishori pounced on her brother. She held him by his chin, looked him squarely in the face and said with eyes breathing fire, ‘O wretch, I know that rand Kalika taught you what to say. She taught you this even before Bhabhi left. And now you have a black face. I loathe you! Have some shame!’ Alak pushed her brother away and gave him a scathing look. Pramaddhan was scared. He sought a way out of his predicament. He was one of those who could resort to a greater lie when caught lying. He turned brazen. ‘Behn, you and Devi are simple-minded. I might be a liar, I might have done wrong, but you recognise this handwriting, don’t you? Look at it, examine it closely and tell me if I have given you false evidence.’ Alak read the torn scraps of paper. ‘Of course! Bhai, you forget that I have spent more years in my life than the number of days you have lived. Bhabhi composed these poems; but they are beyond your comprehension. Bhabhi would write such poems daily. How does that constitute any proof?’ ‘Behn, you are hasty. Take a closer look. This has not been written by your sister-in-law. This has been written by that Navinchandra.’ ‘You wretch! When one lie failed you, you advance another! Was Bhabhi so stupid as to hand you a letter that Navinchandra allegedly gave her?’ ‘No, I retrieved them from under your Bhabhi’s table.’ ‘And you found them conveniently after she left, so that we would believe you and have no opportunity to hear Bhabhi’s explanation, isn’t it? Bhai, that rand Kalika has taught you all this. But your sister is a match for a hundred of those bitches. My brother can’t be so vile.’ ‘I am vile, am I? Aren’t you ashamed? Are you trying to shield your Bhabhi or that Navinchandra? Even I know of some things.’

This enraged Alak even more. ‘Very good, Bhai! Who else but a brother can say such things? It is true—we become like the company we keep. How is it possible that you remain unsoiled by Kalika’s loathsome depravities. Bhabhi has gone, but I pity Devi. Now go away from here!’ ‘Give back those scraps of paper to me.’ ‘As if I am a child!’ ‘What will you do with them?’ ‘I will show them to both Devi and Pitaji. He will judge you, me, Bhabhi and that Kalika of yours. You can tell Pitaji all that you have told me. And also tell that rand Kalika that she can do all that she is capable of—I will not rest until I have driven her away from this town.’ ‘I have evidence. What evidence do you have?’ ‘Forget your evidence; we will have enough evidence if we look for it. That rand was with you in your room, and you had thrown out her buttons from the window. You wouldn’t remember it now, would you?’ Alak retorted acidly. That scene suddenly flashed before Pramaddhan’s eyes. It was Kumud Sundari who had flung the buttons on a chain from Krishna Kalika’s blouse and a flower fallen from her hair at Kalika in rage from the window.⟨fn:62⟩ Pramaddhan turned meek. He couldn’t think. He realised that he had lost. He looked down and walked away, defeated. The matter was reported to Buddhidhan. He maintained equanimity and heard all the charges. He sent Narbheram to his son to obtain answers. Pramaddhan narrated his side of the story. In addition, following Krishna Kalika’s advice he alleged that Navinchandra and Kumud had run away together because he had come to know of their relationship. Their joint departure, he argued, was further proof of their guilt. He said that the decision to run away was taken on the night when he had gone to Lilapur with a message for Russell Sahib. Kumud and Navinchandra were in adjacent rooms and the two educated lovers had planned their escape that night. Buddhidhan thought about it calmly; Pramaddhan’s story did not appear to him beyond the realm of possibility. He thought about this all day long. The matter, he believed, could only be resolved if all the persons involved could be brought face to face; but he was apprehensive as to what that would reveal. He was also concerned that the matter would bring disrepute to the family. That evening his soldiers returned with the captive outlaw Sursinh. Later in the evening, around nine p.m., the coachman returned; he brought news of Kumud’s drowning and reported on the futile search. The family was drowned in sorrow. Their affection and compassion for Kumud increased manyfold, while their anger against Pramaddhan and Krishna Kalika multiplied a hundredfold. Late at night, Buddhidhan called Narbheram and sought his opinion. Narbheram said, ‘Buddhidhanbhai, what has happened cannot be undone. If you stretch the matter, the Karbhar that you have obtained just a few days ago will slip out of your hands. It will be a blot on you. There is no greater stupidity than to declare one’s own weaknesses—please don’t commit this stupidity. Pramaddhan is scared of you and cannot face you. If he does something stupid out of shame and fear, you will repent later. You will blow this issue out of proportion and make a mountain out of a molehill. It will become public knowledge. I believe that your family was almost complete in every respect; it was too good to be true. Your family was certain to attract someone’s evil eye and invite some calamity. You should consider that what could have been potentially a great misfortune is just a minor domestic problem. Thank God for it. Such things do happen in every other family. They were never a part of your domestic life, but now they are. Pramadbhai is a young man, and youth has to manifest itself in some form. Let me be frank, Buddhidhanbhai. If you are too harsh, or foolish, you will be left empty-handed. Your daughter-in-law is given up for dead. Now if something happens to your son, you will lose everything. Therefore, make sure that he is not forced into a misadventure.’ Buddhidhan said, ‘I will keep what you say in mind. But you must come without fail tomorrow and bring along Vanleela and Krishna Kalika’s husbands.’

‘Why do you want them?’ ‘That you will know in the morning.’ ‘Your intention is not beyond my grasp. I will obey your command. But don’t forget the saying: one should not act in haste.’ ‘I will do nothing without hearing your opinion, Narbheram. What shall we do about Kumud?’ ‘We must act swiftly. The coachman said that she drowned in the river and could not be traced even until late in the evening. He does not know anything more.’ ‘Did he also tell you that Kumud, overcome with grief, jumped into the river?’ ‘He can say what he likes.’ Buddhidhan sighed. ‘All right. But before daybreak, send about twenty-five intelligent men to search for Kumud. They should also go and meet Vidya Chatura.’ ‘That is a good thing.’ ‘Oh, I just remembered that Vidya Chatura has sent a letter to me. Read it out to me.’ Narbheram read out the letter. Dear Buddhidhanbhai, I need not emphasise how glad we are that the evil-doers have been eclipsed, and that your Maharaja has recognised your true worth and bestowed the Karbhar on you. It is bound to do good to the king, the people of your state and yourself. This is a matter of great joy. A letter of congratulations written by our Maharaja Maniraj Shri to your Maharana Bhupsinhji is on the way. If I with my limited and shallow experience were to give any advice about administration to you, given your abilities and vast experience, it would most certainly be improper. But if I were to make some suggestions regarding Pramaddhan, it would not be out of place, given my relationship with him. It would benefit Pramaddhan greatly, I feel, if he were to spend some time as a student. Those with learning make much more out of the experiences of life. People like me, who have obtained an English education, believe that just as the minister has certain duties with regard to his king, he also has duties towards the state. A minister’s primary responsibility is towards his king and then towards the state. I believe that a minister violates his duty towards the state if he appoints a son, a brother, a nephew or a son-in-law in high positions in the state. By doing so, a minister is constrained in the discharge of his duties towards the state. People fear greater injustice as justice is harder to obtain under such dispensation. It also harms the person we appoint. Their abilities and industriousness remain unexplored as they are encumbered by the burden of favour done to them. Hence, I believe you should consider sending Pramaddhanbhai to a place other than Ratnanagari and Suvarnapur. Let him learn to swim in strange waters. But of course, the final decision is yours. The remaining part of the letter dealt with domestic matters. Narbheram read it hurriedly. He gave the letter back to Buddhidhan and remarked, ‘Bhai Sahib, Vidya Chatura is a learned man. But our science and our reasoning is different.’ ‘Pramaddhan bears witness to the fact that Vidya Chatura’s learning is not without merit,’ Buddhidhan said cutting him short. ‘Yes, that is possible. Just as you have learnt a lesson from your son, others, too, have learnt their lessons. Allow me to explain to you in vernacular idiom: your son’s father-in-law is pedantic. I will give you another example. In a neighbouring kingdom, the karbhari was over-wise. He invited a Parsi, Jamshedji Manekji. Once the Parsi got a foothold, he got in Nasarvanji and several other Parsis. All the Parsis occupy high positions and ride horses, while that karbhari still walks to work. There are innumerable such examples. If you employ one Dakshini, more Dakshinis pour in after him; brahmins bring other brahmins and banias bring their own caste fellows. I don’t blame them. This is the law of the land. Everyone follows this law; we do not need to reinvent this anew. Everyone likes a feast in someone else’s house. I become your guest and feast on the choicest of sweets; but when you come to my house, you have to observe a fast! It is fine; we should certainly listen to what he has to say. If a liar admits to lying, he ceases to be liar. He will do what suits him, and we must do what is beneficial to us. We should let them say what they want; we should even agree with them but act only for our own benefit—the rest of the world can go to hell. Buddhidhanbhai, if we begin to accept all the advice that is given to us, those who give advice shall be considered wise, and we shall make fools of ourselves.’ For a moment, Buddhidhan forgot his troubles. He smiled and said,  ‘All right, Narbheram, you do that when you become the karbhari.’ ‘What is wrong with what I have said? Bhai Sahib, let me warn you. If you follow this pedantic advice and act stupidly and decide to give even the slightest of punishments to Pramaddhan, I will go to the Maharana myself and ask him to seek your resignation. I will tell him to appoint me in your place and give my position to Pramadbhai. Let me tell you, I will run the Karbhar very well and ensure that Pramadbhai succeeds me as the karbhari. Once he becomes the karbhari, you and I shall renounce the world, pretend that the world is an illusion, and set out in search of Brahma. But for the moment, our world consists of you, me and Pramadbhai; even Brahma is in this world of ours. All else is illusion, which we must shun!’ Buddhidhan could not contain his laughter. He pushed Narbheram away and lay down on the mattress. ‘Is there more to it?’ ‘Yes. Now hear this: The wise seek the company of kings so that they can benefit their friends and harm their enemies. Who does not work to fill their stomach? ‘This is the shastra. Allow me to compose a fitting reply to Vidya Chatura. Meanwhile, you must do as I have told you. Now I shall take your leave.’ Narbheram wore his pagdi and went down to talk to the women. Looking at his retreating figure, Buddhidhan thought, what a character! And how fate has brought the two of us together! His advice cannot be brushed aside. An intelligent man is one who learns even from inanimate things. Then why should I not listen to what Narbheram has to say? He is worldly-wise. As he sat ruminating, Alak Kishori came up, followed closely by Vanleela who was almost hiding behind her. Alak looked like an enraged tigress; her eyes breathed fire, her lips trembled and her hands shook. She stood erect, her chest thrust out, and thundered, ‘Pitaji, this is the limit!’ ‘Why? Has something else happened?’ Buddhidhan asked calmly. ‘Ever since the news of Bhabhi’s drowning, Devi is laid up like a log, Pramadbhai is behaving like a beast, and you have done nothing to search for Bhabhi.’ ‘Alak, if I don’t make efforts to search for your Bhabhi, what else am I good for then? Go and ask Narbheram, haven’t I told him already that he should send out a search party early in the morning?’ ‘Who are you sending? Don’t send anyone who keeps Pramadbhai’s company. They will kill her.’ ‘Why would anyone do that?’ ‘You have fixed a salary of two hundred for Bhai. Have you ever asked him what he does with it?’ ‘No, what does he do with his money?’ ‘I am not like Bhabhi. Even if a fly were to come near me, I would crush it. But if a wasp were to attack Bhabhi, she would gently raise her garment to shield herself, taking care not to hurt the wasp. These two rands, Kalika and some prostitute called Padma, have squeezed Bhai dry. Bhabhi has done what she did to free herself from these two women and my brother. I am now certain that she jumped to her death. Pitaji, we have lost our most precious jewel!’ Alak Kishori broke down and collapsed on the mattress. ‘How can I bear to be alive?’ she sobbed. Vanleela, also weeping, tried to hold Alak but fell on top of her and her hand was crushed under Alak’s body. Buddhidhan helped them both get up. Alak sat beside her father and composed herself. ‘Pitaji, Devi is not herself. You are the only one who can save us. I can’t bear the thought of Bhabhi’s drowning. To top it, Bhai says whatever comes to his mind—it is like a thief punishing the police. Don’t you give him a long rope, Pitaji! Bhabhi is incapable of hurting anyone, and this vile brother of mine accuses her even when she is gone! This fire will burn us all.’ ‘Behn, we will find a way out.’

‘But Pitaji, what do you think?’ ‘We will see.’ ‘No, there is nothing more to be seen. Bhai will make up fantastic stories, and there is no one to tell you about Bhabhi’s side of things. Therefore, you must ask me.’ Alak Kishori relayed to her father the information that Vanleela had supplied her with. Of course, there was something that she could not share with him. Finally, the two women left, and Buddhidhan was once again left to his own thoughts. O’ God, this is not the way of the world, he thought. A sister came to defend her sister-in-law and put her own brother in the dock of an accused. Kumud Sundari, Goddess Lakshmi of my house! This is the result of your pure piety. Pramad did make an accusation that Navinchandra and Kumud both left Suvarnapur according to a predetermined plan. Is he right? No, what Alak said is correct. It was only after Navinchandra’s departure that Kumud’s visit to her parents was fixed. Navinchandra had no knowledge that Kumud was to go and meet her parents. They did not so much as lift their eyes to look at each other! And my house is always full of people. There was no scope that they ever met alone. No, all these accusations are pure fabrication. Vanleela’s story about Pramad and Krishna Kalika also came true. That thing about the buttons is also a fact. But, the handwriting on those pieces of paper was Navinchandra’s. It said: I had a father! I had a brother! Does that not prove his innocence? My son is stupid to be suspicious. No, I don’t think my son is so stupid. Then what is it? It is clear—it is a counter accusation to save himself from the charge. This ploy of putting a counter-charge on Kumud, who is as pure as Ganga herself, is the way of Shathrai’s family. My son would not think of it; it is obviously something that Krishna Kalika has taught him—she is after all from Shathrai’s family. I cannot be certain that only Kalika is to be blamed; but to the extent that Vanleela’s reporting is correct, her guilt is established. The buttons from her blouse and her advice to accuse Kumud prove Krishna Kalika’s involvement. It also proves that my son is debauched. Buddhidhan, although a father, also had to be the judge. He was convinced of his son’s guilt. He could feel Kumud’s anguish. The injustice done to her was apparent. The father-judge was dejected. He realised that even Krishna Kalika’s husband has been wronged and he grew more despondent. Kumud may or may not be traced alive, but to Buddhidhan it seemed plausible that Kumud had jumped into the river to free herself from the evil ways of his son. With this realisation, Buddhidhan’s misery and gloom gave way to seething rage. He said aloud, ‘Beast! I have vowed to punish even those who are nearest to me if they are proven guilty. Pramad—you cease to be my son, and I am no longer your father.’ But then again, Buddhidhan hesitated. He thought: Kumud was bound by fate to her husband; she had to share in his good deeds as also his sins. She, too, would suffer with him for no fault of hers. What could be that punitive action that would punish guilty Pramaddhan but not affect innocent Kumud? Buddhidhan was perplexed. He struck his hand on the mattress in frustration and thought aloud, Vidya Chatura, what you said was correct. If I act unjustly, the innocent will be punished; and if I seek to do justice, I will be punished! Why should one’s administration be such? If we seek to do justice but do not want to be punished for wrongdoing, one’s own conduct must be impeccable. One should not be in a situation where one is required to sit on judgement over one’s own kin. One should be able to exercise control over one’s friends and relatives. There is a saying: a man who asks after the host’s origins after accepting hospitality is an ass. It is true, I have acted in an asinine way. What if I resign? That would be punishment enough for me and my son. Don’t I deserve to be punished? I can take steps for the future, but I can clearly see the implications of my past mistakes. I am certain that I am not even aware of the many mistakes that I have made. There may be others, like Krishna Kalika’s husband, who may have been wronged. My statecraft is not unsullied. Who is responsible for all those mistakes, misdeeds and pain? Who is responsible for all those sins? Buddhidhan, you are responsible—who else? O’ God! I have to account for all those sins. I have to accept punishment due to all others. It is said that those who rule end up in hell; this bears testimony to that wisdom.

Buddhidhan, you deserve punishment. What if I resign? But resignation is an escape from the battle-field, a ploy to save oneself from the real punishment. For all these years, I have prospered because of the Maharana. It is now my turn to be true to my salt. And if I wish to do so, I must stay on in the Karbhar, punish my son and bear the pain, accept the ignominy and disrepute that it would heap upon my family, and in so doing, lay down my duty. If it means that I have to face Kumud Sundari’s suffering every day, that, too, I must endure. I must atone for the sins committed against Kumud. Whatever you may say, Narbheram, escaping the battlefield and deserting Maharana Bhupsinh is not atonement; the saying that you quoted misguides. It is wrong to aspire to authority to promote one’s kin and punish the enemy. This aspiration befits only the lowly. It is sinful; it can only result in immorality. It is certain to lead good men astray. Vidya Chatura, now I appreciate your wise and good counsel. Devi, you have made my heart religious; I will not allow this irreligious thought to take root in it. Tomorrow morning, I shall take the following actions. I shall dismiss Pramad from his position. He shall have no place in court. What about presenting him before the judge? Buddhidhan shuddered at the thought. Tears came to his eyes. He dried his tears and said to himself: All those who commit debauchery are punished by me. Why shouldn’t Pramad be just because he is my son? A deep sigh escaped Buddhidhan and he said aloud, ‘O’ God! Your Will be done! I will do whatever you command tomorrow morning.’ God, You have robbed me of my pride. The fire of revenge that raged within me destroyed Shathrai’s family. I avenged the insults borne by my mother and by Devi. But in my desire to take revenge and be proud of my achievements, I forgot how undeserving I am. I believed the force of that fire to be my own strength; without it I could not have obtained the Karbhar. But that fire is now doused. Will I retain this position of authority? O’ God, the fire that I burnt with was Your fire, Your will, and for reasons known only to You, it raged within me. Now You have suddenly doused that fire—so I was only a receptacle for it. Shathrai, who was consumed by the fire, believed it was powerless to do him any harm. But I will not make the same mistake. I will not play with fire. An insult to that fire is to insult You. You have the power to annihilate the world. You can cause the great deluge. Why would You then be powerless to create such small fires? But God, that fire is inanimate—You are the conscious one. I was a son of a poor widow. You gave me so much wealth. You gave me this family and prestige. This could only be done by Your grace. It is now my turn to perform my duties towards You. If I turn my back to You, would I not be ungrateful? Until You take away everything You have granted me, I am duty-bound. If this act of service is my duty, why should I grumble or be pained by it? Do I even have the right to do so? Shathrai! Dushtarai! The edifice of administration that you created acted as a catalyst for me. I was moved and shaped by it. Hitherto, my Karbhar has been an imitation of the edifice that you created. But beginning tomorrow it will cease to resemble your administration, just as I will cease to resemble you; I will exorcise you, Shathrai. From tomorrow, my Karbhar will be determined by and run on one sole purpose—service to God, service to the people and service to the king to the extent that he remains pure. This purpose will define and guide my ministership. Without this purpose, I am a wretched man who needs a few yards of earth to sleep on and a few morsels of food to sustain this body. With these thoughts, Buddhidhan at last fell asleep. It is said that a king and his minister remain sleepless. But that king and that minister who rule with a sense of duty and uphold dharma receive the boon of sleep. Buddhidhan fell into a deep and undisturbed sleep. At this time, Pramaddhan was not at home. He did not come home even in the morning. The town was abuzz with rumours. A dead body was found floating in the sea. Some said that he had committed suicide. Some said that he was murdered. Some said that he had disappeared. There was speculation even among those close to him. Some said that the shock of Kumud Sundari’s drowning had turned him insane. Some said that Pramaddhan had decided to pursue Kumud with the intention of killing her. Others said that he had followed Navinchandra with murderous intent. It was also said that he was driven by fear and shame. But no one was really certain. Upon his disappearance, many sentiments and statements were attributed to Buddhidhan. ‘My son doesn’t deserve a search party’; ‘It is just as well that he has gone away’; ‘I have nothing more to do with him’; ‘I had already given him up for dead.’ Dear reader, why do we need to dwell further on what the people of Suvarnapur said or did? Suffice it to know that, ‘Such is the atonement of the defeated.’
chapters.summary: Buddhidhan faces a moral crisis as his son, Pramaddhan, is accused of misdeeds, forcing him to question his leadership and family's integrity.

chapters.title: In the Presence of Vishnudas
paragraphs: In the Presence of Vishnudas Sundargiri and Surgram were favourite sacred spots for followers of many religions and sects. The temples and monasteries that dot its landscape provide testimony to this. Religion is a constitutive element of the Aryas who reside in the Indian subcontinent. There are at least four paths to religion: jnana (knowledge), yoga (self-concentration), karma (action) and bhakti (devotion). At various points in history, Sundargiri was the abode of all these paths. The followers of these paths created monuments to their faith. Sarasvatichandra was given a bird’s-eye view of those sacred monuments. Once we know as to which of these four paths Vishnudas’ monastery followed, we shall also acquire the fitness to know Vishnudas. Yoga and karma have withered in our age, but the Aryas have a natural affinity for them. The path of karma is relatively easy to follow if the believer has faith and capability; hence this path still has a large following.
