The path of yoga is complex and its sadhana demands deep engagement; hence it is rare to find a master of this path. The few exponents who have attained mastery of yoga are greatly revered. The teachings of the path of jnana are accessible to all intelligent persons. The fruits of karma are long in coming; they manifest themselves only when the exponent is on the way to heaven. Unless the exponent experiences a mystical moment and obtains the fruits of his actions, the path of karma demands life-long patience. On the other hand, a follower of the path of knowledge receives the fruits of his learning during his lifetime itself. The preference for the path of knowledge in the age of English education is obviously for this reason. Ultimately the path of knowledge leads to Vedanta. The knowledge of Vedanta is mystical and can be obtained only after great effort. Hence, very few are able to realise this knowledge. For this reason, exponents of the path of knowledge are divided into two separate streams: one stream is for those with average intellectual capability and spiritual effort; the other is for those with mystical knowledge. The stream that demands average intelligence and effort is the more popular of the two; this is the one that supporters and critics of the path of knowledge usually refer to in their debates. The paths of knowledge, action and yoga all require capabilities and means. But among the Aryas, the path of devotion is not contingent upon cultivation of any means. It seeks to pave the way to heaven for the devoted. A devotee is not required to cultivate great learning. This path is imbued with the nectar of love and devotion. The devotees sing: A woman bereft of all power Can make him dance to her tunes; The path of love is sublime. Vishnudas had made profound study of all the four paths and sought to amalgamate them in the practices of his sect. Therefore those who wished to cultivate spiritual capability, whether they had the means for this attainment or not, became followers of his sect. Before he took the vows of an ascetic and became known as Vishnudas Swami, he was a brahmin. He had studied grammar, literature, mathematics, the philosophies of Mimamsa, Nyaya and Vedanta in Kashi and Bengal. He had travelled through the sacred Himalayas and dabbled in yogic practices. He had also joined the devotees of Shiva, Vishnu and Shakti and tasted the power of devotion. He returned home to assume the responsibilities of a householder. Vishnudas lived the life of a householder and experienced both the pleasures and pains of a life with parents, brothers, sisters, wife and son. It did not take him long to acquire a mature understanding of life as a householder. He was about thirty-two. One evening he was at the village pond, offering his prayers, when a group of ascetics passed by. He began a conversation with the ascetics. Suddenly, he felt a strong urge to join them. He went home and made arrangements for the material needs of his family. He called his wife aside and said, ‘I am going away never to return. God has given us enough to meet the family’s needs. You have a son. My parents have my brother. I have done my duty towards all, and hence, it is no longer binding on me to be a householder. Therefore, I am going away.’ His wife wailed. His family came to know of his resolve. They all cried. Vishnudas consoled them all; but late that night as the others slept he walked out—he had only a loin cloth on his body. Before daybreak he had joined the ascetics and left his home and family miles behind. He was conscious of the pain he had caused his family. All journeys involve leaving and pain, Vishnudas reasoned with himself. But a traveller returns, and the promise of his return heals the pain faster. In my case it will take a little longer. But this pain is nothing in comparison to the pain they would have felt if I had died. Now they will never know of my death. I have saved them from the possibility of deeper sorrow. But my wife has become a widow even while her husband is alive in the bodily form. Vishnudas could not convince himself that he had not sinned against his wife; but his resolve was not to be undone. He accepted the vows of an ascetic for which he discarded the yajnopavit, the sacred thread worn by brahmin men. He wore his hair long, smeared his body with sacred ash and came to be called Vishnudas. In a short time his learning and experience elevated him to the position of the Guru—the master of the ascetics. As the master, he gained access to the mystical texts of the Yadunandan monastic order. The monastic order and monastery of Yadu Shrunga was ancient. Some learned ascetics had been its gurus in the past. There were instances when the guru was of average accomplishments, but even these gurus had nurtured disciples of great talent and merit. The ascetics of this order were Alakhvadi; they also combined the worship of Yadunandan. The founders of the sect had composed texts to explain their philosophy. The ancient texts defined Alakh as formless, attributeless, Nirgun Brahman. One of the older texts demonstrated that in those days the Yadunandan monastic order was a firm believer in Vedanta; and as Vedantis they accepted the ultimate superiority of Brahman. At some point this monastic order got into a theological debate with Jain ascetics. The Jains argued that the Vedantis believed in a twin reality—one that was illusory and the other, real—and hence their notions of Brahman corresponded with this conception of reality. They further argued that to be non-dualistic and be a Vedanti was a contradiction in terms. The Vedantis entered the debate and argued their position through a nuanced argument drawn from the philosophy of Shankaracharya. They emerged victorious in the philosophical debate that ensued. But average followers did not understand the intricacies of the argument and many adopted Jain faith. The Vedanti ascetics realised that the tide had turned against them. They came up with an ingenious response—they introduced idol worship in their sect. Their sect, earlier called Alakhvad, was now called Alakh-Lakh- Vad. They argued that the Brahman is essentially formless, without any attributes and omnipresent, but that at points this Brahman manifests and assumes a name, a form and accepts attributes. In so doing, the Brahman bears witness to its own manifestations. This manifest form is recognised by different names such as God or Maya (illusion). Human beings may worship these manifest forms and through them recognise the ultimate reality of Brahman. This form of worship was more accessible to people. The ascetic community gained in strength once again. It was easy to incorporate the worship of Yadunandan, Brahma, Mahesh and Vishnu including their many incarnations in forms such as Krishna into the new faith. They drew average devotees through the path of bhakti into their fold and gradually helped them to attain an understanding of the philosophy of Brahman. At the time when Vishnudas became paramount in the monastery of Yadu Shrunga, the charged debates and verbal battles between the various sects and beliefs had not entirely ceased. Some old debates between the Shaiva, the Shakta and the Vaishnava still remained. These debates were distasteful and often violent, and a lot of good people turned away from Sundargiri and Surgram because of them. If Vishnudas had not dealt with these issues with patience, tolerance, immense generosity and tact, the significance of the sacred mountain would have diminished. He propagated equality of all faiths and adopted the maxim that humility was the best means and that one’s own qualities are revealed in one’s appreciation of the qualities of others. Gradually, mutual tolerance and respect took the place of bitter sectarian conflicts. Vishnudas saved his monastic order by saving everyone. He gave equal respect to all sects and they in turn revered his sect. He worshipped their gods and they reciprocated by bowing their head at his shrine. Sarasvatichandra was given these historical snippets of Sundargiri by his sadhu escorts. They praised the virtues of their Guru Vishnudas and spoke highly of his accomplishments. With all these new experiences, learnings and the vitality of his surroundings, thoughts of Kumud Sundari no longer occupied his mind as he approached the temple in company of the ascetics. Sarasvatichandra was now eager to meet this most famous and worthy guru. He was grateful to the ascetics for their hospitality and their learned conversation. He wondered what qualities the master possessed if his disciples were so worthy. He was eager to express his gratitude to the master. The deep sorrow that had enveloped him lifted and his face glowed with joy. As they approached the wide steps leading to the temple, all the ascetics hailed the vision of God, ‘Jai Yadunandan! Jai Yadunandan.’ The temple was not built on the traditional plan of temples. It was part of a large monastery. The monastery was single-storied. A visitor passed through an otalo or platform built of lime stones and entered through a door. The door led to a covered veranda and a large quadrangle where the vedi or altar for performing fire sacrifices was located. A large holy basil plant grew near the vedi. The quadrangle led to the shrine, which was a spacious room. A large idol of Yadunandan was installed in the shrine. Vishnudas usually sat at the feet of the idol on a straw mat. The doors to the shrine were opened for people during the hours of darshan, but were kept closed at other times when Vishnudas sat in meditation. He also used a space in the open veranda to sleep. He gave his discourses there after his early morning prayers and meditation. After the discourse Vishnudas would sit down with all the ascetics and they would have their meal. After the meal, on most days, he went down to the neighbouring villages to spread the word of God. This was also the time when he, along with other ascetics, sought alms. They would return in the evening, offer their prayers, converse among themselves and sleep by midnight. If Vishnudas was late in returning on some days, some other ascetic would offer worship to Yadunandan in his place. Vishnudas had divided his disciples into four categories. The lowest category was called anadhikari or the uninitiated. These novices were allowed to participate in the worship, have their meals with the master and seek clarifications during meals. The second rung comprised ascetics who had been initiated into the sect. These initiates were called the kanishtha adhikari and were invited to listen to Vishnudas’ discourses twice a week. On other days they were required to read and reflect upon the scriptures. Vishnudas discoursed to them on the path of devotion. The third group, the middle order ascetics or the madhyam adhikaris also participated in these discourses on devotion and were also given lessons in yoga by the master twice a week. There were very few ascetics in the highest category of merit, the uttam adhikaris. They were allowed to participate in these discourses but they had special discourses on the Vedanta. Vishnudas would often introduce the ascetics to Nyaya, Mimamsa, mathematics and other such subjects during their excursions to villages or during moments of rest while travelling. He selected deserving candidates to move from the lower rung to the higher rung. The ascetic who was considered best among the highest category was invited to participate in Vishnudas’ personal studies; he would treat such an ascetic as an equal and they would learn from each other. The spaces in the monastery were divided according to these categories. The space closest to the temple was occupied by the ascetics of the highest order. The two large rooms on either side of the quadrangle were occupied by the kanishtha and the madhyam adhikaris. Those still uninitiated used the outer veranda. There were two rooms behind the temple. In one of them all materials required for worship and other rituals were stored. The other room was the repository of all the sacred texts of the monastery; all other precious material possessions of the monastery were also kept there. The space that Vishnudas used had a back door which led to his bath and toilet. This was a large area. On two sides, the ascetics had built walls using large boulders to create a spacious enclosure. There was a big cave which had its opening in the enclosure. A grand banyan tree stood at the mouth of the cave. A perennial fresh water spring provided pure, sweet water. The spring had created a beautiful pond in which lotuses with a hundred petals bloomed. The lotuses attracted bees. There were two large beehives on the mountain side abuzz with the humming of bees. Mango and banana trees grew in the enclosure. There were creepers and flowering plants as well. Swans and ducks swam in the pond created by the spring. Smaller birds like parrots and mynahs also nested in the enclosure. Deer and rabbits roamed around the enclosure, feeding on the lush green grass. It was a beautiful and serene space. The soft green grass, sweet birdsong, fragrant flowers, sparkling water, abundant fruits and the stunning view with the majestic mountains in the backdrop calmed the senses and lifted the pall of gloom even from melancholic minds. There was an all-pervasive feeling of tranquillity and joy. In this natural environment, all doubts disappeared and made way for good thoughts. Vishnudas had decided that this enclosed garden shall be the abode of Sarasvatichandra. Sarasvatichandra was led through the courtyard into the enclosure. Their guru’s decision surprised his disciples, but they obeyed his command and led Sarasvatichandra respectfully into the garden. A deer skin was spread for him to sit under the shade of the banyan. Having seated him comfortably, Mohanpuri and Viharpuri went in to understand their guru’s wishes. Vishnudas was an accomplished astrologer and believed in the science of foretelling the future. He was approaching old age. He was in search of that great soul who could be his successor. He often consulted astrological charts and the position of stars to guide him in his search. His calculations had indicated that his search was nearing completion. His disciples had found Sarasvatichandra during the period indicated by his calculations. Vishnudas was convinced that Sarasvatichandra was that great soul who would succeed him. He was elated at this discovery. Viharpuri gave him an account of their early morning conversation with the guest. This account further affirmed Vishnudas’ belief and filled him with new energy. He was now eager to put his guest through a trial. Vishnudas had finished offering his prayers when Viharpuri and Mohanpuri approached him. He decreed: ‘Bring him to the temple immediately. He knows Sanskrit. I will test his worth.’ Sarasvatichandra was brought into Vishnudas’ presence without delay. Sarasvatichandra stood at the door of the temple and did namaskar to Vishnudas, but he did not fold his hands or pay obeisance to the idol of Yadunandan. The ascetics were surprised. Vishnudas remained unperturbed. He looked at Sarasvatichandra and asked him in Sanskrit: O child! Who are you? Whose son are you? Where are you going? What is your name? From where have you come? O young one, please tell me what I have asked you, for the sake of my love, since you ever increase my love.⟨fn:63⟩ Sarasvatichandra responded without hesitation: I am not a man, not even a divine being or a yaksha; not brahmin- kshatriya-vaishya-sudra; not a brahmachari, not a householder, not a forest dweller, not even a mendicant; I am the nature of Self-knowledge.⟨fn:64⟩ He stood with his arms crossed over his chest and continued his conversation aloud with himself in English⟨fn:65⟩: ‘This is a correct answer, correct in a double sense, true to my philosophy, and true to myself—I alone know me and that I am. I belong to all castes or to none, and my stage of life comprehends all stages. I am my inner self and I know it. The words are true as they were first spoken and also as I speak them now.’

‘Very good. Well spoken,’ Vishnudasji said in approval, and turning to his disciples, addressed them in Hindustani, ‘Look, my prediction has come true.’ ‘Navinchandraji ...’ Sarasvatichandra was surprised that Vishnudas was aware of his assumed name. He waited for the next question. ‘Navinchandraji, all those who enter the temple first bow to Yadunandan.’ ‘That is true, but I pay obeisance only to my personal god.’ ‘Who is your god?’ ‘The Eternal and the Formless One.’ ‘Navinchandraji, but a person and an idol are both manifestations of the Eternal and Formless One.’ ‘That is true. But you must be aware of what Tulsidasji had done.’ ‘What did Tulsidasji do?’ Sarasvatichandra responded enthusiastically, ‘You are a learned man and also a devotee. Tulsidasji refused to bow before Shri Krishna and said: “Your image is powerful and enticing, but Tulsi will bow to you only when you hold bow and arrow in your hand.”’ The ascetics were angry that Navinchandra had insulted their god, but his response set them thinking. Vishnudas was aware of their anger, and he also knew its remedy. He quickly said, ‘Wonderful, Navinchandraji. Well said,’ and turning to his disciples, he said, ‘Listen, this man understands the nature of the Formless One. All that he needs to be taught is the unity of the manifest and the unmanifest. Navinchandraji proved himself superior even to Tulsidas. Navinchandraji would pay obeisance only if the manifest were to dissolve in him and become the Formless One. If Shri Krishna were to assume the form of Shri Ram, the unmanifest would become manifest. This wisdom is indicative of his superior capabilities. Isn’t it so, Viharpuriji?’ ‘Absolutely true, Guruji! This is the resolve of a true devotee.’ The disciples were happy. Sarasvatichandra was also pleased. He said to himself silently in English: This man’s pluck is equal to my wish. He has grasped my position and gracefully assisted me in extracting me from the perplexing conflict between my duty to my conscience and to such kind and gentle hosts as these. Far be it for me to speak a single syllable that will either be untrue for courtesy or for fear, or will happen to offend in the slightest degree the susceptibilities of such noble and innocent souls as these. Gracious God! A disciple asked Vishnudas, ‘Guruji, if this be the case, why not initiate Navinchandraji into our sect?’ Sarasvatichandra was frightened by this proposal. Vishnudas realised the disciple’s naiveté as also his guest’s quandary. He gave a response that satisfied both the disciple and assuaged Sarasvatichandra’s fears. Vishnudas laughed aloud and said, ‘Viharpuri, this disciple is still a novice. He has not yet received initiation and hence he does not understand what the lowest rung of initiates knows. But he is curious and has asked a question which must be responded to. All the initiates shall sing with me.’ Vishnudas stood up and sang the first stanza. All the initiates got up and joined him with gusto. Do not torture yourself, child Only the unseen is true Whether you are white or ochre, Or drape yourself in colourful finery, Whether an ascetic or a householder, A man or a woman, The unseen has wrought the destiny of each: What will be, will be He who can awaken the unseen Cannot escape an ash-smeared forehead Everyone swayed to the rhythm of the song. The robust singing of the ascetics reverberated through the surrounding hills. The questioner stared meekly at the scene and sought forgiveness from the guru. Sarasvatichandra mused to himself in English: Look at this strong doctrine of toleration! Finally, Vishnudas turned towards the novice who had asked the question and said, ‘Child, have you understood? Who are we to offer the ash of renunciation to anyone? If someone does not become a renouncer, that is the play of the Unmanifest One. But if the Unmanifest One so desires, he shall become an ascetic for the welfare of others and shall renounce all—because the Unmanifest One so desires, not due to our persuasion. This ash is merely a symbol; the truth of it is internal. But to understand that you will have to acquire the highest capability. At this juncture it is enough for you to understand that all that is manifest and apparent is a reflection of that which is unmanifest. You should not treat any manifest thing with disdain. This disdain represents the arrogance of demonic illusion. The Unmanifest One has special love for a devotee who remains steadfast in his devotion and to his dharma. It was for this reason that Shri Krishna appeared before Tulsidasji in the form of Shri Ram. Navinchandraji is steadfast in his belief, but your faith is arrogant. I pardon you today, but the next time that demonic arrogance touches you, beware that you shall have no right to live under the protection of this monastery.’ Vishnudas addressed his disciples, ‘Mohanpuri, we have concluded the morning prayers. Today is not a day of study and discourse. We shall spend the day talking about philosophical issues. Our guest can also participate. We shall go to the garden and sit there. All initiates are to remain present.’ All the initiates went into the garden. Tiger and deer skins were spread on the ground. A tiger skin was spread on a flat rock for Vishnudas. A deer skin was spread on an adjacent rock for Sarasvatichandra. The disciples sat around them. Vishnudas turned towards Sarasvatichandra and said, ‘The little that we know of you has pleased our hearts. But I have been told that deep within, your heart is wounded.’ At this Sarasvatichandra smiled and interrupted Vishnudas, ‘Swamiji, that conclusion was based on their assumptions. But this assumption was not entirely without a basis either. Nevertheless, I see no harm in it. What if I were filled with sorrow? Without knowing sorrow we cannot value happiness. Without darkness we do not recognise the path of light. Sorrow often leads to renunciation. Sorrow arouses pity and pity leads to the service of another being. This act of service allows us to recognise that all beings are one. Joy is nothingness that we like and sorrow is nothingness that we do not like. Joy and sorrow both are nothingness. Nothingness is not distinct; then how can joy and sorrow be separate from one another? Like and dislike are constructs of our minds. Therefore, one cannot either aspire to happiness or shun sorrows. I welcome whatever comes my way. But I am partial to sorrows; they sharpen my intellect. If I had not sought out sorrows, I would never have gained this privilege of being in your presence.’ All the disciples were surprised by this opaque discourse. Viharpuri broke the silence and remarked, ‘It is said that nothing by its nature is either pleasant or unpleasant. Navinchandraji, wonderful. Allow me to ask you a question. Assume that the following verses were addressed to you.’ Well hast thou in early age. In these rites thy choice hast made; Aged mortals like myself Oft by worldly things are led. And thy penance, noble youth, Is endued with virtues fair,— Handsome forms we often meet, Handsome virtues,—they are rare! Transient as the autumn clouds, Pride and pomp of human kind;— Pleasures please us for a day, Bitter sorrows leave behind! Mortals’ days are full of evils, Death cuts short our life’s brief span; Therefore in this fleeting world Virtue seeks the holy man. Wise and nobly thou hast chosen Holy rites to virtue dear, But, belying thy great penance, Thy attire fills me with fear!⟨fn:66⟩

‘I am certain that you do not need the meaning of these verses explained,’ Sarasvatichandra replied with a smile. ‘Viharpuriji, these verses are from Bharavi’s Kirataarjunyam. There were doubts regarding Arjun’s appearance, which he resolved. But in response, I must state that I have many failings; consider this to be one more. To me, clothes, white or ochre, are all the same. This is my way of a response. Allow me to pose a question to you. You say that moksha or freedom is not possible without renunciation. But if you consider the manifest as a form of the Unmanifest One, why should it not be possible to attain moksha without renunciation? Please explain this. Moreover, if all that is manifest emanates from the unmanifest, their souls are one. The body is given to decay but the soul is eternal. If that is so, who needs moksha? Is the soul that desires moksha any different from that eternally free soul? What binds a soul to unfreedom? If the soul is eternal, how is it in bondage in the past and how shall it be free in the future? Please explain.’ All the disciples stared at each other in disbelief. It was certain that no one but the guru could provide an answer. Vishnudas looked pleased and eager to explain. ‘What a wonderful question! Navinchandra, one who knows the answer to these questions is given the highest position in our order. The mystery of our philosophy, of the relation between the manifest and the unmanifest is contained in the response. Only those who belong to the highest cadre may stay; all the rest must leave.’ Sarasvatichandra remained. Vishnudas turned towards a disciple and said, ‘Alakhpuri, recite the Siddhant Mantra, the verses that explain the basic philosophical tenets, from the Alakh Rahasya.’ Alakhpuri said, ‘Guruji, I obey your command’ and he proceeded to recite. Neither am I born, nor do I die. I am neither in bondage, nor am I free. This world is akin to an arrow released from the bow. I am one, unique; I abide in me and outside of me. I assume a form and inhabit the world and when I cease to be manifest I still gaze at my manifest form.

One who neither likes nor dislikes either action or inaction is in essence without attributes and devoid of action. A being out of reverence for the manifest one worships a form but retains awareness of the state of the Unmanifest One. Such a soul is self-aware and is intent upon the unmanifest. A soul that inhabits the manifest arises in the unmanifest; why would that being not cause the unmanifest to become manifest? In this way the seeker of Alakh causes the being, the lord and the unmanifest Brahman to become one, indivisible. This was the teaching of the greatest incarnation of the Manifest One, Shri Krishna to Arjun to urge him to perform his duty in war. Doing verily one’s work in the world one should wish to live a hundred years. Such is the saying of the Isa and the object of the manifest. A yogi of Alakh inhabits this world through his soul with the Supreme soul. Is this not the self-illuminating unmanifest, eternally blissful One? He is unattached, yet not free, neither a renunciate nor a householder, he is the Isa of the eternal nectar, He is the self- emanating Purusha. Day is time and so is the night. People perceive the transient day and night; only the enlightened ones know the time in which they are immersed. The ordinary person perceives the fiery manifestation and quiet repose of the manifest as distinct; they cannot perceive the non-duality as they comprehend only the transient. The multitude of senses makes Him the one with a thousand senses and yet, He is self-immanent. The manifest abides in the unmanifest; this is not unwelcomed by the unmanifest. Perceived only by the yogis but unrecognised by the uninitiated, the unmanifest surrounds us. As Alakhpuri recited, the other disciples joined in the recitation. Vishnudas discoursed at length on the meaning of the verses. ‘We divide the Vedanta in two parts: the Shruti and the Shankar Vedanta. The Shruti is the source of all religious sects. The Shankar Vedanta considers renunciation as supreme and urges us to discard all attachments to the illusory world. We revere Shankaracharya. But our philosophy of the unmanifest Brahman differs from his philosophy. The differences will become clear as I explicate the meaning of the verses. The Shankar Vedanta creates a trinity of Being, God and Brahman. We accept this, but we prefer the dyad of the manifest and the unmanifest. This is clearer and pithier as a formulation. Both Being and God are limited by attributes and hence we place them in one category; while we place Brahma, which is without any attributes, in a separate category. Most uninitiated persons can grasp only attributes. Thus we describe Being and God as the Manifest One. Brahman is unseen and not grasped by most people; therefore we describe Brahman as the Unmanifest One. The world of humans is grasped by the mind and the world of gods is the world of illusion. These are integral attributes of Being and the divine. We do not consider them distinct and separate from the manifest. We do not consider illusion worthy of discarding, nor do we dismiss it. Acceptance and denial of a thing is also a sign of preference; it violates the idea of non-dualism. We therefore do not advocate either the acceptance or the rejection of either the world or that, which is illusory. We respect the non-dual philosophy of Janaka for this reason. This dyad has another advantage. We do not prefer to distinguish between the manifest Being and the manifest God. If the manifest Being were to militate against this arrangement, the whole system would collapse. Therefore, God, who governs the manifest world and the being that is so governed are regarded as non-distinct by us. We believe in unity of joy and sorrow as also in the life of a householder and a renouncer. This unity is the basis of non-duality. We do not privilege renunciation. We follow the manifest religion and worship Shri Krishna as the supreme presence of the manifest world. We aspire to understand the nature of the unmanifest through the path of devotion. ‘When a spark is lit in the living being, he acquires knowledge, he receives divine vision, and the unmanifest that was hitherto latent comes to light. We call this the awakening of the unmanifest. ‘The awareness of the manifest implies union of the being with the divine. This union is attained by devotion and performance of one’s duties as a householder, as a king or as a woman. The performance of duties and the path of devotion do not exclude either the path of devotion or meditation on the unmanifest. Through these various means we awaken the unmanifest within us and thereby experience the union of the manifest and the unmanifest. ‘In this grand cosmic play, being and God both are the manifest currents of the ocean of the unmanifest, which is Brahma. The unity of being and divine commences with the body and extends to the cosmic. We move towards this unity like an arrow released from the bow. This movement has both a beginning and an end. The body is composed of both the gross material aspect and the subtle aspect. Therefore, it is born and perishes; that is its destiny. It experiences rebirth eighty-four lakh times. This cycle of birth and death commenced with the birth of illusion at the moment of creation and it will cease with the great deluge that will cause the universe to perish. The state of unfreedom commenced with creation and ultimate freedom or moksha will be attained with the end of creation. But both the state of unfreedom and freedom belong to the realm of this world, or as some say, they are so perceived by the intellect. They may belong to this worldly reality or may be caused by the perception of the mind; but they are not attributes of the soul. There is no primeval cause for this state of freedom or unfreedom and therefore, there is no real salvation possible. They are integral and inseparable from the world but the soul has no relation to it. It is said that the soul attains moksha through renunciation and action that is free of desire. But we do not accept this argument; we believe that we human beings also experience the awakening of the unmanifest within us. Apart from this, there is no other condition described as either the state of unfreedom or freedom. Some Vedanta texts, like the commentary by Shri Gaudapadacharya, suggest that the soul is inherently and eternally free.’ Sarasvatichandra interjected, ‘Are you and your disciples not renouncers?’ Vishnudas laughed and said, ‘Good question, son. Listen to this. Alakhpuri, recite for him the essence of renunciation.’

Alakhpuri recited: The mendicant leaves home to worship the lord of the gopis He covers his body in ash and calls out to the unseen He holds all Gokul in his sway Through this world the itinerant sage Carries the word of the unseen lord He renders the unseen visible and changes the fate of eighty-four lakh lives He ties this world into his matted locks Attached and yet not—such is his asceticism The unknowing sleep while the enlightened one is awake Vishnudas on his perambulations awakens the unseen in us all Sarasvatichandra requested Alakhpuri to repeat this three times, until he felt that he had grasped it. He thought to himself in English: This is true. Those are not apathetic to the world that show their right to live in it by being useful to their fellow men in some form; and the ascetic, that deluges the world with his poetry and philosophy without destroying it, does a duty; and if he does that, he is not bound to confine himself within the rooms where his father has left hoards of money and where his wife wants him to provide for her children. Duty is the best form; it is the motto of these men, and they are not bound to be home-keeping youths with homely wits. The point is Duty, and, in this case at least, asceticism does not murder Duty! Beautiful! Vishnudas said, ‘Navinchandra, we are neither mired in the world nor have we renounced the world; we are detached from it. But in practice renunciation and detachment are regarded as synonymous with each other. We have not renounced the world—it is contained in the locks of hair tied on our heads; we smear it in the form of ash on our bodies. And thus we awaken the unmanifest but we never forsake the manifest. Below the layers of ash lie smouldering embers. The unmanifest lies hidden under the manifest; we remove these layers and bring the unmanifest to light. In short, that is what we strive for. We worship the manifest but awaken the unmanifest. The life of householders is defined by desire. We aspire to a state of desirelessness and to symbolise that we smear our bodies with ash. The long hair tied in a knot that we keep symbolises the complex web of desires that we have knotted up. Both the ash and the long, unshorn hair are thus symbolic. Any great effort requires some uprooting of the old. Our effort is to awaken the unmanifest. We do not renounce the world to be free from sorrow. These symbols are indicative of our striving. We do not seek destruction of the manifest by a violent renunciation of the world. We are seekers; we renounce the state of the householder for the sake of our penance and roam the ignorant world much like the police that patrol the dark nights—as awakened beings making the realisation of the manifest possible. Navinchandra, we shall also awaken the unmanifest within you. All the initiates repeat after me: In this acrid world we smear ash and awaken the unmanifest.’ The disciples chanted these words. Those who were outside also echoed them. The praise of the unmanifest reverberated all around. As the chant subsided, Vishnudas placed a hand on Sarasvatichandra’s shoulder, looked at him with a piercing gaze and asked, ‘Tell me child, has the unmanifest stirred within you?’ Once again Vishnudas was disappointed. His guest had declined to bow before Yadunandan; even now he maintained a strange silence and appeared unmoved. Sarasvatichandra noticed the disappointment. He smiled and replied, ‘Maharaj, I do not consider the unmanifest to be latent within me. Without that admission, can I experience the awakening of the unmanifest?’ Vishnudas appeared pained. Sarasvatichandra realised that he had hurt a good man and sought to assuage his sentiments. ‘Swamiji, do forgive me as I have caused you pain. I heard the mystical verses of your philosophy today. How can I respond to them without proper deliberation? Allow me to ponder over their meaning, let me translate them for myself and then I shall pose my doubts to you. You will have the occasion to dispel my doubts. Through this process my thoughts will mature. Till such time there is no reason for you to be disappointed with me.’ Vishnudas seemed satisfied with this response. Just then the temple bells rang. It was time to offer food to Yadunandan. Vishnudas sent his disciples to participate in the ritual. Once Vishnudas and Navinchandra were left alone, Vishnudas spoke candidly. ‘Navinchandra, before I joined the monastery I was a brahmin. I understand that a learned brahmin like you will only accept our philosophy of the unmanifest after due consideration. But I have to keep this group of ascetics under control. They obey my every command. But I also know when these temperamental ascetics are inclined to disobey me. I am cautious and don’t allow for such occasions to arise. For some reason, I am partial towards you. But if they were to somehow feel that you do not deserve my favour, they will come to distrust my judgement and guidance and they may also cause you some harassment. According to them, those who do not believe in the unmanifest have no right to live in the monastery for a long period. I dislike this insistence of theirs, but that is besides the point. Your departure would cause me great sorrow. Therefore, please do not disregard my request.’ ‘And what would that be?’ Sarasvatichandra asked anxiously. ‘A renouncer cannot re-enter the state of a householder, but in our monastic order that is permissible. An initiate can become a householder among us. It is not mandatory that the ash be smeared on the entire body; it can also be applied on the forehead alone. We mix sandalwood paste in the ash. You may not bow before the idol of Yadunandan, so long as you do not show any disrespect. You may continue to wear your clothes, but they should be ochre coloured. You may continue to follow your own faith, but you should also worship the unmanifest. You can choose the category of initiates that you wish to belong to. ‘An uttam adhikari is allowed to hold any philosophical belief. The monastery has no objection even to your marriage. In the adjacent monastery we have residences for married couples. They are a part of our order; they join us in prayers and we have meals together. If you desire to be a householder, you may also take up residence with them. I would like you to consider this. If, some day, you decide to return to your home and become a householder, do come and speak to me in confidence. But for now you will have to be initiated in the order. This initiation entails that you hear a formal discourse on the philosophy of the unmanifest. The acceptance of the philosophy will be deferred until you have had sufficient time to reflect on it. Please accept this request.’ Sarasvatichandra responded, ‘If this will make you happy I shall do it, because you have given me a new life. But I cannot accept the philosophy of the unmanifest without reservations. It is contrary to my belief.’ ‘That we can tolerate. You have a period of reflection available to you. That period extends up to one year.’ Vishnudas seemed satisfied. He went to the temple, allowing his guest to remain with his thoughts. On his way he said, ‘After the meal we shall go out to seek alms. Some ascetics will stay behind. You may stay with them. In the evening you could go down and visit Surgram. Alakhpuri will give you a commentary on the philosophy of the unmanifest.’ Sarasvatichandra was left to himself. He walked around the garden for a while, quite content. Then he lay down on a boulder in the shade of the banyan tree. He thought of Chandrakant. He decided to write a letter to him, which could be posted from Surgram. His mind flitted to the verses that he had heard. He committed them to memory. He decided that the next morning he would have a discussion on them with Swami Vishnudas. He fell asleep. In his dream he saw Kumud Sundari seated beside him. His companion in dreams held his hand in hers and sang: Now be my teacher, O’ jogi Keep this jogini by your side Jogi, with knowledge may you also find beauty May the vessel of the unseen you now hold be filled with light May you swim in this delightful ocean of dreams Jogi, stay true to your beloved
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra arrives at Vishnudas's monastery, eager to meet the revered guru, who offers him initiation into his order, inviting deep philosophical reflection.

chapters.title: A Discourse on the Philosophy of the Manifest and the Unmanifest: Dream, Awakening, Dream
paragraphs: A Discourse on the Philosophy of the Manifest and the Unmanifest:

Dream, Awakening, Dream Sarasvatichandra surrendered to sleep. Soon after, Alakhpuri came with the text of the commentary. He placed dry leaves as a marker on the relevant pages, kept the text next to the sleeping man and left. Sarasvatichandra woke up, found the text and began to read it.⟨fn:67⟩ Now we shall reveal the secret of lakshya-alakshya, that is the relationship between the manifest and the unmanifest. What can be seen and perceived is the manifest and what cannot be perceived is the unmanifest. When we speak of perception or the lack of it, we speak of ordinary persons because the knowledgeable see and perceive much more. The statement: “When it is night for all others, the disciplined soul is awake” indicates this difference. Great souls have their sights fixed on goals that are diametrically opposite of those of the average individual. Great souls have higher perception. Those who can perceive even the unmanifest, the yogis, have been described in the verses. The first verse says: “Neither am I born, nor do I die.” Just as the sky is distinct from space, we must recognise that the unmanifest soul is beyond birth and death. Similarly, it is neither in bondage nor free. It is only a figure of speech when we describe something as unfree and something else as free. In essence, there is no difference. In other words, it is the worldly being that is either bound or free, but not the soul. The Creator who is omnipotent appears in different forms. But these different forms are perceived as distinct by this-worldly, embodied beings. It is an illusion to say that an archer takes aim of the head and dislodges it from the body. In essence, the archer, the aim and the dislodging of the head are all manifestations of the unmanifest. Samsara, or living in this world, means to lead a good life. It has been described as akin to the movement of the arrow but not as the arrow itself. The moment of commencement of this movement is the moment of freedom. Being, universe, bondage and freedom are all illusory. The common element in them is termed the manifest. Similarly a body with hands and feet is either called purusha or being. A lump of clay can be moulded in many shapes and forms. Similarly, the manifest appears in countless forms and is made up of many such illusions. It is neither in a state of bondage nor in a state of freedom. It is said that each manifest being goes through many cycles of bondage and freedom. This implies that one is born again and again. This is a contradiction in terms. The world and the worldly being both are integral to the manifest, just as the state of dream is integral to the state of awakening. This is called illusion. Illusion is also a part of the manifest. In verses two and three, the unity of the manifest and the unmanifest is established: “I am one,” it is said. The unmanifest soul is cosmic and bears witness. What does the soul bear witness to? Its manifest form, that is, it bears witness to itself. This is the chitta or the conscious aspect of the soul. When the illusory movement ceases, it is the moment of shanti or repose or stillness which is seen as distinct from the illusory movement, but both are aspects of the manifest. Some prefer movement over repose while others prefer repose over movement. It is through likes and dislikes that a person acquires the three gunas or attributes which spur him into action. Some ascetic individuals, often called bhikshuk or mendicants, are no doubt learned and great souls, but they dislike illusion and prefer the moment of stillness. They accept a division between the two conditions. It is for this reason that they are unable to attain the sense of oneness. They are moved by the sense of apparent division and believe that some things are to be accepted, and others to be discarded. The sense of unity, of oneness is attained only through the philosophy of the manifest and the unmanifest. All other beliefs fail to achieve this sense of unity. Philosophers of the Nyaya school classify matter according to its attributes. Other philosophies also have a notion of attributes. We consider it to be a part of the manifest. Some argue that just as the male and female principle are separate, so also being and divine are distinct—this is a false division. The soul bears witness to itself. The soul experiences the bliss of unity. Great souls are capable of experiencing the joys and sorrows of others. This is an obvious example. It proves that the manifest, in variegated forms, experiences itself in others. This unity and indivisibility is the source of bliss. This is true in any condition. Whenever the soul bears witness to itself, it involves birth. It is said that wherever there is mind, illusion persists; its play is apparent. There is no difference between an illusion and the one who conjures up the illusion, because they are contained in each other. The unmanifest extends this illusion through the soul and having extended it, the soul destroys it. In this play the unmanifest attains bliss. Some contend that the bliss so attained is temporal. But that is false, because like truth and consciousness bliss is also eternal and one, while action is temporal and temporary and hence not in-divisive. A yogi thus attains unity of the manifest and the unmanifest. It is asked if such a yogi sees attributes and actions as distinct from each other. We believe that for such a yogi, attributes and actions seem separate but this distinct orientation is like the movement in the world of dreams. But a yogi who has attained a sense of unity remains untouched by them. He is without attributes and indulges in no action. This spark of fire that is the manifest being experiences joy as he reaches out to the inanimate aspects of prakriti. In so doing it extends itself and follows the norms of the manifest, just as the fire that is inherent in the wood but which does not manifest itself. But when that fire is lit, it shows itself like any other matter that can be perceived by the eyes and felt by the skin. It has the same potential to give light and to burn as the cosmic fire. Similarly the enlightened one, in the form of being, appears to follow all conditions of the manifest. It is not sufficient that this spark of fire becomes manifest to others; it is also manifest to itself. It is only when this condition of being manifest both to others and to itself is fulfilled that the unity of one and many, of being and cosmos is attained. A being that aspires to this unity desires nothing else. Such a being is turned away from all other fruits of action. All his actions are good. He has no ego and hence all his actions are detached and selfless. All his actions are dedicated to the cosmic fire. By this dedication he fulfills the obligations of the manifest and of the relation between being and divine. This spark of fire thus attains the power of the cosmic fire and aspires to unity with the cosmic fire. And by this process the unity of being and divine is attained. Some describe it as karma yoga. The Gita says that the unity of being and divine is attained through action or karma yoga. The path of knowledge or jnana yoga attains the unity of being and Brahman. The unmanifest is Brahman. To enter the unmanifest implies knowledge of Brahman. The followers of Vedanta advocate the path of knowledge; they do not follow the path of action to the exclusion of all else. Just as day and night come together to form time, action and knowledge form a unity of approach. Only followers of the philosophy of the manifest follow this unified approach. Thereby, they attain the unity of being, divine and Brahman. All others seek either the unity of being and divine or of being and Brahman. That is, unity for them involves only two elements and to attain this they follow either the path of action or of knowledge. But none of them attain the unity of all the three. Some still argue that unity can only be of two elements and not of three. Such arguments are false because unity can be of many elements; unity does not signify a union of two or three elements only. Now we shall understand the various meanings of the word karma. The shastras and the shrutis use the term in a variety of ways. When it is used along with the idea of fate or destiny, karma alludes to the destiny of an individual just as the term destiny is used as an equivalent of the term karma. Others use the term karma to denote action that is distinct from destiny. Many shastras contend that it is distinct from destiny. Many shastras contend that performance of rituals and offering of sacrifice is karma. The followers of Shankara contend that knowledge of meditation and ritual constitutes action. We believe that karma yoga as described earlier is most appropriate, because one can renounce the fruits of action but not action itself. It is a contradiction in terms to describe the renunciation of action as action. If action is added to the pursuit of knowledge, knowledge becomes temporary because action tends to be impermanent. The Shruti says that the one who knows the play of the atman knows the Brahman. The same is true for a karma yogi. The Shruti also enjoins us to be detached from the fruits of action. Renunciation of fruits of action leads to the dissolution of sorrow and desire. When a yogi becomes desire-less like the Creator, he also becomes free of sorrow. To that extent, such a yogi sits alongside the Creator. The path of knowledge allows for a unity with the Brahman but not with the divine. This unity can only be attained through the path of knowledge. The Gita is the living example of this. Shri Krishna is the supreme embodiment of our philosophy. Shri Krishna urged his beloved Arjun to perform his duties in the manifest world. The Lord reminded Arjun that he was his devotee and a friend and thus enjoined upon him the performance of his duties. This was done to uphold the law, not to destroy it. Shri Krishna’s discourse to Arjun had a purpose—to convince Arjun that he must perform the duties enjoined upon him by the manifest world. The Lord said that this was the path to attain non-duality of the being and the divine. But for this purpose, Ved Vyasa would not have included the Gita in the Mahabharata. In absence of this purpose, the Gita would have become inappropriate and purposeless. Even in the Yoga Vashistha, Shri Krishna has taught us the same thing: that we should cultivate the bearing of the Brahman, that is, we should be imbued with His peace and perform our duties. The Yoga Vashistha propounds the karma yoga. The Isha Upanishad says: “Thus working, may you live a hundred years.” It criticises those who are either steeped into knowledge or ignorance. This is also our view. Similarly, it also teaches us that we should not be mired in either the transcendental or the immanent to the exclusion of the other. It says true knowledge is the knowledge of the self which is attained by desire-less action. The Isha Upanishad urges us to forsake false knowledge which is illusion. Attachment to the fruits of action is the root of false knowledge. The pursuit of knowledge or of illusion, of the transcendental or the immanent, to the exclusion of the other, is a sign of duality. We who seek non-duality forsake this path. When we pursue one to the exclusion of the other, one enters the world of darkness. The Isha Upanishad clearly states that: “Those who combine action with meditation cross the sea of death through action and enter into immortality through the practice of meditation.” It further states: “In the dark night live those for whom the Lord is only transcendent; in still darker night, for whom He is only immanent”; but those for whom He is both transcendent and immanent enter into immortality with the transcendental. Thus it states that only when we grasp the nature of illusion and of knowledge simultaneously and understand the essence of the transcendental and the immanent can we attain freedom. This is positive when action is desire-less and unattached. Our philosophy similarly advocates that only after we grasp the manifest can we understand the unmanifest. When the Isha Upanishad states: “Thus working, may you live a hundred years. Thus alone will you work in real freedom,” it implies the same. Some argue that this is not knowledge of the self but of the divine. This contention is implausible because as the Mandukya Upanishad states, knowledge is that which leads to self-realisation. To argue that knowledge of Brahman is contrary to the path of action is incorrect. Because the knowledge of Brahman precludes the desire for the fruits of action, but not the action itself. It is not possible to forsake and renounce all action. Because the Gita states: “No one ever remains inactive even for a moment” and it further states: “Know that action springs from Brahman and Brahman from the imperishable.” Therefore, we cannot ever be without action. Our philosophy of the non-duality of the manifest and the unmanifest is supported by the Upanishads. The Isha says: “The face of truth is hidden by your orb of gold, O sun; may you remove your orb so that I who adore the true may see the glory of truth.” The Mundaka Upanishad says: “In the golden city of the heart dwells the Lord of Love, without anchor, without blemish. Know Him as the radiant Light of Lights.” The Brahman is concealed. The radiance of the Brahman is protected by that which envelopes it—and this is not to be discarded. When sorrow and desire dissolve, this protective cover is removed and Brahman shines further. If someone were to ask us, what is it that envelopes the Brahman, our answer would be karma yoga. This manifest world is like the golden orb that conceals the unmanifest Brahman. It is described as golden because it is as valuable as gold. Everything springs from the imperishable and will ultimately merge in the imperishable. The manifest is not to be destroyed because it springs from that which is imperishable. The Shruti describes the nature of the manifest. Being or Jiva is not separate from Brahman. It is the spark of Purusha. The Purusha Sukta says: “A man has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet. He pervades the earth on all sides and extends beyond it as far as ten fingers. It is man who is all this, whatever has been and whatever is to be. He is the ruler of immortality when he grows beyond everything through food”; food here means sacrificial offering. The Mundaka Upanishad says: “As hair grows from the body, even so the sages say, this universe springs from the deathless self, the source of life.” Purusha springs from himself and withdraws into himself just like the web that is spun out of a spider and is withdrawn. The cosmic energy pervades both being and divine. Both finally merge with the unmanifest and eternal Brahman. The being is temporal while the unmanifest is eternal. The moment of creation is described as a sacrifice. The Purusha Sukta says: “When the gods began the sacrifice with man as the offering, spring was the clarified butter, summer the fuel, autumn the oblation. They anointed man—the sacrifice born at the beginning—upon the sacred grass. With him the gods, the sandhyas and the sages offered sacrifice.” It further says: “With the sacrifice, the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice. These were the first ritual laws.” The

Purusha was the sacrifice and the one to be sacrificed. We do not advocate the sacrifice of animals. For us, sacrifice is to be taken in its original sense. The man with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes and a thousand feet is Purusha who manifests as Jiva, the Being. But the unmanifest purusha extends as far as ten fingers that are the ten directions. We seek the unity of the manifest and the unmanifest. This discourse, meant for the initiates of the highest category, awakens the unmanifest. What more need be said? The unmanifest is such that both mind and language fail to grasp it. The manifest is complete, so is the unmanifest. When fullness is taken from fullness, fullness still remains. Thus, our philosophy of the non-duality of the manifest and the unmanifest is complete. Because: “All this is full. All that is full. From fullness comes fullness. When fullness is taken from fullness, fullness still remains.” Sarasvatichandra read the commentary with great interest. He knew by heart the Upanishads and the Purusha Sukta. He had studied various commentaries on these texts, and yet he felt he had read an entirely new interpretation. Sarasvatichandra slipped into deep reverie and soon fell asleep. Sleep brought back his earlier dream state. Kumud Sundari appeared in his dream. She sat close to him. But this girl had Kusum’s face. Sarasvatichandra discoursed to her about the philosophy of the manifest and the unmanifest. The young woman heard him with interest and asked many questions. She floated up into the sky and asked, ‘Sarasvatichandra, manifest or unmanifest? Pleasure or knowledge?’ She touched his forehead fleetingly as if in play and sang: My beloved is infatuated with beauty But awakened to knowledge You see the sorrows and joys of this world The wise jogi has claimed you Unseen by me, you worship the formless But your beloved also likes learned discourses We surrender all desires of the body Vraj is dense with tamal trees The sky is heavy with rain and dark as the night

Radha seeks her dark lord Searching for him she wearies and searches again The flute plays further and still further away The melody is heard but Krishna is unseen The flute says, ‘Listen Radha, O’ mad one: I sing from the lips of the one unseen And inspire unnameable love in you.’ The invisible Krishna leaves no trace in the forest O’ you jogini of the invisible one, awaken this love And play it out on the banks of Yamuna Beloved do not forget that we are one The one seeking knowledge reveres language Maya is apparent, but Purusha is not Their union produces this world— It is surrounded by their coming together Maya clings to the heart of Brahma Beloved, these are the ways of love O’ you familiar with the ways of the unmanifest Remember to also take delight in this world Sarasvatichandra suddenly woke up and wondered, What is the meaning of this dream? Who governs the world of dreams? Who is responsible for the sins and merits committed in the world of dreams? Am I responsible? No! Why not? How is this world different from the life lived in dreams? Who is the doer? Who is the one to be consumed? Kumud Sundari, who abandoned you? When were you abandoned? Why do I repent? Whom do I repent for? His eyes closed once more and he dreamt again. But this dream was different. He did not see any visions, but he heard a voice. His soul became omnipresent and his voice rang through in all directions. Sarasvatichandra heard the voice of his own conscience as if it were a voice from above. Two birds: Able of wing and far of sight, Together in friendship and affection, They found great joy. Perched on the same tree branch,

One ate of the peepal’s fruit, the other ate nothing But was resplendent in dawn’s first light; One knew only pleasure, living godlessly, While the other shone in His light. He is the creator of the universe, He is the Supreme Being, the bearer of divine light. As the godless one grew aware of His glory, He went beyond all sorrow To leave behind this web of life, Apprehending the non-dual, he became one with Him; Transcending merit and sin, Able of wing and far of sight, That bird, he took flight. Now replete with knowledge and imperishable, He is not reborn— He is the beloved of God. With these words ringing in his ears, Sarasvatichandra woke up. But the world of dreams refused to recede or relinquish its hold on him. Kumud Sundari appeared before him dressed as an ascetic and posed philosophical questions. ‘How have you become free of sorrow, Sarasvatichandra? How did you realise the Brahman? We are one, you and I—make my condition the same as yours. Free me from sorrow and help me realise myself!’ Chandrakant, too, entered the dream, saying, ‘Dear friends, if the two of you are one, I am not separate from you. Let the three of us unite.’ Sarasvatichandra gave no response to either of them. He listened and allowed the dream to continue. A new dream emerged. Taking flight from the summit of the Sundargiri, Sarasvatichandra soared into the sky. He saw Chandrakant flying by his side. Chandrakant asked him in English: ‘Where, my friend, dost thou fly like an angel upwards?’ Sarasvatichandra, thus halted in his flight, replied, ‘Chandrakant, sweet philosophy brings me up into the heavens! I fly effortless like Dante in his Paradise!’

Kumud Sundari joined them. She held on to Sarasvatichandra’s legs and said, ‘Thou hast no right to rise without me! Am I not that Beatrice whose vision fills thy soul and flies as thou fliest?’ Sarasvatichandra replied, ‘Sweet angel of purity! Thou art—thou art! Fair ethereal spirit, guide us on! Thou shall rise and raise us all—come!⟨fn:68⟩ The sky echoed Sarasvatichandra’s words. The three of them flew through the skies, holding each other in a tight embrace, singing divine songs. But alas, we cannot fly with them into that land of dreams.
chapters.summary: Sarasvatichandra delves into deep philosophy, then experiences a profound dream where Kumud Sundari and Chandrakant join his ethereal flight, seeking spiritual unity.

chapters.title: Kings and Ministers of Ratnanagari
paragraphs: Kings and Ministers of Ratnanagari For hundreds of years, Ratnanagari had been blessed with great kings and able ministers. Given its turbulent history, this could only be considered an act of destiny. The kings were believed to have descended from the Sun God and as a marker of this they wore a gold anklet on one foot. From ancient times, every ruler of Ratnanagari had inculcated and nurtured this pride in the royal lineage and ancestral tradition, both as duty and their privilege. An eternal lamp, a sign of their devotion to the family deities, was worshipped by all kings. From a young age, heirs to the throne were also initiated into the responsibilities of kingly duties and royal traditions, which included devotion to the lamp and what it symbolised. This pride in ancestral traditions was embodied by many valorous reigning kings. It was also their custom to find suitable candidates as ministers, nurture their talents and appoint them to the position at an opportune time. The kings of Ratnanagari thus sought to perpetuate and further their traditions in these two ways. The family tradition was neither complex nor elaborate. But its principles were firm, deep-rooted and allowed for superior practices to emerge. The king should relate to his subjects as a father would to his children. All wise kings realise that it is in their interest to protect their subjects, but the paternal sensibility cannot be cultivated in absence of an enduring affection for the people. The kings of Ratnanagari believed that in absence of this affection, their royal sun lineage cannot remain unsullied—this was the principle underlying all kingly conduct. A king must regard an enemy of his people as his own enemy. If someone, be it an official of the state or even a member of the royal family, were to act as an enemy of the people, that individual must be made to realise the maxim that ‘a king has no friends.’ From this followed the second norm that kings are attached to virtues and not to individuals. The third norm was that the resources of the state treasury should not be wasted and no one should be allowed to exploit the treasury for personal gains. The emphasis was on good and appropriate use of the resources and not on their accumulation. The army must always be battle-ready and its preparedness should be under constant surveillance. The king should always be the commander-in-chief of the army and he should prepare the heir to the throne to assume this responsibility. The king should always guard that his heir be pure-blooded; a child of a mixed marriage could not be appointed as heir as he would contaminate the royal throne. If a king did not have a male heir, he should adopt a male child of the royal household. Such a child should have a pure, uncontaminated lineage and possess all the kingly qualities. This was also a part of the royal tradition and was followed by every ruler of Ratnanagari, be he good or bad, virtuous or evil, wise or foolish. All rulers also looked for able men who could be their ministers. They ensured that the character of such potential ministers matched the disposition of the chosen heir and trained them into statecraft. They encouraged friendship between the heir apparent and the one chosen to be his chief minister. The kingdom of Ratnanagari was ancient. Architectural monuments and coins dating back to the times of emperors like Ashok and Chandragupta had been found during excavations done around the capital, which indicated that the kingdom was prosperous even then. The rulers of Ratnanagari had fought several wars with the Shaka kings. After an initial triumph, they had lost the kingdom and there was a period during which the Shaka kings had ruled over the area. This history was found during excavations and studies of forts, temples, pillars and stepwells done during Vidya Chatura’s ministership. There were also clear indicators that Buddhist, Jain and Vedic religions had flourished in the area. It was also borne out by the studies that during the medieval period the royal family was plagued by dissension, driven by jealousy and foolishness and there had been bitter internal feuds. Muslim rulers had made many expeditions to the kingdom; but the rulers of Ratnanagari had by a combination of diplomacy and valour retained their independence. In a way, God had been kind to the kingdom and had protected it. Towards the west of Ratnanagari were the sea and the hills of Sundargiri, while to its north, east and south were other Rajput kingdoms. The rulers of Ratnanagari maintained peaceful relations with these kings and in times of foreign invasion, they supported each other. The rulers knew that it was their combined strength which protected them. And hence, they did not indulge in displays of false pride with each other; rather they shared their intelligence and resources for mutual benefit. They ensured that no foreign invader could cast evil eyes on the kingdom. They placed so many obstacles in the path of potential invaders that, realising the heavy costs they would have to pay for an uncertain victory, such invaders were invariably deterred. The history of Ratnanagari during medieval times was filled with many such intrigues. It was not in the least difficult for this kingdom with fertile lands to satisfy the greed of the Marathas. The real downfall of the kingdom began when the British took control of the territories controlled by the Peshwas. At the time of the decline of the Peshwa rule, Mallaraj’s father Nagraj ruled over Ratnanagari. Nagraj had defeated the Peshwa’s representative Sardar Vishwasrao. After the decline of the Peshwas, one Colonel Brave started carrying out military expeditions to establish the Company’s authority in the area. With his small army, Nagaraj took on the might of the Company, engaging them in several skirmishes. He fought his last war with Colonel Brave’s forces, a war which lasted six months and during which, the British came to admire both his war strategy and his diplomatic skills. Nagraj had built several fortifications around Ratnanagari. He first transferred all his important officials and wealthy citizens to the securer forts. He then established his headquarters on Sundargiri and from there, carried out periodic raids on the Company forces. Sometimes he attacked from the east, sometimes from the north and sometimes from the south. Twice or thrice he managed to destroy British canons; he also captured two canons and used them against the Company forces. Another time he attacked their supply lines. Always avoiding open and direct confrontation, Nagraj would prefer to launch surprise attacks on the Company forces. Colonel Brave realised that without a direct confrontation he would not be able to subdue Nagraj’s forces. One day Colonel Brave got information that Nagraj’s elder son Hastidant was on his way to Sundargiri along with his army. Brave’s forces intercepted them at the foothills. Hastidant had a small army and his men were tired; but he had no choice but to engage in battle. He rallied his men for a fight to death and they charged on the Company forces. Nagraj was informed of the battle and he rushed down the Sundargiri with his small band of loyal soldiers. He decided to block the British from the rear. Colonel Brave’s forces had more or less vanquished Hastidant’s men by then; only Hastidant along with eight to ten men fiercely battled on, refusing to give in despite being surrounded. But the sudden, unexpected attack of Nagraj’s forces took the British by surprise. It broke their spirit and Colonel Brave realised that his men were about to give in. He decided to attack Hastidant. Nagraj saw through this strategy, but before he could do anything, the Colonel took aim and shot at Hastidant. The bullet pierced his chest and the prince fell. The man who shot him was saddened by his death. But Nagraj did not lose heart. With an act of supreme will he jumped over a boulder two hand-spans high and five hand-spans wide, only to land on Hastidant. Nagraj leapt up from the chest of his fallen son with a war cry and like a flash of lightning cut Colonel Brave’s second-in- command into two. Nagraj’s men joined him and a fierce battle ensued, and they fought until the light in the sky had faded. At dusk, both armies retired to their respective camps. The battle was inconclusive— there was neither a victor, nor any vanquished. Both commandants took stock of their forces. Nagraj’s army was almost destroyed, so were Colonel Brave’s forces. Nagraj received information that the Company forces were likely to get re-enforcements. He had all the forts secured and asked the soldiers protecting the forts to be ready for battle. He then gave a call for all the Rajput men in the region, old and young, to join forces with him; they responded to his call to arms and came together to lay down their lives for their king. Before daybreak, Nagraj had a new army. Colonel Brave knew that he had an upper hand. He also knew that Nagraj would not be able to put up resistance for very long. But the British officer was impressed by Nagraj’s valour, his forbearance and his strategic intelligence. He also realised that the spirit and fierce pride of these kshatriyas was not easy to subdue and subjugate. He felt it would be in the long-term interests of the Company if such a strong ruler were to become a friend. Colonel Brave also believed that extending a hand in friendship was a sign of true valour. He sent an emissary to Nagraj; the emissary carried a letter from Colonel Brave. Dear brave Friend, If we continue to regard each other as enemies, it will result in the destruction of an ancient kingdom and its valorous king. That would be a sad day for me. If you so desire, I am willing to accept you as a friend and have this treaty of friendship ratified by the Company. I am not the Government, but my Government acts on the basis of its faith in the advice of men such as myself. You may wish to use the trust that my superiors repose in me and turn a war into peace and animosity into friendship. I shall await your response. But if you insist upon waging this war, the forces of the Company are prepared.   Your friend, Brave. P.S.: I would not like it that you surrender. I have full faith in the power of your weapons, as in the strength of your words. —Brave. Nagraj dictated a response: ‘We would be blind if we did not recognise that the armies of the East India Company are like a river in flood. But we are like fire—anyone who touches us will be scalded. Not just fire, we also have light. If your flooding armies put out our smouldering embers, both the fire and the light will vanish in it. If you want that our light be preserved but want to extinguish our fire, that can never be. If that is your wish, war is the only option. But if our fire burns on, we shall never lose our light; even if it fades, it will glow again someday.

So we must keep your flood away from our fire. If that is not acceptable to you, we will engage with you in battle. Some will emerge victorious like Ram and others shall be defeated like Ravana. We are all fated to die one day. We do not fear death. All those who are born must die just as all who enter a battlefield must sustain wounds. It is up to you to consult your government. If you do wrong, the consultation is pointless; if you do right, there is no need to consult anyone to walk on the right path. We are strangers to your ways and are not bound to follow your rules. Please bear this in mind. As long as the Sun, our ancestor, shines on us and as long as there is life in us, not an inch of Ratnanagari’s land will fall into foreign hands. We will never bow our heads to you. But we are not averse to friendship with you. We have goodwill for the Company. It is up to you to either further this goodwill or break these bonds.’ Nagraj sent some of his most trusted men to Colonel Brave with the reply. The negotiations also gave him an opportunity to consult with the rulers of the neighbouring kingdoms. He summoned his younger son Mallaraj and instructed him carefully. ‘There are three neighbouring kingdoms. Go and meet their kings and tell them it is time that they wake up. Three bison together can drive out a lion; but if they go their separate ways the lion will kill each of them one after the other. Right now they are all watching the war between the foreigners and us, as if it is some farcical play being enacted for their entertainment. But once this play is over, the foreigners will turn towards them and others with similar attitude, and we shall watch their ignominy. There is still time. Tell them that we do not seek their assistance because we are afraid of death. But even a bania understands profit and loss; if we as rulers do not understand what is good for us, it would be fitting that the foreigners shall rule over our ancestral kingdoms. The throne is like Indrani, divine consort of Indra, the king of the gods; she is married to the occupant of the throne of heaven, and not to Indra. Our illustrious ancestors had established these kingdoms. We are not required to establish kingdoms, only to protect them from aggressors. If we are found wanting, the foreigners will rule over us, and that would serve us right. If you want to protect and preserve your kingdoms, please pay heed to my counsel. But if you do not wish to preserve them, you are masters of your own fate.’ With this message from his king and father, Mallaraj set out to meet the rulers of the three neighbouring kingdoms. There was mutual distrust and jealousy among these rulers, but Nagraj’s words pierced them like arrows. They were shaken out of their inertia. Nagraj’s ancestors had in the past managed to unite dissenting neighbouring rulers against common enemies. It was their combined efforts that had preserved their independence for so long. The same tradition continued. Nagraj’s message, delivered by prince Mallaraj, bore fruit. Colonel Brave received Nagraj’s response to his letter. He read it carefully. He was delighted by it. But his superiors were not as generous as him. They wanted at least one-fourth part of the state’s revenue, failing which a treaty that would benefit them. They did not want a treaty of friendship that gave them no material benefits; they saw this as a sign of foolishness and were not agreeable to it. Brave believed that the friendship of a valorous king was in itself a reward, but his superiors were not convinced. It was not possible for the Colonel to contradict his superiors; therefore he was forced to act against his wishes. He told Nagraj’s minister, ‘The Company does not want your land, but the Company now enjoys all the rights that the Peshwa had. Therefore, you must accept the Company’s rights to collect land revenue.’ The minister responded, ‘We were never subjugated by the Peshwas. We did not allow the Marathas to enter our territories. We do not recognise the rights of the Peshwas, but we are willing to extend our friendship to the Company.’ The claim was true, but Colonel Brave had to act within his authority. He was authorised to renew treaties on terms similar to the ones agreed to by the Peshwas. He was required to get specific sanctions from Bombay for any new treaty. The matter remained unresolved and the day passed. The following day, Mallaraj returned to the headquarters with reinforcements from the neighbouring kingdoms. These kings had also sent their leading men to confer with Nagraj. Statesmen of four kingdoms went as a delegation and met Colonel

Brave. Their unity convinced him that his earlier resolve was the right one, but he needed time to consult his superiors. Brave proposed a truce, which was accepted. He wrote to his superiors, saying, ‘These Rajputs are valorous; they are noble, truthful and are not foolish, evil or wicked. If these rulers were to accept the Company’s friendship, it would be beneficial to the Company in future.’ The treaty was signed. According to its terms the native states and the Company pledged support to each other in times of aggression. The native states accepted that in event of disputes, either among themselves or with the Company, they would accept the Company’s arbitration and the chief arbitrator would be English. The treaty seemed innocuous. The rulers reasoned that they were not required to share any revenue with the Company, their territories were protected and their autonomy was guaranteed. But young Mallaraj remained unconvinced. He was unable to articulate his reservations and was hesitant to speak his mind before his father. At the conclusion of the treaty everyone rejoiced. But Mallaraj remained depressed. From today our state is under shackles, he lamented. Our kshatriyas have been widowed. Like women we, too, have worn bangles. We cannot wage a war. Just as we protect our women, now the English will protect us. We will have our land and our peace, but we shall be effeminate. Kshatriyahood has died. With such gloomy thoughts Mallaraj ascended the throne. Over time, he saw all the major native states drown in the flood that was the British. He remained neutral during the initial period of Nanasaheb’s rebellion. The entire country was passing though a great churning similar to the mythical churning of the sea. He sought to learn from it. He realised that strength alone could not protect the country; statecraft was equally essential. Statecraft required the cultivation of compassion and forgiveness.
