He found his countrymen sorely lacking in these qualities, while the Englishmen had them. Mallaraj was disappointed and saddened. Vidya Chatura’s maternal uncle Jarashankar had recently become his advisor. Jarashankar counselled him on the path of prosperity and happiness. He said, ‘Maharaj, it is good to be on the side of the powerful and the virtuous. We should win their trust and we should also trust them. Every warrior is fond of his sword, but it cannot for that reason be put into one’s stomach. It is wrong and foolish to support the natives if all they have to offer is the destruction of the country. Even righteous action is contextual. From what you have told me, I feel that the good of all the native states, and not just our state, lies in supporting these wise foreigners. They are compassionate and just. Ultimately, they will triumph. If the Muslims and the Marathas manage to defeat the English, they will turn against each other as soon as the common enemy is removed. Whoever triumphs in that conflict will tyrannise the native states. They are like wolves and jackals.’ Mallaraj looked at him sharply. ‘There is little doubt in what you say, Jarashankar. But a brahmin like you will always search for peace, while a kshatriya like me will look for battle. If the English triumph, kshatriya valour will vanish forever. Does that concern you at all?’ ‘No.’ ‘What then?’ ‘Then, what? That would be an auspicious day. The people and the native rulers will both be at peace. I have faith in the English sense of justice.’ ‘Be careful! The English, too, are human. They, too, have their self- interest. They are like the banias. They will become the undisputed rulers of the country one day. No one can be as bad as an unchecked bania!’ ‘Maharaj, that may be so. But what option do we have? If the kshatriyas could unite, why would those seeking to drive out the British be called rebels? If we do not suffer from an incurable disease, the God of Death will not come knocking on our door.’ ‘Do you really think that we kshatriyas have become utterly useless?’ asked Mallaraj with his hand on Jarashankar’s shoulder, his eyes burning red with anger. The brahmin laughed. ‘Maharaj, if all kshatriyas were like you, they would not be considered useless. Among the Kauravas, there was Bhishma. But who remembers him today? There will be few like you. No matter whether the English win or lose, we shall see what the future has in store for us.’

‘What will happen?’ ‘Maharaj, do you not see that many queens have taken up with banias and brahmins? Do you know how many queens have adopted the son of a cobbler or a miller as their prince? One of these robbers will become an emperor. He will either be a Muslim or a Marathi brahmin who are not faithful even to their masters. A time will come when persons of mixed and impure blood will ascend the thrones and pure, blue-blooded kshatriyas will be shamed into hiding.’ ‘What will happen if the English win?’ ‘It is better to have a wise enemy rather than a foolish friend. Maharaj, Ravana told the demon Marich that he should assume the form of a golden deer and be killed by Ram, failing which Ravana himself would kill him. Marich thought that if death were certain, it was better to die at the hands of Ram.’ Mallaraj took his sword and left the room. But he returned promptly, and this time his face betrayed a new resolve. He said, ‘Jarashankar, write a letter to Brave Sahib and inform him that Mallaraj and his army are ready to defend the Company.’ Jarashankar cautioned, ‘Maharaj, I think like a brahmin. You have decided to act upon my advice. But you should also consider it independently. Do not blame me later on.’ Mallaraj smiled and replied, ‘Those who are in my employment should be ready to hear an assessment of both their qualities and shortcomings.’ ‘I do not deny that, Maharaj. But it is my duty to caution you as the implications of my advice will be felt by you and the entire state.’ ‘That is correct. The decision I have taken is not without attendant dangers. The English are like the banias. They will want to convert the Rajputs and make them into banias. The Rajputs will not be able to conduct themselves like banias and they will ultimately lose the game. But if our people emerge victorious, it would amount to placing an infant in the care of monkeys—the English will ill-treat all those who are weak.’

‘Maharaj, my understanding is somewhat simplistic. The English are like rats. They will bite and soothe and thus corrode us, while our natives will pounce on us like a pack of wolves and decimate us.’ ‘In that case, we are not mistaken, Jarashankar. The English appear to be the lesser of the two evils. We should deal with them. We should remember, however, that the English are not sugary sweet but hot and pungent as pepper.’ Jarashankar got up to write the letter. He said to himself, Oh, how times have changed! The English will rule over the land of Rajputs! But my advice was appropriate. I acted according to the principles of statecraft. For, What can a spirited man, though strong, do if without a helper (allies)? Fire, kindled in a place where there is no wind, is extinguished of itself.⟨fn:69⟩ Likewise, the good king Mallaraj is helpless. If these robbers were to take control of the state, how long would they remain friends of anyone? The comfort of clouds, the friendship of the vile, cooked food, women, youth and riches are capable of being enjoyed for a short period. Those who can distinguish between what is permanent and what is short-lived [are] hence able to take proper view of things.⟨fn:70⟩ And what if they were to become the rulers, what would Ratnanagari be reduced to? Formerly a hare and Kapinjala (name of a sparrow) seeking justice and going to a mean judge for decision both met with destruction.⟨fn:71⟩ Jarashankar, what if the English were to emerge superior? The Dutch, the Portuguese, the French, all accept their authority. The English have been equal to them and are likely to retain their superiority. They are a good protective cover for the small states. When there is a master, even at the mere mention of the name of the great before wicked men, good results at once.⟨fn:72⟩ The English are members of an empire. But these robbers have no roots, no allegiance to anyone. One mighty king proves a blessing to the world. If there are many they lead to trouble (or destruction) as many suns at the end of a Yuga cause the destruction of the world.⟨fn:73⟩ They have won some victories but the common enemy is still undefeated. Just a small victory has made them proud and haughty. What havoc would they wreak on the likes of Mallaraj and the people of the state if their victory were to be complete? The crow had said of the owl, What object shall we gain by making this owl which is frightful by nature, very fierce, cruel and of a repulsive aspect, a king?⟨fn:74⟩ These robbers are no different. What does friendship of the Company entail? Mallaraj is certain to be eclipsed by the Company. He will become insignificant before a powerful force. We shall be forced to follow their dictates and be ruined. Friendship and marriage are proper between those whose wealth is equal and whose families are of equal rank, and not between the fat and the lean (rich and poor).⟨fn:75⟩ Should I then advise Mallaraj to remain neutral? Should I advise him against this proposed alliance? Neutrality is the best policy when the outcome of a war is uncertain. One of the two is certain to be defeated. One will gain a friend but also make an enemy of someone. I, Jarashankar, do not have the capacity to predict the outcome of this

Great War, but Mallaraj estimates that the Company will emerge victorious. He has never been proven wrong. If we were to support the Company we shall stand to gain in two ways. If there is any doubt regarding their final victory, our throwing in our lot with them will definitely add to their strength. It is said that friendship with the mighty is not beneficial. But there is an exception to this. In moments of crisis the assistance given by the weak to the mighty is always remembered; the mighty remain grateful for life. Therefore the weaker party should never squander an opportunity. Both these are considerations for the future, and the wise are those who pull the future towards them. The mighty have use for the friendship of the weak. Wise men, even though endowed with fullness (abundance, opulence), should make friends: for the sea, though entirely full (of water), awaits the rise of the moon (to swell up).⟨fn:76⟩ Hence, is it not a sign of stupidity if the weak forgo an opportunity to secure the affection of the powerful? From some cause one becomes a friend and also from a cause one becomes an enemy of another; therefore, a wise man should employ (form) friendship and not enmity in this world.⟨fn:77⟩ Mallaraj’s estimation of the English is unlikely to be wrong. He has the kshatriya’s sharp sense. He does not know the English intimately, but the astute has to taste but one grain to know if the rice is cooked or not. Shrewd men know the mettle of a man although they see him but once; experts know accurately the measure of the pola by weighing a thing on (the palm of) their hand.⟨fn:78⟩ Even a blind man can see that the English are clever. The eggs of a peacock need no decoration.

A young pea-cock that has not yet got its plumage, its distinguishing mark, can be known to be a pea-cock when moving away from a lake with stately steps backwards.⟨fn:79⟩ Even if the English are destined to be defeated, one has to take this risk if one wants benefits of their possible victory. Even if the English prove to be ungrateful in victory and all our expectations remain unfulfilled, we would still have the benefit of knowing the flaws in their character. Knowledge of the weakness of the other is one path to victory. Having entered inside even through a very small hole, an enemy gradually destroys one afterwards, as does a flood of water a boat.⟨fn:80⟩ Moreover, Timidly and timidly at first does an enemy move on the ground with gentle steps, but with great ease afterwards like a paramour of a beautiful woman.⟨fn:81⟩ The English are experts at this game. This is our opportunity to use their game against them. It is not that we are going to be equal to them, but it is an opportunity nevertheless. We do not know what the future holds; our swords will come in use only if we have practiced our swordsmanship. This offers us that possibility. A treaty of friendship does not mean that we trust them implicitly. Distrust and scepticism must be kept alive. That is the first rule of politics. One should not repose confidence in one who is not trusted nor should one confide in one who has one’s confidence; for fear arising from confidence nips off the very roots. One who never trusts (any one) although weak is not destroyed even by very powerful persons; but those who put confidence (in others) although strong are quickly destroyed even by the weak.⟨fn:82⟩

In statecraft, friendship, gratitude and scepticism must all combine. The policy of good action advocated by Vishnugupta, of “the acquisition of friends” by Bhargava and of “distrust” by Brihaspati—thus threefold is the adoption of policy.⟨fn:83⟩ Moreover, When an enemy is wicked and powerful one should deal with him distrustfully, taking one’s stand on duplicity, now proposing peace, now fighting.⟨fn:84⟩ This Company is as vast as the ocean. If we have to build embankments to contain it, the foundations of such embankments must reach the rock bottom and stay firm. Just as one can reach the bottom of water by means of a flight of steps, so the spies can penetrate the very heart of the enemy through the officials and know his secret plans.⟨fn:85⟩ This will acquaint us with the weak points of the Company. If we are seen as friends, we shall use our friendship to get a better measure of their frailties. God willing, there shall not be any enmity between us. But even as friends, knowledge of their weaknesses would allow us to secure and guard our own interests better. Even a pearl, though exceedingly pure, unperforated, well rounded and very beautiful, gets confined (woven in a necklace) when bored through.⟨fn:86⟩ This alliance will secure many benefits for us. The good of the king and the welfare of the people can both be secured by this alliance. It is a great effort. The bitter part is that we will be forced to betray the natives and embrace the foreigner. Jarashankar signed deeply. Tears glistened in his eyes. It is inordinately difficult to fulfill one’s obligations towards the country. One is forced to alienate our near ones and embrace strangers. The only consideration must be the welfare of the state and its people. This welfare can be best secured if one has the five Pandavas as allies instead of seeking the company of a hundred Kauravas. One should not enter into an alliance with a man who is destitute of truthfulness and righteousness; for, although firmly allied, he, on account of his wickedness, will change before long.⟨fn:87⟩ What even if one has to drink a cup of poison to ensure this? Even poison swallowed with the object of accomplishing an end acts like nectar, in the case of all creatures no hesitation should be made in such a case.⟨fn:88⟩ Delayed decision-making and lengthy, unending debates in matters of state administration are both detrimental to it and akin to committing a sin. When a business to be promptly attended to arises and a man delays, the deities, being angry, undoubtedly put obstacles in his way. When any action, and especially one about to be attended with fruit, is not done at once, time saps its juice.⟨fn:89⟩ And therefore, He who takes action before a thing comes to pass shines; he who does not provide for what is to happen comes to grief.⟨fn:90⟩ And hence it is said: one must have foresight and act in time. I must act patiently. The enemy is killed; a friend is gained; the jewel necklace is not lost; and water was drunk by means of a lotus-stalk, well accomplished all this, oh monkey on the fig tree.⟨fn:91⟩

After this lengthy deliberation with himself, Jarashankar the wise minister of Maharaj Mallaraj proceeded to compose the letter to Colonel Brave. Meanwhile, Mallaraj had also reconsidered his decision, and it met with his approval. He thought to himself: In the final analysis, even kings are not attached to any particular piece of land. Which ruler does not have ancestors who were not foreign to the land they ruled? Which heirs to kings will be able to keep their kingdom as long as the sun and the moon shine in the sky? The duties of brahmins and kshatriyas are in some ways the same. The brahmins teach that the soul is immortal and it changes body just as we change clothes. For us our lineage is our soul and our kingdom our body. When one body has lived its life and dies, we must seek another body and nourish it. Kings are not ultimately attached to their subjects either. The shastras say that a king has no friends. Jarashankar sometimes teases me that one should not trust a king. It is true. For parents, a son—be he mad, stupid or vile—is still a son; they cannot deny the blood ties. They also do not admit to the follies of their son. It is for this reason that sons tend to trust their parents. But a king relates only to virtue and he is an enemy of vice. He does not even regard his heir-apparent with complete trust, why would he trust his subjects? Everyone must understand that a king relates to their virtue, but not to their person. So long as the person remains virtuous and trustworthy, the king trusts him. There can be no other ground for trust. A king who considers his queen, his sons or ministers as his own is not a true king. The moment the virtues of a person wither, the king must remove him from his administration—just as one throws away a flower that has lost its fragrance—and punish him for his faults. If this logic were to hold, Mallaraj is not beholden to either the rebels or the people of India. Mallaraj is responsible only to his state and kingdom. The Company has captured the country and they know how to keep it; they are experts in statecraft; they know how to make and spend money; they know whom to please and how; they know the ways of the Muslims, the banias and the brahmins; they are adept at techniques of war and they know their diplomacy; they know how to protect their interests and have transformed a village like Bombay into a metropolis. Five thousand of them, relying only upon their intelligence and not force, can defeat an enemy force of fifteen thousand. They can be generous and thrifty; they are cunning and know how to plunder our wealth, and they know their self-interest as also the welfare of others. Their victory is certain. It is wise to be friends with them. This is also in accordance with my duties as a Rajput. If they do not win, I will have to battle to keep Ratnanagari. I may even lose my life in that battle. So what if I lose my life? If the English emerge victorious, my heirs will also gain some of their great virtues. Even Ratnanagari will produce great men. If all goes well, such will be the benefits. But if the plan fails, my body shall fall on the sands of the battlefield—that is its ultimate destiny and fulfillment. If this alliance proves detrimental, as alliances between the mighty and the weak can well be, my sons and ministers will battle them intellectually and they will learn to match intrigue with intrigue. This will sharpen their intellect. Whether the benefits accrue to all people or are squandered like flowers that grow in the wild will depend upon my heirs. That is how kings play.⟨fn:92⟩
chapters.summary: As King Nagraj bravely battles Colonel Brave's formidable forces, he must weigh a difficult decision concerning Ratnanagari's future and its ancient traditions.

chapters.title: Mallaraj and His Jewels
paragraphs: Mallaraj and His Jewels Mallaraj was deep in thought the day he sent the letter to Colonel Brave. At a time when the foreigner could be driven away and the country could be ruled by natives, he had decided on an alliance with the foreigner. The alliance would soon become public knowledge and that was certain to bring condemnation and censure from the entire clan and community as well as other native states. The possible disgrace perturbed him. But he considered the possible gains of the future and felt less uneasy. This inner struggle made him weary. The letter to Colonel Brave was sent in the afternoon. By dusk a messenger arrived in Ratnanagari. Mallaraj’s favourite Bhayat, his cousin Samant Mulu accompanied the messenger to the king’s presence. Mallaraj sat leaning against the bolsters, smoking his hookah, unmindful of the perspiration that soaked his forehead. He held the hookah in one hand and his sword in the other. The messenger and Samant came in and sat down, but Mallaraj remained oblivious of their presence. After some time Samant spoke, ‘Maharaj, we still have time to reconsider. A fierce battle has broken out in Kanpur. The English judge of Fatehpur was tried, sentenced to death and his body was cut into small pieces which were thrown among the people. The Company’s rule has disappeared.’ Mallaraj pursed his lips in anger and said, ‘A judge is like their brahmin. Did these cowards kill a brahmin? Did the judge kill a few before being taken captive?’ ‘Can any Englishman be captured before he kills a few?’

‘If their brahmins are so brave, what would happen when we fight their Rajputs? Tell me, was it a Rajput who cut up his dead body and threw away the pieces?’ ‘Can a Rajput ever be an enemy of the dead?’ Mallaraj reclined on his bolsters and, putting aside the hookah, said, ‘Aren’t Rajputs ashamed of the company of such irreligious men?’ ‘Maharaj, I did not realise that you would so brazenly take the side of the British. What has to happen shall happen. Tatya Tope’s forces have camped outside the borders of Ratnanagari. Their leader has sent a message,’ said Samant. The messenger relayed the message: ‘Maharaj, about three thousand of Tatya Tope’s men have camped at a distance of about twenty furloughs outside Ratnanagari. Others are likely to join them soon. They demand grains for the men and fodder for the horses. They are willing to pay but claim that if grains and fodder are denied them for payment, they will forcibly seize them. It appears that by morning they will enter the capital.’ ‘Anything else?’ Mallaraj asked impatiently. ‘No. But I heard them talk among themselves. They say that they want friendship with the native states, but that they will capture any state that harbours foreigners.’ ‘Very well. You go back to your post and keep an eye on their movements. I want a report at midnight and before dawn.’ The messenger retreated with a promise to obey the orders. Mallaraj stood up and addressed Samant. ‘Samant, collect all the Bhayat present in the capital and bring them and the chief of our army to my presence immediately.’ Samant hesitated. Mallaraj was irked. ‘What is the doubt? This is not a moment for doubts, Samant. It is necessary to take swift decisions.’ ‘Maharaj! The forces of Tatya Tope do not wish to battle with us; they seek our protection.’ ‘But they will fight us if we refuse to grant protection.’ ‘Is there a problem in granting them protection?’

‘We will deal with that later. We shall consider all opinions. But for now we must be ready for battle. We cannot afford any delay. Now go.’ Samant stared at Mallaraj. His legs refused to move. It took him some effort to leave the king’s presence. Mallaraj ordered an attendant to call Jarashankar. But before the attendant could leave the room, Jarashankar sought permission to enter. Mallaraj was overjoyed. ‘It is a good omen. Very good, Jarashankar! You heard the news and you came for consultations. What a minister! A rift in my forces is likely. I consider an alliance with the British desirable. Samant and some others prefer an alliance with the rebels. It would be disastrous if my forces turn against me at the time of battle. I will have to find a way out. A Rajput’s word is non- negotiable. I have decided in favour of an alliance with the Company. I shall fight alongside them and also lay down my life. A promise has been given. This is not the occasion to reconsider its correctness. Mallaraj has given his word. Mount Meru that holds the earth might shake and the oceans might breach their shores, but Mallaraj will not renege on his promise. War is a certainty.’ The possibility of war filled Mallaraj with new vigour. His legs were ready for action, his lips trembled with excitement and his right hand toyed with his sword as he paced up and down. Jarashankar came in, and even before he could greet the king, Mallaraj placed a hand over his shoulder and said, ‘Jarashankar, it is time for war, isn’t it?’ ‘Maharaj, that is for you to decide.’ ‘But our decision has been made.’ ‘That is so, but your Bhayat think otherwise.’ ‘Who gave them these ideas?’ ‘Those whose interests will be served by it. The talk that you had with Samant is known to others also. You are ready to fight the natives. But all your Bhayat want to fight the foreigner. How can we raise an army without the Bhayat?’ Mallaraj put his hands on his waist, threw back his head and laughed aloud. ‘You do not know my Bhayat. But a decision made and a word given will not change. That is not negotiable. Tell me, what is to be done.’ ‘Maharaj, Samant will soon be here with the Bhayat. If you were to seek their opinion in a congregation, they would all unite against you. It would be difficult to deal with them. It is advisable to deal with each one individually; call them aside and those who differ ...’ ‘Those who differ should be placed under house arrest or held captive in the palace. We should attack the rebels with our supporters.’ ‘Maharaj, that is just what I was going to suggest. How alike we— king and his minister, master and servant—think.’ Mallaraj laughed. ‘Maharaj, this is a difficult moment, not one for laughter.’ ‘Fear not, Jarashankar, we will turn it into a joyous occasion. It is your responsibility to think. The “design” and “execution”⟨fn:93⟩ of a plan are also your responsibility. But when the execution of a design requires a war, that is not your terrain. Then one needs to be kshatriya. It is a game of chess. You step aside and let me play. You have to be a spectator. You watch me deal with my Bhayat. You watch me twirl my moustache. Mallaraj can never be treacherous towards his Bhayat. I cannot imprison them. They are my thoroughbred horses; you just watch me ride them.’ In no time the room was filled with Mallaraj’s Bhayat. They came and took their place around Mallaraj. Mallaraj’s seat was higher. Jarashankar sat behind him. Two torch-bearers of the barber caste stood behind Mallaraj. The light of the torches fell on the excited and eager faces of the Bhayat and allowed Mallaraj to gauge their inner feelings. No one spoke. The pregnant silence of the men merged with the silence of the night and filled the room. Mallaraj broke the silence, ‘Brothers!’ It was only at the time of war that the king addressed his Bhayat as ‘brothers’—an address which carried all the connotations of honour, valour and unswerving loyalty to the king and the kingdom. It instantly captivated the Bhayat and they looked intently upon their king. As the words flowed from Mallaraj, their hearts filled with kshatriya pride and all the doubts harboured in their minds disappeared. ‘Brothers, it is time for war! Samant Bha has brought news that Tatya Tope’s forces have camped near Ratnanagari. Mallaraj does not wish to join them out of fear. They are petty robbers; the light of the sun lineage cannot mix with them. Brothers, our ancestor Nagraj had an alliance with Sugrivji, who was a devotee of Shri Ramji, who also belonged to the Suryavansh. In our Ratnanagari, a son does not break a promise made by his father. Similarly, the Bhayat do not break a promise given by their king. I, Mallaraj, am a son of Nagraj and you are my Bhayat. There is no doubt about this. It is given that I shall honour a promise made by Nagraj, and you shall honour my word. Should there be any doubt or discussion about this? Kshatriyas, rise! Give up this soft-hearted effusiveness of women and bania-like deliberations. Go and return with your forces. It is indeed an auspicious day when war is upon us. After many years. It is time to ride our horses and charge upon the enemy with our swords and guns. You are the protector of my honour. Goddess Lakshmi awaits us; her hands are smeared with the blood of our enemies.’ Mallaraj was charged by his own words. He got up and drew his sword and called out, ‘Brothers! Come, let’s show them who we are!’ As soon as he stood up, all the Bhayat stood up as one man. One of them called out, ‘Victory to Maharaj Mallaraj!’ All doubts and misgivings disappeared and the loyal, brave soldiers trooped out to gather forces for their king. Mallaraj and Jarashankar remained in the room. Samant followed the others up to the door, but once they had all left, he returned. He was soaked in perspiration. His eyes were blood-shot. It was difficult to tell whether he was angry or filled with valour. No words came out of him. Mallaraj asked him, ‘Samant, what doubts bring you back?’ Samant was seething with rage, but he spoke softly and succinctly. ‘Maharaj, you have made a difficult choice. I called them to your presence with the hope that you would consult them. I did not know that you would command us to war. Maharaj, this is an adventure.’

The words came out stiff and heavy as if a shot-putter were throwing iron balls. Mallaraj assuaged his feelings, ‘Samant Bha, calm down. Sit down and breathe easy.’ Samant gave no response and turned his face away. The three of them sat down. Mallaraj continued, ‘Samant, I have thought very carefully about this decision. I know that you would agree with my reasoning. But for a moment let us consider that we differ. Would you go your own way, or would you still follow me? Tell me honestly, what rights do I have over you? If I cannot claim rights over your devotion to the state and your love for me, I would be required to explain my position and I would need to convince you, wouldn’t I?’ Samant became powerless before these words. He removed his pagdi from his head, placed it in Mallaraj’s lap and said, ‘Maharaj, please pardon me. If I do not obey you, whom shall I obey? I may hold a different opinion, but if I follow my own counsel in disobedience of your command, I should be considered a traitor and beheaded.’ With folded hands he said, ‘Maharaj, give me your command that I may follow the other Bhayat and prepare for battle.’ ‘Samant, my dear brother, you are a pillar of this state. You are the elephant that leads my forces. Ram obeyed Dashrath, and Laxman and Bharat obeyed Ram. In the same way, I will obey a command given by Raja Nagraj and you will keep the promise that I have made—such is the glorious tradition of the Suryavanshi kings.’ ‘Maharaj, command me. Why do you not allow me to show my obedience?’ ‘Samant, you are elder to me by four years. You occupy the position that Bhishma Pitamah occupied in the court of Duryodhana. I value your opinion as much as I trust your loyalty.’ Samant trembled, touched his ears as if to cover them and then touched Mallaraj’s feet. ‘Forgive me, Maharaj! Forgive me! I swear by the head of this pure and pious brahmin minister that not for a moment did I feel that your decision was like that of Duryodhana, irreligious and against righteous conduct.’

‘Jarashankar, Karna was like a minister to Duryodhana, but you are a minister to me. How can I disbelieve if Samant swears by you?’ Samant was perturbed. ‘Oh God! Maharaj, if you had awarded me a punishment that would have been my penance. But this is unbearable. I speak the truth. Jarashankar counselled you and you accepted the advice, which may have differed from my opinion. I firmly believe that any advice given to you—the protector of cows and brahmins— would have been righteous and in accordance with dharma. Even if this brahmin had advised you that I should be beheaded and you had accepted the minister’s counsel, and for that reason if I were to even obliquely threaten your minister, it would not be true to my salt. Maharaj, it was not an act of treachery when I swore by Jarashankar.’ Mallaraj was happy. ‘Samant, I am pleased with you. But you must listen to my reasoning.’ ‘Maharaj! Even though I hold a different opinion and know nothing of the reasons that prompted your decision, I have no desire to pry into the secrecy of the deliberations between my king and his minister. I must obey your command in total faith and in so doing I shall prove my loyalty. Please command me and I shall fulfill my duty with unstinting faith. Please grant me this favour.’ Mallaraj embraced Samant joyfully. ‘Go, Bapu, go! As long as Ratnanagari is blessed with gems like you, God has granted me boons far greater than the favour that you seek from me.’ Samant Mulu stepped out of the palace at peace with himself and with renewed resolve to serve his king. ‘Jarashankar, did you see the jewels of Ratnanagari? I have made you my minister so that in time you can test these jewels, and the day I become one with my ancestors you will teach my son to value these jewels among men. If there be such priceless individuals in other states, they should also be invited to make Ratnanagari their home. That is our duty. How can we neglect our own? Kings must know the art of assisting those men who have lost their sheen to rejuvenate themselves—so that their true worth and esteem grows and their light shines forth. You must learn this art and teach it to my heirs. You must appoint a capable minister for my heirs who can learn and appreciate and inculcate this art. Listen to me carefully. My body may fall in the battlefield, but you shall live longer than me and help Ratnanagari attain its destiny. Pay attention to my words, Jarashankar. It is kshatriya practice to confide in the minister at such moments so that nothing remains unsaid.’ Jarashankar grew tearful. Mallaraj continued: ‘The varna division of brahmin-kshatriya-vaishya is an ancient one. It has one benefit. The kshatriyas are warriors while knowledge is the preserve of the brahmins. It is the duty of the kshatriya to lay down his life, while the brahmin must preserve life. There are trees which grow faster when pruned. Similarly among the kshatriyas when the father dies in battle, his sons are infused with even greater courage. When one body falls, from its seed arises a new body, but the seeds of knowledge and art cannot be sowed. Knowledge and art have to be preserved in a family from generation to generation like the sacred fire. What would the people do if the knowledge of statecraft and war strategies were to perish with the death of the king? If kings do not lay down their lives and if they cling on to dear life, why would the kshatriyas respect such cowardly kings? When kshatriya soldiers watch their king battle Yama the God of Death in the battlefield, their loyalty and valour are enhanced. Hence, kings must regard war as auspicious. If the king were to die in battle, his knowledge of statecraft and war strategy should not perish with him, especially if the heir to the throne is a minor. Therefore, the king must make his brahmin minister the repository of the knowledge of statecraft and the art of wielding weapons. The shastras prohibited the killing of the brahmin because he is the inexhaustible repository of knowledge and must be preserved for the welfare of mankind. Let me give you some examples: Dronacharya’s knowledge of weapons and the statecraft of Chanakya. It was only because of Chanakaya that Chandragupta could defeat the mleccha. Even those born into royal lineage require the nurturance of a brahmin. It is only with vast experience that knowledge comes to light. Therefore, kings must have brahmin ministers who must gain experience by bearing witness to great events. The king must ensure a long life for his ministers; this is part of kingly duties. You should instruct my son accordingly, Jarashankar.

‘Moreover, brahmins, kshatriyas and vaishyas should remain within their assigned status; there should be no compromise on this. But the times are changing and the varnashrama will also undergo changes. Do not get me wrong. There will come a time when the son of a brahmin will cease to perform priestly functions and hence his brahminhood will diminish. Under British rule the sons of kshatriyas will have no opportunity to go to war, and to that extent the varnashrama will be destroyed; with it, customs and conduct according to varna will also perish. It is imperative that you remain in tune with the times and that you teach the right conduct as per the varnashrama to others. However hard you might try but a brahmin will never acquire the qualities of a pure kshatriya just as a kshatriya can never become a brahmin. Sage Vishvamitra became a brahmarshi but could not divest himself of his customary disposition. The brahmin Peshwas born in the land of Parashuram may have learnt the art of war, but first they turned traitors to their king; later they turned against each other and now Nanasaheb, the grandson of Kaghoba, shall wreak havoc. Like Bhasmasur he will char himself to death. They fight because of their self-interest. Their actions are cruel. Nanasaheb does not know the generous and noble ways of the kshatriyas, nor will anyone in his lineage be equal to this task. They are not jewels among brahmins but men who will wreak havoc like wild fire. Jarashankar, remember my words even after I am gone. You must not encourage those who are unworthy like stones, hazardous like coal and fiery like embers among the various varnas. Customs and norms of varna are certain to be destroyed among them. Do not make futile attempts to prevent their destruction. Only after a careful examination of hearts and minds, invite the best among the brahmins, the kshatriyas and the vaishyas to Ratnanagari but dump the undesirable ones. Deal with each of them according to their varna. Jarashankar, the night is short and we have much to do. Instruct my heir accordingly.’ The brave men of the army had begun to gather outside. Their voices filtered inside the room. ‘Jarashankar, I forgot to mention one important thing. When I say that you should collect the best among the men at Ratnanagari, do not take my words literally. Some jewels add to the beauty of our home while some shine forth when they are kept in the homes of others. A son and a kshatriya have to be kept at home. One should not trust an outsider with something. Do not forget this. A precious daughter has to be the jewel of someone else’s house. You should also send the best of our brahmins out of the state to gain knowledge. At home their intellect will rust and grow dull, their experience shall remain restricted and they will become lazy; their impartiality and detachment also suffers as they become homebound, pick up internal fights and as a result a small state like ours would lose the few good men that it has. Consequently we would be forced to invite outsiders whose power and capability would be grudged by our worthless men. The money that we spent on worthless people would only bring injury and harm us. We would also not get the benefit of wise counsel in moments of crisis, the state would suffer setbacks and the people would be subject to tyranny. Jarashankar, you must bear all this in mind when you appoint officials and promote them. ‘They might belong to any caste but they will have to do the work that brahmins did in earlier times. The only consideration in appointment should be their capability for the task. You should enable them to do even better. Do not appoint officers only from within the state; they would become bania-like—leonine at home but foxes outside. Remember the maxim that the true value of a person is recognised only when he travels outside. Such are the responsibilities of my ministers. You should cultivate the ingenuity of a bania to accomplish all these responsibilities.’ The clamour outside grew more insistent. ‘That is all, Jarashankar. Our time is up. You must instruct and educate my heir. Before I plunge into battle and leave my beloved Ratnanagari, allow me one last expression of affection for this land. Recite the auspicious verse that tells us how Ratnanagari was named.’ Jarashankar recited: Ratnanagari is blessed with gems found in the mines of the mountains of Sundargiri. These gems adorn the fangs of great serpents. Mighty elephants and glorious lions inhabit this land. Its oceans are filled with pearls. Therefore, since times immemorial this land has been called Ratnanagari. This land also gives birth to gems among men who bring imperishable glory to it. Mallaraj looked up to the sky and said with folded hands, ‘O Mother Ratnanagari! Your Sundargiri, your forests, your oceans, the animals of this land are precious as gems. We pray that the heirs of Mallaraj, their ministers and officers and the people of this land shall never bring disrepute to your name. Today, the best among your sons shall enter battle to protect your glory. We pray that God be with us!’ Just as he spoke these words, Samant Mulu entered with all the battle-ready Bhayat. He laid his sword at Mallaraj’s feet and said, ‘May God be with our righteous King Mallaraj. All of us, your brothers, await your command. We are prepared to lay down our lives. On behalf of all the Bhayat, Samant seeks your command.’ Mallaraj was overjoyed. He said, ‘Samant, the devotion and affection that you and all other brothers have for me is unparalleled. I salute you! As long as I have brother like you, Samant, there is no danger to Ratnanagari. You shall lead the forces. You shall bring us glorious victory. My blessings are with you. Just as Kartikeya battled the demons on the instructions of Indra, I command you and all my brothers to attack the enemy forces and vanquish them. You shall ensure that they shall never again step inside the territories of Ratnanagari. My dear and brave brothers, return victorious before the sun rises. Brothers, give your all to Samant. Samant, you must send me a blow by blow account of the battle. Come, let me embrace you.’ The respect, the demonstration of trust and affectionate embrace of the king caused Samant Mulu’s eyes to well up with tears. Mallaraj shook hands with each one of his brothers-in-arms as they took leave of their king one by one. ‘Jarashankar, there can be no greater strength and fulfillment for the ruler of Ratnanagari than the true love and blessings of his Bhayat, his officials, his army and his people. This is part of our ancient history and you have witnessed it again today. You must teach this history to my son, if one were to be born to me, or to my heirs. Tell them that it does not matter if the English rule India or if someone else runs the empire. No harm shall come to them as long as they have the capacity to follow the ancient traditions and customs of our Suryavanshi family. The times may change, but their rule shall not.’ Mallaraj’s trust in and love for the Bhayat and their devotion for the king had stunned Jarashankar into silence. Mallaraj’s words brought tears to his eyes. He said, ‘Maharaj, I am your culprit and I deserve punishment. I had advised you to neutralise your Bhayat. I think it was cruel on my part. If you did not have so much goodwill for these patriotic men, my advice would have led to evil consequences. I shall never forget your noble way of punishing Samant. You describe the Marathas as capable of thieving from the moment of their conception in their mother’s womb. But you on the other hand were conceived as a great king. I am moved by your kingly qualities and delighted. I am proud that I serve a master such as you. Oh great king of the sun lineage, your words are etched in my heart and I shall instruct your heirs accordingly. But why do you feel that the time has come for you to give your final instructions?’ Mallaraj smiled. ‘Jarashankar, a king and his ministers keep each other within limits. The king’s family keeps the country united by providing continuity. As father, son, or grandson they are ultimately kings and hence they are one. Therefore, the king never dies and the wisdom of one generation is passed on to the next. The king looks upon his state and his subjects as part of his family. But he cannot remain abreast of all the developments taking place around him. He cannot gain all types of experience nor can he be acquainted with different forms of knowledge. He, therefore, needs to be associated with ministers who are both experienced and knowledgeable. It is against norms for a man to marry his sister; he must marry a woman outside his clan. Such are the norms of right conduct. Just as it is undesirable for a state to trouble and torment its Bhayat, it is equally undesirable that the Bhayat be appointed as ministers. When the son of the family marries a woman from another family, the relationship they share is different and personal; neither his father nor his brothers have a right to meddle in that relationship or to know what transpires between them. Similarly, the Bhayat have no right to know as to what transpires between a king and his ministers. Jarashankar, if a man were to be unduly and excessively attached to his mother, his wife is justified in seeking to wean him away and setting some limits. Similarly, if a king were to become unduly partial to his family, his minister must warn him. You were right to advise me. ‘I know my brothers-in-arms. My affection for them ensures the desired outcome. I used my prerogative. But you must always fearlessly think and express yourself. We have to rectify each other’s mistakes. You shall see that my Bhayat will now fight with greater courage, will and intelligence. Instead of leading the battle, I sent them. They will be more cautious. Samant made a mistake but he was rewarded with greater responsibility. I believe that he shall return victorious before the sun rises. But after all, battles are unpredictable; I may be called upon to join the battle and that would leave me no chance to have a word with you. It is said that in olden times warriors impregnated their wives before going into battle to ensure the continuity of their lineage. I am following the same tradition. I leave my thoughts to you to preserve, nurture and pass on. Women and brahmins cannot be killed in a war, but the kshatriyas do die. A seed planted in a woman’s womb and thoughts planted in a brahmin’s mind survive, flourish and come to light at the appropriate time. Who is that approaching us?’ It was Mallaraj’s messenger. He said, ‘Maharaj, two chiefs of Tatya Tope’s army have accompanied me to the gates of the city. They desire an audience with you. At this moment they are waiting at the inn on the outskirts of town. If you so desire, I can bring them to your presence. I have given them my word that no harm shall come to them.’ ‘What is their caste?’ ‘One of them is a Maratha. He claims to be English educated. The other is an elderly brahmin and claims to be learned in the shastras. He has worked in a native state in Gujarat and has done his pilgrimage from Haridwar to Setubandh Rameshwar and from Jagannath to Dwarika.’ ‘Are they accompanied by other men?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘How many?’

‘Only two; one of them is a Hindustani soldier and the other is a Muslim.’ ‘You go back. I will call for them after I have my meals.’ The messenger left. ‘Jarashankar, call them after Samant and his forces march out. These two have been promised that no harm shall come to them. But no such promise has been given to their army.’ Jarashankar got up. The king continued, ‘Jarashankar, I followed your advice regarding relations with the Company. When it came to the Bhayat I followed my instincts. But both of us will have to work together to deal with these two. You must return before they arrive.’ ‘As you desire,’ replied Jarashankar and left. The king asked for his meals to be served. The food arrived in silver plates and glasses. It was tasty, simple and nourishing. He sat down to eat. The servants withdrew. Mallaraj’s queen came in and sat before him. Her beautiful clothes were pleasing to the eyes. She was a tall, young woman of regal bearing. Her sensuality was suggestive. Her lineage was noble and she fulfilled her duties as a wife joyously and with ease. Her tastes were of the high-born. Her pride in being a kshatriya woman was apparent. She spoke sweetly; her voice had an unwavering clarity to it. ‘Tell me, Mena Rani, what news do you bring?’ Mallaraj asked her before picking up his first morsel of food. ‘I have been told that before the day breaks, Maharaj will go to the battlefield. If this were true, does not the woman who shares your bed have a right to know?’ ‘You may have the right, you may not have it. A king has many queens. The battlefield, too, is a queen and she has the first right to share bed with us. When she calls, we forsake all other queens. If she allows us to come to you, we shall come and tell you about the war.’ ‘That is true. If a king like you does not have a passionate desire for the battlefield, who else will? But Maharaj, when you go to meet that beloved queen, it is my right to adorn you and hand you your sword.’ ‘I admit defeat. Yes, that right is indeed yours. Samant has set out with our army. I may or may not be required to lead the forces. But if that time comes, it will be anytime tonight. Now come, eat this morsel of milk, rice and sugar,’ and the king placed the morsel in her mouth. She accepted it coyly. Mallaraj’s hand grazed against her forehead ever so slightly. The queen fed a morsel to her husband in turn. After dinner the king, intent on love, took her hand and walked out on the terrace. A half-moon shone in the sky like the glowing face of Mena Rani leaning on her husband’s shoulder. She longed to disappear into his powerful arms. Her eyes brimmed over. Mallaraj drew her closer. She sang a song for her husband as the tears streamed down her cheeks. You are a Rajputani—harden your heart So that when he who is intent upon the battlefield takes to it Not a tear escapes your eyes Take your husband into your embrace For this brave will soon embark upon foreign lands Hold him close tonight for tomorrow he must leave If a tear were to fall today An inauspicious omen it would be And yet these wretched eyes weep, Bathing him in my tears O husband, return to me victorious Our marital bed I will bedeck as I wait for you Do not beat a retreat—you are blessed by the Goddess; If you bleed on the battlefield, Know that I will weep tears of blood Thoughts riveted on the battlefield, I will wait to hear your horse approach If we find even a moment to embrace today, My whole life will be contained in it What sort of morning will dawn when you join battle? Brahmin women find solace in Brahman; The vaishya woman laments that her husband is away; But I, a Rajputani, know not if my husband will keep me in sorrow or joy. Mena Rani got a grip on her emotions and stood facing Mallaraj. She folded her hands and spoke, ‘Mallaraj, our coming together is true, whether we shall meet or not is speculation. If you have the time, give me your command. I have not borne you a son, but I shall obey your command like a son who obeys his father.’ Tears gleamed in Mallaraj’s eyes. He placed a hand over her head, drew her closer to him and said, ‘You are the jewel of my house, Mena. One cannot predict the future. We Rajputs deal with things as they come. If I live, you and I need not worry about the future. But if I do not return alive and you need to consult someone, Jarashankar and Samant are my most trusted men. Apart from those two, you yourself are wise. The world knows that Rajput women are wiser than their men.’ ‘Maharaj, I shall obey your command like a son,’ Mena said, easing herself out of his embrace. ‘Of that I have no doubt. Rani, have no regrets that you bore no son of mine.’ ‘Maharaj, God will decide who your heir shall be. I have not sought that right when you are present, and I am not likely to assert my claim in your absence. Those kshatriya women who install children of others on the seat of their husbands deserve nothing but contempt. They are more fallen than prostitutes. Maharaj, a woman who has worldly desires even after her husband’s death does so for two reasons: one, that there was something lacking in the life she shared with her husband; and two, that she belongs to an uncultured, lowly family. Maharaj, I have lacked nothing in my life with you. My family lineage is pure and high. Maharaj, what remains for a woman who has lost her husband? Why does she need a son or even a state? If I were to speak any further, it would be self-praise and that does not behove one such as me. Maharaj, I swear by your feet that I shall follow your instructions as dearly as I would care for a son. I will be true to my lineage. Maharaj, go and fight your battle with equanimity—your battlefield is my ornament.’ Mena fell at his feet and kissed them. Mallaraj lifted her up. ‘Beloved queen, I trust your words. I know that women remain virtuous because they desire to remain so and not because of external pressure. Oh pure Rajput woman, I have full faith in your piety, your noble lineage and the words that were spoken from your heart.’

Just then, Jarashankar sought permission and entered. ‘Maharaj, Samant and his army have commenced their march. I have instructed that only two of the four who seek audience with you should come. They will be here soon.’ The queen left the room unobtrusively. ‘Why did you permit only two?’ asked Mallaraj. ‘At such a late hour one should not deal with too many armed men. What they wish to accomplish can be done by one as well, but I have permitted two,’ Jarashankar replied. The messenger entered with two visitors. Mallaraj took his seat. Jarashankar took his place behind the king. The messenger and the two visitors stood facing Mallaraj. Mallaraj nodded in response to their salutations and pointed them to their seats. One of the two visitors wore a Maratha headgear while the other wore the pagdi typical of Dakshini brahmins. The messenger opened the conversation. ‘Maharaj, this is Sardar Shubhaji Rao. And that is Shastri Keshav Pant. They will place before you their proposal. Shubhaji Rao, he is Jarashankar, our minister. There are no unauthorised outsiders here.’ Keshav Shastri was the first to speak. ‘Srimant Sarkar Nanasaheb Peshwa knows that Maharaj Mallaraj is deeply patriotic, and therefore he has sent us to you.’ ‘So you carry a message from Nanasaheb? Do you also carry messages from someone else? What proof do you have that you are indeed Nanasaheb’s messengers?’ asked Mallaraj. ‘Praise on your sharp intellect, Maharaj!’ exclaimed Keshav Shastri. He turned to Shubhaji Rao and said, ‘Shubhaji Rao, Maharaj’s intellect is indeed as sharp as we were told. Maharaj, you know well that in the times of Emperor Alamgir, Shivaji Maharaj had undertaken a yagna, a sacrificial battle to defeat the mleccha. A similar sacrificial battle is being waged these days.’ ‘Even the Muslims are offering sacrifices nowadays and have become the officiating priests in this yagna,’ Jarashankar interjected. Keshav Shastri’s displeasure at this interjection was visible. He changed the metaphor and said, ‘Maharaj, it is like the mythical churning of the seas where the gods and the demons have come together.’

Mallaraj said in jest, ‘Jarashankar, you cannot find fault with this metaphor. It was a futile attempt to spar with Shastri Maharaj.’ Keshav Shastri was delighted. ‘I think that your metaphor carries a hidden meaning. During the churning of the seas, the gods deprived the demons of the nectar and other riches of the ocean. You intend to do something similar,’ said Mallaraj. ‘Maharaj, your understanding of politics deserves the highest praise. Your suggestion is most valid,’ Shastri said with apparent excitement. Mallaraj whispered to Jarashankar, ‘Such treachery is typical of the Peshwas.’ He turned again towards Shastri and said, ‘Shastri, such treachery and ungratefulness are ingrained in the seed of politics.’ Shubhaji Rao felt that the whole display of intellect was misplaced. The discussion was getting waylaid. So he quickly took the proceedings in hand and said, ‘Raja Saheb, Shastriji will present our case in a scholarly fashion, but I will come straight to the point. Just as you spoke frankly, I will also speak plain.’ Mallaraj approved and said, ‘Speak without hesitation.’ ‘Raja Saheb, among all the foreigners who have invaded our country, the English are the most dangerous because they are most cunning of the lot.’ The argument found its mark. Shubhaji Rao was quick to realise that he had found a weak spot and pushed the argument further. He had by now realised that Mallaraj was no fool. He advanced the arguments that would appeal to someone with Mallaraj’s intellect and experience. ‘Saheb, some great men have found a way of bringing all the communities together. This news about the cartridges being greased with the fat of cows and pigs is nothing but a dangerous fiction. But the English army is made up of Hindu and Muslim soldiers; they are ignorant and easily swayed. This story has worked very well. During the times of Shivaji Maharaj we used to have a saying that, “The gods bowed down to the hills.” The present story works similarly. There are many other fictions, but the message that we wish to convey to an experienced ruler like you is something else.

‘Raja Saheb, the fact is that the English have lost their brains. This is a sign that their end is certain. If we do not wake up from our slumber and seize the moment when our enemy is weak, someone else will. Why should leonine kings such as you not seize the moment? The English have become wicked and unscrupulous. They do not even hesitate before causing a breach of trust. Hitherto they were hungry for money, but now their hunger has extended to land. All other types of greed and hunger can be satisfied, but the hunger for women and land can never be met. The English are now hungry for land. They are not going to allow adoption in royal families. Raja Saheb, the rule of our Peshwas is not very old, but see what they have done to Shivaji Maharaj’s Satara—won’t that hurt us? See what they have done to Jhansi, Jetpur, Baghat, Udaipur, Budawal, Tanjore, Orissa, Nagpur, Karnataka, Bihar, Awadh? How many more names shall I count? In some places they say that we shall not allow adoption; in other places they say that the native rulers have tyrannised the people. If we oppress our people, they will turn against us. But what injustice have we done unto the English? All these are mere excuses. It is like that story of the fox and the sheep—if you did not abuse us your father must have, but I am hungry and so for one reason or another, I shall make a meal out of you. The English have signed treaties. They were signed in the past as well; what validity do they carry now? Saheb, such are their ways. You must recognise that your state is not safe in their hands. You are of course free to join forces with them, but be aware that such opportunities do not present themselves every day. Tomorrow, you will be in the same condition that Satara finds itself in today. Saheb, we must unite and fight a common battle against the enemy. The people of the English-ruled territories have rebelled; their native soldiers have rebelled and many native princely states have also joined in the battle against them. Look, how fortunate we are—today, the Hindus and the Muslims have come together to drive out the English. Even the Emperor in Delhi has awakened from his slumber, but the reins of the empire are in the hands of the Hindus. In the past Mahadevji Scindia controlled the empire. Today, the Hindus control it. Have we not driven out the English? From Meerut, from Saharanpur,

Muzzafarnagar, Farooqabad, Kanpur and from many other places, the English have been driven away. I can count many more names. Sikhs, Marathas, Bengalis, Punjabis, Pathans, Purabias, Muslims and Mughals are united against them. The fire has spread far and wide. If you support us, the Emperor in Delhi will recognise you as the ruler and your rule shall become eternal. We shall give you more territories. If you do not help us and fight against us, our victory is certain and your destruction is guaranteed. Raja Saheb, it is our country, our religion and we are one people. We shall drive this pack of monkeys back across the seas. Such opportunities do not come every day. ‘You ask us who our leaders are. The Emperor of Delhi leads the Muslims, while Nanasaheb leads the Hindus. Saheb, I am a Maratha; but for the sake of the country and religion I carry the flag of both the Muslim and the brahmin. The English shake with fear at the mere mention of Tatya Tope. Many other stars have clustered around the sun and the moon that Nanasaheb and Tatya Tope are. Do you want proof that I am their messenger? Take this—it is a decree of the Emperor. And if you still need more proof, there is an army waiting at the gates of your capital.’ Shubhaji handed over the imperial decree to Mallaraj. Mallaraj took it from him and asked without any excitement, ‘I presume all you want from me is a monosyllabic Yes or No.’ ‘Yes, Raja Saheb. Whether you say yes or no, please do so without delay. You must remember that yes translates into riches, while a no would invite the wrath of our armies.’ ‘That we shall see. Messenger, please take these two great men to the adjoining room and look after their comfort. We shall duly consider your proposal and you shall have our response shortly.’ The messenger and the two guests retreated to the adjoining room. Jarashankar walked them to the door, closed it and came and sat facing Mallaraj. Mallaraj twirled his moustache. ‘Maharaj, what is your decision?’ asked Jarashankar. ‘What are your thoughts?’ asked Mallaraj. ‘Hope and threat, fear and affection—Shubhaji Rao’s message was unambiguous.’

‘Jarashankar, do you see this motley crowd fighting each other before too long?’ ‘It is obvious to everyone except them, Maharaj.’ ‘Would we look good in their company?’ ‘Only as good as a parrot in the company of crows,’ came the prompt reply. ‘Was it not you, Jarashankar, who had told me that story of how a foolish brahmin gave life to a dead lion?’ ‘Yes, Maharaj.’ ‘If we join them, we would be as wise as that brahmin.’ ‘There are many other wise men who would bring this lion back to life.’ Mallaraj laughed and said, ‘No, it is not entirely so. Let me explain. Don’t allow his namedropping to startle you. I have thought it through.’ ‘What have you thought?’ ‘Look at their factions. Let us count the states that support the English. Kapurthala, Jind, Patiala, Nabha, all our native states and the Punjab. In short, all the original royal families with pure Rajput blood are with the English. There are some fence-sitters, true, but they will join the English as soon as their fortunes turn. I keep an eye on developments even in far off Himachal.’ ‘Maharaj, you did not include the Gaikwad, Gwalior, Indore and the Nizam.’ ‘But you remembered. Only the old Rajput families come to my mind.’ ‘Do you see the English fortunes turning for the better? The fire has spread far and wide.’ ‘Jarashankar, you brahmins have a short memory. I told you that the English will emerge victorious. They have one failing—they go in a slumber like fools but when they awaken, they are undefeatable.’ ‘How so?’ ‘This issue of adoption is unnecessary. Everyone is greedy for land. The English are no exception. But they are foolish. To begin with they take pity; then they repent, turn cruel and lose their way. They get kicked around and when that happens they hit back, vanquish their enemies and then take pity on them all over again.’ ‘Maharaj, I still do not understand.’ Mallaraj clarified, ‘I have thought about it carefully. The states in which they disallowed adoption were their own creations to begin with. The English had entered into these treaties either out of pity, greed or fear. Then they realised their mistake and wanted to take them back. So they began to swallow them up. But they have never interfered with the old states. As a result all the original states are in their camp. Those opposed to them are their own creations.’ ‘If they swallow their own creations, why would they be restrained while dealing with others?’ ‘If they become greedier, they will not show any restraint. The states they created or propped up are easy to gobble up; they say we created you and now we will destroy you. But that logic does not apply to the older states. However, if we give them a reason they will swallow us as well, just as bigger animals eat the smaller ones. But hitherto the English have not annexed any state without reason. They follow the divine rule of cause and effect. They wait for us to provide a reason. If we give them a reason, they shall become greedy for our state as well. But that would be our stupidity. If there is a tear in the fabric of our state, those monkeys will make it larger. They will bite any hand that comes out. So long as we do nothing to awaken the monkey in them, they will remain their noble selves. They will not annex any state without reason, because they are god-fearing and are cautious in taking bold steps. I do not fear them. But the actions of those who fear them are before you. Do you get it?’ Jarashankar replied, ‘No, Maharaj.’ ‘Some cunning karbharis misled the Rajput women by putting in them the fear that the English would not allow adoption and annex their state. As a result these women passed off the sons of some Koli or Ganchi as their son and installed them on the throne. But these wretched women do not understand that the true heirs of their husband are men from his family, and not sons of Kolis or Ganchis. Once these ordinary men come to power, they will turn against the very women who gave them the throne. If a Rajput were to ascend the throne, he would never allow these women to be disgraced.’ ‘I see. What are we to do now? Those two are waiting for our response, Maharaj.’ ‘Let them wait. Samant will gain time over them. Jarashankar, our decision has been made. The English are not alone in this. All those whom one should side with are with the English. So we shall keep our word.’ ‘Shall I call them in, Maharaj?’ ‘Of course.’ Jarashankar called in the visitors and the messenger. Mallaraj stood up and hence the conversation took place standing. Mallaraj leaned on his sword and said, ‘We have considered your proposal. We have given our word to the Company and we cannot go back on it. We considered the intent of your message seriously, but you have not been able to strike fear in our hearts. All other talk is insignificant. Hence, Ram Ram.’ Shubhaji Rao’s forehead creased while Keshav Shastri appeared concerned. They were about to respond but Mallaraj stopped them and addressed the messenger, ‘You gave them your word that no harm shall come to them. We honoured your word and granted them an audience. Now lead them out of our territories by the shortest possible way. Until they leave the boundaries, no harm shall come to them. Send some men to accompany them to our borders. If they choose to re-enter, they shall be dealt with in accordance with our laws. Jarashankar, it appears that their army is at our gates. They are here uninvited and intend to threaten us into submission. Our army will drive them out. All those who are captured should be handed over to the British so that we do not have to bear the cost of feeding them. You should also attach all the money they have. Robbers are not allowed to enter Ratnanagari. Let the world know that the king of Ratnanagari rules with his eyes wide open.’ Mallaraj called out, ‘Soldiers!’ Some Rajput soldiers promptly entered the room to carry out Mallaraj’s orders. The visitors departed with the soldiers. The king and his minister stayed back. ‘Jarashankar, ensure that all my orders are carried out. Do not hesitate to wake me up if the need arises. You can go home now.’ Jarashankar left. As Mallaraj moved towards his bed chamber, he reflected on the day’s events. The smart ones get caught in their own smartness. The English are forced on the back foot because of the muddle they created out of the policy of adoption. The English understand the simple rule of chess that one should sacrifice a page to capture the bishop. But their ploy misfired. After all they are an army of monkeys. The king laughed at his own simile and continued with his reflections. But remember, if you are good, good people will harbour you. If you do wrong, you will teach others to do wrong. You will stumble and cause others to fall with you. We are pure- blooded kshatriya kings. All others might become sullied, but pure blood flows through our veins. We are ready to shed our blood, but on one condition: you must earn the right for us to shed our blood. You English, remain good and allow others to retain their goodness. Mallaraj recognises your virtues; you must learn to recognise the virtues of native states. We are precious for each other. The kshatriyas might have gathered some dust, but once that is wiped clean, sparkling gems lie underneath. These gems are valuable to you. The native states that support you in this moment of crisis are precious for you—do not apply your monkey justice on them. But if you English behave like Sugriva’s monkey army and step on these jewels, the choice is yours. Who can prevent you from being true to your monkey instincts! Even if you were to behave like monkeys, we shall remain human. Mallaraj could not suppress his laughter. He was near his bed chamber. Mena Rani heard his laughter and came to open the door. ‘Do we have the right to know what amuses his highness so much?’ she asked him with a smile as she wrapped her arm around him and led him in. She removed his finely woven headgear. ‘Of course, my precious one!’ chuckled the king, pulling her in. The doors closed behind them. We, too, dear reader, must bring the chapter to a close for the sake of decorum.
chapters.summary: King Mallaraj faces a crucial decision, as he must rally his Bhayats for war, navigating their loyalty and his controversial alliance with the British.

chapters.title: Mallaraj's Concerns
paragraphs: Mallaraj’s Concerns Yet once more, in justice to this paragon of Heathen excellence, let us remember that Aurelius represents the decrepitude of this era. He is hopeless because the age is hopeless. He cannot rise beyond the sphere of ideas around him. The Heathen world looked for no renovation of a society which was visibly perishing before its face. And now when the popular notion of its degeneration was realised, it accepted its apparent destiny without a murmur.   —Merivale Shubhaji Rao had clear instructions that he should not waste his men and resources on recalcitrant native states. Their efforts had to be preserved for use against the English forces. For these reasons, Shubhaji Rao’s forces did not engage Samant Mulu in a fierce or protracted battle. Mallaraj had permitted only Shubhaji Rao and Keshav Shastri to meet him. Their other associates meanwhile decided to take a look at life in Ratnanagari. They heard that Samant Mulu had set out with his forces. This was enough to indicate to them the fate of the meeting. One of them promptly returned to the inn, while the other rushed to inform the waiting army of the imminent attack. Shubhaji Rao’s forces decided not to engage in battle and prepared to march out of Ratnanagari’s territories. Samant Mulu did attack the retreating army; some men were captured as well. But Shubhaji Rao’s forces made no attempt to either return fire or rescue their captured soldiers. Mallaraj’s soldiers accompanied Shubhaji Rao and his three companions to the borders of the state through another route. The four met with their forces in the morning and abused Mallaraj and Jarashankar to their heart’s content. Samant made sure that Shubhaji Rao had no surprises in store for him; having satisfied himself, he returned to the capital with his forces. Mallaraj released the captives because no war had been fought; he considered such captives to be equal to women. The British captured Delhi, and the tide turned in their favour. The English emerged victorious. Queen Victoria became the Empress of India and made a liberal proclamation written in her own delicate hand. Mallaraj’s predictions came true in every respect; his message to Colonel Brave and his response to Shubhaji Rao further cemented the ties between Ratnanagari and the English. This friendship gave the desired results to Ratnanagari. For long years the king and his minister would remember those difficult and trying days; their memory was not a source of unsullied joy. Mallaraj’s visage would turn sombre whenever he recalled them. Once he remarked, ‘Jarashankar, God has granted us the expected fruits of our efforts. It is a mixed bag. Just as good things have happened, the things we dreaded would happen are also here for us to bear. When father signed the first treaty with the English, I realised that our Rajput valour was about to be widowed. At the time of Nanasaheb’s rebellion, I considered the pros and the cons and further cemented the treaty. But the scales now seem to be tilting for the worse and they will tilt even further. Our thoughts and conduct towards them will have to change accordingly. Brave Sahib is no more; I outlived him. Very few Englishmen with the qualities of Brave Sahib will come to India. The English will not have to fight native states. They will have to draw their swords to punish robbers, cowards, the debauched and such like. But don’t mistake that for a war; it will be like the game of cops and robbers that children play. The English and we alike will lose our valour. They will fight battles elsewhere in their great empire, which will train their armies. But we will not have any such opportunity. We have not surrendered our sword but it should be considered as good as surrendered. We will become vaishya-like. Our fate is to increase the productivity of this land. No matter what their character is elsewhere, the English will become mercantile in this land. They will earn their wealth here and take it away to their country. This will make people of their country develop similar mercantile tendencies. No one can fight destiny but the times have changed. Winds of the new age are blowing from every direction. Jarashankar, it is for you and me to think and act for these changing times. We shall have to consider what to do, how to conduct our affairs, what seeds to sow, how and where; what of the old to retain and what to discard, all these are now subjects of serious consideration for us.’ Jarashankar replied, ‘Maharaj, you are absolutely correct. A new age is indeed upon us and we cannot join in its excitement unthinkingly. The old age still persists and we cannot begin to celebrate the new age. If the new age becomes inebriated and callous, it will be robbed of its glory just as some petty wayside robber defeating Arjun. If the new age forgets itself in the excitement of its newness, it will be like Parikshit who put a dead snake around a brahmin’s neck in anger and then repented. It is clear that the kshatriyas have laid down their arms. Lord Shri Krishna was pledge-bound not to take up arms in the battle of Mahabharata; but unarmed as he was, he helped the Pandavas win a righteous battle. That story told by our sages is most instructive. And there is a message there for people like you. One should not act out of sorrow—this applies to brave men like yourself. Maharaj, do not allow sorrow to eclipse your mind.’ Mallaraj was deep in thought. As he listened intently to his minister speak, tears streamed down the eyes of this brave kshatriya though he seemed oblivious to them. He was biting his lips and they had turned bloodshot red. He twirled his moustache with the left hand. He was frowning hard and his forehead was damp with perspiration. Jarashankar attempted to break the king’s reverie. ‘Maharaj!’ Mallaraj looked up, his hand went to his sword and his visage turned severe. He suddenly got up and said, ‘Brahmin, you speak the truth! For the present, the battlefield, the true beloved of all kshatriyas, has died. Until we mourn her, we shall have no peace. Go, go and tell my queen that her husband is no longer a battle-ready Rajput. He has been converted.’ The king looked vacantly upwards. Frightened by this state of his ruler, Jarashankar urgently called for the queen. Mena Rani rushed in, unmindful of the minister’s presence. Her face was uncovered; she was out of breath. Jarashankar had never before seen the unveiled face of the queen, who was in obvious distress. Tears came to his eyes. With folded hands he addressed her respectfully, ‘Mataji,’ and he described to her the king’s state of mind. The queen composed herself; she observed the king and thought with a clear mind. She asked Jarashankar to leave the room and close the door behind him. She went and stood before the king, who did not notice her. She touched his shoulder, but he did not stir. Mena Rani then gently caressed his head and face and said, ‘Maharaj! Swaminath!’ The king finally looked up at her. He put his hands on her shoulders and asked, ‘Rani, what is it you want?’ ‘What can the queen want apart from her Maharaj’s happiness? In your sadness I lose my all.’ ‘Where is Jarashankar?’ ‘He is waiting outside, saddened by your state.’ ‘When did you come?’ ‘I have been here for long, but so long as my Maharaj did not notice me, it cannot be said that I was present before you. Maharaj, what caused you such sadness?’ ‘Do you have the right to ask such questions?’ ‘I can partake of your joys only when you allow me to, but I have a right to share your sorrows since the day I married you. You cannot take away that right.’ The answer pleased Mallaraj. He sat down on his seat with his queen beside him and said, ‘I am no longer sad. Does that not circumscribe your right?’ ‘Your love is immense, but I am not going to be cheated by it and forsake my right.’ ‘All right. For some reason I was deeply unhappy. But now I have found a solution, and hence the sadness, too, has disappeared. I will confer with Jarashankar and Samant. Tonight I shall be a captive of my Mena Rani and I will share with you all the details. As of now, the narration will be inconclusive. Tell me, what would you prefer?’ ‘Maharaj, I can only be a seeker before you. I do not have any preferences. You said that I exercise power over you at night. I shall then wait for the night. But do not adopt half measures in fulfilling your promise.’ ‘Very well.’ The queen left the room and went back to her quarters. As the king watched her receding figure, he called Jarashankar. Jarashankar came in accompanied by Samant. ‘Samant, I was going to send for you, but I see that you are here already.’ ‘Maharaj, such is your grace; you think of me and I move.’ ‘Samant, tell me what brought you here?’ ‘I came because I was told that you were unhappy for some reason.’ ‘It is good that you came. Jarashankar, why did you go out? Did the queen throw you out?’ ‘Forgive me, Maharaj, but do not speak such words,’ Jarashankar replied, keeping his hands over his ears. ‘I failed to relieve you of your melancholy and hence I requested her intervention.’ ‘So she exercises greater authority over me, is it?’ Mallaraj asked in jest. ‘Maharaj, are words more important or deeds? I failed, but the queen removed the cause of your sadness and hence you are with us again; such is the power of her grace.’ ‘So the Rani is more effective than you?’ ‘Maharaj, efficacy depends upon context. During the day the sun shines bright, but at night it is the full moon that is resplendent; but on a moonless night the stars shine the brightest. Raja Dashrath had such power that Ram went to the forest to keep his promise. Dashrath, Kaushalya, Laxman and Sita, all four of them wished to accompany Ram to the forest. Shri Ramchandraji knew the laws and norms of right conduct. How fine and discerning was his judgement! He declined to entertain Kaushalya’s request and told her that her right and duty were to be with Dashrath. He commanded her to stay with Dashrath. A son can command his mother so she can fulfill her righteous obligations. When a mother begins to act contrary to norms, a son, expert in normative conduct, must show her the right path. Dashrath was Ram’s father and he, too, desired to accompany him to the forest. A son cannot command his father; hence Ram did not do so. But if Dashrath had followed Ram to the forest, he would have violated his duties as a king. Ram obeyed his father to the extent that he chose to go and live in the forest, but he disobeyed Dashrath’s desire to accompany him to the forest as Ram did not wish to be the cause of the violation of kingly duties. Therefore, Ram left Ayodhya at night; such was his discernment. Laxman was devoted to Ram. Ram reasoned with him; when that failed he told Laxman that he was free to accompany him. He showed Sita the hardships of forest life and the comforts of living in the palace. A wife has the right to partake of her husband’s hardships.
