She can exercise this right through anger, reason or force. A husband has no right to obstruct his wife in discharging her duties. Sita used her wrath to convince Ram that she would accompany him to the forest. Shri Ramchandra did not seek either Dashrath or Kaushalya’s consent in this regard; he simply submitted to Sita’s arguments. In certain matters the rights of a wife are supreme and cannot be curtailed either by the husband or the wife. She experiences this pain most intensely and a woman who assuages the husband’s pain exercises unrestrained authority over him in this regard. Therefore, Maharaj if the virtuous queen frees you from pain and restores your joy to you, I cannot seek to undermine either her right or her authority in this regard. If I were to do so, I would be fit for a life in hell. Maharaj, I pray that both her right and her authority in this regard remain eternally undiminished. I also pray that you may come to us every day with your joy restored to you by the queen. I hope that this good fortune of ours will also remain undiminished.’ Mallaraj laughed aloud at this discourse and said to Samant, ‘Did you notice how clever the minister is? He should keep me free of worries, but instead he has cleverly put the burden onto the queen. That should make both of them happy. Samant, I want to share my innermost thoughts with you. I need the minister’s counsel, but more than him, I need your advice.’ Samant replied, ‘Your servant awaits your words, Maharaj.’ ‘Jarashankar, bring two large sheets of paper. Samant will write on one and you shall write on the other.’ Both of them sat in readiness to take down the king’s command. The king dictated: ‘Write down. My state is composed of two bodies— one, my Bhayat, my brothers-in-arms, and the other, the Karbhari. The king and his Bhayat are one. Anyone from among the Bhayat can be chosen as the king. The Karbhari must ensure that all Bhayat acquire the fitness to rule so that on the decisive day, the blind and the unfit are not forced to be recognised as capable. Write that down.’ Jarashankar said, ‘Every word has been taken down, Maharaj. The document is of the highest quality.’ ‘Don’t interrupt. Write silently. The Bhayat must realise that the state belongs to the king. If they were to fight each other, the English will begin to interfere. Initially, they will go after the king but later they will also interfere in the work of the Bhayat. If the state is prosperous, the wealth will be shared by the Bhayat as well; but if the wealth is captured by the outsiders with their tiger-like hunger for wealth, neither the king nor the Bhayat will get anything.’ Samant looked up at the king in admiration. ‘Maharaj, what you say is very true.’ Mallaraj said, ‘Yes, what I say is true. But I fear that my Bhayat will not be able to deal with this truth and eventually, like other native states, the king and his Bhayat will fight each other in our state as well. The native states are staring at further disintegration. States do not multiply. There will be one state and one king, but the number of Bhayat will increase. Hitherto, the king and his Bhayat sought to increase the territories of the state to meet the Bhayat’s demand for a greater share in the state revenue. You must write down everything I say. But now territorial expansion is not possible. The land is fixed and the number of Bhayat will increase. The state treasury will become empty and the states will become smaller. This will be the basic cause of dissension between the king and his Bhayat. The Bhayat will no longer be able to go to war and hence they will fight with words— spoken and written. They have no way with words; so the kayasthas and diplomats will earn at their expense. Ultimately, the judges will be English and we shall become supplicants before them; we shall try and please them with bribes. We will have to swallow their abuse and we shall fight like their puppets. We shall fight like the banias and not like kshatriyas. All kshatriyas, the king and his Bhayat will become paupers, while others will get rich at their expense. We shall become their slaves. Both of you take this down—I do not want such a fate for my state. ‘I have narrated how the kshatriyas will become like banias. Now take down my words that kings will become brahmin-like. They will begin to relish their homes and property; they will prefer life over death; they will be a frightened lot. They will not know how to conduct the affairs of the state. They will lead debauched lives. Write down—I will not have such a king rule over my state. Once we forsake our love of arms and the battlefield, this fate is certain. Write that as well. ‘Kshatriya men will behave like women. Take that down. Oh God! Why don’t I have a son? They will worry about such matters. They will have no wars to fight and no one will come and narrate to them stories of valour; hence they will watch their women fight one another. A kshatriya man will marry many women; some of them will become his favourites and he will be indifferent to others. He will take sides, be partial to his favourite wife, act like her woman friend and deal with others like a mother-in-law. They will also harass former queens and the wives of his brothers. They will play games that women play and become womanly in the process. Both within and outside the house, kshatriya men will behave like women, while their women will seek virile men someplace else. These women would take other men, including household servants, as their men. Write that down.’ Samant could no longer write. Tears flowed from his eyes. ‘Maharaj, I am afraid. I see the future you predict before my very eyes. All around us, the native states are already in such a condition. Maharaj, now ...’

‘Samant, you are already behaving like a woman,’ said Mallaraj, cutting him short. Jarashankar said, ‘Samant, Shri Krishna saw the destruction of the Yadav clan before he gave up his life. The kshatriyas will no longer be able to fight battles, but they must learn to be patient and deal with the problem with forbearance. Such is the duty of all men. Should the kshatriyas be any exception to this? Lord Narayan watched the great deluge take place before his very eyes.’ Mallaraj gave an encouraging slap on Jarashankar’s back, ‘Very well said, minister! Samant, write down what Jarashankar and you have said. Now stop weeping and be a man. Write it down.’ Samant gathered himself, picked up his pen again and wrote. Mallaraj continued, ‘Kshatriyas will become like shudras. They will not know how to read and write and will indulge in depraved acts. They will lead debauched lives. They will learn to plead and please others, revel in low intrigue and will kill and murder stealthily. ‘Write, that the kshatriyas will become like the mleccha. All the vile acts of the mleccha that we hear of from Delhi and other such places will become habitual with the kshatriyas. They will abuse animals, will be evil and cruel. But the kshatriyas will not acquire any of the positive traits of the mleccha. Write that the kshatriyas will imbibe all the bad aspects of the brahmins, vaishyas, women and the shudras, but none of their good qualities.’ Once they had finished writing, Mallaraj said, ‘Samant, now read it out to me.’ Samant read out the entire document. When he finished, Jarashankar said, ‘Maharaj, this deluge, this end of the world that you predict will not come.’ Mallaraj retorted, ‘What do you know? Many states are already living through such deluge. Ratnanagari is an exception where Satyug, the age of truth, prevails.’ Jarashankar said, ‘And it will continue to prevail.’ Mallaraj said, ‘Samant, the age of truth will prevail if all of you commit yourselves to it and if all of us strive together like men to sustain it. Shall I show you the way forward?’

Samant mournfully replied, ‘Maharaj, the seas are breaching the barriers. What are mere men to do?’ ‘Come now, Samant, do not be so despondent! Write down what I say.’ ‘Maharaj, command us.’ ‘I will now show you the remedy for all these problems. First, write down that the kshatriyas may not be called upon to go to war, but if they do retain the art of war, it will come in handy, if not now, then two hundred years later. Jarashankar makes use of the wisdom of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. The brahmins committed these things to memory for a thousand years and have found use for it in this day and age. We, the kshatriyas, should also adopt that method. We may not be able to fight other men, but our forests are full of lions and tigers and we should fight them. We should not come to love our lives so; we must keep alive the virtue of a death in the battlefield, by fighting the wild beasts of the forest. We must learn the use of new weapons. And for this reason, I grant to my Bhayat the privileged access to our forests. The Bhils, the Kolis or foreigners should not enter the forest with a view to hunt without the permission of the king or his Bhayat. The English will come as our guests and hospitality demands that we take them hunting. But they must be accompanied by my heirs or my Bhayat. My heirs should take the lead in hunting and never put life before valour. My Bhayat should be trained to take up kingly duties; they should retain their expertise in wielding weapons, and heirs must ensure that the Bhayat remain good warriors. My Bhayat shall not be called upon to war, but they must treat hunting as a new form of war and discharge their responsibility. My heirs should send the Bhayat to other states to learn the use of arms and join any battle that comes their way. The Bhayat must follow the lead of my heirs.’ Samant was delighted. ‘Very good, Maharaj! Very good!’ But Jarashankar was clearly displeased. ‘Maharaj! That your heirs and the Bhayat should treat the practice of hunting as war appears to me to be the wrong path, and one that will have disastrous consequences.’

Mallaraj lost his patience and cut him short, ‘Stop it, brahmin! You would not understand such things. Just write down what I ask you to. You have to ensure that my orders are carried out in this regard. We are not here to debate these things. Make sure you write down everything and ensure their compliance.’ Jarashankar replied that his commands would be complied with. Mallaraj continued, ‘In case of a dispute among the Bhayat, they should approach the judicial officers of the state. In case of a dispute between the Bhayat and the state, a committee of arbitrators should be appointed. The minister should be the first arbitrator, the second arbitrator should be from the princely family but not a direct descendant of the king, and the third arbitrator should be a Bhayat nominated by the aggrieved party. The decision of the arbitrators should be unanimous and that would be final. In absence of unanimity among the arbitrators a new set of arbitrators should be appointed. The minister or his nominee should be one of the arbitrators. All the Bhayat should suggest names of ten elders among them, of whom two would be selected by the state to serve as arbitrators. If the arbitrators fail to arrive at a consensus then the majority decision should prevail. My Bhayat have to be discouraged from the tendency to fight like the vaishyas; this is the best remedy for that. Third, if their land holding becomes unviable for providing adequate compensation, my Bhayat are forbidden from either selling or pledging their land as collateral to anyone but the state. Fourth, the new garas or inheritance should not be of a land grant but in monetary terms, which should be double of the market price of the land grant. ‘If a Bhayat deviates from the Rajput code of conduct or adopts ways of other castes or breaks the conditions mentioned in this document, he should be held accountable by the rest of the Bhayat and they, and not the state, should impose any punishment or sanctions. The Bhayat should impose a special tax on the errant Bhayat’s lands. The same punishment should be awarded to those Bhayat who do not learn statecraft. The state retains its traditional right of confiscating the garas. And finally, all the customary taxes that the state levies on the Bhayat are stopped forthwith. In lieu of the customary taxes, the

Bhayat should pay a fiftieth part of their garas as taxes—this is their nazrana. If the Bhayat ensure a long life for the king, the taxes that he levies upon them will not increase. Apart from this new tax the state and the king shall place no other revenue demands on the Bhayat. ‘That is all. Jarashankar, keep the original document in my records and place a copy of it in your records. It will be your responsibility to cultivate this sensibility and these norms in the future king and the future minister. Samant, I have no son. As of now, you are my heir apparent. But even you have not fathered a son. Let us see what the future holds for us. This scheme that I have outlined is to the advantage of all of us. It is your responsibility to get the assent of all the Bhayat. Please tell them that I am deeply concerned about the future; we are undergoing immense transitions and if we wish to preserve both kshatriyas and kshatriyahood in the new age, they should all give their assent to the proposal. Tell them that Mallaraj has no son and all his actions are motivated by a desire for the welfare of the kingdom and my Bhayat. Please also tell them that if they have any suspicion of my motives, I am ready to step down from the throne and they would be free to choose a king of their choice. Tell them that Mallaraj would be quite happy to serve as a Bhayat to the new king and would accept these and any other conditions that the new king might wish to impose for the betterment of the kingdom. But so long as I remain the king I would like this new proposal to be accepted by all. Mallaraj is willing to step down for the welfare of the kingdom and will serve as a Bhayat under Samant or any other Bhayat, even if the new king holds the lowest rank among the Bhayat today. Now go, Samant, hurry. Soon, we will be facing the prospect of the English interfering in the affairs of native states. They will tell a king that though he had a right to step down, the choice of the new king now rests with them. They might even bring such a state under their rule. But I still have the opportunity to make a gift of my kingdom. Allow me to use it and secure the future of the kingdom.’ ‘Maharaj, pray let things continue as they are ...’ ‘Jarashankar, stop it! My words must be a command for my officials even if it involves a great personal cost to me. It is I who have chosen to bear it, and I shall bear it happily for my brothers-in-arms. The Bhayat might not appreciate my reasoning and hence I have offered my kingdom. No one has a right to stop me from stepping down from the throne as long as my action is in the interest of the kingdom. Even my queen does not wish to exercise her authority in this respect. Samant, go and meet my brothers and I will hand over the kingdom to a man of their choice tomorrow when the dawn breaks.’ ‘Maharaj!’ ‘Samant, I do not want this moment of bliss to be delayed any further. Go, hurry.’ ‘But Maharaj ...’ ‘Go—that is an order.’ ‘Maharaj, unless I get a hearing, I shall not obey you. It is my right as a Bhayat.’ Mallaraj laughed and said, ‘All right, speak your mind. But keep it short. Don’t lecture me.’ ‘Maharaj, your Bhayat have unconditional faith in your words. They believe that no action of yours could be irreligious. But your proposal to seek their consent, your offer to step down from the throne and the insinuation that they no longer trust you amounts to questioning their devotion towards you. They have done nothing to merit such a charge. The Bhayat of Ratnanagari have always accepted what the kings have offered them and have always given what the king wanted from them. This has been a longstanding tradition. It is not correct to break this tradition and I should not be made instrumental in it. The Bhayat will consider me to be the evil one. We are happy to follow all your commands. Please remove these ideas of consent and conditions from our dealings with you.’ ‘Samant, just yesterday my brothers showed that they were willing to lay down their lives to honour my word. If I put a charge of disloyalty on them, I would be ungrateful. But I have carefully considered my proposal. Listen to me and try to understand, you don’t need to write this down. People have to be cautious when the ruler changes, but in times of transition it is the ruler who must be vigilant. Each family has its tradition; similarly each age has norms that govern conduct appropriate to the time. Samant, you would recall that there are days when the sun is concealed by clouds. Days when it is difficult to tell if it is afternoon or evening, or tell the east from the west. In such bewildering times, a wise man stands and observes as to which side is the darkness denser and so discerns the east from the west. On such days one cannot rely upon the eternal sun to guide us. Similarly, in times of transition one cannot hope to be guided by tradition alone. In moments such as these one has to decide as to what shape the light or the darkness of the new age shall take. One has to find a way out of uncertain times. Because if one allows doubt to debilitate us, the darkness shall envelop all of us and we shall be stranded without a pathfinder. The wheels of fortune turn in a fraction of a moment. We, who have fought battles, ought to know this. We must be clear-sighted and prepared for any eventuality. We cannot always seek refuge in tradition. We cannot go looking for the wisdom of our forefathers when our house is on fire. Tell me, Samant, what do you think?’ ‘All right, Maharaj. We can forget our age-old family traditions for a while. But what is the reason for this charge and this apparent lack of confidence?’ ‘Samant, this new age will bring with it the vaishya way of fighting with paper and pen. Ratnanagari may not remain immune from it for too long. It will bring with itself new modes. What would prevent the charge that Mallaraj was a tyrannical ruler? If not today then tomorrow we will open ourselves to English influence. What kind of relations would the king and his Bhayat have in the future? Can we be certain that those would be relations of affection and trust? We should make sure that our mutual affection remains well-grounded even in these times of transition. This measure is in that direction. ‘Samant, I do not have a son and you are my heir. One cannot be certain about matters of life and death. Therefore, I am letting you into the secret. Today you are a Bhayat, but tomorrow you could be king. You are the bridge that connects the king and his Bhayat. You are related to me and also to the Bhayat. The fortunes and misfortunes of either affect you equally. Therefore, you have to carry my message to the Bhayat. Is there anyone more capable and more devoted to me than you, Samant? By tomorrow morning, bring me the news that my command has been accepted.’ Samant did not respond and, with a frown of concern on his face, sought leave of the king. ‘Jarashankar, you seem perturbed?’ said Mallaraj. ‘Yes, Maharaj. You have embarked on a most adventurous path.’ Mallaraj could not suppress his laughter. ‘Which adventure? My offer to step down, or my attempt to cut the Bhayat to size?’ ‘Both.’ ‘Why should you worry if I cease to be king? We are always prepared to lay down our lives in the battlefield; similarly one should also be prepared to step down from the throne for a great cause. What does a man love more: life or wealth? Most would choose life over wealth. We kshatriyas do not love life and wealth is like the shoes we wear on our feet.’ ‘Maharaj, the shastras say that most men give considered thought to substantial issues. But one must also consider matters that appear insignificant. One must consider such matters like a scholar, one must think of its implications, because small matters when badly executed become a thorn in our side and cause permanent heartburn.’ Mallaraj asked him to repeat the verse. Jarashankar did so. A wise man bent on doing a thing, good or bad, should first carefully consider its consequences. The issue of actions done in hot haste becomes till death, like a dart, poignant to the heart.⟨fn:94⟩ ‘Maharaj, your action will have grave implications. Shouldn’t you have consulted me once?’ Mallaraj mellowed somewhat and replied, ‘Jarashankar, you are right. I should have consulted you. That was obligatory upon me. I cannot deny that. Whose verse was it you recited?’ ‘Maharaj, that was from the wise sage Bhartrhari.’

‘I accept your view. But what has been done cannot be undone. Mallaraj never mourns his actions. Now tell me, what else have I done wrong?’ ‘I do not deny that your proposal, if accepted, will benefit the state, but there is an ancient practice. During war, whenever the gates of the enemy fortification had to be broken down, a camel was placed between the spiked gates and the elephant that charged to break down the gates. This killed the camel but saved the elephant.’ ‘Your example has no relevance to our discussion.’ ‘Maharaj, you are like the elephant and I, your minister, am like the camel. Maharaj, in your dealings with other kings or even with our own people there are moments when someone has to take the brickbats. You represent the royal personage and cannot be expected to face criticism and attacks. To do so would be against morality.⟨fn:95⟩ The royal personage has to be preserved like a precious jewel that is worn only on special occasions. But for everyday affairs, you need the shield of a camel like me so that even if the camel is sacrificed, a replacement can be obtained. A minister is a shield for the king; a minister who does not accept the blows intended for the king upon himself violates his duties and is an enemy of both the king and the state. You told me that Brave Sahib had explained to you the English doctrine that: “The king commits no sin.” The king should only perform deeds that bring him glory. The king bestows honour, prestige, wealth and in return he is loved by all. In England, punishment is awarded by a judge; the queen is seen as merciful. All unpleasant matters that a king wants conveyed to his people should be conveyed through his minister. Thereby, the world blames and abuses the minister, but never the king. The minister is the conduit and repository of all secrets and in the discharge of his duties he must face all the attacks and criticism. The people should have no clue as to what the view of the king is or whether he was even consulted in some decisions. When the king is so shielded, the people’s affection for their king remains perennial and the royal personage remains undented. Maharaj, it was you who told me that the king and the royal family provide coherence and unity to a state. That lesson is etched in my heart. Maharaj, your family tree must be nourished and nurtured; it cannot be exposed to daily blows of axes. It is for this reason that a king needs a minister, and a king who becomes his own minister does damage the royal personage. The king is like a great tree that gives shelter to life. The king is required to weather great storms and not everyday skirmishes. Maharaj, why did you not think of using me as a front in your dealings with the Bhayat? Why did you expose yourself?’ Mallaraj heard this discourse with attention, enthusiasm, affection and joy. His affection for Jarashankar multiplied a hundred fold. ‘Jarashankar, you are indeed a jewel among ministers. Your advice was of the highest order and what you say is very true. But I have considered all these while taking the step I have taken. It was for this very reason that I have put you as one of the arbitrators in all disputes with the Bhayat. The scheme is carefully devised so that the king is not required to sit on judgement on his Bhayat. Therefore, all judicial authority is vested in the minister. If the king had any role to play in adjudicating the disputes of the Bhayat, my heirs and my Bhayat would most certainly have come into conflict and that would have sowed the seeds of family disputes. Kings would have been subjected to ignominy. I have prevented such an eventuality. The task that I have undertaken is a grave one; even a hundred ministers cannot accomplish it. While for me it would be easy to accomplish, as easy as an elephant waving his trunk. Even if I lose a tusk it will grow back but remember that if this task is accomplished, the state of Ratnanagari would be secure for a hundred years.’

‘You have left no scope for any further questions, Maharaj,’ replied Jarashankar. ‘Good. So go home now and watch things unfold. We have done enough for the day.’ Jarashankar left. Samant had to work hard and faced some difficulties in accomplishing the assigned task, but it was made easier by the fact that customary faith and affection for Mallaraj were still intact. Also, the traditional sense of kshatriya identity and devotion to the state were not vitiated by modern mercantile ways. Moreover, the Bhayat had not been influenced by modern methods of doubts and cynicism. Their hearts were uncomplicated. Samant’s deeply affectionate relations with the Bhayat, Mallaraj’s promise to abdicate the throne and the Bhayat’s belief that Mallaraj would prove true to his words held sway. The Bhayat also recognised that Mallaraj’s act was prompted by a desire to do good to the state. The Bhayat appreciated the glory of such acts. Their patriotic sense and devotion to the state increased manyfold and they competed with each other to offer even greater sacrifice. As a result of all these, Mallaraj’s proposals were accepted by his good Bhayat without any amendment or dissent. As Mallaraj woke up the next morning, Mena Rani exercised her right and conveyed to him this good news sent to her by Samant. The king met Samant and took him in his embrace and said, ‘Samant, this is my last gift. Neither you nor I will ever again be called upon to accomplish something as significant as this. And even if we are required to perform such acts of duty, in this new age the king will not be as respected as I am today by my Bhayat. I will now hold court and express my gratitude to all the Bhayat. Neither the state of Ratnanagari nor her king can ever repay their gratitude.’ Mallaraj bid farewell to Samant and went back to his queen. He said, ‘Rani, my minister would have spent a sleepless night. Send a message with our confidant Bhalji that both the camel and the elephant remained unharmed, and that the gates have been opened.’ The queen went out to pass on the message. Mallaraj said to himself, Praise is due to the king while criticism is reserved for the minister! This is a new proposition. Like the camel, the minister faces criticism and harm.

What is his reward? Now I understand the tradition that the king should restrict his own powers and submit his will and authority to his minister and be like a student to the minister. It is impossible to use the minister as a shield where this tradition is not upheld. It is by following this tradition that a king recognises the value of his minister, expresses his gratitude and tries to reward the minister for his cares in whichever way possible. The minister is the camel-like shield in statecraft. And here comes the one who rules my household. I should submit to her authority as much as that of my minister. Mena Rani approached him. The previous night Mallaraj had shared with her his concerns and his proposed solution. Explaining the metaphors of the camel and the elephant to her, he said, ‘This camel is precious to the state. If I had used the camel as a shield, I am certain that the gates would have remained shut but the camel would have perished. The king must take care of his minister. A king who has no compassion for his minister is cruel. A minister with a character fault should be removed from office but a good minister must be protected and neither the king nor his family should add to the worries of the minister. A minister who restricts the powers of a king must also put limits on the king’s family. It is for this reason that so often the minister and the royal family appear to be adversaries. This does not allow a minister to perform his duties well. Rani, you should ensure that no member of our family or our personal staff violates the commands of the minister. No one should act contrary to his advice.’ ‘Maharaj, the minister embodies your authority. He has all rights to know and to reform our follies. Please give him a free hand in the exercise of this authority and empower him that he should without hesitation discuss my misdemeanour with you,’ said the queen. ‘Rani, the minister has often expressed to me his gratitude towards you because you support his efforts and have never been an obstacle. Unlike in many other states, the queen is not opposed to the minister and does not enter into or encourage machinations against the minister. The minister is grateful that you have also accepted measures to bring about financial discipline in the royal household.’

‘It would be a blot on my family if I do not learn your virtues, Maharaj.’ ‘When God is kind, everything else also falls in place; all act in good faith. Common people recognise this as fate. Rani, the good sense that you and my Bhayat have shown is a sign of God’s grace.’ ‘Maharaj, you must reward the Bhayat for their good sense. Neither the king’s anger nor his gift should be empty of substance.’ ‘There is no way I can repay the gratitude of my Bhayat. They have done a great deed.’ ‘But they have one unexpressed desire, Maharaj. You must fulfill this desire. It will give both them and me joy.’ ‘And what could that be?’ ‘Maharaj, first give me your word that my desire will be fulfilled.’ ‘In the Satyug, gods granted boons without enquiring about the nature of the boon sought. Brahma, occasionally and Shiva often granted such boons. But as the creator and the destroyer of the world, they could grant such boons. But Vishnu, the upholder of the universe, never granted such boons. We the kings, who uphold the righteous order, are embodiments of Vishnu. Moreover, by assuming the Vamana avatar, the demons taught a lesson to Vishnu that even he should not grant such boons. Shri Ramchandra wordlessly taught men that if they were to grant a boon unthinkingly in the heat of the moment, as Dashrath did to Kaikeyi, they, too, would come to grief. Rani, ours is the glorious Suryavansh. Would we not follow the example of Shri Ram, the epitome of Suryavansh?’ ‘Maharaj, in matters of love, you cannot take recourse to the Puranas.’ ‘Rani, if you are invoking love, tell me who has greater right—you or my principal queen? Can I grant you a boon without consulting my principal queen?’ ‘Maharaj, I was under the impression that I am your only queen.’ ‘I have never spoken to you about my principal queen in order to avoid a conflict.’ ‘You must tell me the name of my sister. You should test us and see if can live with each other without discord.’

‘There are two-three other queens as well.’ ‘Without first making their acquaintance, I cannot accept any food.’ ‘But you know them already.’ ‘Maharaj, please tell me plainly.’ ‘The first among them is my intellect. She has been my principal queen since childhood; I can do nothing without consulting her. My second queen is Ratnanagari; I am neither allowed to compromise her, nor allowed to love you more. My third queen is the battlefield; I must respond to her call even if I have to leave you sleeping or waiting. These are your three elder sisters. If I were to grant you a boon without their consent they would turn away from me. They would throw a tantrum that would put even Satyabhama’s tantrum to shame, and I do not have the skills of Shri Krishna to assuage their hurt and anger.’ ‘Maharaj, I should express myself clearly. Why should I seek something that is not made explicit?’ ‘Say it.’ ‘Apart from these three favourite queens, you should marry a fourth one. I shall be your fifth wife.’ ‘And who is she?’ Mena Rani spoke sombrely, ‘Maharaj, Samantsinh sent a message through his wife. He wants me to request you that there is a tradition among kings to marry more than one woman from noble families to ensure that his lineage continues through a male heir. The shastras and our customs both sanctify such marriages. Maharaj should give the benefit of this tradition to Ratnanagari.’ ‘Rani, do you have anything to add to this message?’ ‘Maharaj, a woman who has been barren would naturally wish for her husband’s lineage to continue and ensure the good of the kingdom, and she would wish for you to have all the worldly joys.’ ‘And thereby ensure that your own position is endangered.’ ‘This is not a farce, Maharaj. I have harboured this thought long before receiving Samantsinh’s message. Mallaraj mocked her, ‘I, too, do not speak in jest. But pray do continue to harbour this thought until it rots and is destroyed.’

‘Why do you make a mockery of me?’ ‘I do not mock you, Rani. But my three principal queens advise me that your proposal should be rejected. I will not act against their advice. Convey to Samant that I follow the vow of one wife that our Shri Ramchandraji followed. Mallaraj is not about to recognise the authority of either the shastras or customs and marry many women. Mallaraj will not act in an effeminate way. Tell Samant that he shall be king after me; he is free to marry as many women as he wants. Remind him of what I dictated to him just yesterday. I said that a man who marries more than one woman begins to act like a woman, like a mother-in-law or a sister-in-law. The document proscribes polygamy. Tell Samant’s wife that she should act wisely and pass on some of her wisdom to her husband. Mena Rani, do you have anything more to say?’ ‘I have much to say, Maharaj, only if you would consider it.’ ‘Your ploy has failed. Do you have any more dice to throw?’ ‘The same.’ ‘My refusal stays.’ ‘No one can force a king.’ ‘All right then, I shall now visit the palaces of my principal wives.’ ‘Do grace me with your return, Maharaj.’ The king kissed his queen’s forehead and left. The curtains came down on act one of Mallaraj’s concerns.
chapters.summary: Mallaraj, deeply saddened by his kingdom's future, confides in Jarashankar, then Mena Rani attempts to console him with a surprising proposal he ultimately rejects.

chapters.title: Mallaraj's Mani and His Initiation into Statecraft
paragraphs: Mallaraj’s Mani and

His Initiation into Statecraft Mena Rani failed to convince Mallaraj. Samant made another attempt through Jarashankar. One day Jarashankar broached the issue. ‘Maharaj, Samant appears unhappy with you.’ Mallaraj:  ‘What about?’ Jarashankar:  ‘He wished to convince you for a second marriage, and it is said that you dismissed the proposal with disdain.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Just that? Whose message are you carrying?’ Jarashankar:  ‘Samant himself informed me.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Did he tell you who his messenger was?’ Jarashankar:  ‘The queen.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Does he not deserve to be treated with disdain for this stupidity?’ Jarashankar:  ‘He wished to convey that even the queen agreed to this proposal.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Does Samant want me to remarry for the sake of Ratnanagari or for my worldly pleasures? If it was the latter that motivated Samant, he deserves to be treated with utmost disdain. The rulers of Ratnanagari are not moved by worldly pleasures, and if my heir believes that I desire such pleasures, I am pained both by his thinking and his estimation of me. If I were to accept this proposal, both he and I are unfit to be rulers. By my disdain, I showed him the path to acquire the capability to be a ruler. Moreover, he used the queen for something that would have been to her disadvantage. This is the other reason for my obvious disdain.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj, he was motivated by a desire to secure Ratnanagari’s future. You appointed him as the heir apparent and used his mediation with the Bhayat. This idea probably came to him at that time.’ Mallaraj was thoughtful for a while. ‘Yes, I understand. You are probably right. This proposal is the result of his devotion to the state. But I showed disdain for his devotion. I committed an error. Jarashankar you must rectify this mistake. Please explain my reasons to Samant and thank him for it.’ Jarashankar laughed. ‘Maharaj, the king errs and the minister salvages the situation?’ Mallaraj:  ‘This happens every day in other states. For us, this is the first instance.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj, when a king takes a decision without consulting his minister, the king often repents. But if the minister is taken into confidence, even if it leads to repentance later, it is shared by the minister with his king.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Is this advocacy to expand the scope of your authority?’ Jarashankar:  ‘Yes, Maharaj!’ Mallaraj:  ‘I admire your autonomy and courage. How can I not accept my error? But tell me, was Samant not wrong in conveying the message through the queen instead of you? Was I wrong in decrying that choice? You tell me that Samant’s counsel was in the interests of the state, and yet he chose the queen as messenger instead of my minister. Did I have an option but to push him out?’ Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj, your argument has defeated me. But let me come to the main issue. Let us examine the merits of Samant’s message. It has been held desirable that a king should marry more than one wife to have an heir and continue the royal lineage. Samant and the queen both are doing their duty by urging you to do so.’

Mallaraj:  ‘I have considered this. Let me give my arguments briefly. Something that fundamentally violates morality cannot become moral because either Samant or the queen considers it to be moral and part of their duty. A murder committed with the consent of the victim does not become less of a sin for that reason. A person who gives such consent is certainly noble but the one who seeks such consent is a lowly and evil person. One should weigh the costs and benefits of such actions. The costs would far outweigh any possible benefits. A kshatriya married to two or four women is likely to become womanly, and that to me is very harmful. I have decided that this practice must be stopped in the new age. I will set the example for my Bhayat.’ Jarashankar:  ‘But Maharaj, is not the destruction of the royal lineage a matter of grave concern?’ Mallaraj:  ‘A lion cohabits with one lioness; they have one cub. But a pig copulates with many females who give birth to multiple piglets. This destroys the potency of the semen. A lone lion cub is better able to protect the father’s lineage than many piglets. Being with one wife also keeps the passion unsullied. Jarashankar, the kings of Ratnanagari are like lions.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj, this is not a response to my poser. The royal seed, even when dispersed, retains its potency—because it is nurtured in the royal household. Someone born in an average family cannot match that quality. Moreover, I did not suggest that you should sire many progeny. I suggested that you should have multiple wives, one of whom could give you a son.’ Mallaraj:  ‘A clean and smooth mirror gives the best reflection. Its clarity cannot be matched by a multifaceted mirror. Having many wives is like seeing your reflection in a faceted mirror. A progeny born out of a union of deep love for one’s wife is the best.’ Jarashankar:  ‘If the best proves elusive, why should one not settle for something slightly inferior?’ Mallaraj:  ‘If I do not have a son, why can I not have an heir from among my Bhayat. Even they have royal lineage. The one who is closest of kin to the king should be his heir.’

Jarashankar:  ‘That may be so. But they do not have royal upbringing.’ Mallaraj:  ‘That lack has been adequately addressed in the document that the Bhayat have accepted. It will be the obligation of my heirs and my ministers to ensure that the Bhayat cultivate a regal attitude and that their kshatriyahood is strengthened.’ Jarashankar:  ‘There can be a situation where the heir is totally undeserving and is unfit to be educated in the discharge of royal duties. What then?’ Mallaraj:  ‘What prevents us from adopting a suitable heir, even if he were to be distantly related?’ Jarashankar:  ‘This opens up the possibility for intrigue and machinations. Not just that, if an adopted heir has to be selected after the king is deceased, the decision will be taken by women and others.’ Mallaraj:  ‘The right of adoption is only the king’s. That is his sovereign right. If he, during his lifetime, does not adopt, it must be accepted that he wanted his heir to succeed him. No human agency can snatch the throne away from such an heir.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj, I am defeated.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Explain all this to Samant. Tell him that so long as I consider him fit to be my heir, I am not going to adopt anyone. So long as I am alive, I will not forsake or taint my kshatriyahood, my royal pride and my love for my queen by remarriage. If God has to grant me a son, my queen will bear that son. But if God has decided not to grant me a son, even the husband of a hundred queens will remain without an heir. Jarashankar, applaud Samant’s devotion to the kingdom but tell him that brahmins and banias have insatiable desires for a son; it is not for me to have such desires. If the queen is destined to bear a son, she will give birth to one. But if that is not our destiny then I shall not do anything that insults the capability of my Bhayat. But the overriding reason is that I shall not respond to Mena Rani’s love by doing her an injustice. She has sovereign right over my love and I shall not commit the sin of curtailing her right. I would not want to be a witness to injustice and sin committed by my own people. I, as their king, will never commit these sins. Until this point, you had a right to discuss these issues. But now that my principles are known to you, I do not want any further discussion, not even a word more about this. Any breach of this will be regarded as an act of disobedience which shall be punished. Jarashankar, this applies to you, Samant, the queen and all others. You must inform them of my resolve. And if you commit a breach, I will deal with you as sternly as Ram dealt with Laxman.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj!’ Mallaraj:  ‘I have vowed to remain faithful to my wife. No one shall come between my righteous and dutiful wife and me. The decision that we arrived at after consultations cannot be violated even by the king or his minister.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj!’ Mallaraj:  ‘I don’t want to hear a word more. I have given my command.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj, I obey your command.’ Mallaraj:  ‘What were you about to say?’ Jarashankar:  ‘I was about to express my pleasure that it has been my good fortune to serve such a righteous king as you.’ Mallaraj:  ‘I was under the impression that it was the work of bards to sing praises of the king. That even ministers are required to praise the king I only learnt today.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj, please forgive me. It was a wrong choice of words. I am very pleased with your command.’ Mallaraj:  ‘That is better.’ Some years later, God rewarded the unsullied and pure love of Mallaraj and Mena Rani. The queen conceived. Mallaraj intended to inculcate the sanskar fit for a king to the unborn child. One day on his way to the queen’s quarter he ruminated: A man, concerned with the welfare of the unborn child should consider the pregnant woman not as his wife but as a mother-to-be. Hence, he should observe abstinence from the moment of conception till the child is born. He should consider her body to be sacred and allow her to dedicate it fully to the service of the unborn child. The husband should aid her by becoming celibate. After the birth, till the time that the mother breastfeeds the baby the father must act in a way that does not deprive the child of nutrition. This is his duty, both as a father and as a husband. Among the brahmins and the banias, the customs of the elders ensure such conduct. Among them a pregnant woman goes to her natal home and spends the time of her confinement there. Thus, the woman remains free of her mother-in-law’s nagging and the husband’s sexual desires. And thus, she performs her duties towards the baby in the loving care of her mother. But the kings of Ratnanagari have their own traditions. For them the state of householder is not only for the satisfaction of carnal pleasures. They turn celibate whenever required. The king’s mother has affection for his queen. The king’s mother does not tend to be partial towards daughters and harsh on the daughter-in-law, like the commoners. Mallaraj, from today you have become celibate. Mena Rani will now reside in the temple-like palace of your mother. Hastidant, Mallaraj’s elder brother and heir apparent died in the war with Colonel Brave. His widow stayed with Mallaraj’s mother. Hastidant was a martyr and therefore his glory was alive. Hastidant’s widow, for this reason, did not adopt the traditional attire of a widow. On one hand she wore a bangle that signified her married status, but she broke the bangle on the other hand. She did not mourn the death of her husband but lived a sparse life devoid of luxuries. Her life was a complex mix of a woman who, though a widow, lived like a woman whose husband was still alive. She spent her days in prayer and in caring for her mother-in-law. She cultivated a detached attitude to life. Mallaraj’s mother called him and the widowed daughter-in-law to her deathbed and said, ‘Mallaraj, I have lived a life of duty. Now, I must follow your father and your brother to the other world. Do not mourn my death. Your sister-in-law, who has preserved the glory of your brother, should take my place. You and your queen should consider her to be your mother. You are like children to her. I do not have the strength to go on. But in short I have described your duties towards her. You should obey the command issued by me from my deathbed. This is the tradition of the Suryavansh and the royal family of Ratnanagari.’ She then turned towards the young widow and said,

‘Daughter, you must now take my place. We royal kshatriya women do not need any advice. I cannot speak anymore. Daughter, embrace me one last time. Mallaraj, give me your hand.’ Both obeyed her wish. The daughter-in-law embraced her and the son took her hand in his. The mother could speak no more. She seemed to take her daughter-in-law into her arms even as her eyes remained fixed on her son. Her fragile fingers clutched Mallaraj’s hand, but she seemed hesitant to let go of life. Mallaraj said, ‘Mother, I am Mallaraj and this is your daughter-in-law who will henceforth occupy a mother’s place for me. Mother, this is not a moment to worry about anything or anyone. I am your son. I will care for the family and the people of this state just as my father Nagraj did. My brother laid down his life in the battlefield; my father battled on without mourning the loss of his son and when the moment of death came, he allowed his life to ebb away. We kshatriyas travel from this world to the other without any unfulfilled desires. Mother, this is a moment to take the name of our family deity, the sun, and of the God who governs all life. Cherish the moment of being one with their light. Mother, you are a kshatriya. It is our duty to receive Yama the God of Death with you. Mother, a death such as yours is auspicious.’ She looked at her son for one last time and closed her eyes. Her lips parted and people around her heard the faint utterance of the name of God. With that the king’s mother gave up life. From that day on, Mallaraj addressed his sister-in-law as Mataji. He also commanded his queen to respect and care for her as she would for her mother-in- law. Mallaraj was delighted with his idea that his pregnant wife should reside with Mataji. Mena Rani’s unborn child will grow under the protective care of Mataji and imbibe the valour of my brave brother Hastidant, he thought. After years, memories of the elder brother flooded his mind and he was suddenly overwhelmed by sadness. Remembering Hastidant brought copious tears to Mallaraj’s eyes and he wept in silence. Then, as he approached the door to the queen’s quarters, the sadness at the loss of his brother gave way to the joy of fatherhood. The doors were closed. Laughter and banter could be heard. He waited outside and listened. He immediately recognised the voice of Mataji’s personal maid. Mataji had named her Madhumakshika because she buzzed around like a bee. Among the servants she was known as Madhumakh. Madhumakshika said to the queen, ‘Rani Sahib, you must feign a temper tantrum and prepare for a long estrangement from Maharaj.’ ‘But I don’t know how!’ ‘Radhaji had feigned estrangement from Hari. She said, “I will not speak to Hari. He called me Chandramukhi.” You must do something similar.’ Mallaraj opened the door and stepped inside. The queen was on her bed while Madhumakshika sat facing her on the floor. Both stood up as he entered. ‘Madhumakshika, why are you instigating conflict in my house?’ Madhumakshika laughed and said, ‘Maharaj, the science that deals with man-woman relationships speaks of a lovers’ quarrel. It is given to maids like me to spark such lovers’ quarrels.’ ‘So, you do sting!’ ‘It is only by stinging that I give meaning to the name given to me by Mataji.’ ‘Now that you have invoked Mataji’s authority, we will have to accept what you say.’ The king sat down on the bed; the queen stood leaning against the side of the bed. Mallaraj said, ‘Madhumakshika, why should Radhaji object to being called Chandramukhi?’ ‘Maharaj, the moon waxes and wanes. Its light also becomes faint. To call her moonfaced is to insult her. She does not want to wane.’ ‘You should not teach such playful estrangements to us of the sun lineage.’ ‘Maharaj, Raniji was born in the moon lineage; and when you accepted her in marriage you also accepted to partake of the joys of the intellectually pleasing banter that the moon lineage is known for.’ ‘Is that so? We will have to learn all that. We kings of the sun lineage are arid and know nothing of such matters!’

‘Maharaj, the queens of the moon lineage have such light that their mere glance can kill kings of the sun lineage.’ ‘That is true. But Madhumakshika, why are you not with Mataji? What are you doing here?’ ‘Maharaj, I am here as Mataji’s messenger.’ ‘And what is her command?’ ‘Yesterday Raniji visited Mataji, who by looking at Raniji’s body and demeanour knew that she was pregnant and would give birth to a son. The royal astrologer has also come to the same conclusion after his calculations. Therefore, Maharaj, till such time that the queen is delivered of the child and feeds him at her breast, Raniji should come and reside with Mataji. Of course, your palace will always be in Raniji’s heart. Mataji requests that you should permit Raniji to come and reside with her.’ ‘Madhumakshika, Mataji cares for me so much. I am indeed grateful to her. I see that her wish is an act of grace. We shall act upon her wish before the sun sets today.’ ‘Maharaj, the auspicious time for such a departure is only tomorrow. And therefore, I was trying to teach Raniji about a lovers’ quarrel for tonight.’ ‘Have it your way. But if you taught her so much in the few moments that you had with her, what will you not teach her in the next two years that you will be around her?’ ‘Maharaj, I am a mere servant. All I can do is to hold up a lamp and light the path. A good kshatriya woman would see far into the distance with this light. Maharaj, your attendants can hand you the sword, but it is you who wield it with your might.’ ‘All right, what are the other commandments of Mataji?’ ‘Once Raniji shifts to Mataji’s palace, you will have to regularly visit her to inculcate the values of the royal family in the unborn child. These visits are also necessary so that when Mataji is no longer alive, the traditional knowledge of care and nurture of pregnant royal women is carried forward. Maharaj, there is another purpose of these visits. For a kshatriya woman it is impossible to know which meeting with her husband will be her last one. Therefore, it is not advisable to deprive a kshatriya woman of the opportunity of seeing her husband, except when he is at war. Moreover, a pregnant woman craves to see her husband and receive his wisdom. When such craving is fulfilled the unborn child also receives the image of its father. Therefore, Maharaj, though you shall be celibate, to this limited extent you shall be a householder. According to Mataji, this is also a tradition of your family.’ ‘Madhumakshika, I will observe this family tradition.’ ‘Maharaj, the moon approaches Venus only when it is surrounded by other stars. Similarly, you should visit the pregnant queen only when she is surrounded by her maids.’ ‘I will follow this ritual perfectly.’ ‘Among the low-born, pregnant women have debased cravings because of the lowly company they keep. But Maharaj, in your family, ways of promoting noble cravings are adopted. By repeated darshan of the ascetics of Sundargiri, the soul of the foetus is ennobled. The pregnant queen is taken to the temples of Surgram. This pilgrimage to a beautiful and holy place gives a clear intellect to the foetus. Maharaj, when the pregnant queen looks up at the high ranges of Sundargiri, the foetus learns to aspire for higher things in life. When the pregnant queen breathes in the cool breeze of the ocean and looks out at the far horizon, the foetus acquires a sense of beauty, quiet equanimity and foresight. When she walks through your beautiful lush forests, breathing in the fragrance of flowers in bloom and listening to birdsong, the foetus experiences the joy as well. When the brave kshatriya woman hears the roars of lions and tigers, the foetus also acquires the first lessons in kshatriya valour. Maharaj, you must ensure that the pregnant queen is taken to all these places and that her comfort is ensured. You should also accompany the queen on these pilgrimages and visits whenever possible.’ ‘Madhumakshika, I will gladly obey all these commands. Please convey a request to Mataji: if possible you should be a constant companion to the queen during this period.’

‘Mataji has already taken this decision, Maharaj. These were the main requests. But she has also made some other arrangements. I should inform you of them and seek your consent.’ ‘Mataji’s decisions are always taken with our welfare in mind, hence I accept them even before you narrate them. But I do wish to learn about them and experience the joy I know it will bring.’ ‘There will be a few clever maids and a few who can remain in constant service of the queen. The elderly wife of Shastri Maharaj, the experienced wife of Samant Mulu, some three or four young wives of Bhayat and other maids will give the queen company and care for her. Mataji will of course be there. But she does not utter the name of any man other than your elder brother. When Subhadra was pregnant with Abhimanyu, Shri Krishna narrated stories of valour to her. Similarly, Mataji intends to narrate stories of your elder brother’s valour to the queen. Maharaj, when Prahlad’s mother was pregnant with him, Narad Muni also told stories of devotion to him. Maharaj, the character of the child is formed by the stories that are narrated to the pregnant mother.’ ‘Madhumakshika, how can I ever express my gratitude to Mataji? I do not remember my own mother having to worry so much about me. The care and concern shown by Mataji is a thousand-fold higher. Rani, whether I am alive or not, you shall never forget the debt of gratitude that we owe Mataji. You must ensure that our children also remember it always. Rani, what services can we offer Mataji? She must require so many things! We have appointed servants to care for her, but there must be many shortcomings that remain unseen. But the very qualities that enabled her to bear the separation from my brother also allow her to cope with all our shortcomings. Rani, Mataji’s love for us is limitless.’ Mallaraj wiped his tears. Madhumakshika:  ‘Maharaj, it is your tender heart which has placed you in this condition. Your compassion is in keeping with the noblemen of this royal household. Maharaj, a Sanskrit verse aptly captures your noble character. Very few good men are there who, full of nectar of holiness in thought, word and action and pleasing the three worlds with numerous acts of beneficence, rejoice at heart in ever magnifying the minute good qualities of others.⟨fn:96⟩ ‘Maharaj, Mataji is not doing you a favour. This unborn child is the future of Ratnanagari and to care for this child is the principal responsibility of the queen mother. Maharaj, from the day she entered this palace, Rani Sahib has cared for all of Mataji’s needs. A kalpavriksha grants one a boon only when one seeks it, but Raniji’s care goes much beyond that. Even before Mataji expresses a need, Raniji sees to it that it is met. This act of selfless service has melted Mataji’s heart. Her love for Rani Sahib is inexhaustible. I am a witness to this, Maharaj. Mataji’s concern for Raniji is like the rain giving back to the river the water which made rain possible.’ At the conclusion of this little speech, Madhumakshika sought the king’s consent to return to Mataji’s service. In due course of time, the queen gave birth to Maniraj. As the child began to walk and talk, the responsibility of his nurturance came to the men folk. Mallaraj relieved Mataji and Mena Rani of the responsibility and assumed direct charge of Maniraj’s education. Before handing over young Maniraj to his father the king, Mataji sent a message through Madhumakshika. The message was as follows: ‘Maharaj, Mataji wishes you to be acquainted with the care and nurturance that Maniraj received so that you follow similar principles while raising him. This care began with his mother’s milk. Maharaj, this young lion cub has been raised on the milk of his lioness-like royal mother. He has not been robbed of his right by being given the milk of women of inferior castes. Maharaj, eventually a child must leave his mother’s womb and her breast. Now he will come under your care. He has the seeds of manly power. It is your responsibility to nurture, enhance and augment this power so that he grows up to possess powers and abilities greater than what you possess. Mataji requests you to ensure that no partial measures are taken in this effort. Maharaj, we, the worldly beings have to deal with joys and sorrows. This is inevitable. The youthful phase is the period when one must learn to contend with sorrow. Maharaj, a man who wants an active day should spend a peaceful night undisturbed by nightmares. Similarly, this precious child of yours, who will have to wage difficult battles in his youth, should be exposed to nothing but joy as a child. Maharaj, Mataji has ensured that this kshatriya child does not shed a single tear, and has kept him away from tendencies common to women. These were her instructions to Raniji and all the maids in their service. Maharaj, she urges you to show even greater care. Do not allow this tender plant to wither away. Maharaj, a childhood free of worries and filled with joy is a right of every child. Do not please curtail this right in any form. Maharaj, hitherto Mataji and Raniji tended to this child just as a gardener tends his tender plants. A garden that is a responsibility of many gardeners can go untended. Similarly, a child who receives instructions from many cannot obey anyone. His heart is torn asunder. Maharaj, you are his father. Please appoint an affectionate tutor, and the two of you be his instructors and tend to him as a gardener would. Maharaj, it is said that a child’s ears should be pierced by someone other than the mother. Therefore, assign these difficult tasks to this other person. The child should have no doubt that the other person’s authority over him is not complete. But we observe among animals of the cat family that the mother carries the child in her mouth; no one else can do this delicate task. Therefore, the tutor that you appoint must also be under your constant vigil. You have to make sure that the tutor does not put his teeth on the tender skin of your son. Maharaj, you have to be as vigilant as a bird hatching her eggs. A royal child needs protection even from his tutor. ‘Maharaj, even mature and intelligent adults fail to carry out all instructions fully. You will certainly not expect your tender-aged son to do so, but you have to resist similar expectations that others might have of him even in their dreams. Maharaj, a bitter pill has to be sugar coated. You must encourage everyone around him to follow this way. A child can be made to do his work by encouragement. ‘Maharaj, do not allow ordinary men and servants to go anywhere near your son. We have not allowed maids to go close to him; you must also ensure the same. Women out of passionate desire for their husbands give the child away to their maids and the child then learns many undesirable traits from the maids. Your son has hitherto slept either with Raniji or Mataji. He has not spent a night away from either of them. He has not spent time unobserved with anyone else but me, because I am trusted by you. Maharaj, you will be occupied with matters of state and hence cannot be expected to watch over him all the time. But you must ensure that apart from his tutor, the young prince is not influenced by anyone else; he is like the son of Indra and needs the protection of Brihaspati. Maharaj, you can think of many things that we women have not been able to.’ Mallaraj took young prince Maniraj’s hand. He sent a servant to call his minister. As they waited for Jarashankar, he engaged his young prince in playful conversation that also tested the boy’s intelligence. ‘Kumar, will you not miss Mataji?’ Maniraj:  ‘I will not like it, but just as you have to stay away from Mataji, I will also learn to do so.’ Madhumakshika:  ‘Maharaj, his answer lacks nothing. His response fulfills his obligation towards both you and Mataji; it reveals that as the king of Ratnanagari, he would be righteous and discerning.’ Mallaraj looked visibly pleased. He held on to his son and asked, ‘I am required to look after the affairs of the state. And what will you do?’ Maniraj:  ‘Please allow me to be around you when you perform state duties. Please show me how one rules. I will accompany you; I will observe what you point out to me and I will obey your command.’ Madhumakshika:  ‘Maharaj, the young prince has asked that he be initiated into the intricate art of statecraft. You have to decide if you would like to grant him his wish.’ The young prince raised his hand and placed it over Madhumakshika’s mouth and said, ‘Madhumakh, who allowed you to butt in while I was speaking to Rajaji? You should not interrupt our conversation.’ Madhumakshika bent down to embrace the little prince. Tears filled her eyes. She said, ‘Kumar, may you have a long life. Maharaj, just as the first rays of the sun break the spell of darkness, the young prince, even before commencing his education of statecraft, has conveyed to me that my rights over him are over. He has desired that a woman such as me will not exercise any influence over him.’ Maniraj:  ‘Madhumakh, you are still buzzing around. You don’t follow instructions!’ Maniraj turned to his father and said, ‘Maharaj, Mataji told me that the king punishes all those who do wrong. Now it is up to you.’ Madhumakshika laughed and said, ‘So, you have reached the limits of your power?’ Maniraj:  ‘I will not speak with you.’ Madhumakshika:  ‘Maharaj, the young prince understands that he can issue orders; he is intolerant of disobedience and he told you that it was your right to award punishment. And yet, he gave me the punishment that a child could give, by refusing to talk to me. Maharaj, the young prince has all the qualities required of a ruler. They have already begun to emerge in your presence, just as seeds sprout in sunlight.’ Maniraj:  ‘Maharaj, I put my view before you. You get this Madhumakh out of here or you order her to shut up and stop buzzing. Today, I wish to talk with you. I do not like what she says.’ Madhumakshika:  ‘Kumar, I will leave immediately if you ask me to.’ Maniraj:  ‘I am not throwing you out. You go into your hive and stop buzzing.’ Madhumakshika:  ‘All right. I will keep silent.’ Maniraj:  ‘That is good.’ Everyone was quiet. The young prince stared at Madhumakshika, who remained silent. Then he said, ‘Madhumakh, why don’t you speak?’ Madhumakshika just laughed. Maniraj:  ‘Why don’t you speak?’ Mallaraj:  ‘You forbade her. How can she speak?’ Maniraj:  ‘She should speak when I talk to her.’

Mallaraj:  ‘What do you want her to say?’ Maniraj:  ‘She told you everything that Mataji had told her to. But last night, Raniji and she had said something to me. About that she has not uttered a word.’ Mallaraj:  ‘And what was that?’ Maniraj:  ‘Madhumakh will tell you.’ Madhumakshika:  ‘I have forgotten.’ Maniraj:  ‘How can you forget? Say it! Raniji doesn’t call you a liar for nothing!’ Madhumakshika:  ‘She only calls me jhoothi because I eat from her plate.’ Maniraj:  ‘Whatever it is. Say it.’ Madhumakshika:  ‘What am I to say? Give me a hint.’ Maniraj:  ‘That, a real horse and not a wooden play horse, and so on.’ Madhumakshika laughed. ‘Yes, Maharaj, we have given a promise to the prince before he would allow himself to be brought here.’ Mallaraj:  ‘What is that promise?’ Meanwhile Jarashankar walked in. He sat beside the prince, gently lifted him into his lap and said, ‘Maharaj, why are all these questions being posed to Kumarshri?’ Mallaraj:  ‘Kumar will no longer stay with Mataji. He has come to stay with us. But before coming here, he has sought some assurances, it seems.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Is that so? What has he sought?’ Maniraj:  ‘I will no longer play with my wooden horse. I should be given a real horse today.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Anything else?’ Maniraj:  ‘I will not play. I will learn to ride horses, wield a sword and I will give up the company of women. Instead, I will move about in the company of Pradhanji and Maharaj and I will also attend the court rituals.’

Jarashankar:  ‘Madhumakshika, was this the promise made?’ Madhumakshika:  ‘Yes, Pradhanji.’ Maniraj:  ‘From now on, I will have my meals with Maharaj.’ Jarashankar:  ‘For that you need his consent.’ Maniraj:  ‘Either you or Madhumakh get that consent. I will not ask.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Kumarshri, one needs to ask one’s father.’ Maniraj:  ‘Mataji said that kshatriyas cannot be supplicants.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Then how do they obtain what they want?’ Maniraj:  ‘By their own effort, by the use of force and by wielding the sword.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Then you should also obtain it by those means.’ Maniraj:  ‘I have already obtained a promise from Madhumakh—if she does not get it for me, I will have nothing more to do with her. She will be forced to get it for me.’ Madhumakshika:  ‘Kumar, I will not be around you henceforth.’ Maniraj:  ‘Where do you think you are going? I will block your way if you leave without fulfilling your promise!’ Jarashankar:  ‘Kumar, Maharaj will honour your word.’ Maniraj:  ‘I will believe it only if he issues a command.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Take that command as given.’ Maniraj looked up expectantly at Mallaraj. The king could no longer contain his laughter. Maniraj:  ‘Raniji told me that no one can take a single step without your order. Why is Pradhanji taking decisions without asking you, Maharaj?’ Mallaraj:  ‘You should ask him that.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Kumar, Maharaj’s pleasure is a command in itself.’ Maniraj:  ‘All right. I will also please him. Then I shall be able to have my way with him.’ Jarashankar:  ‘That is correct.’

Madhumakshika:  ‘Maharaj, I now seek your permission to hand over Kumar to your care and take your leave.’ Maniraj:  ‘Madhumakh, Mataji taught me that a king and his prince must also learn to reward the services given to them. So, stay.’ Everyone looked on in surprise. Maniraj:  ‘Maharaj, I wish to give all my toys to Madhumakh’s son. With your permission I will go to Mataji’s palace and hand them over to her.’ Mallaraj was pleased that his son had learnt gratitude. He took the young prince into his lap and said, ‘Kumar, you must always remember what Mataji has taught you. Go with Madhumakshika and reward her appropriately. Madhumakshika, till such time that I make adequate arrangements for Kumar, let him stay with Mataji. I will call for him soon.’ Maniraj:  ‘Maharaj, I will not play with toys anymore.’ Mallaraj laughed and said, ‘Of course, Kumar, you will no longer play with toys. You will have a horse to ride and swords and a bow and arrows to play with. Pradhanji will have them sent to you without delay.’ Maniraj:  ‘Who will teach me?’ Mallaraj:  ‘Even that shall be arranged.’ Maniraj:  ‘When will you call for me?’ Mallaraj:  ‘I will take you to the fort in the evening.’ Maniraj:  ‘Madhumakh, come, let’s go. You go and fetch your son so that I can give him my toys.’ Madhumakshika:  ‘You can give them to me. I will hand them over to him.’ Maniraj:  ‘No. You will keep them in the house and not give them to him. You bring him to me so I can give them to him personally. If you take them away, I will deal with you harshly.’ Madhumakshika:  ‘Do what pleases you. Now we must take Maharaj’s leave.’

Maniraj placed his hand over her mouth. Madhumakshika removed his hand and asked, ‘What are you doing, Kumar? Don’t you want to go?’ Maniraj:  ‘Stay here. We will leave after the Maharaj leaves.’ Madhumakshika:  ‘What shall we do till such time? Maharaj has to attend to other matters.’ Maniraj:  ‘We will listen to the conversation between Maharaj and Pradhanji.’ Madhumakshika:  ‘We are not permitted to listen to the secret talks of the Maharaj and his minister.’ Maniraj:  ‘All right. Then take his leave.’ Meanwhile the king and his minister had begun to attend to other matters. Madhumakshika said, ‘Maharaj, I seek your permission to leave. I will take the prince with me for the time being, but before I go I wish to add—insignificant though I am—to the message that I carried from Mataji. I humbly urge you to listen.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Speak.’ Madhumakshika:  ‘Maharaj, even to ordinary folk, a son is precious. That a son should be prized and valued by a king is not surprising. The Shruti says, “Son, you are born of my body. Your place is in my heart. Son, you are my soul. Live a hundred springs.” ‘Maharaj, a son is an embodiment of his father. He must also be imbued with the father’s heart. Just as a new banyan tree grows from the roots of the old tree, mother and father give birth to their progeny. Parents and progeny are of the same lineage. Not just that, they also share a common soul. The son acquires the characteristics of his father’s soul. A son of the king acquires a kingly soul. This ancestral soul of the royal lineage is the true wealth of the king’s people. The body and the soul are distinct, but the body exists because of the soul. The soul is unseen, the body is manifest. It grows and withers because of the soul. A lifeless seed cannot grow. But the seed of the body gives birth to another body because the seed is alive with the soul. This child, in due course, will attain maturity. Maharaj, do not consider the seed to be separate from the tree; do not consider the child as distinct from the adult form that he will acquire. The tree is contained in the seed and assumes its form in due course of time. The seed manifests itself in branches, in flowers and in their fragrance. The soul is concealed by the body; it is without form. But if one were to ask as to what the soul does, the answer would be that the roots that reach the sky and beyond and the seed that grows in the mother’s womb are both manifestations of the soul. O Maharaj! Your son is a manifestation of that soul. The soul of this child is not the body of your son. You and he share a common soul. His soul is imbued with the light of your soul. This child is capable of spreading this light through this land and your populace. His light combines his royal lineage and his personal qualities. He is like a flower that embodies the full glory of the tree. Maharaj, this seed, this child, this light must be nurtured in its delicate stage. It is your duty. The brahmin sages join their soul with the souls of their disciples and create brahmatma. Similarly, a king should join his soul with the soul of his son and create rajatma, a kingly soul. This soul should inhabit the body politic. This can be attained by a self-aware king like you. Wretched though I be, Maharaj, I request you to strive towards this. Maharaj, I clearly see this young prince growing like a grand tree. It is incumbent upon you to ensure that he grows into a grand figure. It will be the result of the power of your soul. Maharaj, I have become verbose and loquacious, but it is my love for this light of yours which shines through your son that forces me to speak. Otherwise, I would never be so bold as to speak thus before you. Maharaj, I have said what I wanted to. I now seek your permission to take your son back to Mataji’s palace.’ Maniraj listened attentively, his gaze shifting from the face of the maid to the faces of the king and his minister. When she had finished, even before Mallaraj could respond, he tugged at Madhumakshika’s sari and said, ‘Madhumakh, are you done?’ Madhumakshika:  ‘Yes. Do you have anything to add?’ Maniraj:  ‘Unless you give me your word, I will not accompany you.’ Madhumakshika:  ‘What word?’

Maniraj:  ‘When Bharat was engrossed in counting the teeth of a lion, Shakuntala and Dushyant forgot about him; neither of them spoke to Bharat.’ Madhumakshika:  ‘What about that?’ Maniraj:  ‘You should tell Raniji that I should not be placed in the situation of Bharat. She tells me stories of Luv-Kush and Bharat all day long.’ Everyone laughed. Madhumakshika:  ‘Do I control Raniji? You should tell her yourself.’ Maniraj:  ‘When we came here, you spoke to Rajaji and got what I wanted. Now you claim that you have no influence over Raniji? Then why did you give me your word? I don’t want to come back with you!’ This produced more laughter. Mallaraj:  ‘Kumar, go with her. You should talk to Raniji yourself.’ Maniraj:  ‘I will not ask Raniji for anything. I am a prince and we get what we want by the power of our force. If you behave like King Dushyant, I will not like it at all. I would like you to talk to me.’ The king and his minister smiled. Madhumakshika also smiled bashfully and said, ‘Kumar, you will bind me to a promise, but you will not make a request. Come, let us go. I will do what you want.’ Maniraj:  ‘Be careful. If you do not keep your word, I will deal with you appropriately.’ The two of them finally left, still deep in argument. The king’s gaze followed them. The prince led the maid by her hand, forcing her to walk faster. The king followed them till they disappeared from view, his face glowing with pride. The minister looked on with delight at the king’s proud, indulgent gaze. As the king was looking intently at the lovely face of his son, with one eye as steady as lotus in a breezeless spot, his intense joy could not be contained in himself, like the flood of the great ocean at the appearance of the moon.⟨fn:97⟩

The joy of watching one’s son is similar. Jarashankar did not have a son, and for a moment, he was saddened by this lack. He had a nephew, Vidya Chatura, who was like a son to him. Vidya Chatura was both virtuous and intelligent. He considered the possibility of appointing Vidya Chatura as a tutor to Maniraj. This possibility allowed him to forget his sorrow. But it gave rise to a new concern. How could he recommend his own nephew? He thought of using the advice given by Madhumakshika to bring up this matter for discussion. But on second thoughts, Jarashankar discarded the idea. He said to himself: My responsibility is to serve the king according to the principles of Dharmashastra. I commit an act of treachery even if I entertain a selfish thought. I will not bring up the matter. I will wait till Maharaj himself has a use for Vidya Chatura. Mallaraj interrupted his thoughts. ‘Jarashankar, we cannot forget the commands of Mataji and the advice Madhumakshika gave us. A father has additional duty towards his son. I am concerned as to how Kumar should be trained in statecraft.’ ‘Maharaj, the mode of instructing the princes is part of our Shastras and have been practiced in your family for generations.’ ‘True, but the Shastras also give us an injunction to act according to the changing times. We must consider that as well.’ ‘Maharaj, hitherto the Muslims ruled over India. Even during those years, our ancient wisdom proved itself useful to your family.’ ‘And it will continue to be useful. But we must not consider knowledge that can be acquired only through our own language. Vidur saved the Pandavas in the palace of lacquer through the knowledge of the Mleccha language. Yudhishthir used the illusion of the demon Maya in his palace. Bhima married a demon and Arjun, a Naga woman. The brahmins think that knowledge can only be brahminical. But the kshatriyas accept knowledge of all people and all lands.’ ‘What is your suggestion, Maharaj?’ ‘The English will be the sovereign rulers of India. We must make use of their knowledge. The rulers of Ratnanagari must learn our traditional ancestral knowledge for the welfare of our people, but they must also learn English knowledge so that they do not become helpless in the face of change. This is their duty.’ Jarashankar appeared deep in thought. ‘What are you thinking about?’ ‘Maharaj, statecraft is a complex subject.’ ‘How so?’ ‘Once they learn English, they will not submit to family traditions. They will become conceited.’ ‘Jarashankar, Rajputs must always look for victory. This is their duty. They should alter their ancient customs according to the times if necessary. Rajputs do not submit to anyone. Now if they become slaves to tradition, they will be reduced to slavery themselves. Rajputs sent their daughters to the zanana of the Mughal emperors. These marriages were intended to win over the Mughals. Many Rajput kings stayed in the outskirts of Delhi and held sway over the Mughal court in Delhi. Such Rajputs and Hindus are around even now.’ ‘That credit should go to Shivaji. But for Shivaji, everyone would have been converted to Islam.’ ‘No, Jarashankar. There were two other means as well. Persuasion, inducement, confidence and coercion are the old means. It is those who also acquire mastery over the new means who will ultimately emerge superior. The Rajputs lacked one of these means and they were forced to retreat. Shivaji also failed to use all the means possible and hence his state came to be ruled by the brahmins, and after them the English. Jarashankar, those who aspire to the knowledge of statecraft must garner all kinds of arms, ammunition and expertise in all kinds of means so that, if the need arises, they can use them at the opportune moment.’ ‘But, Maharaj, once we give up our ancient ways, we shall break all limits. If you decide to change the course, please ensure that it is contained within certain limits, or else we shall give rise to Bhasmasur, demons who will char all that they touch.’ ‘We of the Suryavansh fight demons with an army of monkeys and bears. Even Shivaji owed his success to such a plan.’
