‘If you go looking for monkeys and bears, what will your kshatriyas do?’ ‘My kshatriyas who have descended from the gods will not become monkeys just by dressing up like them. My heirs will use their English knowledge to build a bridge across the ocean and enter the abode of the monkeys. Jarashankar, I have thought it through.’ ‘But, Maharaj, you must secure the banks before the waters flow.’ ‘That is true. If they retain the good sense to work for the welfare of the people, that in itself would set limits to their actions. If the people change but not their king, it will lead to clashes. Therefore, everyone in my family and the state should learn English; but so long as we remain conscious that the objective is to grasp the intentions of the English, none of them shall imitate the ways of the English. This would secure our banks in one way. The other way of securing ourselves would be to take what is best and lasting from our age-old traditions. We need not impose any other limits. Jarashankar, that is it. I have made up my mind. Show me a way of educating Maniraj—that is your duty. Unless the kings of Ratnanagari are able to grasp the knowledge that comes their way from all the four directions, darkness will envelop them. That cannot be permitted at any cost.’ ‘Maharaj, when our children live with someone else they become like the foster family, and we lose control over them. A child reared on a foreign language will respect neither you nor your customs.’ ‘The sons of kshatriyas have to be acquainted with the land, the swords and the shields of the enemy. They have to learn the language and customs of the enemy. Women and brahmins stay at home and look after it, while kshatriyas have to protect the world outside the home.’ ‘That is correct. But it is undesirable that they become slaves to the ways of the enemy.’ ‘Of course! The danger is clear. One will come under the influence of the other when one learns their language and customs even for the purpose of self-protection; this danger is part of any diplomatic warfare. Those who enter the battlefield will either win or lose, will die or get wounded. Jarashankar, I have made up my mind. It is now your responsibility to ensure that my instructions are followed. Go, search for a Dronacharya for my Arjun.’ ‘Yes, it is my responsibility and duty to execute the commands of my king. But to find a brahmin-like Dronacharya to teach English is as easy as looking for a son born to a barren woman.’ Mallaraj laughed. ‘Jarashankar, those who go out wailing come back with the news of someone’s death. You will certainly not find a way for anything that goes against your opinion.’ ‘Maharaj, this accusation saddens me. But you will admit that it is impossible to find someone who is equally learned in English and our Shastras.’ ‘Drona was the teacher of the Kauravas. But the sons of Pandu learnt the art of war from him. My minister should be equal to such a task.’ ‘Maharaj, that is true. Your idea is best. But a man well versed in the knowledge of the enemy will occupy an undeserved position of influence in our state. The prince is very young and impressionable. If you want that his mind should be coloured by the contact with English knowledge and customs, then it is your desire. Arjun was mature enough to stealthily take the best out of Dronacharya. Dronacharya could not capture and subjugate Arjun’s mind. Maharaj, Maniraj is still a child. Sitaji had become infatuated with the golden deer. You are a king, and kings can become adamant.’ ‘Jarashankar, I am pleased with your autonomous views and the accusations that you make to prevent me from taking my chosen path. I am pleased with you. You may ask for anything you like.’ ‘Maharaj, a lion does not allow his teeth to break and kshatriya kings do not tolerate any disobedience of their command. O you best of kings, eminent universal sovereigns like you, who are made by the Creator the receptacles of supreme valour, who, by their peculiar might, subdue kings having a large force of rut- shedding elephants, and who are distinguished by their sense of self-esteem and pride, do not put up with the infringement of their command for any reason whatsoever, just as the lords of beasts who are created by the Creator as the store-houses of strength, who by their fierce vigour conquer the rut-shedding leaders of elephant herds, and whose dignity and haughtiness are distinctly manifested, do not brook the breaking of their jaws on any account.⟨fn:98⟩ ‘But Maharaj, you have shown exemplary patience. You permit me to disobey you. This is a sign of your grace and also of forbearance.’ ‘You have often recited that verse to me. A sovereign ruler cannot allow for disobedience. But we have a powerful ruler above us. I accepted their authority on your advice. Who but you could remind me that I am no longer a sovereign ruler by this act of disobedience?’ ‘Forgive me! Maharaj, please forgive me! I am but your servant and had no intention to hurt you by disobedience.’ ‘Then you must obey my instructions, Jarashankar. I will not be satisfied with my prince becoming a frog in the well. You were instrumental in the treaty that we signed with the English. If the acquisition of their knowledge is as difficult as crossing the black waters of the sea, the prince must do so. The prince must swim across the seas and enter the Lanka-like fortress of the English. It is up to him to drown or swim. We shall take precautions that he does not drown. But the rulers of Ratnanagari do not stop taking risks for the fear of drowning. Maniraj will learn from the teachers of our enemy.’ ‘Maharaj, I accept defeat. I will find a way of obeying your command and taking the necessary precautions.’ ‘You may or may not be able to find a way. But I can show you a way.’ ‘Your suggestion cannot but be the best.’ ‘Appoint your nephew Vidya Chatura. He has studied English; he will also obey you. He has made a good impression on me.’ Jarashankar was satisfied. It was good for both Vidya Chatura and Maniraj. Mallaraj’s injunctions could also be adequately met by it. This seemed to be the best way. He said, ‘Maharaj, you are very kind. I do not know if the appointment of Vidya Chatura would be an act of obedience or an acceptance of your kindness. But if it is an act of kindness, Maharaj, please free me from it and I will give you an opportunity to test my obedience.’ ‘One should not argue about a king’s order and an injunction of the Shastras. This is what our Shastras tell us. But you clearly disobey this injunction.’ ‘Very well, Maharaj,’ and with that Jarashankar left. Mallaraj thought: A king must ensure that the next generation is ready to take responsibility; this is a necessary obligation of the king. One would need a minister to take Jarashankar’s place. The reasons why Maniraj must learn English, the new minister should also know English for the very same reasons. Vidya Chatura will benefit from Jarashankar’s knowledge, experience and wisdom; he will mix as easily as sugar in milk. But that will not be so easy for others. Vidya Chatura is knowledgeable both in English and Sanskrit. It will not take him long to gain in experience like Jarashankar. The old days are swiftly passing us by. New times are upon us. In these times of transition we need a person who can keep note of all that which is passing us by and capture what is yet to come. Jarashankar, Vidya Chatura and I together will do this. The three of us together shall pave the way for Maniraj. We must ensure that he becomes capable of galloping on this path and that he acquires even greater intelligence and acumen than all of us. With such thoughts Mallaraj got engrossed in other matters of state.
chapters.summary: Mallaraj firmly asserts his principles to Jarashankar regarding royal succession and remarriage, while envisioning a modern education for his heir, Maniraj, to lead the kingdom.

chapters.title: The First Surge of Foreign Rule
paragraphs: The First Surge of Foreign Rule Dear reader, in the second part of this novel you will recall that we read about the instructions that Mallaraj gave Vidya Chatura before he took charge as Maniraj’s tutor.⟨fn:99⟩ Mallaraj was alert to ensure that these instructions were carried out. The king also followed the advice given by Madhumakshika. He gave complete autonomy to Vidya Chatura but ensured that this autonomy was not abused. One day, Mallaraj took Kumar and Vidya Chatura on an excursion to Sundargiri. The king’s tent was pitched on top of the hill and afforded a magnificent view. As Mallaraj reclined on a cushion embroidered with golden thread, his fingers toyed with his moustache and his gaze was fixed on the sea. At some distance from the king’s tent Vidya Chatura and Maniraj strolled about; the young prince was holding Vidya Chatura’s hand. Kumar pointed to the sea and asked, ‘Chaturji, how big is the sea?’ ‘You have seen the map of India; the sea is almost twice as big as the landmass of India.’ ‘What comes after the sea?’ ‘Land.’ ‘Does it have people?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘What comes after that land?’ ‘The ocean.’ ‘What after that?’

‘More land.’ ‘Even that land is populated?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘What kind of people are they?’ ‘The English Sahibs come from that land.’ ‘Do they have a king?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘Does their king have a prince?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘The Sahibs come to our land. Do our people go to theirs?’ ‘Very few.’ ‘Why do so many Sahibs come here, Chaturji?’ ‘To rule over us.’ ‘Please tell Maharaj that we should also go to their land and rule over them for a while.’ ‘You could tell him that yourself, Kumar.’ Mallaraj overheard this conversation with interest. Maniraj walked over to his father’s tent followed by Vidya Chatura. He came up to the king and said, ‘Maharaj, let us go to the land of the Sahibs to rule. I don’t like it here.’ Mallaraj was deeply saddened, but he disguised his sadness with laughter and said, ‘Kumar, I have grown old. But you could do that once you grow up. What do you say, Vidya Chatura?’ Mallaraj’s eyes had unshed tears as he said, ‘Kshatriyahood has been widowed. The aspirations of Rajputs are no different from the desires of the son of a poor widow.’ Mallaraj took the prince into his lap and his eyes looked out to the sea, searching the horizon. His lips were pursed and he remained pensive for a while. Then quite abruptly, he stood up. Mallaraj walked up to the edge of the hill with his hand on his sword, his brows furrowed. Finally, he instructed Vidya Chatura in a grave voice, ‘Vidya Chatura, get yourself a blank notebook which you must keep with you at all times. You will be required to write down what I dictate to you; Maniraj will read it once he attains maturity. The writing should be such that it touches his heart irrespective of whether I am alive or dead.

Secondly, the day we return to Ratnanagari, you will remind me to call my Bhayat, their sons, my son and Jarashankar. All of them and I will meet every day at an appointed time, and you shall tell us the story of the British people. We have been hearing stories from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and accounts of the valour of our ancestors. This would be something like it. You can spend as much money as you want to acquire the books you need. You must read to us their story from the very beginning, from the time they were in the state of monkeys till the present times. Moreover, you shall read to us about the condition of the French, the Russians, the Dutch, the Portuguese and the Muslims. But your special focus should be on the descriptions of their wars, their methods of persuasion, inducement and conceit, their statecraft, the countries they visit or inhabit and their activities there as also about their enemies and friends, the people who wield influence among them, the condition of their people, their joys and sorrows, their methods of fabricating canons for war and industries for times of peace, and about their equivalents of our kshatriyas, brahmins and vaishyas. You must learn their secrets about all these things. You must steal the secrets of their arts and learn the way their mind works. Vidya Chatura you must learn, understand and steal all these things and narrate them to us in our language. And you must instruct the prince—the beacon of our hope—in their knowledge as per our instructions. ‘Vidya Chatura, at the right time Kumar must be initiated in our traditional knowledge of the kshatriyas; but in this you cannot be his teacher. Whoever becomes his teacher—native or foreigner, friend or foe—the prince must learn the use of swords and canons alike; he must learn to duel with a brave warrior as also learn the art of commandeering an army similarly constituted. These arts might appear to be futile at present, but I want to ensure that my son and all Rajputs of his generation become experts in these arts. I want to keep the knowledge of these arts alive just as the sacrificial fire is kept alive eternally. I know that this difficult task cannot be accomplished without the help and cooperation of the English. Someday, I will explain to them that their self-interests and our interests are one and the same; the wise English will comprehend this. Vidya Chatura, by these actions we are verily sowing the seeds of a new statecraft. The sowing of the seeds is my responsibility; your duty, Vidya Chatura, will be to be a good minister to me and my son. I have no hesitation in sharing this secret with Jarashankar’s nephew. ‘For this vision to be realised, the sons of my Bhayat should surround my son and contribute to his light, just as the stars surround the moon. The country is passing through a dark night. The stars and the moon must shine together with each other’s light. Vidya Chatura, hitherto my Bhayat have helped us in times of war, and we in turn have cared for them. They sacrificed their lives, and we awarded them land in the form of garas, their traditional inheritance. Now, under British rule, we no longer need their sacrifice and we will not be able to award them any garas; even holding on to the garas we have is going to be difficult. Previously, when Bhayat died in war, their garas was re-distributed to the new generation of Bhayat. Even when we shared our land with them, our own land share did not decline. Now, we will have to award garas to the new generation of Bhayat, but the land will not come back to us—because we will not lose our Bhayat to war. As a result the lands owned by us will diminish and with that our power will decline. Consequently, the British will become more powerful. I have taken certain other steps to arrest this dangerous process. But the wise have likened the mind to the fickleness of a courtesan. The king will have no dealings with Bhayat who fail to prove their usefulness. Selfish and inept Bhayat will not have the opportunity to serve the king—this is one of the weakest links in the state. One will find people who hold the two ends of the chain and make us dance like monkeys. Vidya Chatura, it is my duty to ensure that no foreigner takes control of this chain. You have to find bonds of affection that will act like glue between Kumar and the sons of the Bhayat so that we can mend this broken chain. There may come a time when we will have to wage a war for this country. Shalivahan made a battle-ready army out of soldiers of clay. If these new generations of kshatriyas are joined by bonds of affection, their ancestors will dance with you. Therefore, you must cultivate this clay well. For the present, the English have no use for my Bhayat. But a time will come when the English will feel entrapped by enemies and hostile neighbours. When their own people would have become like brahmins and vaishyas and would be useless in war. The English will feel isolated then. At such a time if my Bhayat have not become like statues and if they have any life left in them, they will go to the aid of the English. It is then that they will appreciate my foresight. Vidya Chatura, when their eyes open, the English will realise the true worth of the native states. Similarly, the kings will also realise the value of the English. But till such time, my Bhayat will be shunned. Till all parties learn to appreciate each other, unhappy times will prevail. You will have to teach my son patience and cultivate the Bhayat. ‘You must remember that the kings of Ratnanagari marry only one queen. If they have no male heirs, the sons of Bhayat become rulers of the state. Thus, my Bhayat and their sons are potential rulers of the state. It will be your responsibility as the tutor of my prince to teach others as well. ‘Vidya Chatura, there will come a time when kshatriyas will become farmers; they will cease to be Rajputs and will be called landlords. Even in those times, the principles I have enumerated must be kept alive like the eternal flame. That is my insistence ...’ The sentence remained incomplete, like the aspiration which was to remain unfulfilled, for just then a messenger rushed in with a letter from Jarashankar. Mallaraj opened the letter impatiently and read the message. His brows furrowed but he somehow retained his equanimity. He got up and walked to the edge of the hill, rolled up his sleeves and said, ‘Hanuman has arrived from the army of monkeys.’ He read some lines of the letter again. ‘According to the terms of the treaty signed by Maharaj Nagraj, the British have a right to appoint an arbitrator to resolve disputes between the native states of the colony. In exercise of this right, their government has decided to appoint a representative. This representative will be called the Political Agent or the Resident. There will be one Political Agent for every four or five states. He will have diplomatic immunity and his residency will be designated as British territory. His task will be to act as an arbitrator among rulers and secure peace in the region. Suvarnapur, Ratnanagari and other native states will come under the Political Agent stationed at Malar Patan. He will appoint other outposts, one of which will be in Lilapur. A British officer, subordinate to the Political Agent will work from Lilapur.’ As Mallaraj folded up the letter, his mind was besieged. All my anxieties regarding the treaty signed by my father are proving to be true, he thought. A Hanuman from the army of monkeys has arrived. Now he will jump about and set fire to our golden Lanka. Now we are the demons and they are the monkeys. Our actions will be constituted as immoral and theirs as moral. The seed sown at the time of the treaty has suddenly sprouted in the form of this Resident. This action will spread fire. What is its remedy? These thoughts and questions passed through his mind like lightning. He chewed his lips as his hand played with his sword. Kumar expressed his desire to go to England and rule, and now the British have laid claims upon our territories! We have ceased to be kings. We are now a colony. The deluge that I apprehended is upon us! Mallaraj looked at his sword. Beloved sword, you have been rendered powerless. Now Rajputs should carry walking sticks instead. Mallaraj turned to Vidya Chatura and said, ‘Vidya Chatura, the pleasure of this excursion must end. We must proceed to Ratnanagari at once. I need to confer with my minister.’ The king’s order was complied with. The next day the king reached his palace and immediately sent for his minister. ‘Jarashankar, write to Brave Sahib that we have no use for his Political Agent. He should be re-called immediately, otherwise ...’ ‘Otherwise we will go to war. Is that what you want me to write Maharaj?’ Jarashankar said with laughter. ‘This is no time for laughter. The treaty with Nagraj does not contain even a syllable about the Agent.’ ‘But the government is convinced that there is a full sentence about it.’ ‘Where is it?’ ‘Of course it is not there. But the government threatens us with its might and says that we must accept its interpretation, or else their army will show us our place.’ ‘If their sword is real, is my sword not real?’ retorted Mallaraj.

‘Maharaj, that question is for your sword,’ replied Jarashankar. ‘Are we their slaves?’ ‘No, Maharaj, we are free, but our sword is shut so tight that it will not open.’ Mallaraj was enraged. Blood rushed to his eyes. The old warrior was overcome with the desire to fight. He unsheathed his sword and began to wield it like a snake charmer showing off his snake. He rushed to the door and shouted, ‘Samant! Samant! Who is there? Prepare the army! There will be war!’ He kicked the floor and roared, ‘Who says that my sword is enslaved!’ Jarashankar considered the situation calmly and urgently sent for the queen and Samant; each moment of waiting was as long as a year. The king stood still, leaning on his sword, his gaze fixed on the rafters of the ceiling. Then, as if he had woken up from a deep, meditative state, he looked around gravely and was surprised by the presence of so many persons. He asked, ‘Why are you all here? Go back to your work. Don’t you know that no one should enter the place where the king and his minister are in conference?’ Everyone went away astonished. The queen who was on her way also turned back. Samant came and joined the minister. ‘Maharaj, you were in a state of intense and valiant excitement. Which is why everyone had rushed here,’ Jarashankar clarified. Mallaraj:  ‘Say it in plain tongue that I seemed mad.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Only Maharaj can describe his experience.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Samant, the minister knows how to speak the truth without being bitter.’ Samant:  ‘The fact that he has the courage to be so bold to your face speaks of your greatness, Maharaj.’ Jarashankar:  ‘You are right, Samant. Maharaj remembered you in his excited state. Hence, you were called.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Why did I want him here?’ Jarashankar:  ‘To have the appointment of the Political Agent annulled.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Apprise him of all the details.’

Jarashankar apprised Samant about the letter and the conversation that had led to the king’s impassioned frenzy. Samant heard him in silence and gave no response. Mallaraj:  ‘Samant, why don’t you respond?’ Samant:  ‘Maharaj, your Bhayat no longer have a right to respond. When Tatya Tope’s men came seeking your support, you decreed that the English were righteous and the Marathas immoral. You decided in favour of an alliance with the English. You also decreed that the Bhayat do not have the right to either question or disagree with a decision that the king had reached in consultation with the minister. My heart burns at your pain, but my intellect has forfeited its right to come to your aid.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Samant, that command was issued because we differed. Today when we are faced with the evil consequences of that decision, to remind me that your opinion was not honoured is the work of a dirty person. Your refusal to be either useful or give an opinion that is sought, just so that you can get even with me is like giving me a punishment. That you actually harboured this hurt for so long shows that you do not know all the duties of a statesman. To harbour hurt for a hundred years is characteristic of women. If you feel that you have been vindicated and have now emerged victorious because God has finally punished me for disregarding your opinion, you harbour within your heart the qualities of a traitor because you act like an enemy of the state. If you wish to throw barbs at me because you are victorious, your tongue is no different from that of a woman. Samant, you are my army. I have the right to rely upon you. I depend upon you more than I do on my army.’ Samant looked down. A tear fell from his eyes. He got up and went out. When he returned, he looked straight at the king and said, ‘Maharaj, your generosity on this wretched self pierces more deeply than a sword would. Maharaj, I am your culprit. I am your servant who deserves punishment, but you treat me with generosity. My heart burns with the fire of expiation. Maharaj, please punish me. I introduced a falsehood in your truth, in your right conduct. I deserve the harshest of punishments.’

Mallaraj:  ‘Samant, my duty is not to destroy my army but to guide it onto the right path. You are my right hand, you are my pride, you are the pillar of my state, you are my army—any punishment to you is a punishment to myself.’ Samant:  ‘Maharaj, that army and this pillar are like a useless elephant who has to be fed for doing nothing. If you set the elephant free, it will crush your people, and if you keep it tied, its hunger will eat into your treasury. Maharaj, what use do you have for us now? What function is left for us to perform?’ Samant sighed dejectedly, looking askance at Jarashankar whom he held responsible for the new politics that had rendered him and the other Bhayat obsolete. The minister ignored the barb and allowed the king and his Bhayat to converse uninterrupted. Mallaraj:  ‘Samant, this is not the occasion for such talk. I want to know if we are free or not to resist the appointment of the Political Agent. It is your right to express yourself.’ Samant smiled vacantly. ‘Maharaj, all things are appropriate in their right context. The time for wielding the sword is over; to bring out our sword at this moment is to invite death. The poet Samaldas has said: “Dissipated wealth shall return, ships will find their course; but an opportunity lost and a lifeless body shall never return.” Maharaj, you chose to act on a brahmin’s advice. We lost an opportunity and kshatriyahood lost its vitality, neither of which shall ever return. If this brahmin, Jarashankar, has the power to bring back lost opportunity and withered vitality, he should do so. But if you allow me, Maharaj, I will slay this brahmin and repay him for the desolation he has wreaked upon us.’ Jarashankar looked at the king, unperturbed. Mallaraj lost control over his temper. There comes a time when a lion stops roaring and uses his paws instead. The king had dealt with a personal insult with utmost generosity. He had in fact shown affection for Samant. That same king now nipped in the bud this opposition to his minister. He ceased to be a brother and spoke in the grave tones of a king: ‘Samant, my minister is a part of me; he is integral to the royal body. You considered slaying him in my presence. For this you shall be punished. I order you to leave this city this moment. You shall not return to

Ratnanagari unless otherwise ordered by me. You shall also not enter within a five-mile radius of Ratnanagari or any other place where either I or my minister could be. Any disobedience will invite further and more severe punishment. Do not utter a word more and pollute the air around me further. Just leave this very moment.’ Jarashankar was shocked. ‘Maharaj! ...’ ‘Silence! Samant, obey my command.’ Samant got up, bowed to the king and left, his body a prisoner of his sorrow and rage. ‘Maharaj, this punishment was entirely inappropriate. You can punish me for speaking thus, but your act is unbecoming of you. You acted out of affection for me, but such punishment without consultation with the minister is inappropriate.’ ‘A king who feels insulted because of a contrary opinion has no right to rule. My command has nothing to do with my affection for you, Jarashankar. It is true that a king’s command issued without consultation with his minister is invalid. But this norm does not apply when the minister is himself a party before the king.’ ‘Should the king act without the counsel of his minister in such matters?’ ‘It is my duty to protect my minister. Let my people know that just as I would hear any complaint regarding my own conduct, I would also hear grievances against my minister and do justice to them. If someone were to attack my person, I would even pardon them. But my queen, my prince, the Bhayat and my people should have no doubt that my officials are my weapons, and just as I would punish anyone who steals my sword, likewise anyone who seeks to curtail the authority of my minister shall receive harsh punishment. I will not show any mercy. In all matters pertaining to the scope of authority and the rights of my minister, I shall follow my own counsel. Jarashankar, issue a royal proclamation that I appoint Samant’s son Mulu Bha as the commander of the army. So long as Mulu Bha is a minor, Samant will from a distance act in the name of his son and carry out my instructions. Samant does not have the right to enter into some areas; in such places he should act through a representative of his choice. The punishment I have awarded will also alert everyone to the meaning and power of my authority. Now let us deal with the issue of the Agent.’ ‘But Maharaj, I do have the right to point out to you the implications of your actions.’ ‘Why do you keep reminding me about implications? Can’t you see that the politics that has rendered my Bhayat useless is being attributed to you? They blame you for influencing my judgement. They are enraged, and Samant is the instrument of their wrath. Would his sword have hesitated before coming down on you?’ ‘I understand very well that for many days now that sword has been hanging over my head, and also that your minister has remained unharmed only because of the shield of your grace. On the other hand, we can already hear the politics of the British at our doorstep; and if those predators were to learn of our internal dissensions, we would become easy prey to them. Maharaj, I have said this to you time and again that your minister is like that camel who should be sacrificed so that you can enter the enemy’s fort. Maharaj, your family is about to be torn asunder, and if not, it shall certainly face divisive conflict. The British are certain to try and take advantage of this dissension. The easiest way of preventing such an eventuality is to place me, your minister, as the sacrificial camel. This would assuage the deep hurt of your Bhayat. This is also in the interests of the state. Maharaj, your Bhayat are neither traitors, nor have they turned against you; their anger is directed towards me personally. You need them and their army much more than you need me—this is a statement of fact. Maharaj, you will find many able ministers, but once you lose them you will not have such brothers-in-arms again. It is improper for you to punish them just for a few intemperate words. It is said: “A neem tree has bitter fruit but provides soothing shade; brothers are given to harsh words but they are like one’s own arms.’” ‘Jarashankar, what you say is not without merit. Hence, the punishment to Samant is in essence a withdrawal of my affection. It involves no other harm. There is scope for him yet to repent and seek my pardon. Samant’s heart is full of anger but not envy, and he is certain to repent. One day he will be with you again and work for the state with all his affection and loyalty restored. The punishment is both necessary and appropriate. Its outcome will be for the best. Only Rajputs understand Rajput temperament. But to sacrifice you would be both inappropriate and harmful. It was you who said, and quite truthfully, that now our swords are sheathed and our armies have been rendered useless. Now one clever and politically astute minister shall do what a thousand warriors cannot. He will act both as the sword and the shield of the king.’ ‘Maharaj has left the possibility of a pardon open and I do not wish to be instrumental in foreclosing that possibility. But I am surprised that you found this solution in response to the fact of your sword having been sheathed. It was the ineffectiveness of the sword that had perturbed you so deeply. Poor Samant was called here to assuage your feelings, and he ended up being punished.’ Mallaraj laughed. ‘True. That was a strange fate. But even in the past such great events have produced such emotions within me. And yet once I bring my emotions under control, I also find a way out of the predicament. This is also a part of my disposition. But for you this seems to be a first experience of its kind.’ ‘Maharaj, my state is somewhat happier compared to yours because I find ways out of predicaments without succumbing to emotions.’ Mallaraj laughed again. ‘That is correct. But in times of war such overpowering emotions are like a brother to a kshatriya. We are not so selfish that we would keep these emotions at a distance at other times. But you have no use for such powerful feelings; therefore, the wise among you keep away from them. This is the difference between us. And it is not in the interest of the state that this difference be obliterated. It is for this reason that it has been considered improper to appoint Bhayat as ministers. Jarashankar, we need your kind.’ ‘Then how has the Maharaj resolved the issue of the British Resident? Your heart has experienced an earthquake. So tell me how you have resolved this quandary.’ ‘Your and my opinions have become one.’

‘I have not expressed my views hitherto.’ ‘But I have understood them.’ ‘Please illuminate.’ ‘First you express your views; then I will speak my mind.’ ‘Maharaj, it is better that your views prevail and not mine. I will speak my mind.’ ‘Tell me.’ ‘Maharaj, I still hold that the decision to have a treaty with the English was a correct one. But even if it were not, we are without any option. That treaty may be a gold mine or a bed of arrows, but the fact of it still remains. We must find ways to derive the maximum advantage from it. And we should not worry about what has not happened because it is not likely to happen.’ Mallaraj’s face was grave. ‘You spoke the truth.’ ‘Maharaj, just at present the circumstances are such that the English are in place of a mother-in-law, and you are in place of a daughter-in-law. They will employ newer means to curtail your authority. The treaty with them sowed a seed for the future, good or bad. If the result turns out to be good we should try to better it even further; but if the result be to our disadvantage we should bear with it anyhow and try to gradually improve our lot. One can entertain doubts while the matter is under consideration; but the time for doubts has passed. Doubt in moments of action is misplaced. It is said that those who harbour debilitating doubt are destroyed. The treaty with the English has been long concluded. Now we must deal with the results of our actions. In such moments the wise who have thought of the appropriate action say that good men do not forsake the fruits of actions that they were destined to do. What should be their conduct? It is said that a good man must, until the very end, deal with the consequences of his actions; this is also the norm that noble men uphold. Those who fail to uphold this are not considered worthy and good men. What does the upholder gain? The wise say that noble and worthy men always follow what has become a part of them. Those who succeed in doing so are fortunate; and they, too, consider themselves to be so. The throne that you occupy can be held only by men who are good and worthy; only the fortunate sit on it. This authority you understand much better than I do, Maharaj. ‘Maharaj, all the considerations that one bore in mind at the time of taking a decision are often not remembered when one has to deal with the fruits of one’s actions. One doesn’t even recall the swift actions taken to implement one’s thoughts. One would always consider all the obstacles before embarking upon a course of action. But the immediacy of those obstacles puts fear in one’s mind. However, such fears are only because of attachment, which does not allow one to perform one’s duties optimally. Such action is appropriate in case of someone like Samant who is experienced only in war. War itself is but a step in the implementation of a decision. The moment the duties of a warrior end, diplomacy commences for a king like you. Only a few like Mallaraj know how to swim against the current. Maharaj, at a time when we are faced with the momentous consequences of our actions, how can I, born to poor brahmins, instruct you, born in the royal house of Suryavansh, regarding matters of diplomacy! The traditions of your family would be far better at showing you the right path. Maharaj, your royal lineage will certainly produce some unique results—of that I am certain. Maharaj, in matters of diplomacy I am but your charioteer; you are the great warrior. I merely drive a chariot in the direction you prefer.’ ‘In short, you advise me to persist with the English, but how that should be done is to be determined by me.’ ‘Maharaj, that is correct. It is now your turn to express your opinion.’ Mallaraj laughed. ‘Pradhan, you are a wily man. You spoke long, but left the burden of a decision on me. Are you scared of Samant before expressing another opinion?’ ‘Maharaj, even if I am scared, I am only a brahmin after all. A person who works under you cannot be afraid of fire. I have the courage to say that despite the knowledge that a weak and scared minister has no place in your service, you still retain me; and that you fail in your duty. I have this courage because of the trust I have in you.’ Mallaraj was very amused. He leaned his head back on the bolster and laughed aloud. ‘Instead of telling a lie, Jarashankar, you have learnt to speak half-truth. I have already lost Samant; I would be foolish to lose you as well.’ ‘Maharaj, we have decided to persist with our treaty with the English. We have to, therefore, accept the Agent. The decision for us now is the proximity or distance that we would like to maintain from the cooking fire that he will light.’ ‘How so?’ ‘Should we allow him to start a fire as far as Bombay or as close as Lilapur?’ ‘They are already in Bombay.’ ‘We are too distant from it. We cannot tell whether the rice they cook remains uncooked or gets burnt. If they are in Lilapur, we will be able to keep an eye on them.’ Mallaraj sat up eager to listen. ‘But if they light a fire in Lilapur, its sparks will fly in our direction, the ash and the smoke will cloud our vision as well. Moreover, we will also feel the heat. Is that an adequate price to pay to watch over what they cook?’ ‘Maharaj, you are a master in statecraft. You decided to get a measure of the English even before you spurned the advances of Shubhaji Rao. And in order to get a measure of our opponent, we have shown our hand as well. But that, too, is a means to an end.’ A major dilemma was resolved for Mallaraj. But some doubts still persisted. ‘Jarashankar, that is correct. But what if we reveal too much of ourselves while trying to get a measure of them?’ ‘Maharaj, that fear is unfounded. The English know us well after the war that Nagraj fought. If they want to know us even more closely, we cannot prevent them. They will even remove our clothes and subject us to an examination. But they will employ cunning and not force to do so.’ ‘It seems as if we are going to bring the axe down on our own feet. Is there a reason for that? Why should we invite them so close to us?’ ‘Those states and rulers who have become devoid of any vitality and rendered effete due to various diseases that plague them must fear the proximity of the English. We look around us and we hardly find one state that is not diseased. They are hollow. The English will penetrate them with ease and drink their blood like a thirsty bear. Poison will flow through the veins of these states instead of blood. I do not think this is either an impossible or an undesirable scenario. Maharaj, there are rulers who prey upon their people, who do not devote even a small fraction of the day in thinking about and ensuring the welfare of their people, rulers who forsake their people and submit to debauched conduct to satiate their passions. If God has created an enemy to suppress such debauched rulers and corrupt realms, what is so improper about them? Maharaj, a king punishes his people, but God punishes even a king.’ Jarashankar caught his breath and continued, ‘Maharaj, I do not know whether the proximity of the English would prove catastrophic for those states which have become hollow and corrupt. But even if it were to prove perilous, I would not regard it as undesirable. Even if such an outcome were to be considered disagreeable, the righteous and virtuous king of Ratnanagari has nothing to fear. Maharaj, as they come to have closer relations with you and your administration, your fragrance and the beauty of your administration will become even more apparent. Maharaj, you are like sandalwood—the more it is rubbed, the more fragrant it becomes. You are gold that glows brighter in fire. Again and again you rub sandalwood on the stone, it produces only a fragrant paste; cut the sugar cane again and again, it produces only sweetness. Burn again and again a piece of gold, it always shines. In the same way when noble people are put into different situations they do not change.⟨fn:100⟩ ‘Maharaj, let alone the English, the whole world can try in vain. They can scrutinise the gems of Ratnanagari until they are satisfied. Our jewel-like men are not afraid of any test. If someone desires to observe our gems, we have nothing to fear. The English can see the treasury that our people are; they can do no harm. If these foreigners take a post at Lilapur, we would also have the benefit of knowing their arts and skills and we could learn some things from them. To me it seems that an opportunity has come looking for us. Maharaj, this is the best scenario for the present.’ Pleased with his minister, Mallaraj stood up, and so did Jarashankar. The enthused king patted his minister on the back and said, ‘All right, Jarashankar. All my doubts have vanished. The gems of Ratnanagari are not under any threat. Go and ask Vidya Chatura to send a response. The progeny of Sugriva were dear to Sitaji. How can we, the descendants of Sitaji, keep them away from us? Those monkeys can sit on any tree they like and jump around as much as they want. They will eat some gram and nuts at most. But they are not capable of either breaking or chewing the gems of Ratnanagari. If they try to bite us, their teeth will break. Jarashankar, the monkeys of Mathura are greedy for gram; we shall be a match for them. If they jump around on our rooftops, they might break a few tiles, but we don’t lack the mud to remake them.’ Jarashankar went home. The king walked towards the quarters of his queen. On his way there, he thought of Samant. Samant was a childhood friend, a companion of many wars and an heir to the throne after Maniraj. Separation from him was unbearable. Mallaraj felt his loss deeply. Tears streamed down his eyes. His heart felt a searing pain at the thought that he was the reason for Samant’s departure and that he had grievously wounded his friend. He cursed himself: Curse on this kingship that forced me to wound a friend! Would it not have been better to have abdicated the throne rather than give up a friend? Samant! Samant, my childhood friend! You were angry because you wanted to protect my interest. And see how I repaid you! A man who does not trust love is evil. It is for these reasons that the world does not trust the affection of a king. Kings are heartless. It is said that rulers end up in hell. This, too, is hell. Oh God! Strange are your ways. Deep in such melancholic thoughts, Mallaraj entered the queen’s quarter. The queen saw his withered and sad face. She knew the reason for his sadness. The news about Samant had spread through the woman’s quarters. Everyone agreed that the punishment was heartless. People judged the king and decreed that the king had relied upon hearsay and not his own intellect while awarding punishment to a brave friend such as Samant. This was the first time that Mallaraj had been accused of such injustice. People said that the king’s views had changed, which was also a sign of the changing times. The king could see that people behaved like strangers; it added fuel to the fire. But the power of Mallaraj was such that no one had the courage to even whisper of such things. The palace looked stricken by death. The queen shared the sentiments of the rest of the palace, but she was not about to mention this to Mallaraj. He had forbidden anyone from the women’s quarters to express any opinion about matters of state; any disobedience would invite severe punishment. Samant’s example left no doubt about that. But the queen took heart from the example of Laxman, who had not thought of punishment while allowing Rishi Durvasa to interrupt Ram’s conversation with Yama, because such an act was in the interest of Ram. She gathered the courage to speak to the king. She decided on something that would relieve the king of his sorrow and give him pleasure as well. She hoped thus to meet two desirable ends by one action. The king, weary of vain attempts to suppress love for his brother by reasons of state, placed his head on his queen’s lap and lay down. The lamps spread soft light, not sorrow. The sea breeze wafting from the west soothed his body as he drifted into sleep. The rustle of leaves produced a pleasant sound. As his worries receded, his body relaxed and before sleep could overpower the king, the queen softly sang a song that she had composed for him earlier during the day, caressing him as she sang. Mena pleads, my lord, your meek Mena beseeches you: A brave man does not live by sword alone; A valorous man does not harbour The smouldering embers of wrath in his heart; The conch-bearer who pierces the hearts of enemies Is the lord of the three worlds But to give solace to his devotees He holds a lotus in his hand He is the compassionate one who Bore Bhrigu’s blows

And incarnated on this earth, abided by its norms Even a helpless woman like your Mena Sees the times she lives in For nine months have I borne our Mani in my womb. O’ husband mine, remember you are the devotee of such a lord. You are enlightened: who can hold up The lamp of compassion to you? The king’s sleep was disturbed. He turned to his side. The queen sang more lustily. Samant, who ought to shine in your crown jewels, adorned your footwear The king opened his eyes and stared at the queen. My lord, you are the jewel on Samant’s crown Manidhar, stay forever compassionate The king was startled. He sat up, his eyes reddening. The astute queen realised that the king was irate. She sang in a mellow voice: Helpless woman that I am, I know I have no place near the throne; Mine is the domain of pleasure and through it I seek subtle influence Enacting the lines, Mena Rani pleaded with him with folded hands as she sang and tried to bury her face in his vast chest. With folded hands and open heart, Today your beloved beseeches you The king took her face in his hands and waited for the next line. The queen sang: My beloved, you are knowledgeable in the scriptures; Give me deep and joyful pleasure My beloved, you are knowledgeable in the art of war; Bear with forgiveness the arrows of pleasure that I aim at you The queen drew the king’s attention to her body. Before he could take control of his desires, she seized the moment and launched an impassioned invitation to pleasure.

My lord, your brave Mena throws darts of love at you My king, beware: your amorous queen attacks Clever warrior, stay alert: this attack cannot be repulsed My king, watch closely my hand Playful one, catch me if you can Even before the last word escaped her lips, Mena Rani flung herself passionately at the king. But Mallaraj brushed aside that beautiful body and got up. He walked towards the door of their bed chamber, and on his way out, he reproached her with scathing words: ‘The king who punished Samant will also punish all those who take his side. Rani, you have transgressed your limits and sought to do something that is beyond your authority. A king forgets relationships while awarding punishment. Rani, I abandoned Samant. Now fate wills that I must forsake you as well.’ The king went out and disappeared into the dark. The queen followed him. She heard him converse with himself or someone else. Unseen in the dark, she sang: O’ beloved, surrender your anger You are the bee and I, the flower, How delightful is our union! If we think of thorns, How can there be pleasure? She found no response. She took a lamp and went in search of the king. She caught up with him and said, ‘My playmate won’t play with me, my dearest!’ The king finally said, ‘Rani, on second thoughts, I understand the meaning of what you said. Samant, is both a gem and also capable of poison like a snake; and hence one should forgive him. But I do not grant women authority in matters of state. What punishment should I award you?’ The queen fell at his feet. She held on to his right leg and said, ‘Maharaj, I did not dabble in matters of state. I do not want to sully your reputation by my transgression. Other women may do so; but Mena is your subject and all my rights are those which you have yourself granted me.’

‘Which right and which authority have you used?’ ‘If you venture into a place infested with snakes, Maharaj, I must alert you through words and if need be, even drag you away. I have had this right since the day I married you, Maharaj.’ ‘Do you think Samant is capable of a poisonous bite?’ ‘Samant will not do so. But your Bhayat are like Samant’s fangs, and these fangs are venomous. Maharaj, your Bhayat are angry with your minister and you. If you pardon Samant, this poison will subside. You have to place the burden of holding up the earth upon the snake. This is one way of saving yourself.’ ‘Rani, I have heard your opinion; but that does not imply that you have not transgressed. I will give you light punishments. You will have to sleep without me tonight. I command you never again to meddle in the matters of state.’ The queen let go of the king’s leg. She got up with tears in her eyes and said, ‘Maharaj, your words are just and your command has both punishment and pardon. I do not have the heart to ever violate your command again. Maharaj, I am your subject. Please enter the bed chamber and sleep on the bed. I will sleep in the courtyard.’ The king lay down on the bed. The bed of love had turned thorny, and he passed a sleepless night. Yet he could not repent for the punishment that he as a king had awarded his beloved. Only a poet with the gifts of Bhavabhuti can capture the mental state of a king who has punished a friend like Samant and a queen like Mena. With an attentive mind he had to govern this world according to the rules of administration; his grief for his dear wife withers his body as heat does a flower; having himself abandoned her he cannot easily have the relief coming from lamentation, but today he can breathe a sigh of relief and thus, lamentation is, indeed a gain to him.⟨fn:101⟩
chapters.summary: King Mallaraj, deeply concerned by foreign influence and his son Kumar's innocence, instructs Vidya Chatura to secretly study the British for future generations.

chapters.title: New Chapters and New Histories
paragraphs: New Chapters and New Histories But no! The imperial theorist will live and die a martyr to his theory.   —Merivale on Aurelius The first shocks of foreign rule were felt through the entire administration of Mallaraj. His Bhayat, his army, his friends, the women’s quarters in his palace, his love—all seemed to dissipate. His friends and relatives turned strangers. Difference of opinion finally led to disaffection among the loved ones. The treaty with the British rendered his kshatriya brethren obsolete, and they felt wounded by it. The Bhayat were enraged by the punishment awarded to Samant. Mallaraj was isolated. His trusted minister was seen by everyone as an enemy. The roots of dissension and machinations went deep. Formerly there was mutual trust, but it proved as unsteady as a stream of water. Mallaraj reclining alone in his chamber could see all this clearly before him. Late into the night he fell asleep. Before yielding to sleep, his thoughts were: A lion does not worry that he is solitary, helpless and alone in the forest. The queen knew of his mental state. She peeped in from a window; for her this did not constitute a breach of the king’s command. Seeing him asleep at last, she, too, went to sleep on the hard floor of the courtyard. A year passed. The ruler of Virpur, a neighbouring state of Ratnanagari, died, and his young son Khachar ascended the throne.

Rana Khachar’s father was a friend of Mallaraj. Ratnanagari and Virpur had together fought against common enemies in the past. The rulers of Ratnanagari believed in keeping their own state united, strong and well-administered. They did not crave for territories of other states. But they helped their Bhayat and Garasia satisfy their desire for acquiring garas in distant lands. The rulers of Virpur allowed their state to be subject to the desires of their Bhayat, while they themselves craved for territories outside their boundaries. The British presence precluded the possibility of wars as a means of acquiring territories, and hence the thirst for land could not be satiated. The Bhayat could no longer fight other armies and consequently, they began to harass the ruler. Young Khachar, thirsting for more land, found a way of grabbing the lands of friendly neighbours without taking recourse to war. The Bhayat became his instruments; instead of harassing Khachar, they turned like a pack of hungry dogs on the neighbours. The Garasia of Virpur began to grab land in the name of their ruler. The neighbouring states took their grievances to the newly appointed political agent. Khachar wanted to establish that he was not the only cause of all troubles. He took advantage of both the foolishness and greed of the Political Agent and filed suits against the neighbouring states. This disease spread to other states as well. The Political Agent’s desire to become an arbitrator among native states was fulfilled. It was like the story of warring cats and a monkey. The scales of judgement went into British hands. For a time, Mallaraj saw this drama of change unfold from afar, and was deeply saddened by it. But he could not remain uninvolved for long; the wheels of time were also moving towards his state. He had managed to douse the fire that had reached as far as his queen’s quarters. But soon flames erupted in neighbouring states and their sparks also flew in his direction. Khachar disregarded old friendship and opened a territorial dispute with Ratnanagari. Khachar’s Garasia also began to plough land belonging to Ratnanagari. The Agent wrote to Mallaraj, soliciting explanations about the dispute raised by Khachar. Mallaraj challenged the authority of the Agent to seek such an explanation. A war of words ensued. Mallaraj called Jarashankar and Samant’s son for confabulations.

‘Jarashankar, the English have assumed the role of a judge in the dispute among kings; the foolish princes will cut each other’s throats and present them to the English. In the times when battles were fought with arms, kings did not covet land; it is unlikely that the same rulers would hold sway when battles are being fought in mercenary fashion like the vaishyas. In times of armed conflict, it was in the interest of the Bhayat and the warriors that the rulers remained hungry for more territory; they sought conflicts to satisfy the warriors’ hunger for land. Now when battles are being fought like the vaishyas, it is in the interest of the political advisors, including ministers that rulers remained hungry for land; and ongoing war through written documents satisfies the hunger of the class of writers. Jarashankar, in the past the jewels among our men were not sullied by greed and hunger. Like in the times gone by, we have among us unsullied, pure jewels among men; and your king does not exchange men of tinsel splendour for pure jewels. For generations, my ancestors have preferred the power of the men of Ratnanagari over the inanimate strength of land and wealth. Therefore, Jarashankar, you must commence a great yajna, a sacrifice to prevent the contagious disease that Khachar has contracted from spreading in this country. You are free to sacrifice as much land and money as required to ensure that this country does not burn in the fires of vaishya warfare and remains free from the subjugation of the monkeys who have usurped the role of the judge. ‘Those times are gone when justice was that which was secured by the power of the sword! It has become a distant dream. Now justice among kings will be secured not by the sword but will be delivered by men! Jarashankar, as long as there is life in me, this Rajput will not allow these times to prevail upon this country. As long as I am alive, I will not permit my kingship to be usurped by the British and I will not accept their authority. What constitutes the loss of my kingly powers in accepting the superiority of the British, or in allowing my neighbourly kings to have their way and acceding to them some land—merely some dust, stones and trees? Jarashankar, rulers lose their powers by accepting the power of others. This has always been so. Let others accept the authority of the British. My ancestor Hastidant chose death over retreat in war, and a father like Nagraj did not hesitate to step on the body of a great warrior such as Hastidant. I, trained by those great souls, will not accept the power of others for the sake of mercenary vaishya-like warfare. Two of my ancestors departed from this earth right before my eyes. Why would I find it difficult to depart from this earth? I have accepted the friendship of the English, but not their justice. I would prefer to honourably accept some demands made by the progeny of those kings who supported me in the war against the English, rather than stand before the English with folded hands. This is what I desire. Go fulfill it. ‘Jarashankar, I have shown you the end I desire. To find the means appropriate to that end is the responsibility of the minister. Mallaraj is not given to labouring over the question of means and the sacrifice involved in it. Put an end to these inconsequential quarrels by whatever means. You know well how to protect my interest and that of my state. In so doing if you were to make a mistake, I am capable of granting a pardon. Hence, go forth with my full authority, absolute trust and all the means at my disposal. Go fulfill the desired goal. ‘But be careful. We must end all disputes. We must enter into treaties even with those with whom we have no quarrels at present, so that no quarrels about mud and stones arise later. Demarcate the boundaries of our state so carefully that even a child will not have any difficulty deciphering them, and even the most cunning person will not find a way of falsifying them. All disputes with other states must be so resolved that they never ever recur. We must bear any expense and even loss of some land, if need be, to ensure this. The sea naturally demarcates our territory on one side. The other three boundaries must be fixed permanently such that so long as the moon and the sun shine no one can raise any dispute regarding them. All outstanding issues must be settled for ever. Once this task is accomplished, no one will have the power to shorten the reigns of the rulers of Ratnanagari or be a hindrance in our pursuit to secure the welfare of our people.’ Mallaraj turned towards the adolescent Mulu Bha, held his hand and spoke with unbounded joy, ‘Mulu Bha, just as Samant Bha is a pillar of my state, you, too, are fit to be a pillar of Maniraj’s reign.

Samant Bha was by my side when I had to go to war. His intellect and love proved beneficial to me. Maniraj is still a child; but you have reached an age where you must learn and gather experience. Hence I have decided that you should accompany Jarashankar so that you become acquainted with matters of state and rulers of different lands. En route, go to Virpur and take your father along. You must obey him.’ Mulu Bha touched the king’s feet. Mallaraj blessed him. Mulu Bha said, ‘Maharaj, I can never repay the debt of gratitude for your mercy towards my wretched father. Your command is a sign of your grace, and I shall obey it. My father, who is unhappy to be separated from you, will experience the joy akin to having seen you when I shall relate your command to him.’ This response satisfied Mallaraj. He did not want to lose an opportune moment. ‘Jarashankar, go with Mulu Bha and meet Samant. When you meet me next, Samant should be with the two of you.’ Jarashankar was clearly overjoyed. ‘Of course, Maharaj! Can there be a moment of greater joy? You have granted Mulu Bha’s request and shown great mercy for Samant. There can be no more auspicious beginning to this great task. The goal that you desire shall be attained. What can a master who has jewels like Samant and Mulu Bha lack?’ Jarashankar and Mulu took leave of Mallaraj. Mulu’s family customarily wrote the father’s name before that of the son. Thus, Mulu was known as Samant Mulu, and at times Mulu Samant. Mulu’s heart was touched by the winds of a new age. He was greedy for land and power; he harboured anger for the insult meted out to his father, and nurtured jealousy and animosity towards the minister and his family. He was keen to fuel trouble for the kingdom. Such ghosts danced a macabre dance in Mulu’s heart. He had inherited instrumental cruelty from his mother’s side of the family. He had received nothing but intellect, imagination and valour from his father’s family. With great effort, Mulu kept his ambitions secret. After he was gone, Mallaraj had a momentary apprehension that Mulu’s speech hid his treachery, that his smile betrayed a secret weapon and that his heart was demonic. Mallaraj considered this apprehension unnecessary and turned his attention to other matters. Vidya Chatura will gather political experience and meet other men of politics, he surmised. As we have decided, he should be trained to take over Jarashankar’s responsibilities; Maniraj and the state will stand to benefit. And so thinking, Mallaraj ordered Jarashankar to take Vidya Chatura as his assistant. For Jarashankar, it was as if the doctor had ordered what his heart most coveted. This great task took many years to be accomplished. In the course of these years, they came to be acquainted with many rulers and British officials. The demeanour and the conduct of the British revenue officials changed over the years. Mallaraj prophesied that in the years to come they would herd the natives like a shepherd herding his cattle. The British government acted as a court of appeal in disputes among kings. Just as common people appeal over a judgement not in their favour, the rulers went in appeal over the orders of the Political Agent. Consequently the English courts came to be established above and over the rulers. Kings forgot their kshatriyahood and fought battles like vaishyas. They sought redress of their grievance in English courts and went in appeal to higher courts. They begged for justice, became supplicants, and the prestige of the English courts multiplied. This form of justice was formed on the evidence and testimonies of witnesses. The fates of kings came to be controlled by lowly witnesses. It was necessary to believe one evidence and testimony over the other. Consequently the prestige of kings and their ministers came to reside in the courts; with the loss of prestige, the glory of the kings inevitably declined. As their power and glory declined, the grip of the British administrators became firm. Sometimes the kings challenged their authority, but a weak challenge often only further strengthened the power and authority of the British. If a political agent was considered a just man, defeated rulers gambled with their chances and fell deeper into decline. The process of decline hastened if the agent was unjust. The inevitable decline of the rulers became a source of joy for some. Mallaraj keenly observed this and remarked to Jarashankar, ‘Jarashankar, have you seen what pleasure this evil Fox Sahib derives from insulting and extracting money from this cunning and exploitative Thakore, who is a messenger of death for his people?’

Jarashankar replied, ‘Maharaj, someone has said that it is cunning nature that brings at one place the ripe fruits of neem trees, a tongue that relishes their taste and a crow adept at eating the fruits. The person being punished is like Yamaduta, the messenger of death, and the one awarding the punishment is Fox Sahib; the Creator has thoughtfully made this pair.’ Mallaraj sighed, ‘Jarashankar, because of one such ruler, all others will stand to lose. How many kingly powers has this messenger of death transferred to the English!’ ‘Maharaj, because of the inebriated, debauched Yadavs, a spear eventually killed Shri Krishna. That divine being lost his life because of his association with the Yadavs. If one like him can meet such a fate, who are we?’ ‘If the English officers were bad, one could blame the English for appointing them. But if our own kings and natives turn good officers into bad ones, how can we blame the English? It is certain that the English Sahibs are not as fallen as they are made out to be. It is our tendency to fight like vaishyas that is the cause of our downfall. A good wife can reform her evil husband. Would not our kings and ministers cultivate the art of reforming the Sahibs? Jarashankar this fire is raging; one cannot say when its flames will singe us. A forest fire engulfs not just dry trees but lush green ones as well. We must not allow this fire to burn us. We must not allow any weakness to creep into our state. It would be better to lose land, wealth, prestige and even this crown than allow debilitating weakness to corrode our state. If my progeny have any kingly glory, they will regain the state by the strength of their own acumen and ability. But those who seek to keep their rule but bargain away kingly glory will lose both their state and their glory forever.’ ‘That is the truth, Maharaj. A king is subject to temporal time. A king must overcome that through his endeavours. Your efforts will bear results.’ ‘It is because of the English that we native rulers fight amongst ourselves. They will play their game; but Mallaraj will watch their moves in this game of chess.’ Mallaraj seemed delighted at this thought.

Virtue and shaping state policy for the welfare of the people is in itself a state of joy for a good king. Over time, courts came to be established to adjudicate the disputes of native rulers. Laws were framed to govern the conduct of common people. Any attempt on part of the British to codify laws to govern the rulers would certainly have been seen as a clear sign of erosion of kingly authority. Hence the kings did not demand codified laws, and the British refrained from framing them. Therefore, the decisions of the courts became laws. This measure ostensibly adopted to protect the authority of the rulers became the source of many problems. In the absence of laws, judgement depended solely on the discretion of the judges and their predilections. There were not required to explain or assign reasons for their decisions. In this reign of darkness, the rulers stumbled around seeking favourable decisions. Often the judges were military men, and in such instances the real power of decision making was exercised by their lowly clerks. If the judges were learned men, they wrote reasoned judgements that could not be reversed even by the government. These judgements systematically eroded the authority of the rulers. The stories of such vaishya-like quarrels wafted into Ratnanagari like smoke from distant fires. It roused irritation in Mallaraj. At a time when other native rulers were subject to injustice and insult, Mallaraj drew his senses within himself and like a yogi meditating upon the eternal truth, he meditated upon the nature of kingly authority. One day, Vidya Chatura opined, ‘Maharaj, our native rulers have become corrupt. If the foreigners were to become equally corrupt, the rule of the Mughals would certainly return. But the norms of politics by which these foreigners are governed make it imperative for them to follow the norms of justice, even while furthering their self- interest. There are three reasons for the difficulty that native rulers face in securing justice. First, the laws are not entirely virtuous or in accordance with our customs. Second, the officials who implement these laws are either corrupt or inefficient; there are learned or effective men among them, but they are few in number. Third, even if we were to discount the evil among our rulers and their advisors, even the good ones do not have either the desire or the ability to remain abreast with the changing tides of time. We have no alternative but to bear the burden of the foreigner’s self-interest. But these three factors can be ameliorated provided we are true to ourselves and our identity. Maharaj, it is impossible for all rulers to cultivate your attitude of non- possession, your generosity and self-control. It is not a small matter to deal with the kicks of our neighbours with equanimity. Hence, other rulers are unlikely to immediately acquire the ability to deal with these factors. The type of education that is being given to Maniraj ought to become common in all our royal households; only then they will acquire the ability to deal with difficult times. The path that you have adopted can become an infallible weapon, like the arrow of Ram, in the hands of noble rulers. No one can deny that. But Maharaj, there was only one Ram capable of wielding that infallible weapon!’ Mallaraj gave a patient hearing to the discourse of this young man. Two or three years passed. A new chapter opened, and the nature of British adjudication changed. Disputes among the rulers were adjudicated by the British. This arrangement was tolerable, but there arose disputes between rulers and their subjects, which also went to the English courts. This unprecedented situation was not envisaged in the treaties between native rulers and the British. The native rulers had not imagined such an erosion of their authority even in their worst nightmares. They were for long years embroiled in disputes with each other, neglecting the welfare of their people. In the golden days, the kings ruled by their sword. They were always battle ready. They had no inclination to think of the welfare of their subjects. Kshatriya warriors were constantly at war with each other. They also tortured the people. Rulers lacked the courage to place limits on them. Inevitably, the people were crushed, just as trees fall when two elephants fight. But when subjected to torture, even the meekest of animals attack, cowards find courage and the foolish begin to find their intellect. By the same logic when subjected to injustice, the smouldering embers of discontent would suddenly turn into fire. Meek but clever banias would harass the rulers by going on strike and shake up the Rajputs, who were clueless about the world of business. The guild of traders was capable of shaking up the very foundation of the royal households. Similarly, the brahmins had cultivated the art of interfering in the royal household from a distance—much like causing the water to ripple by blowing air onto it through a pipe—by their hold over royal women, and it would create quite a storm that would blur the sight of men and women alike. In all castes and communities, from the highest to the lowest, from those doing customary manual work to those engaged in trade, in narrow streets, in large neighbourhoods, on the streets of brahmins, at the dharamshalas of banias, at the town squares of the Patels, in the otalas of the elderly, at the ponds and wells frequented by women, at the shops of petty traders, inside the barracks of soldiers and the huts of the lower class, everywhere the discontent of the people would simmer and the deafening noise of their combined whispers would rob the rulers of their sleep, as if the discontented held the garment of the goddess of sleep to prevent her from entering the royal households. But when rulers continued to remain indifferent to the pleading, pleasing and the treachery of their subjects, people would rise up in open rebellion and shake up the thrones of their rulers. At such times, to appease the rebellious subjects, rulers and their ferocious henchmen would dance to the tunes of their subjects like Mahadev before Chandi. In the early days of the British Empire the English gave a blanket assurance to the rulers, which turned the subject population effete, and the rulers and their cruel henchmen danced like ghosts over the fragile and withered bodies of the people. Some compassionate English officials were moved by the plight of the people. They realised that their protective treaties with the rulers had rendered the people powerless, and that the English were responsible for their plight. They felt that it was their duty to empower the people. Other selfish and power-hungry officials used this compassion to further their interests by robbing the rulers of their already frayed and withered authority. Selfishness and compassion became strange companions. The combined intellect of the good and the bad Englishman worked towards the same purpose. The question of means and ends was set aside, the only consideration being the efficacy of the means. The kings were like the slavish Pandavas, unable to fight Duryodhana having lost their all in the game of dice. The Political Agent played the role of Dushasana and robbed the royal authority of all vestiges of prestige. Like the Pandavas, the kings watched in silence. The English brazenly disregarded the sensibility of the mute elders just like Duryodhana who, disregarding the presence of Bhishma, Drona and Vidur, had invited Draupadi to sit on his thigh. The English invited the royal authority to sit on their lap and, like Duryodhana, said ‘disrobe her’. The enfeebled royal authority did not possess enough life to say ‘God, help the helpless.’ Mallaraj discussed this sorry state of affairs with Vidya Chatura and Jarashankar. ‘It is the same country and the same lessons, but the times are not the same. The Pandavas were deserving of Panchali, but our kings are undeserving of royal authority. Jarashankar, when an Indra devoid of merit falls on earth from the heavens, Indrani accepts the new Indra as her new husband. Royal authority is like Indrani; it does not stay with an undeserving master. Royal authority is wedded to the virtue of the ruler. A king who tortures his subjects is no king. The moment the stench of the king’s debauchery reaches the nostrils of royal authority, it deserts the king. If the English are more deserving, royal authority will come to them. On close and dispassionate examination, I for one certainly do not see this as inappropriate.’ Hitherto, Ratnanagari had remained untouched by raging fire, but a sudden gust of wind changed that, and the fire reached Mallaraj’s palace. The state officials emerged from hibernation and stood up to face the challenge with all senses alert. Kumar Maniraj was in the direct line of succession to the throne. In the event of his death, Samant and then Mulu were second and third in line for the throne. It was customary in Ratnanagari that all potential heirs to the throne were trained to acquire the fitness to rule. Samant was trained by Nagraj in statecraft. It was with similar intent that Mallaraj had sent Mulu with Jarashankar on a political mission. At the same time care was taken that the direct heirs and the secondary heirs did not develop close proximity. This was done to ensure the personal safety of the direct heir and to curb jealousy or greed that the secondary heirs might develop. Yet, cordial and affectionate relations among the heirs were necessary for the welfare of the state. In times of peace the heirs were usually brought together to foster this. But Mulu Bha was discontented. The perceived insult of his father further fuelled his displeasure. He became unreasonable and impatient. He regarded Mallaraj as an enemy and interpreted Mallaraj’s respect for him as a sign of appeasement by the weak. He thought of Maniraj as an effete, lustreless and stupid child. He rued Ratnanagari’s fate in the hands of Maniraj. A thought took root in his mind that ultimately, it was Vidya Chatura who would wield authority. Such thoughts possessed his excited mind, but he lacked the courage to express them before his father who was a loyalist. Sometimes he spoke his mind to his mother, and received encouragement. One day, at a moment he felt was opportune, Mulu spoke to his father, albeit with hesitation. Samant instantly realised that a gun was being pointed at his master and he leapt up just as a ferociously loyal dog protects his master. Mulu grew sad and disheartened. Shunned at home, he sought solace and support outside. During his travels with Jarashankar, Mulu sought the friendship of Rana Khachar. He kept in touch with Khachar, and their friendship deepened. He passed on state secrets to Khachar, who found in Mulu a willing instrument of his machinations. Anonymous letters maligning Ratnanagari were sent to Fox Sahib, the Political Agent. A letter was sent to him, suggesting that Mallaraj’s attempts to resolve disputes with other rulers were a clear sign of disrespect to the English. But a king has four eyes; before long Mallaraj became aware of these machinations. He remained calm and appeared indifferent, pretending to be a mere spectator in this affair. Both Mulu and Fox Sahib believed that their secret was intact. Jarashankar and Samant had secured an understanding with all the neighbouring rulers except Rana Khachar. Fox Sahib began an inquisitorial correspondence with Mallaraj; the response sent by Jarashankar proved ineffective. Fox Sahib insisted that all disputes between Mallaraj and Khachar be resolved immediately. Mallaraj had not shared his knowledge of Mulu’s treachery with anyone, not even with Jarashankar who suspected Samant for the present trouble. Samant was aware of this suspicion, but did not make any attempts to correct Jarashankar’s impression.

Before long, Fox Sahib, Mulu Bha and Rana Khachar became allies; they corresponded in secret code. One day, Samant intercepted a letter from Fox Sahib to Mulu. This was Samant’s opportunity to clear any suspicions regarding his loyalty. He took the letter to Mallaraj. The letter stated that Mallaraj was an enemy of the English Queen’s representative, and that his attempt to forge a treaty with Rana Khachar was a part of this treachery. Mulu was asked to bear witness and provide evidence of Mallaraj’s disloyalty. Samant wept as he placed this letter before Mallaraj. ‘Maharaj, a traitor lives in my family. He is as destructive as fire. He has no right to live. Order his execution, and if there is any hesitation, allow me to bring you his head. Never before has Ratnanagari produced such a degenerate son.’ Samant shook with anger and sorrow as he spoke, his eyes bloodshot. Jarashankar said, ‘Samant Bha is an epitome of loyalty. Loneliness in old age is not the reward for such loyalty. We cannot punish Mulu Bha on the basis of mere suspicion alone.’ Mallaraj smiled and said to Jarashankar, ‘Explain to Samant the meaning of that verse cited by Vidya Chatura.’ Jarashankar recited: The elephants, whose temples are soiled with rut, are heard (to have run away) to the end of the quarters; the female elephants are an object of pity; while the deer are indeed not a footing of equality.
