Where should then this lord of the beasts exhibit the sharpness of his nails, the ends of which are incomparable.⟨fn:102⟩ ‘The verse says that in the distant horizon where the earth and the sky meet, mighty elephants roar, flanked by the female of the species, and grazing deer idle. But who is there to equal the lion, and whom should he test his might against? ‘Only Maharaj knows why he asked me to recount this verse to you, Samant Bha, but we have been reduced to little worms in the face of your fierce loyalty and the readiness to sacrifice your son. Mulu

Bha will also grow up to be a pillar of this state one day—this is a brahmin’s blessing. Many Jarashankars will come and go, but only the house of Samant Mulu will gift loyal, lion-like men to the state.’ Samant paid scant attention to Jarashankar. His eyes were fixed on Mallaraj. No one spoke for a while. Then Samant broke the silence, ‘Maharaj, I am not here to hear my praise. You have to give your assent to my request.’ Mallaraj:  ‘My response was that verse.’ Samant:  ‘I do not understand verses. Give me a straight response.’ Mallaraj:  ‘You will understand my response only if you comprehend that verse.’ Samant:  ‘It is your right to demand that I understand that verse.’ Mallaraj (laughing):  ‘You shall not be able to bring yourself to say, “Maharaj, please explain.” I want you to comprehend it. In our times, the subject people are as helpless as the forest deer; to oppress them even more is like a man showing his might to a woman. Let other kings hunt female elephants; theirs is not the hunt of the brave. The English are like the mighty roaring elephants. Brave are those who match them in strength. Maharaja Nagraj showed them that the men of Ratnanagari were truly brave. We have to care for our meek subjects. Hunting deer is an act of cowardice, and that is what you ask of me. Do you have a response?’ Stunned, Samant stared at his master, at a loss for words. Then he said, ‘Yes, we must protect our subjects, but that does not mean we should allow them to overpower us! Maharaj, if you make such norms, you will soon have to give up your throne and become a mendicant.’ Mallaraj smiled. ‘What is wrong if a kshatriya king becomes a mendicant for the sake of his subjects?’ Samant:  ‘Maharaj forgive me, but I cannot see how this will secure the welfare of your subjects. This is your generosity, but generosity is often a foolish way of seeking popularity among subjects. Your generosity might turn the people brazen and instead of securing their welfare; it could cut the very branch that supports them.’

Mallaraj:  ‘Samant, you do not seem to realise that Mulu is not only my subject, he is as much a son to me as is Maniraj.’ Samant:  ‘If that is true, you ought to give him punishment that is a hundred-fold harsher than what you gave me. Maharaj, you do not want to punish him because you do not regard him as your own.’ Mallaraj:  ‘A father who distances his son so much that the son cannot approach him allows the son to behave as if he is not the son.’ Samant:  ‘Maharaj, I accept defeat. Then you must punish him wherever he ceases to act as if he is not your own.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Now you speak intelligently, Samant, and not driven by rage. A king should not hear advice given in rage, nor should he act in rage or jealousy. Now that your intellect is unclouded by anger, you have acquired the fitness to discuss the matter. Justice is one of the responsibilities of a king. But statecraft occupies a place higher than justice; justice is only one of the instruments of statecraft. The sword of justice must always remain sharp so that subjects do not quarrel. But sometimes in case of conflict this weapon is used, but such use is rarely ever called for. The relationship between a ruler and his subjects is sometimes like that of a man and a woman; in such cases the man should deepen their love and union. At times their relationship is like that of a father and son; in such instances the ruler should deepen the trust between them; childlike subjects should remain in awe of the paternal power of the king. The king should nurture and nourish his subjects like a gardener tends his delicate plants. Infallible means are those which enhance, and not reduce, the power of the king. A king who does not choose means appropriate to the context and acts unreasonably, driven by rage or jealousy, also encourages others to walk the wrong path. Such a king merits hell. Samant, Mulu is intelligent. He has made an error, but we should not believe that he has been doing so for long. We must find a way wherein he is made to realise his mistake and give up the wrong path. Mulu should realise that the promised land contrived by the English and Khachar holds poison and not sugar; they have urged him to swallow poison. Mulu must acquire the discernment to distinguish between sugar and poison, and not seek the latter.’ Samant:  ‘Maharaj, I do not comprehend this roundabout way of speaking. Please talk to me straight.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Jarashankar, I have destroyed Samant’s defences. It is your responsibility now to find suitable means and satisfy Samant’s query.’ Jarashankar was deep in thought for a while as he searched for a way out of the quandary. When he spoke, his words were slow and deliberate; as he spoke his thoughts became clearer. ‘Samantraj, the first hurdle in our intended treaty with Rana Khachar is Mulu Bha—this you have showed to us quite clearly. Khachar himself is an obstacle to our treaty. Agent Sahib is the third hurdle. Khachar does not stand to benefit from the delay because the treaty we have proposed is such that he is the sole beneficiary of it; in fact it is we who stand to lose. Khachar would gain both territory and wealth from the proposed treaty, but he shuns them. We have to ask whether this decision is due to his stubborn, unthinking nature. But Khachar is not stubborn, nor does he happen to be insistent. It is likely that he views our accommodative stance with suspicion. It is equally likely that the Agent has promised him something and that his actions are driven by greed. It is also likely that Khachar and Mulu Bha, being of the same age, are close friends and wish to use this friendship for mutual gain. These are the probable reasons for his conduct. Samantraj, I believe that you have forgiven me; but Mulu Bha still harbours a feeling of deep hurt and resentment. You know and are well capable of recognising that I as a minister had no role to play in the decision that Maharaj took in your case. However, it is but natural for young Mulu Bha to think otherwise. In such a state of mind, he will not take kindly to your loyalty to Maharaj. Hence, my first advice to you is that he should have no inkling whatsoever of our alliance.’ Samant bit his lips and said, ‘What else?’ Jarashankar:  ‘You must become a close friend of Mulu Bha; he must come to trust you to the extent that he opens his heart to you. You have to ensure that he trusts you enough to reveal the machinations of the Agent and Khachar without any fear. Eventually, even Khachar should come to trust you. Samant Bha, an enemy’s enemy is a friend— use this maxim and seek entry into their camp. Use Mulu Bha, who is clever enough to gain an entry into Khachar’s house. We should not punish Mulu Bha but use him intelligently to secure the treaty with Khachar.’ As Samant’s trust and comprehension grew, he seemed less agitated. He softly said, ‘One acts either under duress, or with a hope for future gain. Mulu has nothing to fear as you have resolved not to punish him. What can he hope to gain from this?’ Jarashankar:  ‘Samantraj, at present, I am the eyes and ears of the Maharaj. But if Mulu Bha secures the treaty, he will take my place for the Maharaj. In the present scenario I occupy a position of prominence; but the future scenario erases me and paints Mulu Bha in bright, resplendent colours. This aspiration will be enough for him to trust you. Samantraj, for Mulu Bha friendship with Khachar is a means to acquire power in the state. Show him the way to power. Mulu Bha’s tender heart is possessed by a ghost; he must be freed from this possession. With the intent of removing me from power, you, Mulu Bha, Khachar and ultimately the Maharaj should form an alliance and secure the treaty.’ Samant:  ‘What about the Agent? Eventually both Khachar and Mulu will remain dissatisfied and retaliate with even greater force. We will be back to the same quandary but with fewer options. Have you considered that?’ Jarashankar:  ‘Once we come together with Khachar, the Agent will be isolated. We will have a letter bearing his name, which may be true or may not be true. If it turns out that it is not the Agent’s letter, any accusation from us will make us more vulnerable. He will have many instruments and occasions to cause us harm. Even if he is the author of this letter, he is not likely to admit it. His superiors will hold that he was right, and we were wrong. So he will not be hurt at all; it will be held that he is not the author of the letter. He will accuse us of disloyalty. If we accuse the Agent, we will have to fight a strong enemy openly and approach his seniors for justice. If we win, we get nothing but if we lose, we lose it all. If God has willed that we should take that course and go to war with the British, then so be it. But we should not bring it upon ourselves; it will be like cutting our own feet. And even if we were to succeed, what guarantee do we have that the new Agent will be any better than the present one? How can we be certain that the new official will not take revenge for his countrymen? If the new Agent were to start fresh proceedings against us, we will have to go in for an appeal. The superiors will come to believe that we complain habitually. Our situation is like that of the daughter-in-law who is blamed for all ills in the family of her in-laws. Samantraj, if Khachar can strike a deal with the Agent and we cannot, it is our inability. The best way out for us is to keep the matter of the letter a secret. At present, the Agent thinks that we are without any support, but once Khachar and we become allies, he will hesitate to strike at us. From being an arbitrator of the treaty, he will be reduced to being a mere registrar of it. This course will moderate animosity.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Samant, are you capable of this?’ Samant:  ‘I will learn and become capable of all that the Maharaj commands. I am not bothered about the Agent. But if that son of mine turns to devastation, I will have to raise this question once again. What about that? Maharaj, even a sage like Kashyap had a son like Hiranyakashyapu. My state is similar. Statecraft demands that an enemy be nipped in the bud. It would be stupid to let the enemy become powerful and then seek his destruction. Maharaj, I deserved the punishment you gave me for having insulted the minister. God is my witness that I harbour no other thought. That punishment saved me from grave fault. If I fail to express my gratitude to you for showing me the true nature of royal duty, it would be said that I did not deserve to be born in our glorious Suryavanshi family. Maharaj, I swear that I did not once grudge Jarashankar. If you and Jarashankar have truly forgiven me, allow me like Bharat of our glorious sun lineage, who abandoned his mother Kaikeyi, to both abandon and destroy the evil son born to me. Like Bharat who submitted to Shri Ram, I fall at your feet and swear that my conscience is pure.’

Just as a great storm subsides and surrenders to the lofty mountain, the powerfully built warrior fell at Mallaraj’s feet, his head touching them. Samant’s eyes rained tears and the lament of his saddened heart could be heard. Jarashankar was stunned; he stood petrified. Mallaraj melted. He bent down to raise his old friend and loyal Bhayat. At that moment, a song wafted in from Mena Rani’s quarters. My lord, you are the jewel in Samant’s crown Manidhar, stay forever compassionate Helpless Mena begs of you Mallaraj raised his brother and embraced him. Jarashankar watched the great warriors in tight embrace. His lips expressed what his heart felt, ‘Maharaj, we pitiable brahmins can never rise up to such loyalty. Maharaj, today the son of this loyal friend has raised his head against you, but one day he shall fall at your feet with equal loyalty. The fruit of such seed can never be sour. Maharaj, do not forsake such men from your midst for the sake of this poor brahmin. Ministers will come and go, but such loyal, pure-blooded friends will come rarely.’ Mallaraj released Samant from his embrace. The three of them sat down. ‘Samant, the duty of the king is so complex and unfathomable that he is often required to perform tasks repugnant to his conscience. The punishment that I awarded you was one such task.’ Samant interrupted the king and said, ‘Maharaj, let us drop that matter. You must however decide upon my request.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Samant, you will not rest easy till I punish my child Mulu. But listen, he needs to be given a chance to reform himself. If God willed that he should have treacherous thoughts, the same God will also fill him with good sense. The fiery ordeal of today will allow him to cherish the cool shade of tomorrow. He will repent and that will be his punishment; you will know from your own experience that such repentance is in no way less than any punishment that I might award. And yet if Mulu fails to reform and constitutes himself to be an enemy of the state, we will use all our might to crush him.’ Samant:  ‘Maharaj, I cannot fathom your statecraft. I have come to believe that since you punished me, you hesitate to punish Mulu.’

Mallaraj:  ‘We have decided to use Mulu against his wish as a means of securing a treaty with Khachar, and in emerging victorious against the machinations of the Agent. But if Mulu remains treacherous even after we secure our goals, that will be his defeat and for a treacherous man, defeat is a punishment in itself.’ Samant:  ‘What then?’ Mallaraj:  ‘If any other punishment is required, I will have Samant punish Mulu.’ Samant:  ‘Is that certain?’ Mallaraj:  ‘Has Mallaraj ever been untrue to his words?’ Samant:  ‘Maharaj, consider your wish as good as fulfilled.’ Samant took his leave. Mallaraj said to Jarashankar, ‘Some days ago Fox Sahib was my guest, and we went hunting in our forest. We spoke about a lot of things, but we could not bring up this matter. I knew that he wanted to raise this issue.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj, the power of your virtue is such that the evil- minded turns cowardly and retreats. Evil becomes powerless when faced with a great soul who combines virtue with valour. Let me remind you of a verse which I once told you. A king, while entering a forest inhabited by sages, said: “This forest has a quiet beauty but my heart treads softly.” Even ferocious animals like lions and tigers turn tail when faced with a brave man who looks them in the eye. Why would a clever but evil Englishman not hesitate before expressing impure thoughts to you? If an Englishman ever succeeds in expressing lowly thoughts before a king, know that to be a measure of the withered authority and virtue of the king, and not a measure of the Englishman’s character.’ Jarashankar took leave of Mallaraj. Samant accomplished the assigned task with faith and acumen. Days passed. Months went by. Samant gained Mulu’s trust. Khachar and his associates submitted to the will of the ruler of Ratnanagari. The treaty with Khachar was signed. The Political Agent stood witness to the treaty and the British government confirmed it. All four boundaries of Mallaraj’s kingdom came to be definitively demarcated. Young Mulu believed that all credit was due to him; even Khachar was no match for him. In this game of chaupat, there were four players: the Agent, Khachar, Mulu and Mallaraj. Mallaraj was the only player who secured all the houses. Mulu became proud of his success. The fall of the minister seemed imminent to him. He reckoned that he had earned the right to seek reward from Mallaraj and his father. Samant’s fears about Mulu seemed to be coming true. Mallaraj was keen to satisfy all of Mulu’s aspirations. He was willing to shower all possible generosity over Mulu. But his desire and resolve to protect his minister were even greater. Samant had personal experience of this policy. He had come to regard both his personal banishment and the policy behind it as beneficial to the state. Mallaraj wanted his rule to benefit his Bhayat. He believed this was good for the state. At the same time he recognised that unchecked aspirations of his Bhayat would spell the demise of the authority of the state officials. Just as Ganga and Yamuna originate from the same source, the power of the Bhayat and the authority of the officials emanate from the same source— the person of the ruler. Yamuna merges in the Ganga and finds the sea. Similarly, the power of the Bhayat can be harnessed for the state only by the sagacity and authority of the officials. Therefore, Mallaraj remained alert that the unchecked, inebriated power of his Bhayat did not act to circumscribe the authority of his minister. Even if he so much as suspected his Bhayat of transgression, he came down on them like a lion on its prey. Samant, at one point, viewed this policy as detrimental, but with time and maturity he came to regard the policy as necessary and beneficial. Samant now wanted Mallaraj to use all possible force to curb his son, Mulu. Mulu had proved himself useful to the king. The king made every possible effort to satisfy Mulu’s aspirations. But a person consumed by the fire of animosity remains discontent even when all his aspirations are satisfied. While Samant had overcome his resentment about being punished and the resultant rage and had proved to be an example of loyalty, his son could not forgive Jarashankar for the same act. In his devotion to his father, Mulu destroyed all traces of loyalty towards the state that he might have felt. His statecraft was consumed by loathing. He had hoped that the treaty with Khachar would spell the doom of the powers of the brahmin minister, but his hopes were dashed. All other desires became insignificant compared to the desire to defeat Jarashankar, which possessed him. As Mulu failed even in this mission, frustrated rage took hold of him. Rage leads one to act indiscriminately in every sphere and it sullies every action. An enraged person is incapable of distinction; wrath destroys everything that it touches. Chandika in her rage danced on the body of Shiva. Mulu’s anger towards Jarashankar inevitably turned into rage against Mallaraj. If Mallaraj does not get rid of the minister, why should one not get rid of Mallaraj, he asked himself. But this was not feasible in Ratnanagari. Mulu could not take such an issue to the Agent. Hence, he decided to finish off the minister rather than wait for his authority to be eclipsed. Like a dog that sniffs its way around, Mulu sniffed around for some weakness of the minister. His search failed. Instead, he decided to cultivate a friendship with Jarashankar. Gradually, he gained entry into the house of Jarashankar and Vidya Chatura. Jarashankar, who had a measure of Mulu’s mind, was not deceived. Their relationship did not grow beyond formal cordiality. Jarashankar, experienced as he was in palace politics, remained undeceived; but inexperienced Vidya Chatura accepted the offer of friendship from the king’s nephew. This was enough of an opening for Mulu, who made his move with the dexterity of a warrior. Jarashankar warned Vidya Chatura, but Vidya Chatura, educated in English ways, did not agree with him. He could not distance Mulu completely. Thus, Mulu retained some foothold in Vidya Chatura’s house. His father, Manchatura, disliked Mulu and each time Mulu came visiting, Manchatura remained alert like a tiger. One day Manchatura was not at home. Mulu seized the opportunity and went to Vidya Chatura’s house. All the servants were busy. Sundargauri was at the neighbour’s house. Vidya Chatura had not yet come home. In the guise of playing with Kumud, Mulu sought Gunasundari’s company. Gunasundari was quick to suspect Mulu’s intentions. She trembled with fear but swiftly ran to the inner chambers and shut the door. She was concerned about little Kumud but reassured herself that it was more important to save herself and her family from ignominy. She left her daughter and the house to the care of the gods. Before long, Gunasundari regained her composure but still thought it prudent to stay behind closed doors. She peeped through an opening; Mulu, on the pretext of handing over Kumud to her mother, had entered the house and was looking around. Just then, Manchatura returned. He was quick to grasp the situation and he could imagine Gunasundari’s state. He took Kumud in his arms and, in his brief exchange with Mulu, ensured that such a situation would never again arise in the future. Manchatura said, ‘Mulu Bha, you are a scion of the royal household. When you visit our poor home, it creates complications and people get a chance to talk ill about you. Hence, all that you need to do is to send a message, and Vidya Chatura will present himself before you. In any case you will find him at the palace daily. Therefore, you should not trouble yourself by coming here. It is in the fitness of things that Vidya Chatura should come and visit you. You are a wise man, Mulu Bha. If you were to ask Samant Bha, his advice to you would be the same.’ Mulu’s guilty conscience enabled him to understand the true import of this statement. Mulu lacked the courage to give a retort to the elderly but robust Manchatura. He looked down, mumbled, ‘That is true,’ and left. Manchatura called out to Gunasundari. His words were clearly audible to the retreating Mulu. He said, ‘Gunasundari, the evil one has left. From tomorrow onwards, appoint Arab guards to protect you so that such an evil incident does not recur.’ Gunasundari came out and said meekly to her father-in-law, ‘Pitaji, I have told you more than once that the custom of a joint family is good. In a joint family, such difficulties do not arise. When Mataji, my sisters-in-law, brother-in-law and his family all lived here, no stranger, no matter how powerful or evil, ever had the courage to so much as peep inside our house. I do not know what wrong I have done that you have to go and live in Manoharpuri every now and then.’ Manchatura laughed and said, ‘Then we will appoint Arab guards, won’t we? Those who learn English must live like the English in separate households.’ Gunasundari sat down, and somewhat dejectedly said, ‘You are our elder, Pitaji, and can say what you like. But God is my witness.

A mere blow of air from the mouth of an Englishman is enough to destroy a mountain. Even kings tremble in their presence. English madams can live in forests all by themselves, and our men will be afraid to even glance at them. If, like them, we, too, kept an open house, every passerby and even dogs would want to enter. When our families disperse, we lose our protection. Elders like you are our fortification, and when these forts are breached, women like me and all else that is precious in our households will be robbed in broad daylight.’ ‘Gunasundari, I provoked you because I wanted to hear these words from you. You speak like wizened elders. But these days, young people sing to a different tune in which the elderly cannot join in. You will find your words falling on deaf ears. In our household, I am the elder and all of you are the young ones. It is good that our household has remained untouched by new-fangled notions. But who can foretell the future? Do we know even the present? Therefore, we will have Arab guards. And I am of course around as long as there is life in me.’ Manchatura changed the subject and made Gunasundari feel lighter. Angered by his failure, Mulu walked towards his pleasure garden outside the city. Gunasundari had proved smarter than him. He had to swallow Manchatura’s insult; he felt humiliated. He was also afraid that now Vidya Chatura, Jarashankar and the Maharaj would come to know of his misadventures. As he walked on dejectedly, he passed by a market. People had gathered around a brahmin, who entertained them with a song. Hoping to lighten his heavy heart, Mulu joined the crowd. She whom the world calls ‘helpless’ makes A man dance to her tunes, Compels even one born of a queen To stand as her water-bearer Such are the scenes of this Kalyug. She draws the debauched even deeper, Drowns the very scriptures of the priests, Entices the most accomplished yogis, Blindfolds the wise— Even the sages and seers have succumbed to her spell:

The woman’s sinful body ensnares them all Such is the blazing Kalyug. All the Satis have descended into the netherworld The debauched have become the high-priestesses; Their gaze entraps all those Who come into their line of vision; The brahmin’s verses have become their charms, The Rajput’s weapons, their toys. Someone went up to the brahmin and asked, ‘Is your woman like the one you described?’ There ensued a scuffle. Young lads tossed around the brahmin’s headgear. Mulu got the brahmin out of the melee, and he went on his way, the words of the song still ringing in his ears. ‘She ... Compels even one born of a queen to stand as her water-bearer ... The Rajput’s weapons, their toys.’ This is so true! No! No! There are pure unsullied women. It is we the Rajputs who have become debauched. Mulu’s excitement ebbed. He reasoned: There can’t be anyone as stupid as me. I went the wrong way. War can only be among equals. This Jarashankar and Vidya Chatura—mere brahmins! Ministers are after all servants of the king. I harboured animosity against the lowly, and I was driven to low means. What would I have gained even if I had succeeded? I failed, and lost face. One must fight an equal. Mulu walked on, deep in thought. A new plot came to his mind. Excited, he twirled his moustache and said to himself: A Rajput is one who breaks norms given by the brahmins. My grandfather was two years younger to Nagraj, and he was for that reason denied the kingdom. Such are the rules of the devious brahmins! But I, his grandson, have the capacity to make the living join the dead. The day this effete Maniraj dies, Mulu will be crowned king! All he needs is one blow of my sword. Why should this Rajput not act like one? Why deal with the brahmin? Whom should a Rajput fear? The man who deserves to be king shall be crowned king! This calamitous thought that came to him at an inauspicious moment took possession of Mulu. He was caught in a whirlwind. Maniraj was now an adolescent, and was being trained to hunt in the large forests of Ratnanagari. Scions of royal households accompanied him on the hunt. Mulu decided to take advantage of such an expedition. Samant had become a confidante of his son. Before long, he became aware of Mulu’s machinations. Samant had Mulu seized, placed him under arrest and put guards to watch over Mulu. Samant was not in the least surprised by the evil designs of his son. He now understood Mallaraj’s reluctance to punish Mulu. He knew that Mulu had a short time to live; he wanted the enemy of his king dead. Samant was delighted that Maniraj was unharmed and safe forever. He felt proud that his forecast had come true. This Rajput father felt no remorse or sadness at the certain death of his son. He set forth for the palace, resplendent as the noon sun, to hold the king to his promise. Samant lodged a complaint against Mulu, accusing him of plotting to kill the prince and heir apparent. Mallaraj gave him a patient hearing. Samant demanded death for Mulu. Mallaraj promised to consider the request. Samant said, ‘What is the need to deliberate in a matter as clear as this? What could be a greater crime? You must remain true to your promise, Maharaj.’ Mallaraj considered the matter and ordered Jarashankar, ‘Both Samant and you are aware of the resolution under which such matters are to be placed before a tribunal of the Bhayat. Read the resolution again and appoint a tribunal as per its terms. That tribunal will decide the charges against Mulu.’ Samant:  ‘Does that mean that you will not sit on judgement? The resolution does not cover criminal offences.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Read the resolution carefully. It clearly states that in case of any dispute with the state, the tribunal should be constituted. It is incorrect for me to sit on judgement in any matter that involves Maniraj. If you want my justice, withdraw your complaint and set Mulu free.’ Samant:  ‘He will be released only in the next life. You are bound by your pledge to me.’ Mallaraj:  ‘In that case, the tribunal, to which you and other Bhayat have committed to, will adjudicate the matter.’

Samant:  ‘Maharaj, in that case, the tribunal will also award punishment. I am entitled to be a member of that tribunal.’ Mallaraj:  ‘You are not impartial, Samant. You are the complainant. You are not fit to sit on judgement.’ Samant:  ‘I am also the father of the accused. Maharaj, the other Bhayat will be torn between conflicting loyalties and will not award punishment that is deserved. As per your promise, I am entitled to be on that tribunal, failing which it will be a breach of your promise.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj, it is for such reasons that I had said that such a resolution should require the consent of the minister.’ Mallaraj:  ‘You brahmins are wise in the hindsight; you will not understand such things. Samant, I authorise you to be on that tribunal. I am bound by my promise. But read and act according to the terms of the resolution, so that I am not constrained to appoint another tribunal to review your decision.’ The tribunal was constituted; it held Mulu guilty of the conspiracy to murder Maniraj and awarded him death penalty. The king refused to abide by this extreme punishment. A fresh debate ensued between Samant and Mallaraj. The king asked Mulu, ‘Mulu Bha, it was my attempt to satisfy all your desires. But I failed. I take pity on you. For that, I am chided by your father. Have either Maniraj or I done a personal wrong to you?’ Mulu was in shackles. He raised himself to his full height, looked up straight at the king and said, ‘Maharaj, but for your treaty with the English, we would not have seen such sorry days. You signed the treaty. You were misguided by this brahmin. If you had stripped him of his powers, I would not have been forced to act as I did. So be it. You proved to be a weakling in moments of political crisis. You are mesmerised by this lowly brahmin, and so long as you do not free yourself from his snare, I consider you undeserving of this throne. I have the courage and the capacity of shouldering the burden that you are incapable of. I chose the path that would give me the responsibility of the state. I have done no wrong. In this world there are many undeserving and ineffective rulers such as you who take the lives of capable men to perpetuate their rule. You can do the same and take my life. I am ready to die.’ Samant was enraged. He got up and hit his fist hard on Mulu’s forehead. Blood flowed. The king restrained Samant. Mallaraj said, ‘Mulu Bha, your father’s anger and punishment must bring back memories of childhood. Hear me out. I am happy that you became my judge before I could judge your conduct. Mulu Bha, you admit to the charges levelled against you, but the veracity of the charges that you place upon me can only be decided by time. You require the maturity that comes with experience to realise this. If I give you death penalty and shorten your life, you would never gain this experience, and I would never have the opportunity to be freed from the charges levelled against me. Given my desire to be freed from those charges, I cannot award you death penalty.’ Samant jumped up and said, ‘What? Maharaj, that cannot be! You have to accept the punishment decided by the tribunal of the Bhayat.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Samant, be patient. We will give you the opportunity to be heard. Mulu Bha, no one in your family has been as depraved as you. This is a sign of our times. One day you will acquire the fitness to be a member of our family, and till such time, I do not have the right to take your life. Only a criminal who cannot be reformed deserves death penalty. I have not yet given up hope. Hence, you do not deserve to die. Mulu Bha, you have insulted this throne, and for that reason you are a criminal in the eyes of God. But I cannot say that this throne will never need someone like you. And it is my duty to see to it that you have a long life only for such an eventuality. Mulu Bha, you were intent on taking Maniraj’s life. Someday, Maniraj will occupy this throne, and at that time he may decide to pardon you. I hope he will have the generosity to forgive you, and I do not wish to forsake that hope by taking your life. Therefore, Samant, Mulu will be placed in your custody today. Tomorrow, we shall decide on his punishment in a way that respects the decision of the tribunal, and also my hope.’ Samant put Mulu into the prison and returned to be with the king. Mallaraj, Jarashankar and Samant sat together to reflect on the fate of the royal household.

Mallaraj:  ‘Jarashankar, you heard the judgement of the Bhayat. They are authorised to adjudicate on the crime but cannot award punishment. I felt that their decision was extreme and so I gave a punishment that he deserves. It is your responsibility to think of ways of executing that punishment. Samant:  ‘Do I have the right to know the reasons underlying your decision?’ Mallaraj:  ‘Of course. The reason is the same as what I told Mulu.’ Samant:  ‘But I am not satisfied. Such generosity towards an enemy is stupidity. This snake does not deserve to be cared for and raised. He will become a baharvatiya—he will form a band of outlaws and evil-doers from among our people, our Bhayat and the English; he will foster many enemies of the state. Maharaj, I clearly say that Mulu does not deserve to live. Death is the least punishment for those who seek to poison the state.’ Mallaraj:  ‘You should recall that it was because of the threat of English presence that we decided that Bhayat should sit in judgement over other Bhayat.’ Samant:  ‘Yes.’ Mallaraj:  ‘We gave juridical powers to the Bhayat in order to fortify our state even further.’ Samant:  ‘Yes.’ Mallaraj:  ‘The English might use some of the Bhayat to attack us, and at that time our Bhayat should have the strength to defend the state. This arrangement was made with the consent of the Bhayat.’ Samant:  ‘That is true.’ Mallaraj:  ‘The English and Mulu may use their combined strength to attack the state; this would also show up our weakness, and when that happens, you, Samant, will be authorised to use every possible force to meet with such a challenge.’ Samant:  ‘All that is there. But I do not like this way of inviting the axe to chop our feet.’

Mallaraj:  ‘The present arrangement will save our feet from being chopped. Think of a time when neither you, nor I, nor even Maniraj are alive. At that time, the man we consider the enemy of our state will become its master and protector. If we were to finish him off now, we would have acted as enemies of the state.’ After long deliberation, the validity of Mallaraj’s decision was accepted by the other two. It was decided that Mulu be banished from the state and be allowed to live in exile in a place of his choosing; he was to be provided with enough resources to meet his needs. It was also decided that after Samant’s death, his garas would vest in the state. If Mulu were to run away from his place of exile or act against the interests of Ratnanagari, his annuity would be stopped. If he were to enter the territory of Ratnanagari, he would be arrested and imprisoned for life. Maniraj was authorised to commute any part of this sentence, or pardon Mulu altogether. Mulu wanted to live in exile in Rana Khachar’s state. His wish was granted. The tribunal of the Bhayat signed the document. Mulu was banished from the state, but he left behind many burning issues. The Agent was informed of this banishment; he wrote a letter to Mallaraj, seeking information. Samant was quick to accuse Mulu of conspiring through the Agent. In response, Ratnanagari asked the Agent as to who had initiated this inquiry, for what reason and under what authority. The Agent responded, ‘It is the office of the Political Agent that wishes to be informed of the events. If the information about Mulu’s banishment is correct, it is likely that he would become an outlaw. This would threaten the peace and security of the country. It is in this exercise of the sovereign powers vested in the British government that this information is sought. In matters of peace and security of the country, the interests of the native rulers, subjects and the sovereign power are one.’ In conclusion, the Agent made a personal appeal to Mallaraj, saying, ‘I regard you as a friend, and as a friend, I urge you that a virtuous king like you should have no hesitation in accepting the power of the British government. If you were to defy this power, it would needlessly sow the seeds of suspicion. I do wish to inform you that the British government has the power to seek compliance of its desire.’ Mallaraj was enraged by this letter. ‘Initially, the Agent assumed the powers of arbitration. Now he wants to police the state. Jarashankar, this is the outcome of your statecraft.’ Jarashankar, keen to observe Samant’s reaction, looked towards him. Samant realised this. He spoke not impatiently but in a grave tone, ‘Maharaj, if this is the outcome of the minister’s statecraft, its resolution also lies within it.’ ‘Samant, have you jumped from the king’s chariot to that of the minister? Am I awake or in sleep? Is this you?’ Mallaraj spoke with genuine surprise. Samant smiled and said, ‘Maharaj, how can I say that you were asleep? Earlier, whenever issues of statecraft were discussed, the two of us were on the same side as brothers. But eventually you would go across to the brahmin’s way of thinking, and I would be left holding on to the earlier opinion. I have learnt from my experience. I have decided to join the party that you are eventually going to join.’ Mallaraj shook with laughter. ‘Samant, the punishment has clearly been beneficial to you. You have to speak your mind. I do not want you to conceal your opinion.’ Samant:  ‘Maharaj, if I were to speak a lie, either because of fear or for any other reason, I would disqualify myself to be your brother. Maharaj, during the period of banishment, I had the opportunity of quiet reflection. I have become a devout follower of the statecraft of Jarashankar. Therefore, I have the courage today to defend his statecraft against the charge that you place on it.’ Mallaraj:  ‘How so?’ Samant:  ‘Maharaj, the minister has given us the broad contours of the policy of our times. The British government is in the mood of feasting at our expense; it will have many desires. It will insist that some of these be satisfied whether they are just or unjust. It will use force or persuasion to secure our compliance. We cannot engage them in battle. We can only carry on a war of words, which will cause ripples in quiet waters. We will have to oppose a force far superior to us; each time we oppose them, we are likely to lose and we will come to be regarded as an enemy. We would decline and eventually, we will have to give in to their demands. Maharaj, I do not think that we should bring upon ourselves this situation. It is better to abdicate the throne than commit this folly.’ Mallaraj:  ‘What should we do?’ Samant:  ‘We should enter into a war of words with the British government only when we think they are ready to accept our point of view; we can decide then either to sweet-talk them in a friendly way, or use some bitter remedy. Whenever the government places a new demand, we should ask ourselves if in the final instance compliance with it is inevitable or negotiable. If the demand is one on which negotiation is possible, we should oppose it. We should not resist inevitable demands; we should comply with such demands as friends, and not be forced into submission as weak opponents. This will earn us their friendship and even their gratitude. Maharaj, those like us who learnt to swim in different waters will not feel comfortable with the new situation. I prefer death to this submission; but Maharaj for kings and kshatriyas, adherence to duty is much greater than personal emotion. It is the royal duty to submit to the demands of the time and seek space for manoeuvre within that.’ Mallaraj, mesmerised by these words, carried on the discussion with Samant, disregarding Jarashankar. ‘Samant, your words today have the depth and wisdom of experience that even our minister cannot match; Jarashankar would agree to that. So tell me, what are we to do with this desire of their government to police our homes? The British government might want that when their dogs bark at us, we do not even shoo them away. Would you consider such a demand as inevitable or negotiable?’ Mallaraj was so full of anger that his eyes had turned red and his body was bathed in perspiration. Samant fully sympathised with this kshatriya sentiment. He said, ‘Maharaj, you were born to command and rule; you do not know what it is to carry out orders. In former times, the emperor of Delhi or his governor or the Peshwa of Poona or his officials used to lay siege and coerce the rulers to accept their demands. Today, the British government keeps its forces in the barracks and sends out their Political Agent, who is still backed by their military might. Rulers have no means to fight this coercion and must submit to it while retaining whatever autonomous authority they can. You have operated under similar constraints ever since you sat on the saddle.’ ‘Samant, you are right. I, too, had foreseen this day when we signed the treaty with the British. But clearly, my body and mind have become feeble with age. Both my intellect and authority have withered. Old age has made you wiser, but my mind has become blurred. Jarashankar, so long as Samant was opposed to your views, in order to protect you, I considered it my duty to shoulder the responsibility of the state. You no longer need my protection; Samant is with you, not opposed to you. Maniraj is still a child and cannot shoulder the responsibility of the state. I am old and hence incapable of ruling. From today onwards, you and Samant have to think of the welfare of the state. Leave me to think of God.’ Both Samant and Jarashankar were overcome with emotion but did not allow the tears welling up in their eyes to roll down. No one could speak for a while. Samant wiped his blurred eyes and broke the silence, ‘Maharaj, all these years we have lived in the protection of a great banyan tree. We are incapable of providing that kind of shelter to the state. Maharaj, we are fit to obey. You are the soul of this kingdom. Only you can infuse life into this state, not us.’ Mallaraj stood up. He appeared as tall and sturdy as the pillars of the palace. Hitherto, his bearing had the visage of valour and authority; today he seemed detached and unconcerned. Religious quest had replaced royal authority. His gaze seemed to have turned inwards; his ears seemed eager to listen to a hitherto unheard voice. Mallaraj seemed uncertain of the path that awaited him. Samant and Jarashankar also stood up. The minister appeared to have found a way of fulfilling the new aspiration of the king, as also a way of ensuring that he continued to discharge his duties. Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj, if you have decided to withdraw from worldly life and accept Vanaprastha, I am willing to follow you into the forest.

Hitherto, I have advised you on statecraft; henceforth, I shall join you in deliberations on the matters of the soul. But when the hour of death approaches, each one of us is required to perform one final duty: the one about to die must ensure the welfare of the living.’ Mallaraj smiled and said, ‘All right. That shall be done. You and Samant think of a solution. I am not about to run away like a truant child. I am open to all kinds of suggestions except one.’ Jarashankar:  ‘We will think about it and implement it with your consent.’ Mallaraj:  ‘This means that you will involve me in the final decision. This is not part of the duty of a man ready to meet his maker.’ Jarashankar:  ‘Only you can decide whether our decision is in accordance with your religious duty.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Is that so?’ Jarashankar:  ‘It simply means that you will have to participate in the discussion and decide for yourself as to what constitutes your duty.’ Mallaraj:  ‘If I have to participate in the discussion and decide regarding my duty, what will the two of you do?’ Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj, who are we to decide for you?’ Mallaraj:  ‘Samant, don’t you think our Pradhan is cunning? He got me to agree to his proposal against my wish. Now he persuades me to change my mind without even opposing me!’ Samant:  ‘Maharaj, it is for this very reason that he is fit to be your minister. There are ministers who plead and please their kings, garner benefits and consider their duty fulfilled. They do not have the interest of the king or of the people at heart. They never speak their mind. Moved by greed for wealth or power, they deceive their master. They tell lies. They have no regards for their masters, whom they consider to be fools. These treacherous ministers are enemies of both the king and the people. Maharaj, such ministers deserve to be thrown into the gutter.’

Mallaraj:  ‘But even Jarashankar did not speak his mind freely. He took a circuitous route, he deceived me and he finally got me to agree to what he wanted of me.’ Samant:  ‘That is the correct thing to do. One cannot be brazen and call one’s mother as our father’s wife. Maharaj, once upon a time I was brazen. The minister spoke the truth in a civil and courteous way. This is a sign of his acumen, and my brazenness was a sign of my stupidity. It is the duty of a minister to speak the truth in an agreeable manner.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Then he could speak an agreeable lie as well.’ Samant:  ‘No, the scriptures do not encourage a lie. The scriptural injunction is to speak the truth that is both agreeable and in the interest of the listener—which I interpret to mean a clear disavowal of a lie. It also suggests that a truth that is not in the interest of the listener, or one that is disagreeable, should not be spoken. A minister proves his worth by speaking the truth that is both agreeable and in the interest of the king.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Jarashankar, is that so?’ Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj, when I have a pleader as clever as Samant, why should I complicate matters by speaking for myself?’ Mallaraj:  ‘Do you think that kings are incapable of hearing the truth?’ Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj, you know what your capacity is. Your wrath was unbearable when the functionary of a powerful sovereign asked a question. Would I have the strength to remain steadfast in the face of your wrath? Maharaj, I know my weakness, you know your strength.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Is it desirable that the king be possessed of such capacity?’ Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj, the answer is contingent upon time and context. In the Shanti Parva of the Mahabharata, Bhishma’s counsel to Yudhishthir was that in times to come, kings will be surpassed by their advisors.’ Mallaraj:  ‘And what is the injunction of our times?’ Jarashankar smiled and said:  ‘You are determined that I should speak my mind. I cannot go contrary to your wish. Maharaj is well seized of the imperatives of our times. Our context would depend upon whether you are angry, excited or possessed of equanimity as also whether I am moved by selfishness or act out of consideration of your interest. If a king has to deliberate on all such matters, it is burdensome and it can also be dangerous. Hence it is good for both the king and the counsellor to remain steadfast to the advice of Bhishma.’ Mallaraj:  ‘What should the king do?’ Jarashankar:  ‘A king must encourage his counsellor to speak the truth that is both agreeable and beneficial; he should be intolerant of untruth and yet not crave for agreeable counsel. He should at the same time not accept brazenness. A king should not tolerate any insult and must punish any transgression immediately. The authority of the king should be such that his counsellors and servants do not deviate from their duty. These qualities are necessary for a king, regardless of whether they be regarded as strength or weakness. Maharaj, I have spoken fearlessly.’ Mallaraj heard his minister attentively and said, ‘Jarashankar, you gave us a long discourse, and I shall imbibe these qualities. Tell me, what should we do about the Agent?’ Jarashankar:  ‘Maharaj, our responsibility is confined to our state. The British have to keep an eye over hundreds of native rulers of India. It is the duty of the sovereign to be seized of all developments, however insignificant, in their territory. They have to observe what tiny kingdoms and petty rulers cannot see. They have to institute processes for a common good and also protect and further their larger interests. It is the duty of the sovereign to be alert, inquisitive and informed. They also have to keep native rulers on their guard. In order to meet with different situations, they will have to assume more powers. We have to ensure that they do not get any opportunity to exercise more power over us. In a given situation, we should, according to Samantraj’s advice, decide if the outcome is predetermined or if it can be negotiated to our advantage. We committed a mistake by raising a question on the authority of the Agent. He seized the opportunity and gave a cunning response. We shall not commit such mistakes in the future; we shall also try and undo this harm. A king who has no weakness has nothing to fear from prying eyes.’ Samant:  ‘Maharaj, let us drop this long-winded discussion. This problem has been created by that wretched son of mine. For me he is dead and I have already performed his last rites. Now our cry announcing his death should be heard by that Agent. Maharaj, Jarashankar is right. Our authority will not be compromised. We should send copies of the tribunal’s decision and the final punishment awarded by you, to the Agent. Jarashankar and I will take care of the rest. We must announce that Mulu is dead for us, and if the Agent still wants to be possessed by his ghost, we know how to deal with possessions. For the present, we must announce Mulu’s death. Jarashankar, let’s go.’ All three men got up. Samant followed Jarashankar. Samant’s anger was evident from his demeanour; he bit his lips and clenched his teeth; his hand seemed poised to draw out his dagger, but sheathed it. Mallaraj observed this as he saw his minister and Bhayat walk away.
chapters.summary: Amidst escalating territorial disputes with Khachar and the Agent, Mallaraj consults Jarashankar and Samant, determined to protect his kingdom's sovereignty and future.

chapters.title: Mallaraj's Retirement and Maniraj's Youthful Reign
paragraphs: Mallaraj’s Retirement and

Maniraj’s Youthful Reign The day passed. Night fell. All of a sudden Mena Rani came running, out of breath, to Mallaraj. She apprised him of the latest developments. Samant recognised that Mulu had instigated the Agent to fight his battle, and this was just the beginning of trouble. He feared that both Mallaraj’s throne and Maniraj’s life were in danger. Samant was also troubled by the anxiety that the Agent had caused Mallaraj; he did not want his ruler to be anxious. He saw his path clearly before him—his evil son had to die. He did not want to wait for any royal decree. He saw no violation of duty if the murder of his son was committed in the territory of another state. For him, the punishment for such a crime was as glorious as death in battle. At eight o’ clock that evening, he took five trusted men, fully armed, and set off towards Rana Khachar’s state. Mulu’s mother got wind of her husband’s intentions. The certain prospect of her son’s death gave her the courage to approach Mena Rani to seek her intervention. The queen ran to the king and informed him of the developments. The king set out in the dark and caught up with Samant. Samant was angry but powerless before the king. The king took a promise from him that he would not set out on such an adventure without royal command. Samant returned home, but resolved that he would not so much as look at his wife from that day on. Days turned to months, and months into years. Samant’s men kept a watch over Mulu. Mallaraj relied more and more on Samant and Jarashankar, and kept Maniraj by his side. Mallaraj placed more and more responsibilities on Vidya Chatura. Jarashankar retained the title of minister, while Vidya Chatura performed all the duties of the minister. As Vidya Chatura grew in stature, he was made the minister. Maniraj was appointed the crown prince and he performed all royal duties. The king and the former minister kept a distant watch on the new minister and the crown prince, while they spent their days in spiritual quest. Jarashankar became his counsellor even in this quest. They studied the scriptures and drew upon their wisdom gained through statecraft to enlighten their path. They sought the company and guidance of scholars and ascetics. Loss of royal power appears hellish to most people, but for these two it became heaven. The crown prince and his minister also benefited from this wisdom and aspired to have similar experiences at appropriate stages in their lives. While Jarashankar and Mallaraj retired from worldly affairs, Samant had other desires. It was Samant’s duty to look after the welfare of the crown prince and the new minister. He knew that Mulu was a constant threat, and that his destruction was the only guarantee of their security. Samant constantly thought of ways to eliminate this enemy. Hitherto, Samant had been unable to eliminate Mulu entirely because of the king’s order. He made several attempts to seek Mallaraj’s permission, which he never could secure. Mallaraj did not entertain any discussion about eliminating Mulu. This irritated Samant, who could not bring himself to disobey the king. Mulu also remained disaffected. He kept close watch over Maniraj’s movements. Sometimes he roamed the banks of the Subhadra in the company of outlaws; Sursinh of Suvarnapur was his companion. Mulu enjoyed his company and relished the hardships of the life of a baharvatiya. Rana Khachar also instigated and encouraged him. Samant kept himself informed of Mulu’s movements and appraised Mallaraj of the developments. Despite the knowledge of Mulu’s intentions, Mallaraj refused to order his execution. Samant thought of giving a false sense of security to Mulu. He allowed him to enter and roam within the territory of Ratnanagari without apprehension. Samant’s plan was to ambush Mulu and kill him in battle, or at least capture him alive. According to the decree, Mulu was to be given life imprisonment if he violated the code of conduct. However, despite Samant’s efforts, Mulu remained free. Khachar supported him, and Mulu’s distrust of his father ran deep. Mulu openly associated with Sursinh’s band of outlaws. Samant appealed to Mallaraj that the annuity paid to Mulu be discontinued as he had joined the baharvatiyas. Mallaraj laughed off the matter by saying that Mulu would learn to yield weapons and become brave in the company of the baharvatiyas. Mallaraj eventually asked Maniraj to capture Mulu, because Mulu had questioned Maniraj’s capacity as a ruler. Samant did not approve of this plan, but he had no choice. Henceforth, he accompanied Maniraj on all his expeditions. This matter did not remain secret from Mulu, who saw this as his chance to eliminate Maniraj. He began to frequent the territories of Ratnanagari and robbed people in open defiance of royal authority. Complaints were also sent to the Political Agent that Mallaraj lacked the capacity to capture the baharvatiyas. The Agency in turn posed questions to Ratnanagari. The problems seemed to multiply for Ratnanagari. The terrain was suitable for the outlaws to operate at will. Jadsinh and Shathrai of Suvarnapur harboured antipathy towards Ratnanagari and gave their support to the enemies of the state. It was not possible for the forces of Ratnanagari to chase the baharvatiyas once they entered British territory. Meanwhile, Mallaraj took ill. His days seemed numbered. Once again Samant sought permission from the ailing king to kill Mulu in Khachar’s state. He was even willing to be hanged by Khachar for his crime. Mallaraj not only refused the request, he obtained a pledge from Samant that he would never ever attempt such a thing. Samant had no choice but to give his word of honour to the ailing ruler. Samant came up another plan. He proposed to give his daughter in marriage to Rana Khachar. In return, he wanted Khachar to hand over Mulu to Ratnanagari. Samant obtained the support of some greedy courtiers of Khachar’s court. Khachar accepted the proposal of marriage, but broke his promise subsequently and refused to hand over Mulu. Samant’s daughter also took her mother’s side. Samant felt cheated.

These failed machinations of Samant amused the ailing Mallaraj. But Samant was not one to accept defeat. He bribed the baharvatiyas and some of Khachar’s men. They were willing to lead Mulu into a trap. Mulu had no inkling that a new plan had been hatched. Mulu was secure in his abilities; he considered himself superior to any machinations of inferior men. Samant and Maniraj keenly followed every move that Mulu made. One day they had camped near Manoharpuri when they received information that Mulu had also camped nearby. Some of Mulu’s men had shifted their loyalty to Samant. Samant, Maniraj and their forces moved swiftly towards Mulu’s camp. Mulu received information that Maniraj was leading the charge. He decided to move ahead and face Maniraj. Those of his men who had turned disloyal broke off and went in the other direction. Mulu’s remaining forces were taken aback by this development and their movement became uncertain and slow; the group scattered because of this change. Samant pursued the breakaway group, believing that Mulu was part of that group. Meanwhile, Mulu, who had gone a long way ahead, was isolated from his men but pressed on in anticipation of meeting Maniraj. Maniraj and his men charged at Mulu. Mulu knew the forest well and he moved his horse onto a treacherous trail. Maniraj followed after him. The chase continued for three-four miles. Mulu jumped over a deep gorge. Maniraj crossed the gorge from another point and continued his pursuit. Mulu rode up to a steep rock precipice and stopped. From this high ground, he looked below for those pursuing him. He saw no one; all he could hear was the trotting of a lone horse. Before Mulu could decide on his next move, Maniraj took his position on a rock facing him. Maniraj fired a bullet, which pierced Mulu’s horse. Both rider and horse tumbled into the gorge. Mulu’s leg got entangled in the stirrup and he fell along with his horse, losing his weapons in the fall. Some were swept away by the force of the water. Maniraj watched Mulu fall. Mulu somehow managed to disentangle himself from his horse and slowly got up. He had miraculously survived the fall; but his horse was dead and his weapons useless or lost. He looked up and saw Maniraj standing high above him. Mulu shouted a challenge, ‘Maniraj you are armed; I have lost all my weapons. I am ready to fight. But if you have the courage for a righteous battle, discard all your weapons and fight me with your bare hands.’ Maniraj replied, ‘Muluraj, there is no escape for you. Your life and death are at the mercy of my weapons. Do not make a show of your courage. The choice is not yours, but mine. I am ready to dismount and fight you with bare hands. But I do not trust you. I am not going to send away my horse along with my weapons. If you want to fight, come up, and I shall engage you in a duel. Maharaj Mallaraj has authorised me to kill you or capture you. I am eager to follow his command.’ Mulu climbed up. Maniraj dismounted and faced him. For a while they matched each other in strength and skill. Finally, Mulu fell and, pinning him down, Maniraj sat astride his chest. ‘Muluraj, you are my prisoner. It is your choice whether you wish to come along without further resistance, or force me to use my weapons and take you captive. You have lost the duel.’ Mulu had concealed a dagger in the folds of his clothes. He made an attempt to push the dagger into Maniraj, but before he could do so, Maniraj unsheathed his sword and cut off Mulu’s hand. Blood gushed out. Mulu made one last attempt and kicked Maniraj. Maniraj flew into the air and, landing expertly on his hands, in one swift movement of his leg sent Mulu tumbling down the rock and into the gorge. Mulu fell unconscious. The stream turned red with his blood. Meanwhile, Samant realised his mistake. He gave up pursuing Mulu’s men and went in search of Mulu and Maniraj. Samant divided his men into two groups, which went in separate directions. One of these groups, not led by Samant, witnessed the duel. For a moment, fear gripped them when Mulu kicked Maniraj. They went down the ravines to capture Mulu. In a short time Maniraj also reached the spot where Mulu lay unconscious, bleeding to death. Maniraj’s eyes welled up with tears to see Mulu’s plight. He ordered his men to immediately arrange for Mulu’s treatment. Samant, Maniraj and their troops came together at Manoharpuri. They sang praises of Maniraj’s bravery. Samant was overjoyed. Maniraj had fulfilled his duty. Samant and his troops marched triumphantly towards Ratnanagari with Mulu as their prisoner. Maniraj expressed his intention to go on a hunting expedition in the forest of Sundargiri and Subhadra. Maniraj and his hunting party roamed the hills, the forests and the banks of river Subhadra. He feasted on the beauty of nature, felt awe in its grandeur. He walked and rode in the forest from dawn to dusk, drenched in sweat, hunting wild animals. One day, as he stood exhausted under a large tree, gazing at the distant mountains, he saw a great eagle soar with a small animal clutched in its claws. Suddenly he heard a gunshot. The bullet found its mark; the wounded bird let go its prey and fell on the mountain top. These were royal grounds where hunting was prohibited unless sanctioned by the king or the crown prince. Maniraj was surprised. He wondered if there was a trespasser or some member of the royal family or some English officer who had come to hunt in the forest with the king’s permission. He galloped in the direction from which the gunshot had come. He reached the banks of Subhadra. There was a lovely grove of trees on the river bank. Wind wafting over the river water cooled the grove. Its coolness soothed one even at the height of a summer noon. Maniraj saw some foot marks. He followed them. The grove was so thick that it was not possible to ride a horse. He dismounted; he looked closely at the footmarks. They were made by a group of persons walking bare feet. They were small and delicate as if made by children or dainty women. He reasoned that a man out on a hunt was likely to be wearing heavy boots. His curiosity was aroused. What were women doing in a place like this? Could they be young boys? He tied his horse to a tree trunk and moved silently ahead. Then he saw them—it was a group of three or four young women. They were led by a nubile beauty of fifteen or sixteen. The group seemed to be her friends and servants. ‘Ratni, I am tired. Let’s sit and soothe our feet awhile in the flowing water,’ said that nubile beauty. ‘Kamalaba, what if there are crocodiles in the river?’ ‘We shall deal with it when we see one. Let us sit, and don’t forget to bring the flowers,’ said Kamala.

They sat on the bank, dangling their feet in the flowing water. Maniraj watched them in raptures of pleasure. Though he was a young man now, he had hitherto exercised great control over his passions. But today he was curious about these women and wanted to watch them at play. These women are like the beautiful and meek deer which play fearlessly in the forest, unmindful of the predatory tiger, he said to himself; it is wrong to disrupt their play. Maniraj hid behind a tree and watched them. But he felt a sudden pang of guilt; a man who watches unknown women at play is unfit to be a ruler, he thought. He changed his position. Now he could see their backs, but not their faces. He murmured to himself: In public spots my dignity I show, On high-born dames I hesitate to gaze.⟨fn:103⟩ He could hear them talk. Kamala’s hands rested on the shoulders of her friends as her feet played with the water. She looked admiringly at her own feet. ‘Ratni, how do my legs look?’ she asked. ‘Your legs are as smooth and delicate as the stem of a lotus flower, the soles of your feet as radiant as the lotus and your toes are as beautifully formed as lotus petals.’ ‘And this water?’ Kamala asked as she played with the water. ‘It is as clear as the dew that gathers on lotus leaves.’ A friend chirpily said, ‘Kamalaba, do sing us a song!’ Kamala continued to admire her feet splashing in the water. ‘What do you want me to sing?’ ‘The one which you have composed.’ Kamala sang her song. I don’t want a beloved delicate as a jasmine I must have a rose Not for me the smooth lotus I desire the thorns of the ketak flower Friend, go tell mother

Friend, do tell father Hear me, mother and father This I have resolved: My beloved must be like a rose Like a kevda I cannot abide a good, soft husband— Everyone, calling him ‘good,’ will want to touch him! A prickly husband must I have Attractive and fragrant But able to prick anyone who comes too close He will yield himself only to A clever gardener like me— All mine to enjoy his fragrance and colour Other women shall be jealous Such a husband I call a rose or a kevda For the sake of Kamala He must be born of the Suryavansh ‘Why don’t you pluck one such flower yourself?’ teased one of her companions. ‘I, too, am a flower. I will marry the one who can come close to me and pluck me,’ Kamala replied. ‘What kind of a flower are you? And why is it difficult to pluck you?’ ‘I am the lotus that blooms in the delicate rays of the moon. I open up on solitary nights—the one who wants to pluck me must approach me at night, breathe in my fragrance and take delight in my beauty.’ At that very moment, Maniraj leapt out like a tiger, lifted Kamala in his arms and carried her away from the water. Her retinue of companions looked on in bewilderment. Just then a crocodile raised its head at the water’s edge. Maniraj lowered Kamala on her feet. ‘Your splashing feet and your song attracted that crocodile to you. I saw it and carried you to safety before it could devour you. Forgive me that I carried you in my arms.’ Kamala blushed and could not utter a word. She could not bring herself to look up at his face; her eyes furtively gazed at the strong hands that had carried her to safety. Her friend Ratna spoke up, ‘We are grateful to you. We wish to know our saviour, his name, family and lineage.’ ‘I am Maniraj, son of Mallaraj, the ruler of Ratnanagari. My code of conduct forbids me to be inquisitive about women. I can be your guide and take you to safety out of this dense forest.’ ‘Prince, we do not need an escort. Our Kamalaba rides and wields weapons. Her father, Maharaja Khachar, is a guest of your state. His camp is nearby. We know the shortest way to the camp. We can be your guide, if you wish to come and pay your respects to him.’ ‘Has Kamala Kumari used her weapons in this forest?’ inquired Maniraj. ‘Yes, she shot an eagle that was preying on a lamb.’ ‘In that case, she has violated the laws of this state. I will have to arrest her,’ Maniraj said, smiling mischievously. Kamala’s retinue of women did not know what to say. Kamala spoke up, ‘Is there a law in your state that I should be arrested twice?’ ‘No, only once.’ ‘You held me captive just a while ago, and then set me free!’ ‘Of course, we shall not arrest you again. How do we know that you committed this crime? We have not heard of women who use guns.’ ‘That is right. I am ready for a test, provided you agree to compete with me.’ Kamala’s friends and servants quietly withdrew, leaving them to their banter. Rana Khachar had two queens. Kamala was the daughter of the elder queen. Samant’s daughter, the younger queen, had proposed marriage between Kamala and Maniraj in the hope that this alliance would put an end to the longstanding animosity between Samant, Khachar, Mulu and Mallaraj. She sang praises of Maniraj’s qualities to Kamala. She told her that in Mallaraj’s family, the men remained faithful to their wives and Kamala would never have to share her husband with another woman. Kamala was thus infatuated with Maniraj even before they met. She was a brave and pure kshatriya woman. Her father showered affection on her. But Khachar was against the idea of giving his daughter to an enemy. And Kamala was determined that she would marry none else but Maniraj and refused all other alliances. After Mulu’s arrest, Khachar’s younger queen and Mulu’s sister persuaded him to visit Ratnanagari as a state guest. For years Khachar had harboured animosity and hatred towards the rulers of Ratnanagari. With maturity and experience, however, he had come to appreciate the nobility of Mallaraj and wished to learn from the grand old king. He accepted the suggestion of his younger queen. They were on their way to Ratnanagari and had camped in the forest for rest. It was these fortuitous circumstances that brought Kamala face to face with Maniraj. This was Maniraj’s first experience of being alone with a young woman; he felt the excitement of it. Kamala was the daughter of the enemy of Ratnanagari; he wondered if he should trust her or maintain cautious distance. The words of her lovesick song were fresh in his mind and they removed all traces of mistrust. He was secure in his valour and had nothing to fear from Khachar. He leaned on his gun, stole glances at her and asked, ‘Where have your friends gone?’ ‘They went away to present you with an opportunity to hold me captive.’ ‘That was just a joke. I do not stay alone with a woman not known to me. If you do not need me any longer, allow me to go.’ Kamala leaned against a tree and wept, ‘Crown prince, I am not someone else’s woman. Hitherto, I have not accepted anyone in marriage, and I shall be the wife of none else but you, Maniraj. You say that I should allow you to go if I do not need you. Maniraj, I need you till the very end of my life. How can I allow you to go when I want to draw you nearer?’ Maniraj felt pity for her. ‘Princess, you are unmarried. It is your duty to marry a man chosen by your parents.’ Kamala sighed with dejection. ‘Maniraj, just as Rukmini had given herself to Shri Krishna, I have given myself to you. You are capable of accepting me in marriage just as Shri Krishna accepted Rukmini.’ She looked at him, her gaze expectant, infatuated and hopeful; her eyes filled with tears. Maniraj held her gaze.

‘Kamala Kumari, your father considers us his enemy. If you think that I have the qualities of the rose and kevda, you pluck me and make me your own. I do not ask for anything. How can I ask your father for your hand?’ ‘Kumar, when you permit me to enter your garden, I will pluck my rose. You have to take the initiative and pick this lotus from her pond. Marry me, like Shri Krishna married Rukmini.’ Kamala came forward and rested her head on his shoulder. Maniraj’s instinct was to push her away, but hesitated lest she should fall. Her touch was exciting and delightful. Kamala took his hand in hers and intertwined her fingers with his; they both felt surging desire. Torn between a sense of rectitude and desire, Maniraj caught her by her shoulders and held her at some distance from himself. He spoke gently but firmly, ‘Kamala, we have already transgressed all limits. We are not yet married. A man destined to be king must obey all norms of rectitude. Who shall uphold the norms if we, the rulers, break them? Hence ...’ But before Maniraj could say, ‘stay away,’ Kamala leaned forward and held him in a tight embrace. She concealed her face in his broad chest and said, ‘You could have asked me to stay away so long as you were not my husband. But both our bodies have felt the same surge of desire and passion. We are joined by the same fire. We are now married. I am no longer my father’s daughter; I am now your wife, Maniraj. My dear husband, you must now take me with you, as Shri Krishna took Rukmini.’ Maniraj was speechless. A conflict raged within him. He had not sought his father’s permission. A part of him wanted to push her away. Mallaraj had received many proposals of marriage for Maniraj. In each case, Mallaraj’s response was unambiguous. ‘According to the custom of our family, a man upon maturity selects his own wife. You must wait for my son to grow up.’ It occurred to Maniraj that his father’s consent would not be a problem. He saw their meeting as an act of providence. He had won the heart of the enemy’s daughter. It would be politically beneficial if this alliance could result in friendship between the two families. By all measures, this was a favourable alliance. Maniraj was not guided by reason alone; his passions, too, came into play. Kamala was a pure-blooded kshatriya woman, brave and an expert shot! She appealed to his sense of valour. He gently lifted her face and looked at her, but did not know what else to do. He held her close. She was tall and voluptuous; he liked the feel of her body against him. He surrendered to desire. Kamala responded passionately, holding him close and leaning over him. At length, Maniraj caressed her back and said, ‘Kamala Rani, please return to your father now. We shall decide on the future course once you reach Ratnanagari.’ In a day or so, both parties reached Ratnanagari. The decision regarding Mulu awaited the crown prince. The decree of punishment was clear. Mulu had to be awarded imprisonment for life. Samant could not appreciate the uncertainty and hesitation. He urged Mallaraj to issue the orders. Mallaraj declined, saying that he had cultivated detachment from worldly affairs, and left the final decision to Maniraj. Rana Khachar met Mallaraj and benefited from his Bhishma-like wisdom. Khachar felt a newfound reverence for Mallaraj. Meanwhile, Maniraj reached Ratnanagari. Khachar met Mulu, who informed him about the circumstances that led to his defeat and capture; Maniraj had won their duel in every sense—in strategy, in strength, in rectitude and in forgiveness. Hitherto, Mulu had always held that Maniraj was effete and unworthy of the throne. He now accepted Maniraj’s superiority. He felt humbled and deeply repented that he had turned against such a noble state when he should have, in fact, been its strength. Mulu shared his feelings with Khachar, who laughed and mocked him. Khachar had to revise his opinion of Maniraj, but he viewed Mulu’s attribution of superior virtue to Maniraj as a sign of the weakness of a wounded and defeated person. Khachar said that Maniraj had missed his mark, and the bullet from his gun had killed the horse and not Mulu. He categorically expressed that the day Maniraj assumes the throne of Ratnanagari, it would indeed be an unfortunate day for the state. Samant demanded that Maniraj agree to life imprisonment for Mulu, as per the punishment decreed. Maniraj sought time to decide on the matter and called Mulu’s mother and sister for a meeting. He told them that Mulu had to choose between life imprisonment in

Ratnanagari and life as a free man in Khachar’s state. He asked them to get a clear response from Mulu. Mulu told his mother and sister, ‘Please tell Maniraj that hitherto I had a low opinion of his abilities, but now my views have changed. In my encounter with him, I learnt about his strengths, his statecraft, his generosity and intellect. My pride and hatred have melted—I am humbled. I have sinned against the state by supporting its enemies. I can never be free of this sin. Tell the crown prince that Khachar is their enemy, and it is for that reason he was my friend. He remains an enemy of Ratnanagari, and for the very same reason I do not wish to even look at his face. Imprisonment would be my reparation. I prefer incarceration to a life of ignominy. But, on the other hand, I also feel that I should work to establish friendly relations with Khachar and weaken his animosity towards Ratnanagari. I can do this service to the state, which I can render only if I were to live freely in Khachar’s state. The decision rests with Maniraj. Please tell him that he should not set me free and allow me to live in Ratnanagari. I would never be able to live with such an act of generosity. Moreover, the two brahmins— Jarashankar and Vidya Chatura—are dear to him; but I will always remain their enemy. If I were to live freely in this state, someday I will commit the crime of killing not one, but two brahmins.’ Maniraj left the choice to Mulu’s mother and sister. They asked that Mulu be allowed to live as a free man in Khachar’s state. Maniraj cautioned them, ‘I will set him free on your guarantee that henceforth, he will not do anything to harm the state or participate in intrigues against the state.’ The two women gave their word of honour. Maniraj further said, ‘One of you is my aunt, and the other, my sister. I must fulfill your desire. Samantraj insists that we should take guarantees from both Khachar and Mulu Bha; but tell Mulu Bha that your word of honour carries greater value for me. Mulu Bha has said that Khachar is our enemy, and for that reason, even his. We would not ask an enemy to stand guarantee. What greater guarantee can a kshatriya have than the word of honour of his aunt, his sister and brother? If and when there is a breach of such trust, the kshatriyas will face each other with whatever strength they are capable of. I accept your promise. Please tell Mulu Bha that expectations lead to despair; I have none from him. I have been true to myself. Now it is up to him to be true to himself.’ Having decided Mulu’s fate, Maniraj went straight to the palace of his mother, Mena Rani. Kamala Kumari had gone there to meet the queen, but her eyes pined for Maniraj. Maniraj saw his opportunity, called his mother aside and briefly narrated to her his encounter with Kamala. Seeing Mena Rani hesitate, Maniraj told her, ‘Mother, there is no scope for either hesitation or deliberation. I have given my word and accepted Kamala as my wife. Father cannot have any objection as he has left the decision to me. Hence, Kamala will stay in your palace. Please tell her that she is not to go back to her father, even if he were to command her to do so.’ Mena Rani was surprised. ‘Kumar, you can marry anyone of your choice. But this is abduction. The British government is watching over us.’ ‘Mother, it would have been a different matter if we had abducted her against her will. But in this case, the woman herself says that she has accepted me as her husband. Her abduction—if it is that—has become necessary only because her father is our enemy.
