Both she and you come from the moon lineage, and since the time of Krishna, it is customary among you of the Chandravansh to abduct women as wives.’ ‘What if your enemy complain to the British, and they harass you? You should consult the minister.’ ‘Mother, Kamala will not hesitate to give her testimony to the British, but we must help her. Let us see what Khachar does. We will consult the minister and others as well.’ Till late that evening, Kamala did not return to her father’s quarters. Khachar sent word that it was time for her to return. She replied, ‘My Chhoti Ma will apprise my father of all the developments. How can I leave my husband’s house? My husband has not placed any restrictions on me. I will come when I wish to.’ Khachar was enraged. He was given the details of all that had happened. He went to meet Mallaraj and complained to him. Mallaraj gave him a patient hearing, but could not help laughing. ‘Ranaji, your daughter appears willing and has given her consent.’ Khachar:  ‘Maharaj so what? These two have deceived me.’ Mallaraj:  ‘You! Deceived by mere children! Ranaji, please do not say this to anyone else.’ Khachar:  ‘You of course cannot see that your son has done anything wrong, but I have to take some steps.’ Mallaraj:  ‘Ranaji, if you will kindly regain your composure and become a little less agitated, I will say something to you.’ Khachar:  ‘All right.’ Mallaraj:  ‘You claim that these children have deceived you. But Ranaji, Maniraj has not sought my consent either for this marriage. Let that be. Do you consider this a suitable match or not?’ Khachar:  ‘No, it is not suitable.’ Mallaraj:  ‘How so?’ Khachar:  ‘First, Maniraj is not adept in the use of weapons, while my daughter is an expert.’ Mallaraj:  ‘What else?’ Khachar:  ‘Maniraj is naïve. He does not have the cunning mind required of a ruler.’ Mallaraj:  ‘And what else?’ Khachar:  ‘Nothing else. He is suitable in all other respects.’ The two rulers were in Mallaraj’s garden. A lake separated this garden from that of Maniraj’s. Mallaraj pointed towards Maniraj’s garden and said, ‘That one is Maniraj’s garden. He is likely to be there. Let us go there incognito, and you might get a chance to test his ability. What if he emerges triumphant and you lose?’ Khachar:  ‘I will accept the relationship.’ Both rulers changed their appearance and assumed the dress of Kabulis and walked towards Maniraj’s garden. The guards stopped them. They pleaded with the guards, ‘We would like to see the garden and also meet Prince Maniraj. Please go and obtain permission for us.’

The guard replied, ‘The crown prince and his queen are in the garden. I cannot permit you to go in, nor can I go in to seek their permission.’ The garden was fortified, but not on all sides. Mallaraj and Khachar went to a corner where the fortification gave way to a hedge. The hedge was made of a thicket of thorny branches and trees. The hedge was impenetrable. They could not see inside the garden, but voices from within were audible. The voices came nearer. ‘Crown prince, you showed me the garden, but did not talk about an important matter.’ ‘Which one?’ ‘When a man holds a woman captive, it is considered to be a rakshasa vivah. You forbade me from going back to my father. Does your custom approve of such a demonic marriage?’ Maniraj laughed and said, ‘You wanted me to accept you in marriage and so we came together in gandharva vivah, a union akin to that of celestial lovers. Moreover, it is just to take the enemy’s daughter in a rakshasa vivah once a gandharva vivah has been consummated. Kamala Rani, it is our family custom to show our demonic power to our enemy.’ ‘Kumar, I had also challenged you to a test of marksmanship. You are yet to meet that challenge.’ At that moment, a bird flew up from the lake with a fish held in its beak. Two gun shots were fired; one of them hit its mark, and the other missed it. The two kings heard Kamala laugh. ‘Fortune favours men. Crown prince, never before has my bullet missed its mark. But today I missed.’ ‘That is not the case. If my bullet had not hit the bird, yours would have. You did not calculate the distance between my bullet and yours as also the flight of the bird. If you had done so, yours too would have found its mark.’ ‘You are right. But I am not as good a shot as you are, Maniraj.’ ‘There is some movement behind that thicket; it could be some men. The guards must have been negligent.’ ‘There is someone or something there.’

Khachar and Mallaraj grew alert. ‘Let them be. What can they do to us?’ Kamala said. ‘No, that cannot be allowed. They could also be thieves. Do they think I do not know how to be on my guard?’ ‘What is impossible for a man who can deceive Rana Khachar and hold his daughter captive?’ teased Kamala with an alluring smile. Mallaraj could not suppress a chuckle and whispered, ‘Rana, you called my son naïve, but your daughter thinks he is cleverer than you. She knows both you and him, and she has expressed her opinion.’ Rana Khachar urgently signalled to Mallaraj with a finger on his lips that he must keep absolutely quiet. He pulled Mallaraj to a more secure place. Maniraj asked a gardener to bring him a sickle attached to a long bamboo rod. He pushed and poked in the hedge, making any movement difficult for the two rulers dressed as Kabulis. When no one came out, he pushed the sharp sickle into the hedge. Rana Khachar tried to hold onto it, but Maniraj pulled hard. The sickle came out strained with blood. Maniraj alerted the guards at once. Mallaraj and Khachar jumped into the lake and swam back to safety. They hurriedly changed into their regal clothes and sat ponderously in Mallaraj’s garden. Maniraj’s guards returned empty-handed. Maniraj went over to his father’s garden. In a corner of the garden, thrown in a heap behind a hedge, he saw wet Kabuli dresses; he also noticed injuries on Rana Khachar’s fingers. He instantly understood who the intruders were. He came back to the palace and informed Samant about the curious happenings. They went over with some guards to Mallaraj’s garden. Maniraj addressed his father, ‘Maharaj, two thieves tried to enter my garden just now. One of them is the master of this land. But the other thief deserves punishment. I request you to hand him over to me.’ ‘What is the identification of that thief?’ Samant replied, ‘Maharaj, Aniruddha’s grandfather had cut off Bana’s hands. But our Aniruddha has himself cut Bana’s fingers. This Bana does not have a thousand hands. What are we to do? When

Aniruddha’s father himself has become an accomplice of Bana, Aniruddha has to take matters in his hands.’ Khachar was defeated and felt ashamed. He accepted his daughter’s choice. Mallaraj came to be regarded as fortunate in every respect. He had a brave son and an able heir. Mulu was conclusively defeated. Khachar gladly gave his daughter in marriage to Maniraj; his animosity gave way to genuine affection. Moreover, Fox Sahib was transferred and the good Buskin Sahib, who held the position at Lilapur, became the new Political Agent. Buskin Sahib was an old friend of Brave Sahib. The Agency ceased to be a source of trouble or anxiety. Maniraj, Vidya Chatura and Samant ably administered the state. Mallaraj moved out of the palace and made the garden his dwelling. The old king and Jarashankar passed their days in spiritual quest. One day, the king felt that the hour of his death was approaching. He called his family and counsellors by his bedside. The king lived in a bamboo hut. Its floor was made of mud and cow dung. He slept on a simple string cot. He had worn a dhoti and a loose kurta. Despite his weakness, Mallaraj had bathed early in the morning. He was too weak to sit up and hence lay in his bed. His once stout body had withered and he looked emaciated. He had smeared ash over his large forehead. His long white hair was neatly tied; his moustaches had turned white and pale. His eyes shone with light. His speech was clear and measured as ever. Mena Rani sat on the floor by his side; she was inconsolable. A vaidya sat on the other side, measuring the pulse and administering medicinal preparations to the king. Maniraj visited his father every day, sometimes four or five times, and spent the night by his father’s side, sleeping on the floor. He was called. He came and stood watching the life ebb out of his father. Samant, Jarashankar and Vidya Chatura also rushed to the king’s side. The king signalled to Samant to approach his bed. Samant bent down to hear the king’s last wish. Mallaraj said, ‘Brother, you have been an integral part of Ratnanagari’s statecraft. Look after Maniraj, and ensure that Mulu takes your place. I am ready to meet my Maker. Send Vidya Chatura.’

Samant wept, choking on his words, ‘Maharaj, please do not worry. Do not worry about the state, the ministers, your people and even Maniraj.’ Turning to Vidya Chatura, Samant said, ‘Maharaj would like to speak with you.’ Vidya Chatura approached the king’s bedside. Samant said to himself: What a great soul! He showed grace and generosity towards that evil Mulu even at the moment of death. Maharaj, you will not forsake your nobility, but that Mulu will not abandon his evil ways. God has summoned this great soul, while that rascal lives a living death. What more trouble won’t he cause! Oh God! Why did I father him? Samant wept. Mallaraj spoke to Vidya Chatura, ‘Vidya Chatura, you are the gardener. You must take such care that not one plant withers. I have nurtured you as one nurtures a plant. Don’t forget that. What more can I say from my death bed? I have withered. This is the age of the British. I have accepted their friendship. I cannot think clearly anymore.’ Vidya Chatura spoke soothingly, ‘Maharaj, my body and intellect are dedicated to you. Your soul is immortal. You have led a life of virtue and done good deeds. Your heir is equally worthy and virtuous.’ Mallaraj signalled Maniraj to approach nearer, and said, ‘Maniraj, all my energies were spent in dealing with the enemies of our state and making it secure. In all this, I have not cared for our people. I give you a state that has no enemies. You must work for the welfare of its people. The people are meek; they are silent. But do not forget that I have not been able to do anything for them. You must give up the pleasures of food, drink and the body and work for your people. It is your responsibility to care for your subjects.’ Mallaraj felt all his strength ebbing from him. His eyes turned misty and he closed them. Everyone in the room wept. Mallaraj stretched a feeble hand towards his queen and mumbled, ‘Mena ... Mena.’ Mena Rani came forward, took his hand in hers and said, ‘Yes, Maharaj.’ Mallaraj opened his eyes and looked at her. ‘I punished you that night for no fault of yours.’ The Rani somehow managed to say, ‘No, Maharaj. I was at fault. You did the right thing.’ ‘Now Kumar is the king. You must obey him.’

‘Of course, Maharaj. Kumar will be the king, and I his subject. My conduct towards him will be like that of your mother towards you, once you assumed the throne.’ ‘And Kamala will get precedence over you, Rani,’ the king said, extending his hand as if seeking a promise. The queen put her hand in his and said, ‘Maharaj, you are my god. I promise that I have no claims on the state now. In my childhood I obeyed my father, and after marriage I obeyed you. Like your widowed mother obeyed your wishes, it is my duty to obey the wishes of the new king and queen. I am blessed that they are my son and daughter- in-law.’ With these words, the distraught queen fell unconscious. But before his mother could fall to the ground, Maniraj caught her in his arms. Mallaraj had closed his eyes and did not see the plight of his queen. He murmured, ‘I have spoken my last words. Is there anything else?’ Jarashankar came forward and said, ‘Maharaj, Raghu’s journey to the forest!’ The king had sought guidance from the conduct of the Raghu dynasty. These verses were very dear to him. Jarashankar stood close by the king and recited: Now the king Raghu, finding that his son was firmly established among his (ministers) and subjects, became indifferent to the objects of pleasure, even though situated in heaven, which are perishable by nature. For verily the descendants of Dilipa’s race, when they grew old, transferred by royal fortune to their accomplished sons, and curbing their passions, betook themselves to the life of anchorites, wearing garments of the bark of trees. The son with his head adorned with royal turban, prostrated at the feet of his father who was about to repair to the forest, and begged that he should not be abandoned. Raghu, who tenderly loved his son, granted that desire of him whose face was covered with tears, but did not resume his kingly fortune, once abandoned, just as a serpent does not put on the slough it has once cast off. He, having entered the last stage of life, lived, it is said, in a convent outside the city, where he was served, his senses not being affected, by the goddess of the royal fortune, as by a daughter-in-law, enjoyable only by his son. The illustrious (royal) family, with the old king leading a life of spiritual tranquillity, and the new king just entered upon his kingly career, was comparable to the sky with the moon almost set and sun newly risen. Raghu and his son, being (respectively) the emblems of the ascetic and the king, seemed to the people like the portions of the two dharmas, come down to the earth, whose rewards are final emancipation and earthly glory. For the acquisition of what was (yet) unconquered, Aja took for his companions ministers well-versed in politics, while Raghu, in order to reach the state which is not subject to decay (salvation), associated himself with the contemplative ascetic who had got true insight into Yoga and whoever spoke the truth. The youthful king took his judgement seat in order to look into (the affairs of) his subjects; while the aged monarch seated himself, in solitude, on the holy seat of kusa grass, in order to practice the abstract contemplation of the mind. The one (Aja) by the super eminence of his sovereign power reduced to submission the neighbouring princes; while the other (Raghu) by virtue of his constant metaphysical exercises brought under control the five vital airs existing in the body. The new king completely foiled the efforts of his enemies; while the old one engaged himself in burning down, by means of [the] fire of knowledge, the fruits of his own actions. Aja employed the six expedients beginning with peace, with a due regard to their results; Raghu, on his part, who regarded gold and clod of earth as equal, established his mastery over the three primary principles, the constituents of Prakriti. The new lord, steady in action, did never desist from his undertakings until they bore fruit; nor did the lord other than the new one, firm in mind, desist from the practice of holy meditation, until he obtained a vision of the Supreme Spirit. Thus the two (Aja and Raghu) who were watchful of the enemies and the senses (respectively) whose course was checked, and who were bent on (attaining) prosperity and absolution, obtained their (respective) desired objects.

Then Raghu who regarded all beings with equal eye passed some years out of regard for (the desire of) Aja and then obtained, by means of profound contemplation, the Supreme Spirit that is imperishable and that is beyond mental darkness.⟨fn:104⟩ The visage of the dying king was saturated with peace and joy. As the last verse was being recited, Mallaraj murmured, ‘Shiv, Shiv ...’ Then all speech ceased. His hand fell limp on Jarashankar’s shoulder, and life left his body. The king’s body was consigned to the sacred fire. His hut and his state felt his absence. It was only after a few days that Mena Rani and Maniraj could begin to mourn his loss. In a few months, Maharaj Mallaraj became a part of fading memory. What remained were the fruits of his actions, the benefits of his statecraft, the lessons that he had taught. The seeds he had sown grew into trees. Like the many sacred basil plants and Shiva temples erected in his memory, the good deeds of Mallaraj’s statecraft remained for posterity.
chapters.summary: Young Maniraj bravely pursues the rogue Mulu through treacherous terrain, leading to a tense, weaponless confrontation that tests their resolve and skill.

chapters.title: Maniraj's Sorrow and the Vision of His Father
paragraphs: Maniraj’s Sorrow and the Vision of His Father O star of strength! I see thee stand And smile upon my pain; Thou beckonest with thy mailed hand, And I am strong again. —H. W. Longfellow Maniraj, devoted to his father, decided not to assume the throne. He felt that he should place his father’s footwear on the throne and rule in his name. He conveyed his decision to all the officials of the state. The period of ritual mourning came to an end, but the dark shadow of sorrow continued to mark his face. The crown prince refused to fix an auspicious time for his accession to the throne. Maniraj wrote to Buskin Sahib, informing him of Mallaraj’s death, but made no mention of the new ruler. He gave no response to the repeated entreaties of Samant, Jarashankar, Vidya Chatura and Kamala Rani. The saying: ‘The king is dead, long live the king!’ proved false in his case. If anyone dared to address him as ‘Maharaj’, that person was certain to be insulted. Buskin Sahib was informed of these happenings. He wrote an affectionate letter to Maniraj and urged him to shoulder his royal duties. Buskin Sahib reminded him that the Father in Heaven does not die and urged Maniraj to perform his duties by submitting all his actions to that father. It was Maniraj’s duty to abide by both his mortal father and the Immortal One, Buskin Sahib wrote. The letter also mentioned that Buskin Sahib would attend the ceremony of Maniraj’s ascension to the throne of Ratnanagari. Maniraj read the letter and put it into his pocket. He reclined on an easy chair. It was seven in the evening. His mind was full of his father, and he wept silent tears. Weeping, he fell asleep and dreamt that he was in a small boat in the middle of a stormy sea. The boat rose and fell with the high waves and was tossed about by the strong gales, but it somehow remained afloat. The moon shone brightly. Unperturbed by the storm, Maniraj lay watching the moon. A figure emerged from the moon and sat facing him on the boat. It was Mallaraj. He took Maniraj into his arms and spoke lovingly, ‘Kumar, Samant was present at the time of my death, and hence I could not share all my secrets with you. I have come to you in this moment of solitude. I chose to remain silent as I did not want any ill feelings at the time of my death. I have come to share some secrets of my statecraft with you. Listen carefully. ‘Maniraj, you must retain your affection for Samant and Muluraj. But they do not know the reason for our relationship with the English; I share this with you from the heavens. Agnidev, the God of Fire, handed over Sitaji to Ram after her trial by fire. As she prepared to leave Ayodhya for her heavenly abode, Sugriva, Angad and Hanumanji approached her with folded hands and asked her as to what should be done to the bridge that they had built across the ocean. Sitaji said, “Son, the bridge has no further use. It must be destroyed so that no one else can cross the sea and attack Vibhishana’s kingdom. Only a portion of that bridge should be preserved so that the bridge of dharma and rectitude does not perish from memory. That portion will survive as long as the sun and the moon shine. It will be sacred to all religions.” As they sought her leave, Sitaji gave them a boon and said, “You are divine beings; in this life you will build a bridge of dharma and help establish the righteous order. In the Kali Yuga, you will be born as men and establish a new Ram Rajya in this land.” ‘Maniraj, Shri Krishna married Jambuvati, a daughter of the king of bears. The flag on Arjun’s chariot has the sign of a monkey. Wherever you find that flag—the kapidhwaja—dharma and victory prevail.

Shri Krishna became the charioteer of the kapidhwaja. Maniraj, it was foretold that fair people shall rule in Kali Yuga. That was also the boon given by Sitaji. It has come true, and the English now rule over this land. The monkeys of Sugriva’s army were the progeny of gods; the English are the bearers of the same divine seed. ‘You may ask: How did I recognise them? When we ruled this land, it was the reign of untruth and fratricidal war. Like the ten- headed Ravana, thousands of Ravanas ruled this land and perpetuated falsehood. The earth trembled under their terror. Maniraj, you have no idea of those terrible times, but I have lived through them. I saw monkeys and bears who had received Sitaji’s grace emerge triumphant over those Ravanas. Have you seen rulers without an emperor? I have seen a community of traders become rulers! Who was Ram and who was Sugriva? Monkeys and bears rushed to the aid of Ram. Similarly, a community of traders came to the aid of dharma in this land. ‘Maniraj, Samant will say something quite to the contrary. But on this one matter, do not take his counsel. The new monkeys and bears have slayed a thousand-headed Ravana and established a new Ram Rajya! Why did I sign a treaty of friendship with these foreigners of a different race? Why did I trust them over fellow countrymen? You might ask me all these questions. Samant will lead you on the wrong path; hence do not pose these questions to him. ‘Maniraj, what is greater—one’s brothers or one’s religion? Is mother earth more precious or is dharma? If you really want to know who is a brother, ask Vibhishana, ask Bharat. Ask any great soul, ask the scriptures, ask the philosophers. Remember, where there is dharma, there is victory. Ramji believed so. Vibhishana, too, believed the same. The Pandavas held the same faith. And Shri Krishna taught the same truth. ‘Maniraj, how did I divine that the English will emerge victorious? At the time of the war of Mahabharata, when two great armies clashed, how were dharma and victory decided? Maniraj, the victory of the kapidhwaja was certain—I, too, saw the victory of the new bearers of that standard. Samant could not see it, but I did. You might want to ask if the English have never done any wrong. Maniraj, in this world what matters is a wrong which is the cause of things, not an action done as a consequence of that wrong. Disrobing Draupadi was wrong, not Bhima’s act of breaking Duryodhana’s thigh. The Pandavas accepted banishment because they were bound by a promise; that is right conduct. Their final victory was the triumph of dharma. ‘Maniraj, do you think these monkeys and bears do not trouble me? Have I not been perplexed by them? Samant will cite my example and mislead you; do not take his advice. I, too, was startled by their presence just as children are frightened by monkeys jumping around. But those who lost their all to the monkeys were wrongdoers and perpetrators of adharma. I was merely frightened by the strange sight of bears, but the wrongdoers were vanquished. The monkeys and bears have emerged victorious; there is no conceit in them. They have become humble in victory. ‘Maniraj, the bridge of dharma near Lanka was destroyed. But a new bridge is coming up in our land; stones will float on the water, and the army of monkeys will cross over it. Our rulers want to get on to that bridge; they want to run after that monkey flag. The enemies of the English are your enemies, and your enemies will be the enemy of the English—Maharaja Nagraj taught us that lesson. Maniraj, do not be stingy like a bania nor should you live like a brahmin. Victory is guaranteed if you climb onto that bridge and fight under the kapidhwaja. Maniraj, do not show your teeth to the monkey—play with them and win them over. ‘Maniraj, do not follow Samant’s advice on this. But take his son along with you and make him run by your side. If Mulu does not have life enough in him, become his Shalivahan and breathe life into him. Fight those who fight against the warriors of the new monkey army; you will benefit by associating with them. If you cannot run with them, you are certain to be left behind. But if you run with them and feel tired during the run, they will carry you on their shoulders and run.’ With these words, Mallaraj’s form faded and disappeared. The boat disappeared; the stormy sea disappeared. Maniraj woke up from his dream and reflected on it. The words ‘kapidhwaja’ and ‘dharma’ echoed in his mind. He recalled the poem about Akbar’s dream. He got up and recited it to himself. Me too the black-wing’d Azrael overcame, But Death had ears and eyes; I watch’d my son, And those that follow’d, loosen, stone from stone, All my fair work; and from the ruin arose The shriek and curse of trampled millions, even As in the time before; but while I groan’d, From out the sunset pour’d an alien race, Who fitted stone to stone again, and Truth, Peace, Love and Justice, came and dwelt therein⟨fn:105⟩ ‘Maharaj, give me the command to perform my duty and build the bridge of righteousness,’ Maniraj said aloud, beseeching his father and king. His reverie was broken when he saw Kamala. Approaching him, Kamala said, ‘Mother’s sorrow has deepened seeing your condition. Instead of alleviating her sorrow, you have drowned in yours. There is no one to give her succour.’ ‘You are right. Her bond with the Maharaj was much deeper than what I could ever cultivate. Maharaj had taught me that it was the duty of the one whose sorrow is less to console the one whose grief is deeper; a son must console his mother, and a man his woman.’ Kamala came closer and placed her hand on his shoulder. Maniraj permitted her this proximity after many days. Encouraged, she said, ‘I am told that Sahib is to come tomorrow morning to commiserate with Maharaj in his times of sorrow.’ Maniraj did not show displeasure at being addressed as ‘Maharaj’. He sat down and made Kamala sit beside him. He said, ‘I feel that I have been lax in my duty and have not met Mataji as often as I should have.’ ‘That is correct. It not only provides solace to both of you, it also gives us a sense of relief.’

‘Kamala Rani, it is also your duty to ensure that I do not deviate from the performance of my duties,’ said Maniraj, getting up, a vacant, distant expression in his eyes. Kamala held his hand and gently guided him towards their conjugal bed. ‘Maharaj is preoccupied with something.’ Maniraj did not respond for a while. Then he said, ‘Do you see our shadows at play?’ ‘Yes. Even our shadows are playing a game of love.’ ‘Our limbs appear disproportionately elongated or fat. Look at that hand!’ ‘Yes.’ ‘Our heads appear large and disfigured.’ ‘Such is the illusion created by God. Look at that, now our headless bodies are moving.’⟨fn:106⟩ Maniraj stared at the shadows. ‘Rani, the illusions of the dream world are similar,’ he said, reflecting on his dream. ‘Maharaj, even this real world is like that.’ Kamala had no inkling of Maniraj’s dream. Her endeavour was only to help him forget his sorrow. ‘In a dream, things appear disproportionately significant. It often lacks context, and it is difficult to decipher its meaning.’ ‘Even in this world a lie masquerades as truth, Maharaj.’

‘The world of dreams is shadowy.’ ‘The world is as intricate a trap as a spider’s web.’ ‘Kamala, a dream is constructed like a beehive; but when you wake up, there are neither bees nor honey. What remains is an empty shell of a few lingering memories.’ ‘The world as it is today is not what it was yesterday and it will not be the same tomorrow.’ ‘Yes, one cannot remember a dream that one had just a while ago.’ Kamala led Maniraj towards a large swing which was shaped like a bed. He lay down in her lap. As she fondly caressed his body, he said, ‘Even faces appear strange in dreams.’ ‘People change their minds in a flash, Maharaj, and so their appearance also changes. Especially, the features of children change often.’ ‘The dead sometimes appear in a dream and say things which they never said while alive.’ ‘Maharaj, do not let such dreams trouble your heart.’ ‘Rani, sometimes the sweetness of dreams is preferable to the wakeful state.’ Maniraj’s eyelids grew heavy with sleep. Kamala moved her hand over his body, wishing for him a dreamless sleep. She sang him to sleep. Beloved, may you dream sweetly Know that I dream of you often You played in the laps of your parents Like the monsoon cloud in the month of Ashad Your father was a yogi and an ascetic: He was the supreme bearer of compassion He has now ascended to the heavens Leaving deep wounds in the queen’s heart King, you have been devoted to your parents Contain now your tears One cannot forget the virtues of your parents Their like is impossible to find Beloved, at a time such as this, remember your duties Know the will of God Your father entrusted you with caring for the people

But the King’s subjects stand orphaned Mourn no more Hold firmly the reins of your kingdom Draw your mother and your people Out of their sorrow Establish peace and prosperity instead Bee-like one, roam the forests and flowers Seek the nectar sweet Mountains, seas, forests and palaces Saints and sages, people of all four castes Men and women They are each thirsting for your benevolence They wait for you— Wake up and arise my king Enthuse your people And receive their blessings
chapters.summary: Maniraj, consumed by grief for his father Mallaraj, receives profound guidance in a dream, urging him to embrace his royal duties and forge strategic alliances.

chapters.title: A Look Back at Sarasvatichandra and Kumud
paragraphs: A Look Back at

Sarasvatichandra and Kumud It was the third year of Maniraj’s reign. A small but beautiful Shiva temple called Malleshwar was built in the garden where Mallaraj had lived his last days. Ratnanagari’s rulers were devotees of Shiva. Large parts of the population followed the Vaishnava sect. The rulers respected their faith and as a sign of this respect, numerous plants of the sacred basil, the tulsi, were planted in the garden. Mena Rani lived in that garden. She slept on the floor of the hut in which Mallaraj’s soul had left his body. She refused to entertain any talk about the state or worldly affairs. She ate one sparse meal daily. With the exception of Maniraj and some gardeners, no male was permitted to enter the garden. Every day she woke up early, remembered her departed husband and wept, prayed to be united with him in the other world and sought solace in the recitation of God’s name. At sunrise she worshipped Malleshwar and watered the tulsi plants. Soon after, Maniraj and Kamala Rani would come to visit her. They would touch her feet, sit on the ground and seek religious advice and her blessings. Maniraj would return to the palace to attend to his royal duties, but Kamala would stay back, prepare Mena Rani’s meals, clean her hut, wash her clothes and try to alleviate her sorrow; only then would she go back to the palace to serve her husband and king. Every afternoon, Madhumakshika would go to Mena Rani, read to her from the Puranas and discuss scriptural matters. Kamala and other women from the palace would gather at the hut to hear stories of the virtuous royal women of Ratnanagari from the old queen. Mena Rani would invariably speak of the greatness of Mallaraj, which would fill Kamala with pride and she would often weep, moved by her mother-in-law’s pain. Kamala would stay with her till she was asked to leave. Mena often wondered if she deserved such doting care and affection of her virtuous children, and would invariably retire to bed in tears. She neither knew nor cared whether her bed was hard or soft. She would lie awake, talking to herself: How generous Maharaj was towards me! He left for his heavenly abode, while I cling on to life! I did not deserve his love and affection. I gave him nothing but sorrow. Eventually, sleep would take pity on this grieving royal widow. After receiving the news of Kumud Sundari’s drowning, Vidya Chatura and Gunasundari returned to Ratnanagari from Manoharpuri. Vidya Chatura’s attempts to console Gunasundari proved futile; she could not bear the weight of her sorrow. Maniraj and Vidya Chatura decided to send her to Mena Rani. They reasoned that the intense mourning of the widow would help Gunasundari forget her own pain. At seven in the morning Gunasundari arrived at the garden, accompanied by Sundargauri and Kusum Sundari. They saw Mena Rani deep in thought, leaning against a platform on which grew a tulsi plant; the water from her pitcher had drenched her clothes, but she seemed oblivious of it. She had worn a borderless black sari. Her body had withered and appeared fragile, as if about to snap under the weight of her sorrows. Kamala Rani had given clear orders that Mena Rani was never to be left alone under any circumstances. Female servants followed her everywhere, ensuring her comfort and safety at all times. Their constant hovering presence often irritated Mena and she would often ask them to leave her alone. That day, too, she had told the servants that she wanted to be left alone. She was deep in remembrance of her departed husband. In her mind’s eye, she saw his form; her eyes were shut tight as if to capture that fleeting image. Her body was so emaciated that her bones could be counted. The constant flow of tears had made deep lines from her eyes to her sunken cheeks. Her face had turned pale, her skin was deeply furrowed, and her lips had become parched and white. She felt faint and looked as if she would collapse any moment. Anyone who saw her was certain to be moved to tears. The servants came out from their hiding places behind the trees and shrubs. Mena Rani often experienced such fainting spells. The servants took care that she did not fall and hurt herself, but they had orders that they were to make no attempt to revive her. Mena had composed many devotional songs. Being a widow, she did not sing, but she had taught these songs to the servants. Kamala Rani had instructed the servants to sing these compositions and play the tanpura whenever Mena Rani experienced her fainting spells. A servant signalled to Gunasundari, Sundargauri and Kusum to stay out of sight. One of the servants approached Mena Rani and stood close to her. She plucked the strings of the tanpura and began to sing. Tell the world there is but one God: The one who lives in Vaikunth is the one who resides in Kailash Brahma and Hari are the same omnipotent Purusha The unknowing see the difference But their devotion is the same He who seeks differences in the One Is only fit for hell Knowing the divine to be One I have chosen a personal god In the palace of Ratnanagari, Shankar is the presiding deity For those who aspire to death on the battlefield Must draw their strength from Him Mallaraj worshipped Shiva, Vishnu and Shakti alike He treated destitute beggars and queens alike His rule, his vision and his devotion were all one The Rajyogi has departed, but his God remains with us He whose devotion was steadfast has gone But he has charged Mena with the worship of Shankar Mena Rani seemed to revive with the last lines. She opened her eyes, but they closed again. Just then Kamala arrived. She was told in hushed tones what had happened. She took the tanpura from the servant and began to sing another song. The servants also joined in.

Shankar, who is both formless and not Entices the world His presence permeates the universe Even as he remains steady, unmoving He resides in the crematorium Bearing witness to the destruction of the world This equitous god drinks the poison of the world The serpent that spews venom wraps itself around Shankar’s body The purveyor of destruction destroys all differences Subsuming them into one formless being Mallaraj, who worshipped him, has Now merged into the formless Shankar Leaving behind the body of Mena As she sang the last lines with difficulty, Kamala, too, felt faint with sorrow. My husband has become one with God Leaving this world a crematorium Mena is alone here Singing to her Lord Kamala fell at the feet of her mother in-law. The strings of the tanpura broke. Her song, her soulful rendering and her touch revived Mena Rani. She opened her eyes and saw Kamala prostrate at her feet. She bent down and picked Kamala up and held her in fond embrace. Kamala said, ‘Mataji, after Pitaji’s demise, you are our elder. Do not rob us of this shelter. Please forget your sorrow for a while and give us succour. Maharaj has become one with the divine; you are his earthly representative. You are a great devotee of Malleshwar; you embody him. All of us are your children and subjects. I beg you to rain upon us like a shower of mercy.’ ‘Kamala Rani ...’ Mena murmured. ‘No, Mataji, I am your subject. If you love me, please call me Kamala. Laugh with us, spend time with us. Give me orders; I rejoice in your service, in obeying your commands. I shudder at the thought of giving anyone an order. I feel inadequate to shoulder this burden.

Mataji, the one who has to obey has to think of only one thing, but the one who commands has to think of many. Please keep the burden of issuing commands and directing all of us in your holy and pious hands. Please free me from this burden, at least for a few days. I will observe and learn from you.’ This noble kshatriya woman made an attempt to reinstate her widowed mother-in-law with all the authority and responsibilities of a queen. She hoped that this enormous responsibility would help alleviate Mena’s suffering. But if Kamala was determined to engage her mother-in-law in worldly affairs, Mena was equally determined to follow in letter and spirit her late husband’s advice and the promise she had given him. She touched Kamala’s face and said, ‘Kamala, you are devoted to your husband. Why then do you ask me to break the promise given to one who was the head of our family? Let us forget that. I see that Gunasundari has come. Let us go and receive her.’ Everyone got up. Pain and sorrow were momentarily forgotten as they engaged with practical matters of worldly affairs. ‘Gunasundari, come let us go to my ashram.’ They walked in a row, side by side, Mena, Gunasundari, Kamala holding Kusum’s hand and finally Sundargauri. The female servants walked behind them. They broke up this formation only when dense trees narrowed the path, but as soon as the path widened they would re-group. Mena said to Gunasundari, ‘Gunasundari, the pain of a diseased person or someone like me is apparent. You saw my condition a while ago. I am an old woman; you are young. What ails you?’ Gunasundari:  ‘Mataji, Pradhanji sent me to you, so that I could share your grief.’ Mena:  ‘For a kshatriya woman death is preferable to the pity of others.’ Gunasundari:  ‘Mataji, our sorrow is fleeting. We should understand what you are going through so that we do not wallow in our pain. Mataji, the news of Kumud’s drowning has been a source of great shock and grief for us; her father’s words did nothing to lessen my anguish. He advised me that my pain was insignificant compared to your deep suffering and that I should come to you and seek solace.’

Mena was shocked to learn about Kumud’s drowning. Gunasundari told her about the mishap. Just then a Jain arja, a woman ascetic, came, followed by Samant’s wife. They, too, heard Gunasundari’s narration. Samant’s wife said, ‘Gunasundariba, this is how the world is. You moan the loss of a virtuous daughter, while I bemoan the fact that my wicked son is still alive.’ Her interjection was disregarded. They continued talking, until they had nothing more to say. Samant’s wife pleaded attention. ‘Mataji, you are aware of my condition.’ ‘A woman who prefers the son over the husband is not regarded as devoted to her husband and does not deserve her husband’s love. Thakurani, I have no sympathy for you.’ ‘Mataji, my fate is such that even in my old age, I am punished like a young bride.’ ‘A woman, and an old one at that, is certain to turn senile. You must live as your husband keeps you, have faith in him and do not utter a word in contempt.’ ‘Mataji, I do not criticise him. Thakore is on his deathbed; even then he refuses to see my face. He has banished me from his life. I cannot bear this pain any longer. I know that my son Mulu is undeserving. But I was once misled by my mother’s instinct. My husband is unwilling to forgive that one mistake even on his deathbed. How can I bear this? I am tired of the ways of my son. But if I am not forgiven at the moment of death, when will I be forgiven?’ ‘Thakurani, you have again spoken ill of Samantraj in the presence of outsiders. You do not deserve forgiveness.’ ‘Mataji, I have not spoken ill of him. I have come to you to seek your guidance so that I can seek his forgiveness and see him on his deathbed,’ wept Samant’s wife. ‘Mataji, no one but you can persuade him to grant me forgiveness. A wayfarer seeks the protective shade of a banyan tree. Mataji, if the lake refuses to quench thirst, where would the thirsty go?’ ‘That is no longer in my sphere and authority. Now Kamala Rani, my child, has that authority. It is pointless to speak to me, disregarding her authority.’ ‘How can I, in my old age, plead with a child?’

‘When God decides to bestow a certain authority in a child, He also grants that child light and wisdom. It is your conceit and pride which makes you say that your queen is only a child. Your son imbibed this conceit with your milk and destroyed all your husband’s aspirations. Even in your old age, you are filled with this pride. Knowing this, how can I plead your case with Samantraj? There has never been and there will never be an equal to Samantraj in this state. It is your and Muluraj’s duty to seek and obtain his forgiveness. What can Mena or Kamala do?’ Kamala informed Mena, ‘Muluraj’s brother has sent him a letter, inviting him to meet Samantraj.’ ‘Look at this, Thakurani! You were ashamed to ask for two drops of rain, but the rain did not wait for you to plead and showered its mercy upon you. Maniraj has already sent a letter to Muluraj; if you want to know what more he can do, you should ask him.’ Mena appeared to be deep in thought for a while. Then she addressed Kamala, ‘Daughter Kamala, my pledge not to concern myself with worldly matters was broken today. I felt involved in Thakurani’s problems and deviated from my religion. You must ensure that such matters do not come to me hereafter. If a platter of food is kept before one, one is likely to be tempted to have a morsel.’ Before Kamala could respond, Madhumakshika, herself an elderly woman now, came and said, ‘Mataji, I met Pradhanji Vidya Chatura at the gate. I have come with a message from him and one from Maharaj Maniraj. Samantraj’s body is now ready to give up life; he might slip into a coma anytime. He keeps repeating Maharaj’s name and says nothing else. Maharaj Maniraj felt that his presence was required at Samantraj’s bedside, and for that reason he has not been here to meet you. ‘Maharaj and Pradhanji were on their way to Samantraj’s house when the security officers who had gone to fetch Muluraj met them on the way. Muluraj was with them. He was captured from the ravines near the Subhadra. At the time of his capture, he had in his hand someone’s decapitated head. He was charged with murder. Before the guards brought Muluraj, Pradhanji had received a message from Manchaturbhai; the message was about Kumud Sundari.’ Gunasundari and the others eagerly awaited further details. Madhumakshika continued, ‘Pratapsinh, a baharvatiya from Suvarnapur, dived in after Kumud behn as she fell into the river; his intention was to abduct her. A man called Shankar was also in pursuit of Pratapsinh. Pratapsinh caught Kumud behn by her leg. Just then, Muluraj came to Kumud behn’s aid—he jumped into the water and beheaded the outlaw. Muluraj came out with Pratapsinh’s head and met Manchaturbhai. Maharaj has granted pardon to Muluraj. This good news will allow Samantraj’s soul to leave his body without any remorse or rancour. Maharaj has taken Muluraj with him so that father and son could meet and reconcile.’ Samant’s wife wept tears of joy. But this news gave no succour to Gunasundari; all her anxieties and fears remained as before. Madhumakshika continued, ‘Gunasundari behn, Pradhanji said that if Muluraj had the use of both his hands, he could have saved Kumud Sundari and fought Pratapsinh at the same time, but having only one hand, he could not do so. Kumud behn was dragged by the flow of the river. Earlier, there were two things to worry about—Pratapsinh and the river; now the only concern is the river.’ Fresh tears rolled from Gunasundari’s eyes. She bit her lips hard to prevent sobs from escaping her throat. Madhumakshika understood her plight and said, ‘Behnji, Manchaturji and his men are now searching the river bank. Muluraj said that if Kumud behn was dragged by the river, she would eventually reach the sea. But it is now time for the high tide when the sea water enters the river; therefore, she is unlikely to be dragged into the sea.’ That was some ray of hope. Madhumakshika continued, ‘The place where the Subhadra meets the sea is made shallow due to sediment deposits and the water there is crystal clear; Muluraj said that it would be the best place to search for Kumud behn. Manchaturji has gone to that spot with his men.’ ‘God’s will be done,’ Gunasundari said with a forlorn sigh. ‘God will be merciful,’ said Mena Rani.

‘Mataji, your blessings will help Kumud. But she has drowned. It is futile to hope until we get some final news,’ said Gunasundari. Madhumakshika:  ‘Mataji, Muluraj begs your forgiveness. He feels that he has pained you deeply.’ Mena:  ‘Madhumakshika, please convey to Maharaj Maniraj that before the ruler of this land and our master, the late Maharaj, became one with the immortals, he gave me a punishment. If I had felt that the punishment was undeserved, I would have been unhappy. I deserved it and did not once feel pained. Through penance, I regained the trust of the late Maharaj. Now, Maharaj Maniraj must decide what he wants to do with Muluraj.’ Samant’s wife:  ‘Mataji, please have mercy and speak one word of forgiveness.’ Mena:  ‘Muluraj’s crime was not against my person. His crime was against the state, the decision for which can only be taken by the Maharaj.’ Madhumakshika:  ‘Mataji, furthermore, Muluraj fell at the feet of the Maharaj and, with tears in his eyes, sought his forgiveness. He said that in the inebriation of youth, he had caused great misery to Maharaj Mallaraj. But his insults and crimes against you and Maharaj Maniraj were even greater, and that for this reason he was not even worthy of begging your pardon. He said that his crime was so grave that even if he were to go to all the four sacred places and do penance, his sins would not be washed away. Speaking with the Maharaj’s permission, Muluraj said that earlier he held the Maharaj in low esteem, but he had now realised that the Maharaj was like a pure-blooded lion, while he was a wily, low-born fox. He praised Maharaj Maniraj’s intellect, his valour, his virtues and royal power, and declared himself to be a lowly being. He further said that his pride—which held even when Maharaj Mallaraj had punished him—had melted and he fell at the Maharaj’s feet, just as Vishwamitra had fallen at the feet of sage Vashishtha. He said that if the Maharaj gave him the chance to do penance, he would consider himself somewhat cleansed.

‘Mataji, Muluraj further said that he was guided by his mother and failed to recognise the wisdom of his father and that instead of a sword, he chose a nail clipper. He said it was only because of the intercession of Maharaj Maniraj that his father had pardoned him and the meeting at the hour of his father’s death was possible only because of the Maharaj’s grace. He took a pledge in the presence of his father that just as Bharat had forsaken Kaikeyi, he, too, would forsake his mother.’ Hearing this, Samant’s wife turned pale. Madhumakshika continued, ‘Muluraj then turned to Pradhanji and said that the differences between them were divinely ordained. He held Jarashankar responsible for the treaty with the English, which had made the English so powerful; and he would not be able to forget that. After much debate with himself, he had realised that he had to obey Maharaj Maniraj’s minister, Vidya Chatura; and as proof of that new resolve, he had slain the man who wished ill of Kumud behn, Pradhanji’s daughter. ‘Furthermore, Muluraj said to Pradhanji that he was a trusted friend of Pratapsinh, and that Pratapsinh had confided in him that he coveted Kumud Sundari. Muluraj did not confront him on this issue as Pratapsinh would then stop confiding in him. Muluraj was on the river bank when he saw Pratapsinh chasing Kumud. Muluraj killed him, something that Shankar had failed to do. Muluraj said, “I killed a friend—an evil one—but why? When Kumud Sundari was still a child, I had once played with her as a father would. No one knows— perhaps not even Gunasundari—that on that day I had cast an evil eye on Gunasundari, the penance for which was long due. A brahmin, whom I had met fleetingly, made me aware of the evil nature of my desire. As an act of penance and in order to reform myself, I slayed a friend who cast an evil eye on Kumud Sundari. If I am able to spend time with another brahmin, Pradhanji Vidya Chatura, I may be able to reform myself even further. I have no worldly desires left in me.”’ Madhumakshika turned to Samant’s wife and said, ‘Thakurani, Maharaj Maniraj has said that you should proceed without delay in the company of Kamala Rani and be present by Samantraj’s bedside.

Samantraj has expressed his desire to meet Kamala Rani. Maharaj has also said that Samantraj occupies the place of his father and hence, Kamala Rani should not keep purdah. He said that it is our duty to fulfill Samantraj’s last wishes and seek his blessings. With Mataji’s permission, Kamala Rani and Thakurani are to proceed immediately.’ Mena:  ‘Daughter Kamala, the king’s command is a just one, and you should obey it without hesitation. Please convey this message to Samantraj: tell him that I lead a useless existence ever since Maharaj Mallaraj became one with the immortals. He had entrusted Maniraj to Samant, who was a protective shield for Maniraj. But the gods have sent for him, and His ways are not for us to fathom. Moreover, tell Samantraj that without him, Maniraj will now be left without a companion and guide; therefore, Samantraj should trust Muluraj and hand over this responsibility to him. Muluraj has learnt his lessons from life and experience; he has become a patriot and his devotion to the state and the king should not be questioned. I will join Samantraj and Maharaj Mallaraj as soon as the Creator sends for me.’ Everyone got up. Kusum walked alongside the Jain ascetic. A gosai, who was a woman ascetic from Sundargiri, and a pujaran or devotee of the Mother Goddess also walked with them. Kusum moved in- between the three of them, trying to join in their conversation. Kamala Rani, Gunasundari and Sundargauri walked ahead of everyone, but Sundargauri’s attention was on Kusum’s movements. She was aware of young Kusum’s newfound desire to remain unmarried and perturbed by her niece’s fascination with three women leading a life of devout asceticism. Sundargauri signalled to Kusum and beckoned her to join them. Kusum indicated with a movement of her head and her hands that she was not inclined to join her mother, her aunt and the queen, and she carried on her conversation with the ascetics. Finally, as they neared the gate, Kusum had to go and join her mother. She weighed in her mind all that she had heard and surmised: The Jain arja is obviously unmarried and leads a religious life. Can I, too, become an ascetic? The pujaran has a good life; she worships the Goddess, but she is married. The gosai is happy; she can choose to marry or remain unmarried and sing Mira’s songs. Kusum sang to herself:

Mira has become one with Mohan She has taken Shri Girdhari as her husband As if the world did not matter She repeated these lines three or four times. As she sang, Kusum intertwined her fingers with Sundargauri’s and walked with a spring in her step. At the gate, the group separated. Kamala Rani and Samant’s wife went away in their carriage, while Gunasundari, Sundargauri and Kusum got into the carriage waiting for them. Sundargauri promptly enquired, ‘Kusum, what was it that you were discussing so intently with the arja, the pujaran and the gosai? What is so attractive about them?’ ‘Why? Shouldn’t I be talking to them? Was I talking to some men?’ Kusum responded, making a face. ‘Were you plotting with the Jain arja to become like her?’ ‘I might have been. They are certainly happier than any married woman.’ ‘What is wrong with the married ones?’ ‘There is three-fold sorrow that befalls them—the pain of finding a husband, the pain of living with one and then the sorrow of his death. There cannot be anyone who has not experienced at least one of these.’ ‘Nonsense! You, a mere girl, have not experienced any of the joys of marriage and are talking of the pains of married life!’ ‘I may not be married, but I have seen marriages. Kumud behn found a good match, and his going away became the cause her misery. She had an unhappy married life. And look at my mother—she is happy in marriage but is in grief because of her daughter.’ Gunasundari snapped out of her pensiveness, pinched Kusum’s cheek sharply and said, ‘Stop! Stop, I say! You shameless girl! Speaking of your mother like this!’ Kusum turned shades of red with embarrassment and looked down. But presently, she perked up again and said, ‘All right. Shouldn’t one take a lesson from Samant’s wife? Or from the Maharani, who exemplifies the pitiable life of a widow? What pain! I was stunned by her sorrow. Kumud behn exemplifies the agony of living with an undeserving husband. And the Maharani mourns the death of a good husband.’ ‘Why do you look at such examples alone? These are just your tricks to avoid marriage.’ ‘Do I have to go looking for examples? They are all around me, even in our own home. I am not blind that I cannot see them. Marriage means a certain fall.’ ‘There you go again! You keep speaking of others. You spoke about me, and now you talk about your aunt!’ Gunasundari scolded her irrepressible daughter. ‘All right. I will not. I spoke of her joy, not of her sorrow. Kaki, if father were to allow me to remain unmarried, I would grow into a fat cow.’ ‘As if your father is mad like you! Have you ever seen a spinster among our people?’ ‘That, too, we shall see.’ The carriage moved forward as did their conversation. Vidya Chatura had spent much time ruminating his decision to send Madhumakshika with a message for Mena Rani. Many thoughts assailed him. He thought: Ultimately, Maharaj Mallaraj has been vindicated. After all these years, Muluraj has returned to the family fold—Maharaj was right in insisting that Muluraj must not be given the death penalty. Samant and Muluraj have consistently opposed the treaty with the English. Is this because they are obstinate and unreasonable? Can one say that their opposition is not because of their devotion to Swaraj and national pride? Maharaj Mallaraj and Jarashankar Mama had assessed the political scenario and accepted this treaty. I, too, am in favour of this treaty. But can one say that there is no other aspect to it? If the natives had continued to rule India, is it not possible to imagine that like Japan, India, too, would have risen and progressed? Is it an impossible dream for a country that once had men like Madhavrao Peshwa, Madhavrao Scindia and Nana Phadnavis that it would give birth to other such jewels among men to work for the uplift of this land? Could not men of sterling qualities, like the men we have in Ratnanagari, usher the dawn of independence on this land? For kshatriyas like Samant and Muluraj, war has become a distant dream. Should it not be a cause of anger to them? A Hindu who despises them is an Anarya, not an Arya. But Samantraj and Muluraj, that was our past. You still burn with anger towards Jarashankar. It cannot be doused. What is the reason for it? Your desires have no anchor. What if Jarashankar had reconsidered his advice and given asylum to Shubhaji Rao? I am his nephew and I can well imagine what he would have said. Like one who doubts an elephant, Though seeing him stride by, And yet believes when he has seen The footprints left; so I.⟨fn:107⟩ Muluraj, why should you not feel aggrieved? You are a lion among men! But even Maharaj Mallaraj was a lion among men, one of the best! But unlike the lion, he was not grounded—his intellect was like an eagle, capable of soaring high and surveying a vast area, which gave his perspective both depth and breadth. He was virtuous, generous, possessed a high intellect and he nurtured virtue and righteousness in others. He surveyed the earth and gazed at the sky to ascertain his target. The treaty that Mallaraj signed with the paramount authority of the British appears to us as beneficial and necessary as the one forged by the great Akbar with his people.⟨fn:108⟩ But I am not surprised that Muluraj could not see its wisdom. How was Muluraj to fathom the great depths of Maharaj Mallaraj’s heart?

Vidya Chatura’s mind turned to his elder daughter. Kumud! Kumud! As I contemplate your fate I am tempted like all others to believe in destiny. Happiness has never been your lot. We looked for a groom from a good family, but he proved unworthy. Wherever you went, fate snatched away sweetness from your life. You were saved from the outlaws, but the river took you away! I believe you are lost to us forever. It is futile to hope for your safe return. Your mother cries out in anguish, but I am a man; politics has made my heart stony and dried up all my tears. Perhaps what Kamakandaki said to Malati is true. But how can those Feel natural affection for their offspring, Whose souls are sunken in schemes of policy?⟨fn:109⟩ No, that cannot be entirely true. If ... if both Pramad and Kumud are dead, it is a closed chapter. If Kumud has died, the matter is closed for me. But what if both of them are alive? How am I, the father of an ill- starred daughter, to save her from calamity? I educated her; it is up to her to navigate the worldly sea with the help of that boat. A daughter suffers the consequences of the wrong choice of husband made by her parents, and parents can do nothing but weep from afar. It is for this reason that our people do not want daughters. Yes, so long as Buddhidhan and Saubhagya Devi are around, Kumud will be cared for. But what if the news about Pramaddhan’s death is correct and Kumud is found alive? How are we to bear the pain of a widowed daughter? My Kumud, a widow! A widow, my Kumud! Oh God! Will you have no mercy upon me! Pramaddhan, you did not know how to savour the fragrance of my daughter; she withered. Vidya Chatura heaved a deep sigh. But as a practical man, can I not see my remedy for a disease which threatens to be a fact? Other nations have it. Mine bars it. Conventional widowhood! Social terrorism! Must you stand between me and my love and duty to my elder child? Here—here is a calamity; here is escape from it—and yet the poor one must suffer and not escape! And why? Because the stronger sex controls her lot. Is it proper in a father to submit to the control and see the child writhing before his eyes because he is a social-moral-coward?⟨fn:110⟩ Kumud, Sarasvatichandra is still alive. He behaved foolishly, but his heart is still aflame for you. I have the courage to marry my daughter to him, and he has the courage to accept her in marriage. Sarasvatichandra, would you who gave up so much wealth be afraid of taking this step? Oh God! Dear Kumud, suffering and pain has robbed your father of his sanity. I do not act upon decisions taken in a state of unreason. My father and maternal uncle are both alive. Can I act against their wishes? One does not need to consult a fortune teller to know what their verdict would be. Should I be bold and act contrary to their wishes? My old father took up the sword to protect Kumud. Is she a daughter only to me and not him? A man who dares take such a step must in the interest of the state step down from the position of minister; my self-interest is not larger than my love for my daughter. That is indeed true. But I do not serve Maniraj just to fill my stomach. I can put aside my self-interest. But how is one to forget his generosity? How am I to scorn his affection? Kumud, tell me which path should I take for you—this one or the other? I cannot see my way. Vidya Chatura went blank. He lay in his carriage, feeling desolate and melancholy. Then he thought, There is no reason why one should think of the uncertain future. Who knows what news awaits me? Only, should I worry about good or bad at this point? Meanwhile, Madhumakshika returned and informed Vidya Chatura of the events that had taken place inside the garden. By then Chandrakant, who was travelling with Vidya Chatura, had stepped outside the carriage, allowing the minister to be with his thoughts.

Chandrakant stood on the bank of the lake, thinking about his lost friend. Sarasvatichandra, just when Vidya Chatura had promised help to look for you, we got the news about Kumud and you were forgotten. Maharaj Maniraj, too, had broached the subject, but then Samantraj took to his deathbed and you were again forgotten. I search for you, but you do not wish to be found. Even fate conspires against me. Let fate favour you, but I am not going to return without you. I receive letter after letter from home urging me to give up this futile search and return. But my foolish relatives do not know that a crown jewel has been lost. Many worthless stones like Chandrakant cannot make up for one Sarasvatichandra. As long as there is life in this body, I will not give up my search for you, Sarasvatichandra. A mendicant was on his rounds to seek alms. He saw Chandrakant and approached him. ‘Brother, you are not a resident of this city, are you?’ he asked. ‘No, I am from Bombay.’ ‘And your name?’ ‘Chandrakant.’ ‘Chandrakantji, on the other side of this lake, what appears hazy on the horizon is the beautiful mountain, Sundargiri. We live there in an ashramic community. Do visit us; it would do you good. If you visit us without such royal paraphernalia, you will see more and also receive more.’ ‘Alakh!’ the mendicant called out and set out on his way. An ordinary English-educated person would not give a second thought to such invitations. But Chandrakant was in search of a friend. He considered: Is it not possible that Sarasvatichandra has gone there? If he has managed to escape from the outlaws, one road would lead him to Manoharpuri and the other to Sundargiri. Yesterday, I saw the map of this area with Vidya Chatura. The mountain is close to river Subhadra. Kumud drowned in that river. Destiny is strange; if Kumud has been dragged in that direction, couldn’t fate have taken Sarasvatichandra there as well? Oh friend, alluring are the ways of your love!

A shadow of gloom darkened Chandrakant’s face. How can Chandra and Kumud now love each other? Such love is sinful. My dear Chandra ran away from the possibility of that sin and wanders in unknown places. Yes, this is a plausible idea. Sarasvatichandra, I know you have an inclination for the life of an ascetic. I also know how you strive to attain what is dear to you. I will not impute any motives or accuse you of vile conduct. Chandrakant gazed in the direction of Sundargiri. The play of light and shadow on the clouds took for him the shape of Kumud and Chandra. He remembered the lines of a poem that Sarasvatichandra was fond of. The path through which that lovely twain Have passed, by cedar, pine and yew, And each dark tree that ever grew, Is curtained out from Heaven’s wide blue A curtain divides us. But wherever you are, dear friend, it must be a lovely place. Like mine, there are so many minds you have captured. You shine over them like a bright star. And what does that star do? It scatters drops of golden light, Like lines of rain that ne’er unite; And the gloom divine is all around; And underneath is the mossy ground. ... My wings are folded o’er mine ears; My wings are crossed o’er mine eyes; Yet through their silver shade appears, And through their lulling plumes arise, A Shape, a throng of sounds. May it be no ill to thee O thou of many wounds!⟨fn:111⟩

As he recited the last lines, tears welled up in his eyes; he took out his handkerchief and wiped his tears. Just then Vidya Chatura’s coachman came up to him and said, ‘Bhai Sahib, Pradhanji has asked for you.’ Chandrakant composed himself. Madhumakshika had left, but a policeman stood near the carriage. Vidya Chatura gave Chandrakant a ring and said, ‘Chandrakant, do you recognise this ring? The rich in these parts would have such precious jewels but the shape is not familiar to these parts. I recall having seen such a ring with Sarasvatichandra.’ Chandrakant took the ring and examined it closely. There was a tiny button, which he pushed. The ring opened, and inside it was an image of Sarasvatichandra! Chandrakant enthusiastically showed it to Vidya Chatura and at the same time he asked the policeman a few questions. ‘This ring and this photo are of Sarasvatichandra. Who brought it here and what is his story?’ The policeman said, ‘Pradhanji, this ring was recovered from a bania called Aarthdas. He says that a man called Navinchandra gave it to him. Our people caught Aarthdas. But someone called Hiralal from Bombay claims that Aarthdas has killed the owner of this ring.’ ‘Who is Hiralal?’ ‘He is an employee of a Bombay merchant called Dhurtalal. He claims that he is here in search of Sarasvatichandra.’ ‘Dhurtalal’s employee!’ exclaimed Chandrakant, stunned. He apprised Vidya Chatura about Dhurtalal. Having heard him, Vidya Chatura said, ‘Chandrakant, you go home in the police carriage and send it back immediately. Meanwhile, I will proceed to Samantraj’s house. I will get to the root of this.’ Vidya Chatura, accompanied by the policeman, went to Samantraj’s house. As Chandrakant got into the police carriage, his mind went into a whirl as if keeping pace with the turning wheels of the carriage. What has destiny in store for us? Evil Dhurtalal, both you and I are searching for Sarasvatichandra. I want to bring him back home and you want to keep him out. I am his friend and you, his enemy. I cannot even imagine what you are not capable of doing! Sarasvatichandra, are you alive, or have these evil ones killed you and with you, all our hopes? I can neither hope nor feel dejected.

Fate robs me of my happiness. My heart is rent—my fibres fall apart. The world is blank. I burn with inward fires— My soul sinks plunged into the glooms of hell, And dim obscurity veils every sense. What shall I do?⟨fn:112⟩ No, I shall not be forced into such a situation. I believe that Sarasvatichandra is alive and with us, and I will find him. Like Alexander the Great, I will always be hopeful. I will try and push these people, whether they show any enthusiasm in finding him or not. I will acquaint myself with this area. I will roam the mountains, the forest and the villages. I will call for additional men from Bombay to help me or I will employ some local men. But find you, Sarasvatichandra, I will. Aarthdas’ version appears plausible. It is quite like Sarasvatichandra to give precious things away. As the carriage moved on, Chandrakant looked intently at the distant peaks of Sundargiri and berated himself for having failed to ask the mendicant about Sarasvatichandra. As he reached home, he saw Kusum standing at the window. A new thought struck him. Some resemblance, something of Kumud’s light, And some shadows ... The heart pants with the effort of catching her. Sarasvatichandra, what is this unique power of your inner world that makes others dance to your tunes and yet, their rhythms can never be in harmony with your own music?
chapters.summary: Gunasundari seeks solace with Mena Rani, sharing profound grief over Kumud's reported drowning, while Chandrakant relentlessly searches for Sarasvatichandra.
